samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want for 2500 words.
samples.result:
**The House That Kept Its Measure**

When my mother sold her house, the buyers asked for the marks inside the pantry door. They wanted the freezer removed, the lilac cut back from the path, and the dents in the hall plastered over, but the marks were to stay. There were forty years of them: pencil strokes, dates, initials, a few smudged thumbs. Apparently the buyers had seen a photograph online. They thought the marks gave the house a history. My mother, who had spent three afternoons trying to get that house clean enough to suggest it had no history whatsoever, took this as a personal criticism.

“Tell them they can have the lilac or the children,” she said. “They don’t get to pick and choose.”

I was in the pantry with my phone, negotiating on behalf of people who had never asked me to negotiate. Beyond the open window my mother was tying string around the lilac, as if preparing to send it somewhere by post. I looked at the highest mark bearing my initial. Seventeen years old, five foot six. I have been telling people five foot seven for thirty years, on the strength of a measurement taken in boots at a county fair. It was disagreeable to find a witness for the prosecution in my own childhood home.

The first mark was not a child’s. It said *Fridge*, and beside it my father had written a fraction so small and painstaking that you could tell he was the son of a watchmaker. Before moving in, my parents had come to the empty house with a folding rule to see whether their refrigerator would fit. Finding the opening barely tall enough, my father marked the appliance’s height on the pantry jamb. No one remembered why. The refrigerator was in another room. My mother’s theory was that he had finally found a nice sharp pencil and wanted to make the most of it.

The first human mark was mine. The second was my brother Paul’s, although what it recorded was not his height but the highest he could reach with a piece of toast. I remember the mark being made. I remember the toast dropping, butter side down, on the sole of my father’s slipper as he knelt beside the door. I remember my father saying, quite gravely, “Well, now I have to eat my shoe.” Or perhaps I remember being told these things. The joke was very much his, and it is possible that over the years I have furnished it with the slipper it deserved.

Paul wanted the doorframe. I called him in Vancouver and explained the buyers’ request. There was a pause during which I could hear a dog drinking prodigious quantities of water.

“They can’t buy that,” he said at last.

“It’s attached.”

“So’s the toilet. They asked us to change that.”

The toilet was avocado green, manufactured during a brief period of national confidence in the color of avocados. My mother had agreed to its replacement on condition that she never receive a photograph of the new one. She thought white bathrooms made you look sick, which was about the last thing you needed in a bathroom.

“What would you do with a seven-foot piece of painted wood?” I asked Paul.

“Put it somewhere.”

“Where?”

“In my house, Jane. I’d put it in my house.”

He said this with an anger that surprised us both. The dog finished drinking. In the sudden quiet he added, “It’s the only place where all three of us are together.”

There had been three children. Between Paul and me came Daniel, who died at nine. On the pantry jamb his marks began low, overtook mine briefly, and ended between *Paul, 7, in socks* and a blue line labeled *Flood*, which had nothing to do with water. Flood was a neighbor’s greyhound, a creature so obliging that it had stood on its hind legs while three children balanced a dictionary on its head.

What I remember best about Daniel is an afternoon when he and I found a green armchair on the curb. It had wheels at the front and legs at the back. We figured out that if one of us lifted and pushed, the other could ride down the sidewalk in considerable state. Daniel installed himself first. At every driveway he raised a hand in acknowledgment of the crowds. When it was my turn he pushed me into a hedge. I climbed out with a split lip, and he spent the next hour trying to persuade me that if I would only push him into the same hedge, neither of us would have to tell. His faith in justice was almost entirely mechanical.

I told Paul I would see what I could do.

At lunch my mother ate half a pear standing up and wrapped the other half in a dish towel. She was moving to an apartment with a balcony and a view of the back of a cinema. She had chosen it because the balcony faced east and because she liked seeing the employees come out in the afternoon to shake popcorn from the mats. A view, in her opinion, ought to do something. She was eighty-one and still perfectly capable of moving herself, an impression she maintained by lifting boxes whenever anyone was looking and sliding them along the floor with her foot when they weren’t.

“Paul wants the jamb,” I said.

“Paul lives four thousand miles away. It’s easy to want timber at that distance.”

“He says it’s the only place where the three of us are together.”

She stopped chewing. “There’s a photograph of you all in the bath.”

“He’s probably thinking of something he can display.”

She considered this, then went back to her pear. “Ask him to pay for the shipping. We’ll see how deeply he feels.”

I went to the hardware store, where a man named Ellis had cut keys for my father and mixed paint for my mother and once sold me a packet of sunflower seeds from which, despite the picture on the front, nothing whatsoever had emerged. Ellis was retired. His granddaughter was in charge now. She had the same heavy eyelids and the same unnerving patience with questions asked by people who were about to purchase the wrong thing.

“What are you trying to save?” she asked. “The wood or what’s on it?”

I said I wasn’t sure.

“Gets expensive when you’re not sure.”

She suggested taking photographs with a ruler laid alongside the marks. A print shop could reproduce them at full size. Or I could trace everything onto transparent paper. Or, if the wood itself was important, a carpenter could remove that side of the jamb and fit a new one. She drew me a little diagram on the back of a receipt. Her pencil moved quickly and left a firm, pale groove in the paper. For years afterward, whenever I saw a carpenter’s pencil, I would think of that girl, although I never learned her name and have forgotten nearly everything else I bought that day.

Back at the house I found the buyer standing in the pantry. He had come to measure for shelves. His name was Martin, and he taught music at the middle school. He had taken off his shoes without being asked. In his right sock there was a small hole through which a little white moon of heel appeared whenever he rose on his toes. I found it difficult to resent a man who had exposed so tender a portion of himself to our kitchen floor.

“We heard about the marks,” he said. “I hope we haven’t been awful.”

“What do you want them for?”

He looked surprised. “Our daughter liked them.”

“Does she know whose they are?”

“No. She thought houses came with them. Like the lines on the wall at the doctor’s office. You move in and find out how big you are.”

He examined the ruler I had brought home. “Of course you should take them. We thought you were going to paint them over. That was why we said something.”

There is a particular embarrassment in discovering that you have spent a whole morning courageously defending yourself from a kindness. I put the ruler on the counter. My mother came in through the back door trailing lilac leaves and announced that she had found a terracotta pot large enough for the smaller of the two suckers. Martin offered to help her dig it up. Within five minutes she had learned that his wife played the cello, his daughter was named Bea, and none of them had the faintest idea when to prune a lilac. She gave him a lecture on the subject, distinguishing between what the books said, what the neighbors said, and what the lilac had consistently indicated it preferred.

That evening I began the tracing. I fixed a length of translucent paper over the marks with low-tack tape, knelt on a cushion, and copied each date and initial. The early marks clustered tightly. Later ones rose by larger intervals as we became too busy or too self-conscious to submit to measurement. At fourteen I had apparently insisted on being called Jaine, with an extra *i*. Paul had passed five feet on Christmas Eve. Someone had measured a broom. There was a row of question marks at the height of my knee and, near the bottom, in my mother’s square printing, the mysterious words *No, Robert*.

“Dad wanted to get a tortoise,” she explained when I asked. “That was how tall he said it would eventually be.”

“Did he mean long?”

“That was one of several objections.”

We sat on the floor with our backs against the flour cupboard. It had grown dark outside, but the kitchen light was on, and from our angle we could see beneath the table a yellow crescent of old linoleum that had escaped the sun. My mother touched the tracing at Daniel’s last mark.

“He cheated on that one,” she said. “There was a magazine under the mat.”

“Did you know at the time?”

“Of course. I put it there.”

She had measured him the week before a hospital appointment. He had been worried he wasn’t growing. She slipped a gardening magazine under the mat, stood him on it, brought the dictionary down gently onto his hair, and marked the place in red. He was delighted. At the hospital he told the nurses he had grown half an inch, and my mother stood behind him daring anybody to say otherwise.

“I don’t think I’ve ever heard that,” I said.

“No reason you should have. You were at clarinet.”

We had lived in the same small house, breathed the same hot weather, eaten beans from the same chipped bowls, and still I had been at clarinet while all sorts of things were happening. I had imagined our childhood as a room the three of us occupied together. It was more like one of those old railway compartments with a corridor running past it: faces at the glass, a door sliding open, a little while in company, then someone getting up to go and find a lavatory or a sandwich, taking a whole stretch of countryside with them.

The carpenter came on Thursday. He was a quiet man with silver eyebrows and an alarming habit of saying “Interesting” whenever he encountered anything that ought to have been straightforward. The jamb came away in one piece. Underneath, on the naked plaster, was another pencil line. It was short, dark, and sloped slightly upward. No date, no initial. The carpenter said it was probably a leveling mark, although if it was, he added, the man responsible had enjoyed a generous lunch.

We laid the old board on the kitchen table. Removed from its place, it looked at once precious and ridiculous. Paint flaked along one edge. There was a dead spider in the recess behind the latch plate. My mother brought a toothbrush and cleaned the dust from its little brass screws. I sent a photograph to Paul. A minute later he called.

“God,” he said. “It’s only a piece of wood.”

“That has been the local understanding for some time.”

“No, I mean I thought I’d look at it and feel something.”

“Do you want me to send it?”

He was quiet. I heard the dog begin its endless drink. “Yes,” he said. “I’ll see what happens when it gets here.”

We packed it in a long narrow crate that cost more to ship than any of us felt able to discuss. At the print shop I ordered two copies of the tracing, one for me and one for my mother. Mine went into a drawer. My mother cut hers into strips, taped them together in the correct order, and hung the result behind the pantry door in her apartment. It was a shallow pantry, barely deep enough for cereal packets. On the first morning there, she took a pencil and measured herself. She had lost an inch and a quarter. Beside the line she wrote *Disputed*.

A month later Martin sent us a photograph. In it Bea stood against the new jamb, her chin lifted and her eyes crossed in the effort to see the book resting on her head. They had used a music dictionary. A cello leaned against the table. Outside the window, the lilac had put out fresh leaves. My mother enlarged the picture on her phone, examined the foliage, and declared herself provisionally satisfied.

Paul eventually put the board up in his hall. The first new mark belonged to the dog, measured sitting down, since nobody could persuade him to stand still. The second belonged to the woman Paul married the following spring. When I visited, he handed me a pencil and told me to take off my shoes. I stood with my heels against the wood while he searched for something with a hard cover. He came back with a road atlas. For a moment neither of us moved. Then he lowered it onto my hair.

“Well?” I said.

“Five six.”

“Try again.”

He did. Same result. I asked for a gardening magazine. He didn’t know what I meant, so I told him, and when I was finished he went into the living room and returned with a glossy catalog of bathroom fittings. He laid it on the floor. I stepped onto a double spread of gleaming white toilets, drew myself up, and waited while my brother made a small, deliberate mark in the wood.

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want for 2500 words.
samples.result:
The map was nearly finished when Mrs. Bell came in to say that the hill was wrong.

I turned my monitor toward her. The hill rose behind the school in a series of brown contour lines. We had measured it from an airplane. I was rather proud of the airplane.

“Yes,” she said, “it looks like that from above. But I live down here.”

She put a finger on the library, where we were sitting, and walked two fingers along Orchard Street. At the corner she stopped.

“Here I change hands.”

She carried a shopping bag in her left hand as far as the corner, she explained, and then in her right hand as far as the dentist. At the dentist she set it on the windowsill and pretended to be interested in a poster about gums. After that there was a railing. Then there was a stretch of forty yards about which she had nothing polite to say.

“Your map makes it look as if I could go straight home.”

I told her that was more or less the idea of a street map.

“Well,” she said, collecting her shopping, “you might come up sometime and see how you get on.”

On Thursday I went up to see how I got on.

Mrs. Bell bought potatoes, a cabbage, milk, a newspaper, and a jar of little onions. She refused my offer to carry anything, on the reasonable grounds that we would then be measuring a different hill. Instead she gave me the newspaper. By the time we reached the corner I had read the same headline seven times upside down.

At the dentist we stood looking at a magnificent pink cross section of a tooth. Rain began to fall. The windowsill was exactly the right height for a shopping bag; Mrs. Bell merely had to relax her elbow and the weight was gone. I had passed that window twice a day for eleven years without noticing the sill. I knew the name of the dentist, who had retired, and the telephone number, which was painted on the glass and no longer worked.

“Good sill,” I said.

“It would be better with an awning.”

At the top of the hill she let us into a narrow brick house and made scrambled eggs. The little onions went on the table in a chipped blue bowl. We ate the lot between us. I had imagined, without ever quite admitting it, that the onions were an extravagance she might eliminate to make the climb easier. Having tasted them with the eggs, I would sooner have thrown out the newspaper.

I went back to the library and drew a small square at the dentist’s window. Then I erased it. A person looking for a dentist had troubles enough without being directed to a convenient ledge.

Our commission was to produce five thousand folding maps in time for the summer festival. On the front would be streets, public buildings, and places of interest. On the back would be advertisements for the businesses that paid for the printing. Folded correctly, the map would display the town arms. Folded incorrectly, as all previous maps had been, it would display half a sofa and the word LEGAL.

I mentioned the windowsill to my colleague Dev, who was pasting photographs into the local history album. He considered the matter with his usual care.

“You could put it on a map of places to put things down.”

“How many such places can there be?”

He lifted a photograph. Underneath it, holding the corner flat while the glue dried, was my coffee cup.

We found seventeen places before lunch. Most were benches. One was a disused drinking fountain with a stone basin broad enough to hold a birthday cake, a fact verified by the woman who had once stopped there to tie her shoe while carrying a birthday cake. Another was the low wall outside the courthouse. Dev proposed the roof of a parked car, which I disallowed on the grounds of impermanence and the likelihood of meeting the owner.

We put a sheet of paper by the library entrance. Across the top I wrote: WHERE CAN YOU STOP ON YOUR WAY HOME?

For three days nobody wrote anything. On the fourth, somebody wrote HOME. Below that somebody else wrote PUB. I was about to take the paper down when a boy in a yellow football shirt came in and drew a tiny, accurate plan of the alley behind the butcher shop.

“There’s a pipe,” he said. “Warm all winter.”

“Is it somewhere you sit?”

“No, it’s where you put your gloves before football. Then after football your gloves are warm.”

“Do you leave them there the whole time?”

He gave me the pitying look children reserve for adults who might conceivably be in charge of something.

“You put them there at halftime.”

We added the warm pipe to a fresh sheet. By the end of the week somebody had marked a doorway where you could get a pram out of the rain, a clock visible from the bus queue, and the one place on Mill Lane from which you could see whether the bridge was up before committing yourself to the descent. None of these things belonged on our official map. I began spending quite a lot of time on them.

People disagreed. A red-haired man described the steps of the Methodist church as a good place to eat lunch; someone else observed that on Saturdays there were weddings. The red-haired man returned to write, in small neat capitals, ESPECIALLY THEN. A nurse recommended the garden behind the clinic for its quiet, and a patient objected that the whole point of the garden was that nobody knew about it. I removed the garden. That evening the patient came back to make sure.

There were places whose value depended on the month, the hour, or the direction from which you approached. Under the railway arch you could hear rain beginning ten seconds before it reached the pavement, unless a train was passing, in which case you could not hear your own name. The west face of the bank caught the last of the afternoon sun. A brass plate set there in memory of a merchant nobody remembered became warm enough in October to ease the joints of your fingers.

I tried the brass plate. It worked.

One morning I found Mrs. Bell examining our collection. She had dressed for rain in a clear plastic bonnet that tied beneath her chin. She read every entry, including the pub.

“You’ve left off the difficult bit,” she said.

I knew at once which bit she meant. The forty yards above the railing were bordered on one side by a high fence and on the other by the road. There was no sill, wall, doorway, or warm commemorative merchant. There was nothing to mark.

“If I put down all the places where there isn’t somewhere to stop,” I said, “the map will be nothing but ink.”

She undid the knot beneath her chin. It took a while. I watched her work at it, resisting the urge to help, until she said, “Oh, for heaven’s sake, have you got scissors?”

I fetched the scissors.

“You keep thinking I’ve come to give you information,” she said while I cut the ribbon. “I came because I’d like a bench.”

I had been working for the town for fifteen years. I could tell you which committee named a street, who maintained a drain, and what form you needed to put a flag over a public footpath. I had no idea how a town acquired a bench. The benches we had seemed as permanent as punctuation in a printed book. Occasionally one lost a slat. Often somebody died and a little plaque appeared. I had vaguely supposed that the bereaved supplied the whole thing.

The parks department dealt with benches in parks. The highways department dealt with obstructions on highways. Orchard Street was not a park, and if we were proposing an obstruction, they would be happy to send the form by post. The woman at the council said there was a small fund for improvements but that we had missed the deadline. The next deadline was in November. That was not the deadline for improvements; it was the deadline for asking to have an improvement considered when they next decided what qualified as an improvement.

“Is there a fund for buying a chair?” Mrs. Bell asked.

We were having eggs again. I had brought the onions this time.

“I own a chair,” I said.

“So do most people. Curious how none of us can sit down.”

On Saturday I carried a kitchen chair to Orchard Street. It was green, with one white foot where I had once failed to finish painting it. I set it halfway between the railing and the top of the hill. I sat in it myself for twenty minutes to establish, if necessary, that it had not been abandoned.

From the chair I could see a narrow slice of the river between two warehouses. A gull traveled through the slice from left to right. A minute later, possibly disappointed, it traveled back. I had always thought of Orchard Street as a street without a view.

A man pushing a bicycle stopped beside me. “Are you selling tickets?”

“No.”

He looked down the hill, then up it. “What for?”

“I’m not selling them.”

“Right,” he said, and pushed on.

I went home. When I returned after lunch the chair was gone.

What bothered me most was the white foot. I had intended for six years to finish that foot, and now somebody might reasonably conclude that I had considered the job complete. I walked to the top of the hill and down again. There was a faint impression in a patch of grit where one leg had stood. I was inspecting it when a window opened in the fence.

It was not really a window. Two upright boards swung inward on hinges, revealing the upper half of a woman in a purple apron. Behind her was a garden full of washing, every towel straining east in the wind.

“Looking for your chair?”

Behind the fence, she explained, the pavement belonged to the town, but the little wedge of gravel beside it belonged to her. She had taken the chair in because rain was forecast. She had also tightened a loose screw under the seat. Her name was Ada. She had lived there thirty years and had never seen anyone sitting outside her fence except a plasterer who had been taken ill in 2009.

“Did he recover?”

“He married my sister. Would you like your chair?”

We agreed that the kitchen chair was unsuitable for permanent outdoor use. Ada suggested a folding seat attached to the fence, like the ones in old cinemas. Her brother had made such a seat in his hall so that he could lace his boots without being thrown to the floor by his dog. We went inside and telephoned him. He still had the pattern. He no longer had the dog, who had died at nineteen after a life of exceptional happiness and, it seemed, very little discipline.

By Wednesday there was a seat on Orchard Street. It folded flat when not in use. Ada painted it the same dark green as the fence, and I painted the last foot of my kitchen chair with what was left in the tin. The greens did not match. After six years of waiting to get around to the job, I found that I preferred it that way.

Mrs. Bell tried the seat on Thursday. She lowered herself onto it with her shopping between her shoes. Ada watched from the opening in the fence. I stood by with a notebook, prepared to record suggestions concerning height, angle, splinters, and so forth.

Mrs. Bell looked through the gap between the warehouses. An orange boat passed along the river, carrying three men in orange jackets. For a moment the boat looked empty, as if it had grown three upright parts peculiar to its design. Then one of the men lifted a hand to his mouth, and the illusion broke.

“Somebody ought to trim that buddleia,” Mrs. Bell said. “In another year you won’t see a thing.”

Ada fetched her secateurs.

The official map went to the printer on time. It showed the school, the library, the river, the festival grounds, and the correct position of every contour on Orchard Hill. There was no room on it for our collection. Instead Dev made a little book out of folded paper, with one observation on each page and several pages left blank. We kept it on the counter. People could borrow it, copy it, argue with it, or add something. The boy in the football shirt drew his own gloves on the cover. They had fingers of wildly different lengths, which he assured us was accurate.

In August a visitor asked me for the best way to get to the river. I gave her the official map and showed her the short route down Mill Lane. She thanked me but did not leave. She was looking at the drawing on the little book.

“What’s that one for?”

I almost said it was another map. Instead I asked how much time she had.

She had an hour before her train. She had new shoes and a blister coming up on one heel. She liked boats but did not particularly care about getting close to the water. I sent her up Orchard Street, which was in precisely the opposite direction. I told her about the folding seat and the slice of river and the possibility, if Ada was home, of a conversation through the fence.

An hour later she came back into the library, walking in her stocking feet. She asked to borrow a pencil. On one of the blank pages she drew the front of the station and the shallow step beside the entrance. The stone, she wrote, was smooth and clean and still warm from the day. If you had made an unfortunate choice of shoes, it was a good place to take them off.

Then she put her shoes back on and ran for her train. I went outside to collect the book, which she had left open on the step. The afternoon had cooled. I took off one shoe and set my foot on the stone. There was just enough warmth left for me.

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want for 2500 words.
samples.result:
The first thing we learned about the clock was that nobody wanted it fixed to the correct time. They wanted it fixed to seven minutes fast. It had been seven minutes fast since 1981, except for a brief period in 1996 when it was eleven minutes fast and a bus driver named George had climbed onto the roof of the bus shelter and adjusted it with a broom. People remembered the broom. Three people claimed to own it. Nobody could explain how you adjusted a clock through glass with a broom, including George, who was still alive and eating breakfast most mornings at the counter in Bell’s Pharmacy.

“You had to be there,” he said.

I was there to take the clock down. My company had bought the old market hall and was turning it into apartments. We had a drawing of the finished building in which a woman in a yellow dress carried a baguette across the square. There was nowhere within a mile of the square to buy a baguette. There was a bakery, but it sold doughnuts and something called a lunch pocket that had to be held upright. I knew this because on my first visit I had held one horizontally over a set of plans.

My job was to find somewhere to keep the clock during construction. It was eight feet across, weighed six hundred pounds, and had spent ninety years telling people more or less when to go home.

I put a notice in the library. By noon on Friday I had received seventeen proposals. The dentist wanted it on his house. The rowing club offered an interior wall, though their door was thirty-two inches wide. A girl called Mina wanted it in her yard because her brother had told her that if a clock was big enough you could hear it in your sleep and never have to set an alarm. Her proposal included a drawing of herself asleep while a tremendous clock stood guard over her like a sunflower.

The best offer came from the municipal swimming pool. It had a loading entrance, a blank wall, and a facilities budget with enough money left to pay for the mounting brackets. I drove out to meet the manager, a tall, stooped woman named Fran who wore two watches. One was for ordinary time. The other counted backward from the moment the chlorine delivery was due.

“If I miss them, they go to the other pool,” she explained. “Then we’re closed for half a day and everybody gets religion about it.”

She showed me the wall. It was at the deep end, above a faded mosaic of a dolphin. The clock would fit. My company could borrow the town crane. There was even an electrical outlet, previously used to illuminate a plastic starfish at Christmas. I shook Fran’s hand and said we had a deal.

“You better swim here once before you decide,” she said.

I thought she was making a joke about the water. She wasn’t. On Saturday morning I paid six dollars, borrowed a pair of goggles from the lost-and-found, and swam six lengths before I understood the problem. Every time I came up for air at the deep end, I looked straight at the blank wall. Put a clock there and every swimmer in the pool would spend some portion of every length being told the time.

Afterward I mentioned this to Fran.

“That’s not the problem,” she said. “The problem is Thursdays.”

On Thursdays from ten until noon, the pool was reserved for people who needed help getting in and out. Some had been coming for years; others were learning to move after operations or accidents. There were two volunteers, a physical therapist, and a radio that received the country station perfectly provided nobody sat on the blue bench. The sessions lasted as long as they lasted, within the two-hour limit. A man might spend twenty minutes on the steps before going in. A woman might float on her back for an hour, holding somebody’s hands.

“We had a clock there once,” Fran said. “People kept apologizing.”

For taking too long?

“For taking any time at all.”

We stood by the vending machine. Inside it, a packet of cheese crackers hung from the end of its spiral by one corner. Fran gave the machine an absent, affectionate slap. The packet fell.

“Still want it?” I asked.

“Sure,” she said, opening the crackers. “Just wanted you to know what you were offering.”

At the office on Monday, my supervisor suggested the dump. He made the suggestion gently, in the tone you might use to propose a nursing home for somebody’s father. We had a crane booked for Wednesday, he reminded me. The scaffolders were coming Thursday. The clock was not listed on the historic register. We could photograph it, salvage the hands, perhaps have the face reproduced on the wall of the residents’ gym.

“What time would the reproduction say?” I asked.

He looked at me for a moment. “Ten past ten. They always say ten past ten.”

That afternoon I went to see George. He was having a late breakfast, eggs and fried potatoes, and wore a tie tucked between the second and third buttons of his shirt. He made room for me by moving his hat to his knee.

“Everyone thinks the broom part is impossible,” I said.

“The broom part is easy. The glass was out.”

“Why was the glass out?”

“Because I broke it with the broom.”

He ate a potato. The woman behind the counter filled my cup without asking if I wanted coffee, then poured a small measure into George’s saucer. He dipped a corner of toast into it.

“Weren’t trying to fix the time,” he said. “There was a bird in there. Making a holy racket. I thought I could lift the door with the broom handle. Next thing, here comes the glass.”

“And you set it seven minutes fast?”

“Must have knocked the hand. You’re looking for an intention where there was mostly a pigeon.”

Outside, the square was full of delivery vans. A boy in a green apron pushed handcarts of tomatoes down the ramp into Bell’s. The clock said twenty to twelve. I had begun the week by checking it against my phone; now, without meaning to, I found myself subtracting seven. It was odd how quickly an inconvenience could become a skill.

I asked George where he thought we ought to put it.

“Why’s it have to go up somewhere?”

“Well, it’s a clock.”

“It’s also six hundred pounds. Lay it down.”

He meant we could store it flat, on blocks, in the bus garage. His son ran the garage now. There was room behind the old ticket booth, where they kept the snow tires in summer. In winter, when the snow tires went on, there would be even more room.

“Come to think of it,” he said, “that’s the wrong way round.”

The garage was a brick shed with a roof the color of a bad tooth. George’s son Arthur took me through the side entrance and showed me a patch of concrete occupied by two traffic cones, a broken fan, and a cardboard carton marked GOOD ROPE. I looked inside. It was good rope.

“We could put it here,” Arthur said. “Run a little fence around it so nobody backs over it. You’d have to sign something.”

I had spent the better part of my adult life signing things. I assured him this would not be a problem.

On Wednesday, the crane arrived at eight. By nine, a crowd had gathered. Mina was there with her brother. Fran came carrying a paper sack of lunch pockets, which she distributed vertically. George stood beside the bus shelter, denying to a reporter that he had ever climbed on top of it. He had stood on the seat, he said. What did they think a broom was for?

When the clock came away from the wall, something unexpected happened. The square grew lighter. It wasn’t much, but you could see it: a pale wash passing over the windows of the pharmacy as the white face tilted in the sun. For two or three seconds a bright oval moved along the brickwork and over the awning and across the coats of the people watching. Mina ran after it. Then the crane turned, the angle changed, and the light was gone.

Behind the clock was a circle of original brick, dark red, untouched by weather. Near the bottom of the circle, somebody had painted a name in white letters: EDITH. No date. No heart around it. The letters were square and careful, the E slightly fatter than the rest.

Of course everybody wanted to know who Edith was. By lunchtime she had been identified as the architect’s wife, the builder’s daughter, a racehorse, a lady electrician, and an acronym for a municipal department that had never existed. The reporter called the historical society. The historical society called George, who said he was old, not eternal, and went home for a nap.

I went with the clock. We lowered it onto padded blocks behind the ticket booth, face up, and Arthur connected the motor to an extension cord. The minute hand moved, paused, moved again. We watched until we were sure.

“Seven fast?” he asked.

I checked. “Six and a half.”

“Leave well enough alone.”

For the next few months I had other work. We discovered a drain that ran uphill, a wall that appeared on no drawing, and an entire room full of empty mustard jars. There were four hundred and sixteen of them. I counted because we were being billed by the hour for their removal and because, once you have counted two hundred mustard jars, it seems foolish not to learn how many there are. We advertised them as free to a good home. A single person took them all, which was somehow less reassuring than if nobody had wanted them.

In November I stopped at the garage to ask Arthur for a receipt. A bus was up on a lift. Somewhere a radio announcer was describing a football game with the mournful insistence of a man reporting damage to his own fence. I found Arthur behind the ticket booth, sitting on an overturned bucket beside the clock. Across from him sat a young mechanic in red coveralls. Between them, on the glass face, stood two paper cups of tea and a chessboard.

“Don’t put that in your report,” Arthur said.

I told him there was no report. The young mechanic moved a knight. Under the chessboard the minute hand crept on, carrying its black tip into view between Arthur’s elbows.

“Who’s winning?”

“She is,” he said.

“He means generally,” said the mechanic. “This particular game is in dispute.”

Her name was Sal. She told me the clock made an excellent table except during lunch, when the minute hand came out from under your sandwich and made you feel you ought to be getting on with something. On nights when it snowed, the drivers sat around it waiting for word that the hill road had been cleared. One driver did his accounts there. Another spread out maps of walks she planned to take when her knees were better. Somebody had put a sheet of clear acrylic over the glass to keep it from scratching.

I asked what would happen when we wanted it back.

Arthur glanced at Sal. She considered the board.

“We’ll need a table,” she said.

By the following spring, the market hall had windows, balconies, a laundry room, and a name: The Market Hall. A consulting firm in another city had been paid to come up with that name. I saw the invoice. The woman with the baguette had disappeared from the drawings, replaced by a man walking a dog so small it looked like a glove he had dropped.

We were ready to restore the clock. The town paid for new glass. My company paid to have the case repainted. Arthur asked if we could make the replacement table exactly eight feet across, since the drivers had grown accustomed to the distance and had found that at eight feet you could hold a private conversation on one side without making the people on the other side feel excluded. At six feet, apparently, this was impossible. I ordered the table.

There remained the question of Edith. Once the clock went back, her name would disappear, probably for another ninety years. The historical society had searched its records and found eleven Ediths with plausible connections to the building, along with one Edyth whose granddaughter insisted that she would rather have died than spell it with an I. There was talk of a plaque. There was talk of moving the clock three feet higher, which would have put the numeral twelve into a bedroom on the second floor.

In the end Mina settled it. She came to the square on the morning of the installation, carrying an envelope and a glue stick. Inside the envelope was a photograph of everybody who had come to watch the clock come down. The reporter had taken it just before the crane turned. In the photograph most of us were looking up, but Mina was a pale blur at the edge, already running.

“Put us behind there too,” she said.

We did. I climbed the scaffold myself. I pasted the photograph to the brick just below the name, then stood aside while the riggers guided the case onto its brackets. From up there I could see the roof of the bus shelter. It was dented in two places about a shoe-length apart. Down in the square, George had both hands folded over the top of his cane and the expression of a man prepared to deny absolutely anything.

The electrician switched on the motor. I set the clock seven minutes fast.

I don’t work for that company anymore. Last autumn I passed through town again and stopped at Bell’s for breakfast. The coffee was better than I remembered and the potatoes were worse. George’s usual seat was occupied by a woman helping a little boy peel an orange. I didn’t ask after him. I wish now that I had.

Across the square, a tenant on the second floor had opened a window and hung a red quilt over the sill to air. Its bottom corner brushed the top of the clock. While I watched, a hand reached out and drew the quilt up a little, just enough to let the second hand pass without catching. Then the hand disappeared and the quilt stayed where it was, bright in the cold morning, keeping its own hours in the sun.

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want for 2500 words.
samples.result:
The first thing we bought for the library of things was a ladder too long to fit through its door. Six of us stood on the pavement holding it at shoulder height while Mrs. Vale, who had opposed the entire project, watched from her upstairs window. “Have you considered,” she called down, “lending it to someone?” This was generally agreed to be the best available solution. By four o’clock the ladder was at the home of a man called Anil, who had been meaning for eleven years to clean the little round window above his stairs. At five he brought us a photograph of the view. None of us had known that from his landing you could see the river.

The library occupied a former travel agency between a bakery and a shop that sold nothing but lamps. Its window still promised WINTER SUN in letters that resisted every solvent we tried. We put our opening hours underneath. People passing on the bus must have supposed that winter sun was available on Tuesdays and Thursdays, six until eight, and Saturdays until noon. For a long time that was more or less what we offered: a warm yellow room where you could spend twenty minutes discussing a problem with people who had no financial interest in making it sound complicated.

The idea had been my sister Ruth’s. She owned a carpet cleaner, which she used once a year and stored the other three hundred and sixty-four days beneath the coats in her hall. One November she calculated what proportion of her rent the cleaner ought to pay. The result annoyed her enough to call a public meeting. Fourteen people came. Nine wanted to borrow the cleaner. One wanted to explain why this sort of arrangement had never worked in any society at any point in history. The remaining four, myself included, had understood there would be cake.

We developed rules. Nothing alive. Nothing you would be heartbroken to lose. Nothing requiring two adults to lift, a rule adopted shortly after the donation of a piano and shortly before its removal. Borrowers had to live locally, though we never established quite where locally ended. There were no fines. If something came back late, Ruth rang and asked whether the person was all right. Often they were not, and the call turned out to be more useful than the retrieval of the folding chairs. Sometimes they were perfectly all right and had simply forgotten the chairs. Ruth permitted them to be embarrassed for no more than thirty seconds.

I took the Saturday shift. I liked the quiet first hour, when the bakery next door was busy and our shop was empty. I would turn on the lamps, straighten the shelves, and inspect the returns. A borrowed object comes home bearing a little weather from another household. The jigsaw smelled of cedar. The cake tin had flour caught in the ridge around its base. Someone returned the telescope with a silver paper star stuck to its case, and nobody ever took it off. There was usually a note tucked into the carpet cleaner: *Thank you, especially from the dog.* Or: *You wouldn’t believe what came out.*

My official task was to enter every transaction into a spreadsheet. Ruth had chosen me because I worked in an office, a qualification that implied, in her view, a broad mastery of electricity and the written word. In practice I kept a pencil behind my ear and wrote things down on whatever was handy. Our records for the first year included three entries on bakery bags and an entire month on the back of a poster advertising cruises to the Norwegian fjords. This became a problem when the council offered us a small grant and asked for evidence of impact.

“What sort of impact?” I asked the woman on the telephone.

“Whatever you measure.”

I looked around. On the counter lay a tape measure whose first six inches had been chewed by a puppy. Depending on how you used it, everything in town was either half a foot too short or approximately correct.

“How long have we got?” I asked.

The council gave us six weeks. I bought a ledger and devised a form. What had the borrower used the object for? How much money had borrowing saved? Had the loan enabled an activity that otherwise would not have taken place? Members regarded these questions with deep suspicion. Mr. Bell, who borrowed a socket wrench every few months, wrote *socket purposes* in the first box and drew a line through the rest. A child borrowing the telescope estimated that buying her own would have cost a million pounds. I asked her father for a more realistic figure. He said it depended how good a telescope she had in mind.

Then a woman named Leila came in to borrow the ice-cream maker. She was perhaps thirty, with a baby asleep against her chest. She read the form carefully and asked whether it mattered if the activity had already taken place. Her father, she explained, had made peach ice cream every August when she was small. He had died in February. She had found his recipe on a card in the kitchen, though it was less a recipe than a list of ingredients followed by the instruction *you know how*. She didn’t know how. That was the trouble.

We found the manual in a drawer. On the page about fruit, a previous borrower had written, *Mash half, leave half in bits.* Leila touched the pencil mark with one finger. “That sounds right,” she said.

In the savings box she wrote zero. Without the machine she would not have bought one. She would have put the card back in the drawer, where it might have stayed until the baby grew old enough to find it and ask whose handwriting that was. I copied her zero into the ledger. It looked accusatory sitting there among all those respectable sums.

After that I added a final question: *Anything the next borrower should know?* This received better answers. The wallpaper steamer took slightly longer to heat than the green light suggested. The left-hand clasp on the picnic hamper needed lifting before it would shut. For the binoculars: *There are kingfishers behind the old mill, but if you go specifically to see one you won’t.* For the folding table: *Seats eight if friendly, six if family.* We copied the answers onto labels and tied them to the handles with string. Within a month the place looked like an orchard of small, unusually practical wishes.

That winter Mrs. Vale came downstairs. It had snowed overnight. She wore boots with grocery bags tied over them and brought a wooden box lined in green felt. Inside was a device consisting of a little brass wheel, a handle, and a dial. Nobody knew what it did. Mrs. Vale set it on the counter and turned the wheel against the street map we kept under the glass. The needle moved. Her husband, she said, had used it to measure walking routes. He had trusted neither signposts nor the estimates of other walkers, especially other walkers who described a hill as gentle.

“Does it work?” I asked.

“It knows how far,” she said. “It doesn’t know how steep.”

We entered it into the catalogue as a map measurer. For weeks nobody borrowed it. People picked it up, turned the wheel against their palms, admired the box, put it down. In March a teenage boy asked if he could take it home. He refused the offer of a map. The following Saturday he returned with a figure written on his cuff: 4.7 miles. This was the length of the corridors in the hospital where his mother worked, if you walked each one once. She had been saying for years that she walked miles every shift. For her birthday he had measured how many, and made her a card in the shape of a shoe.

When I told Mrs. Vale, she said, “My husband would have asked whether he counted the stairs.”

“Did he count the stairs?”

“I should hope he had better things to do. He’s a young man.”

The grant application was less successful. We could demonstrate that a hundred and seventeen households had used the library, that our most popular item was still the carpet cleaner, and that one household had apparently saved a million pounds. We could not demonstrate vast environmental benefits because we could not honestly claim that everyone borrowing a melon baller would otherwise have purchased one. The truth was that a person might spend her whole life content to eat melon in slices until, one wet Saturday, she came upon an instrument capable of producing little orange planets and thought of her nephew, who was interested in space.

I kept trying to turn such incidents into evidence. One evening I read Ruth a sentence I had drafted: “The project generates opportunities for low-cost intergenerational engagement through the circulation of underutilized domestic assets.”

“Is that about the melon baller?”

“Yes.”

“Did the little boy like the planets?”

“Apparently he ate Saturn and put the others in his pockets.”

“Put that.”

I didn’t put that. I wish I could say I did. I submitted a competent application in the language expected, and we received enough money to pay six months’ rent. There are occasions when the proper use of an underutilized domestic asset is to take your sister’s advice, and occasions when it is to make sure the landlord gets paid.

By our third year the ladder had become famous. It had still never spent a night in the building. From Anil it had gone to a woman painting a stairwell, then to the school for the hanging of paper birds, then to the cricket club, then to somebody whose name we lost. For a frightening fortnight no one knew where it was. We put a notice in the bakery. On Monday a postcard arrived: the ladder was safe, the guttering almost finished, sincere apologies from number sixteen. We did not know which street. By then we trusted the ladder to make its own arrangements.

There was one item I privately disliked lending. It was a portable record player in a blue case, donated by a man moving into a smaller flat. My mother had owned one like it. On Sundays she used to play the same four records while she ironed. When the last side finished she would fold the board away, even if clothes remained in the basket. As a child I thought this was because ironing could not be done without music. As an adult I have come to consider it a radical and sensible position on the limits of housework.

One Saturday a young man in a good suit borrowed the player for a wedding. He returned the following week carrying the blue case with both hands. His face told me before he spoke. Someone had put it on a windowsill. Someone else had opened the window. He had gathered all the pieces, including a hinge he found the next morning in the flower bed. He offered to buy us a new player. I heard myself tell him we did not want a new player. We wanted this one, which was a cruel thing to say to someone who had spent part of his honeymoon kneeling in wet geraniums.

Ruth took over. She accepted the pieces and gave him a cup of tea. After he left she asked whether I remembered rule two. Nothing you would be heartbroken to lose.

“It wasn’t mine,” I said.

“No,” she said. “It wasn’t.”

That evening I sat at the counter with the pieces arranged on the green felt from Mrs. Vale’s box. What had broken was mostly the case. The turntable itself might be all right. I wrote *Does anybody know about these?* on a card and put it in the window. On Tuesday three people came. One knew about hinges, one about wiring, and one had misread the card from the bus and thought we wanted information about geese. He stayed anyway. It was his idea to build a new case from the wood of a drawer.

The repaired player looked nothing like my mother’s. Its lid was too thick and its handle was a leather belt. In the bottom, where nobody would normally see it, the drawer still bore a pencilled note: *Buttons, stockings, good gloves.* The young man who had borrowed it brought in a record from the wedding. We played it after closing. Mrs. Vale danced with the goose man, whose name turned out to be Peter. They did not fall in love or get married. She said he danced too fast and he said the record was warped. Both things may have been true.

I stayed on Saturdays until my job moved to another town. On my last morning a girl I didn’t recognize came in for the map measurer. She had drawn an island for a story she was writing and needed to know whether her heroine could reach the lighthouse before dark. I asked what scale the map was. She looked appalled. Evidently I was the sort of person who, presented with an island, would immediately demand paperwork. Together we decided the island was four miles wide, the heroine had a bicycle, and the road along the cliffs was closed because of sheep. The answer was yes, but she would have to hurry.

At noon Ruth took my key. I stood outside for a while, reading the old promise of winter sun. In the window sat the ice-cream maker, the telescope, the record player with its handsome ridiculous lid. There was space on the wall reserved for the ladder, though by then no one seriously expected it back. Across the street a bus was drawing away. Up on its top deck a small boy pressed his face against the glass and looked into the shop, trying, I suppose, to work out what we sold.

I nearly raised a hand to explain, as if there were a gesture for it. Instead I watched the bus turn the corner. Then I walked to Anil’s house. I had his key because he was away and his plants needed water. I watered the fern in the hall, the basil in the kitchen, the improbable lemon tree that had never produced a lemon. Before I left, I climbed the stairs. His little round window was dusty again. Beyond it were chimneys, the hospital roof, a strip of playing field, and, between two buildings that from the street appeared to touch, the river, bright as a dropped pin.

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want for 2500 words.
samples.result:
The first thing I wrote in the book was that we owed Mrs. Vale a window. This was on a Tuesday in March, and the window in question had been broken since November. Four men from four different offices had inspected it. Each had stood in her kitchen, accepted a biscuit, and explained why the window was somebody else’s responsibility. By the time I came along, Mrs. Vale had stopped buying biscuits. She gave me a chair facing the broken pane and sat opposite with her hands in her lap, as if we were on a train together.

“What do you see?” she asked.

“A piece of cardboard.”

“Exactly. I used to see a pear tree.”

I worked for the town of Calder as an assistant recorder, a job whose chief qualification was the ability to distinguish a copy that had to be kept for seven years from an identical copy that had to be kept forever. The town had recently acquired a computer to make this distinction for us. While we waited for someone to connect it, my supervisor sent me out to settle old complaints. He gave me a bicycle, a pencil, and no particular authority.

The trouble with the window was that a stone had flown out from under a municipal mower. The mower belonged to Parks, the man pushing it worked for Roads, and the land he was mowing had been left to the library by a woman who wished it used for the advancement of poetry. There was no department of poetry. I spent an afternoon trying to establish which office had paid for the petrol. Then I went to the glazier, paid him twenty-eight pounds, and took the receipt to work. My supervisor looked at it for a long time.

“You ought to have got two estimates,” he said, and gave me twenty-eight pounds from a tin where he kept the tea money. His name was Emil. He wore a green visor when reading, although our office faced north and even at midsummer had the atmosphere of a cupboard. He was a man of delicate loyalties. He would not falsify a receipt, but he would spend the next three months persuading people that they preferred their tea without milk. I opened a black exercise book and wrote down what had happened, including the matter of the tea.

After the window came a bench. Somebody had removed it from the top of Quarry Hill because one leg was rotten. Repairing the leg took half an hour. Getting the bench put back took nine months, during which it stood in a passage at the depot and became a popular place to eat lunch. The depot men were understandably reluctant to lose it. In the end, the carpentry apprentices made them another, a much better bench, with a broad shelf along the back for mugs. I rode up Quarry Hill the morning the original was returned.

An old fellow was sitting there with a string bag between his feet. I asked if he was pleased to have the bench back. He said he had never been there before. I confess I was disappointed. I had wanted somebody to tell me how hard the climb had been all winter, how dear this spot was to his heart. Instead, he reached into the bag, took out a small orange, and began to peel it with his thumbnail. Looking out over the roofs, he divided it neatly in two and handed half to me.

I called my exercise book Matters Arising. At first it was simply a way of remembering who had promised what. Then people began asking to see it. The woman who ran the swimming baths wanted to know how I had got hold of the glazier; the glazier wanted the recipe for a seed cake Emil had brought to a public meeting; Emil wanted it understood that the cake had been made by his brother and was not, as I had recorded on page eleven, a little dry. He struck out those words. Their impression remained legible on page twelve.

By June the book contained diagrams, telephone numbers, a pressed violet, and the names of six people willing to help move a piano without necessarily agreeing that it ought to be moved. I had learned that Calder possessed a ladder long enough to reach the clock above the market, but that the only person insured to climb it was expecting a baby. I had learned that a brass band needs somewhere to empty the water from its instruments. I had learned that if a notice says “temporarily,” nobody has to decide when to take it down.

The piano belonged to the ferry waiting room. There had not been a ferry for seventeen years. A bridge carried traffic across the river now, high enough that most drivers scarcely noticed the water. The waiting room survived because nobody could agree what to do with it. Its roof was sound, its windows looked west, and the council continued to receive an annual invoice for tuning the piano. This invoice had been paid every year. In Calder, a man who wanted a hole in the pavement filled might grow old waiting, but a correctly submitted invoice was practically a sacrament.

I went down to the river with the tuner, a young woman called Kit whose father had held the contract before her. Inside, the waiting room smelled of cold stone and the sweet dust inside a vacuum cleaner bag. Somebody had swept the floor. The piano stood against the wall beneath a timetable giving the last crossing as twenty minutes past ten. Kit opened the lid, lifted out a square of faded blue felt, and played three notes. From the other side of the wall came three answering knocks. Neither of us moved for a moment.

“That’ll be Leonard,” she said.

Leonard lived in the adjoining cottage, once the ferryman’s house. He was ninety and had been the ferryman’s son, then the ferryman, and finally a man whose front door opened upon a job that no longer existed. He let us in through his kitchen. On the table were two cups, a butter dish, and a newspaper folded to the racing. He had heard his piano being tuned every June since the bridge opened. He liked the first part best, he told us, when the notes were almost right and you could hear what the tuner was for.

It turned out that the waiting room was in use. A woman came there to practice the cello because her husband worked nights. Two brothers repaired fishing reels on the long table. On wet afternoons the school crossing guard sat by the window to work on a translation of an Italian detective novel. She did not know Italian particularly well. That was why she was doing it. Leonard kept a list of names on the back of a cornflakes packet. There was no charge, although anyone who came on a Thursday was asked to put his bins out.

Here was a difficulty my book was poorly equipped to handle. The council believed the building empty. A report saying otherwise would summon a committee. The committee would consider locks, charges, supervision, and whether people repairing fishing reels required access to separate lavatories. On the other hand, Leonard’s cornflakes packet was a rather frail constitution. If he went into hospital, who would know where to find the key? I asked him. He picked up the butter dish. Underneath it, on the oilcloth, someone had written in blue ink: SPARE WITH JOAN AT NUMBER EIGHT.

I ought perhaps to have left it there. Instead I took a photograph of the room in the late afternoon, with the piano open and a bar of sun across the floor. There was a vase on the windowsill holding three stems of something yellow. I pinned the photograph above my desk, partly because I liked it and partly, I think, because I wanted someone to ask. In August the deputy mayor came looking for a street plan and stood for a while in front of the picture. “Wherever is that?” she said. So I told her.

Within a month the ferry waiting room had a future. There were drawings of a café counter and little round tables. A company from the county capital offered to run it as a destination for cyclists. Their proposal included a pump for inflating tyres and a mural showing a ferry that bore no resemblance to any vessel ever seen on our river. The council liked the proposal. Leonard liked the pump. Kit rather liked the thought of coffee. At a public meeting I stood up, flushed with indignation, and discovered I did not know precisely what I objected to.

I said something about the cello. The company director, who had driven an hour to be there and had missed his supper, said he would be delighted to host live music. I explained about the fishing reels. He suggested a local crafts evening. He was not a bad man. Everything I named he tried sincerely to accommodate. Yet with each accommodation the thing itself seemed to slip further away. The crossing guard helped me out at last. “What if I come down on Wednesday,” she said, “and I don’t buy coffee and my translation goes badly?”

The director thought about this. “I suppose you’d have had a fairly disappointing morning.”

She laughed. So did everybody else, and the meeting went on to discuss refuse collection. Afterwards I found the two of them talking beside the coat stand. He wanted to know which novel she was translating. His mother was Italian; perhaps she could help with the difficult bits. The crossing guard tore a page from her notebook. It concerned a corpse discovered in a vineyard and a remark made by a police inspector which, as best she could tell, meant either “such is life” or “leave the onions whole.”

In October the river rose. Not dramatically; there were no pictures on the national news. It rose the way a large man gets out of a small chair, in stages, with intervals of apparent reconsideration. By Friday the water covered the lower steps. On Saturday it entered the waiting room. Leonard rang Joan, who rang Kit, who rang me. I opened Matters Arising to the page about the piano. Of the six people listed, one had moved and one had a bad shoulder. The other four arrived with a furniture trolley, some rope, and strong opinions about casters.

The café director came too. His name was Paul. He had returned the Italian page and been invited for lunch. He spent most of the afternoon standing in river water in a pair of very good shoes, passing things through a window. We moved the piano into Leonard’s kitchen, which was three steps higher than the waiting room. There was just enough space if we took out the table. Leonard sat on the draining board directing operations. In the middle of everything the butter dish fell and broke. Under it were the words about Joan, scarcely smudged.

When the water went down, it left a gray line along the wall and a smell so remarkably like boiled cabbage that we searched the cupboards. The floorboards buckled as they dried. An assessor came and walked about making small, unhappy noises. Paul withdrew his proposal. The likely cost of insurance, he explained, would put too much pressure on the onions. This was now his word for all matters of Italian origin or excessive difficulty. The council fenced off the steps and put up a notice. I did not have to go and look to know which word would appear on it.

Winter passed. My computer was connected. It produced clean lists of outstanding complaints, arranged by date and optionally by street. I appreciated it most on days when I had to answer the telephone while eating lunch. Matters Arising went into a drawer. In February Leonard died, not of anything to do with the flood. His daughter came from Leeds and found herself trying to sell a cottage with an upright piano occupying most of the kitchen. Kit offered to take it. This time we moved it properly, in a van, with men who knew how to lift.

I would like to say we saved the waiting room. For a long time I meant to do something about it. So did quite a few people. But there were other things to attend to, some of them urgent and some merely near at hand. The cello player’s husband went onto days. The brothers quarreled over money. The crossing guard finished her translation and began learning to drive. One afternoon I cycled down to the river and found a surveyor measuring the building for demolition. He asked me to hold the far end of his tape, and I did.

Years later, clearing my desk before retirement, I came across the black book. Out fell the photograph, a little bleached at the edges. I turned it over. On the back, in Emil’s narrow handwriting, was the address of his brother and, below it, the instruction to soak the seeds overnight in milk. I had forgotten that he wanted me to try making the cake myself. I had forgotten a great deal. For instance, the flowers in the photograph were not yellow. They were white, in a yellow vase. I had been picturing them wrong for almost thirty years.

On my last afternoon I took the bicycle up Quarry Hill. The bench had been replaced again, this time with one made of a brown composite material that would never rot and was surprisingly comfortable. Below me the town extended in all its red and slate-colored particularity. I could identify the library land by the stand of poplars at its edge. Beyond that stood the houses on Mrs. Vale’s street. The pear tree, if it was still there, would have been in bloom. It occurred to me that I had never gone back to see the window after it was mended.

A boy came laboring up the hill, pushing a bicycle with a flat rear tyre. He asked if I had a pump. I had stopped carrying one years ago, after discovering that the rubber seal had perished at precisely the moment I needed it. We sat together while he considered his options. Then I remembered the depot at the foot of the hill. “Go round to the side door,” I told him. “There’s a little bell. If nobody answers, they might be having tea. Give them a minute.” He thanked me and set off, riding the good pedal, rattling downhill.

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want for 2500 words.
samples.result:
The first object my father borrowed from the library was a fish kettle. This was in the days when you could still astonish somebody by bringing home a whole salmon. Our neighbor Len had caught one in Scotland and carried it south on the train, wrapped in yesterday’s racing results. When he unwrapped it on our kitchen table, a blue number seven was printed just behind the gills. My father regarded the fish, regarded our assortment of round saucepans, and put his coat back on. An hour later he returned with a galvanized vessel long enough to bathe an infant.

I remember the kettle better than the salmon. It came with a perforated rack you could lower by two handles, and on one end somebody had soldered a small brass plate: BOROUGH OF WEST MERE, LENDING DEPARTMENT, 1968. Imagine the meeting at which this purchase was approved. Somebody in municipal government had stood up before witnesses and argued that from time to time the people of West Mere would need to poach a very long fish. Somebody else had seconded the motion. I was nine. This became, and has remained, my highest conception of what a government might do.

Thirty years later, when I moved back to West Mere to help my father, the library occupied the same building, though the lending department had migrated from the basement to a former carpet showroom across the street. I went looking for a folding wheelchair. Dad could still walk, but the distance between where he could walk and where he wanted to go was growing. He wished, specifically, to see the last ten minutes of amateur football matches without having to sit through the preceding eighty. He liked the moment when tired men began to make unreasonable demands of one another.

The woman at the desk said they had no wheelchairs. They did have a wheeled garden seat, she added, in the tone of somebody whose duty obliged her to mention an absurdity. Behind her, on steel shelves, were thirty or forty cardboard boxes, a carpet stretcher, two accordions, a projector screen, and a plastic skeleton wearing one red mitten. The woman followed my gaze. “The mitten keeps his hand on,” she said. Her name was Viv. I asked if they still had the fish kettle. She reached under the desk without getting up and set it down in front of me.

It was full of keys. There were little silver keys for cashboxes, big black keys with teeth like ruined battlements, and two identical keys on a tag marked POSSIBLY CUPBOARD. Viv was retiring in October. The council meant to combine her department with the main library, where there was room for perhaps a quarter of the collection. Everything else would be sold. I looked around the showroom, already furnishing a sentimental argument in my head. Then I noticed six trouser presses standing shoulder to shoulder by the wall. “Yes,” said Viv, seeing me count them. “That’s how the trouble starts.”

I found Dad a wheelchair through a charity shop, and soon we had established a Saturday circuit. At half past three I wheeled him through the park. We stopped behind whichever goal the wind favored, saw somebody in a muddy shirt shout an accusation across forty yards of open grass, and went on to buy two custard slices. On the return trip we called in on Viv. Dad had been a plumber for most of his life. He could identify tools that had defeated her, though once he confidently described an apple corer as a device for tightening a certain Belgian tap.

What interested him was the condition of things. He would take a pair of bolt cutters from a shelf, feel the resistance in the hinge, and tell Viv they needed oil. What interested me was who had borrowed them. Each object still had a card in a brown paper pocket. The projector screen had gone out nineteen times in one December, many years ago. The smaller accordion went out every March to the same address. A set of pastry cutters shaped like the nations of Europe had been borrowed once, on a Tuesday, and returned the following morning, minus Portugal.

I began volunteering on Wednesdays. Viv gave me a cloth, a yellow pencil, and a stack of forms on which I was to record each object’s dimensions, condition, and probable value. Probable value was the difficult one. A dressmaker’s dummy with an adjustable bust might fetch good money, but there were three within walking distance, and everybody who sewed knew whose spare bedroom they occupied. The department’s single left-handed wallpaper brush, worth almost nothing, was apparently the only one in the county. I put a question mark in the value column so often that Viv suggested I have a stamp made.

By June I had worked my way to the back wall, where strips of the old carpet samples still hung from hooks. Behind a square of plum-colored shag I found a narrow door. It opened onto a storeroom no larger than a railway compartment. There were no shelves. Instead, objects hung from the walls on carefully spaced nails: a white dinner jacket, a pair of wooden crutches, a bell with a cracked handle, an enormous aluminum numeral three. On the floor stood a blue suitcase. Across its lid, in white paint, somebody had written, in a very steady hand, RAIN.

Inside was a watering can, its spout fitted with a remarkably broad rose. There was a tin tray, a plug of bath chain, two coconut halves, a square of silk, and a leather tobacco pouch full of dried peas. The pocket inside the lid held a script for a play called *The Captain’s Daughter*. Pencil marks in the margins specified an approaching carriage, the opening of a sash window, a summer shower, and, on page seventeen, “the sea, getting up a little.” I took the case out to Viv. For the first time since we had met she looked cross.

“That was supposed to go home with Arthur,” she said. Arthur, it emerged, had been her husband. He had run the sound effects for the town’s amateur dramatic society until the society discovered recorded sound and Arthur discovered bowls. He had died eight years before. Viv had assumed the case was in their attic. I asked whether she would like me to carry it to her car. She shook her head. “We bought the watering can with public funds.” She took out the silk and rubbed it briskly between her palms. From somewhere close by, an audience began to applaud.

I told my father about the suitcase over supper. He knew Arthur, of course. They had gone to school together, as had most people whom Dad liked and all the people he particularly disliked. “He could do horses on cobblestones,” Dad said. “Any fool can do a horse. Arthur could have it lose a shoe.” He put down his spoon and tried it with his fingers on the tabletop: a regular, hollow drumming interrupted by a single, slightly flustered beat. He tried again. The soup cooled while a procession of unfortunate horses made its way down an invisible street.

It was Dad who proposed putting on the play. More accurately, he asked why we didn’t, by which he meant that he would enjoy attending provided somebody else took responsibility for everything before and after. His suggestion arrived at a fortunate moment. The council had requested a public event to mark the merging of the collections, and Viv had been threatening to arrange a demonstration of all six trouser presses working simultaneously. We could use the carpet showroom as a theater. There were folding chairs in stock, naturally, and the projector screen would serve as a curtain if nobody minded it going up sideways.

The play was terrible. The captain’s daughter, Eleanor, had promised herself to a man believed lost at sea, while her father favored a wealthy landowner with access to his own gravel pit. For two acts people came in from the terrace to report conversations they had held on the terrace. Then the missing sailor appeared, the landowner conceded that gravel was insufficient grounds for marriage, and everybody went back onto the terrace. What the play had, however, was weather. Arthur had annotated it far beyond the author’s requirements. Even the gravel man had a personal breeze, described as “fussy, inland.”

We found our Eleanor at the bakery. She was called Dee and could make herself heard above the bread slicer without appearing to raise her voice. The man who repaired bicycles played her father. A pair of teenage brothers agreed to divide the role of the sailor, one taking him before the interval and one after, on the understanding that neither would have to remove his glasses. Viv took charge of the effects. I was the gravel man. Dad undertook to collect tickets, although the performance was free and there were no tickets. “There will be,” he said, and made some.

For a month our rehearsals consisted chiefly of shifting objects from places in which they were inconvenient to places in which they would become inconvenient later. Then one wet evening Dee read a passage in which Eleanor explains why she has refused the gravel man. “When I hear his step outside,” she read, “I do not stop what I am doing.” We waited for the rest, but that was the whole explanation. Dee looked up from the script. The bicycle man took off his cap. From behind the projector screen came the small, dry sound of Viv putting down her peas.

I had been divorced for four years. People who knew this, including me, had generally explained it in terms of our working hours, the cost of living in two cities, and the foolishness of buying a house that needed so much attention from people who were seldom in it. All these explanations were true. None excluded the possibility that my wife had once heard my key in the lock and gone on peeling a carrot to its slender orange point. I wondered when it had happened the first time, and which of us, if either, had been relieved.

On the afternoon of the performance my father woke from a nap with a fever. It was not dramatic. He was simply too hot, then too cold, then very tired of being asked which. The out-of-hours doctor prescribed antibiotics and told me what to watch for. By six he was sleeping comfortably. My neighbor offered to sit with him while I went to the showroom, but I had lost my taste for playing a disappointed owner of gravel. I rang Viv. She listened, asked two practical questions about the medicine, and said, “Put his tickets outside. I’ll send the sailor.”

At seven a boy on a bicycle collected the tickets. At eight my father opened his eyes and asked how many had come. I said I didn’t know. He asked me to open his bedroom window. We lived only three streets from the showroom, but between us and it stood a pub, a busy junction, and a substantial Victorian building in which people learned accounts. We could hear none of the play. We heard a motorcycle changing down, somebody putting bottles into a bin, and, after a long interval, the clean double note of a pedestrian crossing giving permission to nobody.

“Your mother played the daughter,” he said. I thought he was confused. My mother, a quiet woman who had worked in payroll, had been dead for eleven years. I had never seen her on a stage, not even to collect a raffle prize. But Dad was particular. She had played Eleanor in that same production, with Arthur backstage and the terrace made from the vicar’s garden gate. “Couldn’t act,” he said fondly. “Finished everything too fast. Came in out of the rain while Arthur was still getting it started.” I asked what part he had played. “I went to watch.”

He had gone on all three nights. After the final performance he helped stack chairs, an activity during which, in West Mere, a surprising number of courtships had apparently begun. I waited for him to say more. He asked for some water. When I brought it he was examining his hands, turning them under the bedside lamp as if they constituted a complicated tool returned in uncertain condition. “It wasn’t a salmon,” he said. “That fish of Len’s. It was a sea trout. He always said salmon because of what the railway charged him to bring it down.”

The play raised no money, saved no institutions, and received one review, in the local paper, which praised the chairs. Forty-seven people came. The second sailor forgot his entrance and had to be summoned from the pavement, where he was trying to establish whether his brother’s bicycle could clear three trouser presses laid on their sides. During the final shower Viv tilted the watering can over the tin tray, exactly as Arthur had specified. Several people turned to look at the showroom windows.
