This, she told me when she visited the next morning, was as much applause as she required.

In October the collection crossed the street. The accordions went, and the wallpaper brush, and the European pastry cutters, now including a handmade replacement for Portugal that was slightly too big and produced a pleasingly generous biscuit. The trouser presses went to auction; a guesthouse proprietor bought all six. Viv took the blue suitcase home after purchasing the watering can for its assessed value of eighty pence. My father recovered slowly. By Christmas we were back behind the goal, where a goalkeeper in purple blamed a duck for something that had quite plainly been the fault of his left back.

The fish kettle lives in our kitchen now. Viv emptied out the keys and I bought it at the sale. I had an idea that I might put plants in it, but it is the wrong shape for our windowsill, and anyway I like being able to lift the lid. Inside are the unused tickets in my father’s handwriting. There is also a button, a foreign coin, and the address of somebody who can repair the zip on my coat. When the lid comes down it makes a little hollow note. Given a second kettle, you could do a passable horse.

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want for 2500 words.
samples.result:
The first thing Ada Vale learned about keeping a public clock was that nobody wanted to know the time. They wanted to know whether they were late. A man running uphill would call, “Is that right?” and point at the clock above the market. If Ada said yes, he ran faster. If she explained that the minute hand was accurate but the hour hand had slipped its collar, he went on running at much the same speed. Eventually she learned to call back, “You’ve got a minute.” This was generally true in one sense or another, and it seemed to help.

The clock had four faces. The north face overlooked the station, the east the wholesale flower market, the south a row of apartments, and the west a brick wall erected in 1974 by a bank that had neglected to look up. Every Thursday Ada climbed eighty-six steps with her lunch, a flask of tea, and whatever tools the maintenance book suggested. She ate behind the west face. Here the afternoon sun came reflected off the bank in a dim red square, like the light inside a closed eyelid. Of all the rooms she had known, including rooms in houses she had owned, this was the one where she felt least obliged to improve herself.

In March the council sent a woman named Lecia to inspect the tower. Lecia wore white trainers and carried no clipboard, which made Ada underestimate her. She climbed the stairs without stopping. At the top she put one palm against the winding drum and closed her eyes. “My father had a printing press,” she said. “Different noise. Same feeling in your teeth.” Then she measured everything, including the width of the trapdoor, and took a photograph of the place where Ada had pencilled the dates of every new pair of work boots on the wall. Ada had no explanation for having done this. Lecia did not ask for one.

The proposal arrived six weeks later. The market needed a new roof. To pay for some of it, the council would lease the tower to a communications company. The mechanism would be removed and the four hands driven by small electric motors. A receiver would keep them precisely synchronized. There would be no winding, no weekly visit, no possibility of the station face gaining three minutes whenever a hard frost came up the valley. Ada read the letter twice. Then she sat at her kitchen table and ate six dry crackers, one after another, though a tub of perfectly good butter stood within reach.

She was sixty-eight. She could afford to lose the money, although not, as her brother put it, to an extent that justified mentioning it quite so often. What she could not picture was Thursday. Monday she swam. On Tuesdays and Wednesdays she repaired domestic clocks in a little shop that smelled of wet coats even in July. Friday was groceries and her brother’s lunch. Thursday had a staircase in it. Take out the staircase and the whole week went flat. She tried explaining this to her brother, who said he understood completely and suggested the stair machine at his gym.

At the consultation meeting a surprising number of people spoke in favor of saving the mechanism. A teacher called it the beating heart of the district. A florist called it a witness to history. A young man who had recently opened an expensive bakery said the neighborhood was losing its authenticity. Ada knew him slightly; he had bought her old kitchen table for his window display, then sanded off the marks where her children had done their homework. The points were all entered in the minutes. At last Lecia asked Ada whether she wished to speak.

“It’s not especially old,” Ada said. “The frame is 1890. Most of the train is from 1936. I put in the escapement myself in 2008.”

People looked disappointed. The teacher lowered her phone.

“Does that mean you support the proposal?” Lecia asked.

“No,” said Ada.

“Would you like to say why?”

She had meant to talk about repairable machines, about the cost of replacing sealed units that failed. Instead she said, “There’s a stool up there that fits me.”

Somebody laughed, not unkindly. The secretary put down her pen. Ada found this surprisingly irritating. “You can take that down,” she said. The secretary did.

After the meeting a girl in a green school blazer followed Ada to the bus stop. “What happens to the old clock?” she asked. Ada explained that the faces would stay. “I know. That’s why I said the clock.” Her name was Mina. She had a gap between her front teeth and a violin case with a sticker that said FRAGILE, as if anyone opening the case might reasonably expect to find a hammer. Mina wanted the mechanism for the school. There was a landing, she explained, where they kept a dead rubber plant. The floor was probably strong enough. The plant had been very large.

Ada told her the mechanism weighed nearly half a ton. Mina considered this. The bus came and went while she considered it. Then she asked what it weighed in pieces. It was a good question. There were younger clockmakers in the city, men with excellent credentials, who would have spent ten minutes explaining why half a ton could not go up a school staircase before it occurred to them that it need not go up all at once. Ada gave Mina the shop number. “Call on Tuesday,” she said. “Have the measurements. And find out if that plant belongs to somebody.”

By Tuesday Mina had the measurements, a note from the head teacher, and the news that the plant was not dead. The school caretaker had scraped the bark with his thumbnail and found green beneath. It had been moved to a window beside the chemistry lab. Unfortunately the landing was eleven inches too narrow. “We could leave out the striking train,” Mina said. “It wouldn’t sound, but it would run.” Ada looked across the counter at this child who, four days ago, had not known that the striking train existed. “What have you been reading?” she asked. Mina unzipped the violin case. Inside lay three library books and a cheese sandwich.

It turned out there had been no violin for over a year. Mina had rented one through school, discovered she disliked it, and returned it in good condition. She kept the case because her mother, who worked nights and had a great deal to remember, sometimes still called from bed, “Don’t forget your violin.” It was easier to take the case than to go upstairs and sort out the misunderstanding. Besides, it kept the rain off her books. Ada found this arrangement both ridiculous and entirely sensible. She took Mina up the tower on Thursday, with written permission from her mother, who signed herself, Yours gratefully, though I am not clear what the violin has to do with it.

At the top Mina did not go straight to the mechanism. She went to the south face, where a little gap beside the numeral eight admitted a blade of daylight. She bent and looked through. “That’s our flat,” she said. Ada bent too. Beyond a fire escape and a treetop she saw a balcony with a blue towel over the rail. “My mum looks at the clock when she gets home. If it’s before seven she makes eggs. If it’s after seven she brings home rolls.” Mina put her hand on a girder. “I like rolls best. Can you make this side fast?”

For the next month they searched for somewhere to put the clock. The museum had no space. The library had space but no money for a structural survey. The station had space, money, and an absolute prohibition against clocks not connected to the national rail system. In the meantime the market roof began leaking over the fish stalls. The fish sellers, who had been tactfully silent during the public consultation, put buckets beside their displays and pinned photographs of the buckets to the council noticeboard. Nobody, not even the teacher who had called the clock a heart, could look at a photograph of a wet man selling wet fish under a wet umbrella without conceding something ought to be done.

The solution came from Ada’s brother. He had listened to an account of the week’s disappointments over lunch, mopping the last of his gravy with a piece of bread. “You can put it in my gym,” he said. Ada assumed he meant this in the same spirit as the stair machine. But he owned the building. The ground floor had once housed industrial laundry equipment. There were steel beams, a loading door, and a bare stretch of wall forty feet long. “People stare at that wall all day,” he said. “I’ve tried putting on the news. Nobody wants the news when they’re already doing something unpleasant.”

They went after lunch. The gym was bright and smelled faintly of oranges. Six people walked uphill on machines without advancing an inch. At the far end a very old woman was lifting a weight from the floor while a young instructor watched with the grave attention of a person observing a moon landing. Ada stood before the blank wall and imagined the clock there, its frame waist-high, all its ordinarily hidden workings visible. For the first time since the letter came she wanted, positively wanted, to take the mechanism down. Then her brother said, “Of course, it would need a face,” and the old difficulty returned in a new shape.

The original faces had to remain with the tower. A new dial could be made easily enough, but what should it look like? Her brother favored large luminous numerals, suitable for people who had removed their glasses to exercise. Mina wanted no dial, just a pair of hands traveling over the bricks. Lecia, who had secured council money for the move by filing it under both heritage retention and improvements to community health, suggested they ask the members. The members wanted a clock that went faster between six and seven in the morning. The old woman with the weights wanted a second hand. “I rest ninety seconds between sets,” she said. “I don’t care which ninety.”

One Thursday, eating lunch in her red square of light, Ada noticed that the bank wall was being painted. A platform hung across it, and two painters in paper overalls were turning the bricks pale gray. Already the color in her room had gone lavender. In another hour it would be white. She set her sandwich down and felt a foolish impulse to lean out and ask them to leave her one red square. But which square? The light came off the whole wall. To preserve exactly what she had, she would have to ask two men to stop painting, a bank to stop maintaining its property, and the sun to hold still in the sky.

She finished her sandwich. The new light was cooler but better for seeing by. On the floor beneath her stool she noticed a little brass washer that she had dropped the previous winter. It had rolled under a joist and she had sworn at it for five minutes before getting a spare from her bag. Now it shone in plain sight. She picked it up. At the shop she drilled a hole near the rim, threaded a chain through it, and hung it around her neck. It looked like nothing in particular. Her brother asked if it was some kind of medical alert.

In June they dismantled the clock. Ada labeled each part in black pencil, and Mina photographed it beside its label. The hard part was not lowering the frame. Professional riggers did that in forty minutes. The hard part was getting the stool out. It had been assembled inside the room by some ingenious predecessor and was half an inch wider than the trapdoor whichever way they turned it. Her brother suggested a saw. Ada told him where she kept it, then went down to the market and bought three peaches. When she came back the stool was on the pavement, intact. Mina had taken the trapdoor off its hinges.

They set up the mechanism at the gym behind a low glass partition. For the dial they used the wall itself, with twelve different people invited to paint one numeral each. The teacher did a neat blue two. The florist painted a five with leaves. One of the fish sellers produced an eight formed by two silver fish biting each other’s tails. Ada’s brother did the eleven, saying it was the only one he felt qualified to attempt. At six, the old woman who lifted weights painted a small black dot, perfectly round. It took her the better part of an afternoon. The dot was visible from everywhere in the room.

On the evening they started the clock, Mina came with her mother, who had changed shifts and wore a yellow dress. Lecia brought her father. He stood beside the glass for a long while, his fingers making minute adjustments to an invisible press. At seven Ada released the pendulum. The escape wheel advanced one tooth, paused, advanced again. The long hand shivered and began its almost imperceptible climb away from the six. Across town the new electric motors would already have taken the tower hands to exactly half past seven. Ada had deliberately set this clock thirty minutes slow. When somebody finally asked why, she said, “Because we started late,” and set it right.

Afterward there were paper cups of lemonade. The riggers came in from another job, still wearing their boots. The old woman did one ceremonial lift. Mina’s mother learned the truth about the violin, took a moment to count backward through an entire year of Thursday mornings, and laughed so hard that she had to sit down on Ada’s stool. Ada stood near the loading door. She had imagined this evening would feel like the end of a long repair: tools wiped, fault corrected, an orderly entry in the book. Instead there were peach stones wrapped in napkins, condensation running down the glass, and a child trying to lick the painted fish.

The following Thursday she woke early. For a few seconds she could not account for the weight in her chest. Then she remembered there was no tower to climb. She got dressed and went to the gym. Her brother had given her a key. Inside, the clock was running well. Mina had done the figures: with the weights hanging in a shallow pit where laundry water had once drained, it would need winding twice a week. Monday and Thursday would do. Ada put the handle on the square and turned it. Outside, a delivery van reversed. Upstairs, someone dropped a shoe. In the glass she saw the old woman waiting at the door, gym bag over one shoulder. Ada let her in.

“Am I early?” the woman asked.

“You’ve got a minute,” Ada said.

The woman put down her bag. Together they stood in front of the clock, waiting for the other lights to come on. It was possible, if you held quite still, to see the long hand move.

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want for 2500 words.
samples.result:
The first thing we recorded was the drawer that held the spoons. My mother pulled it open, waited for my signal, and pushed it shut. Through the headphones I heard a quick silver commotion followed by a wooden knock. It was a fair recording of a drawer and a terrible recording of breakfast. At breakfast nobody waited for a signal. Somebody was usually standing in the way, buttering toast over the cutlery, and the person who wanted a spoon had to reach around that somebody with the particular tenderness or irritation the morning deserved.

“Do you want me to get in your way?” my mother asked.

We were selling the house. She had lived there forty-three years, I had lived there eighteen, and my brother Daniel claimed twenty, counting two summers when he kept his belongings in the garage but slept almost exclusively at his girlfriend’s. Our father had died in February. By July my mother had chosen a flat near the railway station, with a lift and a balcony just deep enough for two chairs, provided the people in them had no immediate plans to stand up. She had measured both chairs. The measurements, unlike most assurances offered to her since February, had made her feel better.

The recordings were my idea. I worked editing radio documentaries and had spent much of my adult life asking strangers to repeat things they had said more beautifully by accident. I knew enough to regret this habit and not enough to stop. I had brought a portable recorder, two microphones, a stand, several cables, and a pair of headphones with a repaired headband. My mother had expected something smaller. When I set it all out on the table she took the good tablecloth off first, as though I were about to clean a fish.

“What are we recording next?”

“The stairs,” I said.

“They’re not going anywhere.”

“Neither is the drawer.”

“Well,” she said, “you’ve got me there.”

On the stairs the fourth tread clicked at the left edge, the seventh gave a long complaint, and the little square landing made no sound at all. As children we had believed we knew a silent route upstairs. Listening to Daniel demonstrate it that afternoon, I discovered that the route would have deceived only a very generous audience. He planted one foot against the skirting board, swung the other over the seventh tread, grabbed the banister, and arrived at the landing breathing like a man bringing a wardrobe up behind him.

“Dad always knew,” my mother called from the kitchen. “He just didn’t fancy coming out to discuss it.”

Daniel played the recording back twice. The first time he laughed at the breathing. The second time he took the headphones off before the end and asked whether I had anything of Dad. I said I was sure I did. There were birthday videos, messages, a cassette from a holiday in Wales. What he meant, it turned out, was whether I had Dad saying Daniel’s name. On the birthday videos Dad usually held the camera. His messages began with “Hello, it’s me,” and ended, rather formally, with “Your father.” Neither of us could remember what was on the Welsh cassette.

We put it on the list. The list had begun on the back of an envelope with six items: stairs, drawer, front gate, boiler, rain in the conservatory, and the kitchen clock being wound. By supper it occupied three sheets of paper. Daniel wanted the old letter box, which delivered the post in two movements, a slap and a squeal. My mother wanted the bathroom tap before the plumber came on Wednesday. It made a noise she disliked and wished to play for the plumber, who had already failed on two visits to hear it. Her contributions tended to have a practical advantage over ours.

The gate was a disappointment. In my memory it announced each visitor in advance, giving a child on the sitting-room carpet enough time to decide whether to run to the door or hide behind the sofa. In fact the gate had been replaced in 2009. Its successor opened with the soft, costly efficiency of a hotel wardrobe. I stood by the hedge holding a microphone while Daniel went in and out three times. A woman walking a terrier crossed the road to avoid us. At last my mother leaned out of the upstairs window and told us the old hinges were in a tobacco tin in the shed.

There is a sort of hope peculiar to people clearing out a house: the hope that the next container will explain the contents of the last one. The tobacco tin contained four hinges, none in pairs, a brass number six, the broken pink leg of a plastic animal, and a Canadian dime. We never found the animal or the tobacco. Daniel put the six in his pocket. He lived at number forty-two, but that seemed a mean point to raise. I kept the dime because it bore the year of my birth and because nobody else wanted it, two qualifications that have filled a good many cabinets.

That night I slept in my old room on a mattress whose hollows no longer corresponded to my body. The recorder lay on the floor beside me. Around two in the morning I heard a train from the goods line beyond the allotments. It had been the last sound I heard on hundreds of childhood nights, though I could not remember ever hearing its beginning. I would become aware of it already under way, a low iron rhythm traveling through the dark along with my thoughts. By the time I found the recorder and worked out which way it was facing, the train had passed.

Instead I caught a minute and forty seconds of my mother downstairs. Water ran. A cupboard closed. There was a faint scrape that might have been a chair moving back from the table. Then I heard her laugh. It was a short, unguarded laugh, not one I had heard much lately. In the morning I asked what had been funny. She had gone down for a glass of water and found Daniel’s imitation of a council notice propped against the bread bin: RESIDENTS ARE ADVISED THAT THE FRONT GATE IS CURRENTLY UNDERGOING AN EXTENSIVE PROGRAMME OF LISTENING. Underneath, in smaller letters: NO DISCERNIBLE IMPROVEMENT IS ANTICIPATED.

“Did you record me in my nightdress?” she asked.

“Only the sound.”

“Thank goodness. It’s a dreadful nightdress.”

I offered to erase it. She thought for a moment and said I might erase the water running, if that was possible, since she had left the tap on longer than necessary and did not like to set a bad example. The laugh could stay. I tell this because it was the first time any of us had considered that the house might contain sounds a person did not wish to keep. Until then we had treated the microphone as a net drawn through clear water. Now we had to decide which things to put back.

At work I could spend an afternoon removing a refrigerator from an interview. Not the refrigerator itself, of course, but its low continuous note beneath a woman’s account of leaving home at sixteen, or a retired surveyor’s description of a landslip. Cut the note too aggressively and the speaker began to sound weightless, an oracle transmitting from a tiled lavatory. Leave it in and listeners in their own kitchens might never notice. I generally left a little. A human voice ought to sound as though it comes from somewhere, even if the somewhere is an appliance in need of service.

On Tuesday we found the cassette in a biscuit tin marked PHOTOGRAPHS, under some photographs in an envelope marked GUARANTEES. We borrowed a player from Mr. Shah next door. He came with it, reasonably enough; Daniel had borrowed his stepladder in 1998 and had yet to return it. The cassette began with several seconds of wind, followed by my own high voice explaining that we were at the seaside. More wind confirmed this. Then Daniel, aged seven, gave the football results for a league in which all the teams were named after puddings. Rice had beaten Sponge away from home in what sounded like difficult conditions.

Our father came on about halfway through. He said, “If you put your thumb there, love, all you’ll get is your thumb.” This was plainly advice about the camera and not the tape recorder. There followed a stretch of beach noise so vivid that Mr. Shah looked down at the carpet when a dog shook itself. My mother sat with her elbows on her knees. Daniel’s face had assumed the careful vacancy it wore when he was trying not to influence a penalty kick on television. We listened to the side run out. Our father had said eleven words, depending on what you did with “you’ll.”

“Other side?” Mr. Shah suggested.

The other side contained a French lesson. A brisk woman wanted directions to the municipal swimming pool. A man offered directions of such complexity that she would have been better off taking a bath at the hotel. We listened for nearly a minute, reluctant to be the one who pressed stop. Then my mother repeated the woman’s last sentence in an excellent accent. All those years, she said, there had been another cassette, and all those years she had wondered why the course started at lesson nine. Mr. Shah took his player home. Daniel followed him with the stepladder.

On Wednesday the plumber heard the tap. It happened before I could set up, and by the time I had attached the microphone he had diagnosed a loose washer. He replaced it in four minutes and stayed for tea and a discussion of parking regulations. My mother crossed the tap off the list with satisfaction. I felt briefly cheated, as if he had painted over a small fresco. Then I went upstairs to wash my hands and enjoyed the smooth, quiet turn of the handle. There were advantages to the future which had not been adequately represented on our sheets of paper.

Rain was forecast for Thursday. I set a microphone in the conservatory, which was what we called the narrow enclosure my father had built against the kitchen wall. It held a washing rack, a dead radio, and a geranium of fabulous age and uncertain loyalties. The geranium flowered whenever my mother announced that she was getting rid of it. Its latest reprieve had come the previous week, when a single red head appeared above the packing boxes. Daniel had agreed to take it home. His girlfriend from the summers in the garage was now his wife, and had stipulated that no additional furniture accompany the plant.

The rain arrived at four. The first drops clicked separately overhead; then their intervals shortened until the whole roof spoke at once. I had forgotten how loud it got. My mother came in carrying tea, and Daniel brought the last three biscuits on a saucer. For a while we watched runoff collect at the low corner where our father had repeatedly intended to fit a gutter. Through the headphones the roof sounded magnificent, broad and intricate. Without them it sounded even better, because I could feel the table trembling faintly under my wrist. I took them off. Daniel offered me a biscuit. It was soft.

“You know what I’d like?” my mother said.

Neither of us heard her over the roof, so she had to say it again. She wanted a recording of us trying to remember the name of the man who used to deliver potatoes. Not the name itself. She knew the name. She wanted the conversation in which we tried to remember it, because at some point Daniel would be so sure of a wrong answer that he would offer money, and I would start listing unrelated men with vans, and she would get to sit back knowing something. We gave it a go. Within forty seconds Daniel had lost five pounds.

By Friday we had thirty-seven recordings. Some were excellent. In one, the kitchen clock ticked its way through the silence after my mother finished winding it, and the sound seemed almost visible, like the neat punctures a sewing machine leaves in paper. Others required their labels. Without the words “airing cupboard” I would have identified that file as somebody taking a thick jumper off in a hurry. I copied everything onto my computer and made folders. Daniel asked me to send him the Welsh tape, including the puddings. My mother asked for the potato conversation. Neither requested the gate.

We moved her on a clear Monday. At the new flat the lift doors made a small bowing motion before they closed, as if apologizing to passengers for what was bound to be a short and unremarkable journey. The balcony faced west. From the left-hand chair, provided you turned your head a little, you could see the station platforms and a strip of countryside beyond the car park. My mother sat there while Daniel and I argued about the bookcase. Eventually she told us to put it where she had asked in the first place. A train pulled out. You could not hear it through the glass.

Several months later she rang me at work. She wanted to know how to make a recording on her phone. I began explaining where the microphone was, but she had already located the application and wanted to know what the red circle meant. I said it meant record. She said a circle hardly conveyed that information to a person coming fresh to the subject. A square for stop she could understand: it had the look of something planted solidly in your way. While we were discussing the triangle, she recorded both of us for almost three minutes and sent the result to Daniel, who replied that it was good to hear adults getting to grips with shapes.

That evening she sent a second file. At first I could hear only a faint traffic wash. Then came a rattle, a pause, and three descending notes of astonishing sweetness. Across the road from her balcony, my mother explained in the accompanying message, a boy was learning to play the trumpet. Every evening he began with those three notes. After that things deteriorated considerably, but the beginning was lovely, and she had thought I might like it. I listened again. Just before the trumpet started, there was my mother setting down her cup and drawing the other chair a little closer, to rest her feet on it, I suppose. She had left the balcony door open.

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want for 2500 words.
samples.result:
The first thing my father did when the town hired him to move the library was go home and weigh a book. He put a dictionary on the bathroom scale, found that the needle barely stirred, then tried standing on the scale himself, holding the dictionary. My mother came upstairs to find him taking off his trousers. He wanted a clean number, he explained. She said that unless he planned to move the library naked, the trousers could stay on. This was in August, when the new library was finished except for a front door that had been made in centimeters and ordered in inches.

My father moved pianos for a living. There were not enough pianos in our town to sustain this occupation, so in practice he moved refrigerators, filing cabinets, elderly people’s bedroom furniture, and once a plaster Saint Anthony who had lost three fingers to a ceiling fan. His truck said IVES & SON in letters that had outlasted the partnership. The Ives in question was my grandfather, dead eleven years. The son was my father. I was a daughter and therefore, according to the sign, free to spend my Saturdays as I pleased. According to my father I was due at the old library at seven.

I was seventeen and saving to leave. My intention was to become a photographer, a profession I had chosen largely because the verb attached to it was *shoot*, which sounded decisive. I owned a camera with a sticking shutter and had taken approximately four hundred photographs of the railway bridge in different weather. In every photograph the bridge looked patient and I looked, by implication, like somebody with nowhere else to go. My father offered me eight dollars an hour, cash, plus lunch. I calculated that the library contained at least a hundred dollars’ worth of Saturdays. I said I would come.

The old library occupied the second floor of a building whose first floor had been, successively, a saddlery, a savings bank, and a shop that sold things made of wicker. There was no elevator. The staircase turned twice and narrowed near the top, as though the architect believed that people became smaller as they approached literature. At the new library, across the square, broad windows looked onto a bus stop, and a ramp climbed through beds of lavender to the enormous temporary opening where the door should go. Pigeons had discovered the opening. The first employee to use the new building was a man with a broom.

Mrs. Vale, the librarian, had strong opinions about moving books. Her basic principle was that a book should be able to find its neighbors at the other end. She had devised a system involving colored tape, numbered slips, and diagrams drawn on the backs of obsolete tax forms. My father listened with the interested expression he reserved for clients right before telling them why their sofa would not fit. Then he surprised me by asking for a pencil. For half an hour the two of them leaned over a table discussing the travel arrangements of nineteenth-century Russians. Neither appeared to think this funny.

We began in geography. My job was to take books from a shelf and set them upright in a carton, spines facing the same direction. My father’s job was to lift the carton, decide I had made it too heavy, and remove a country. By ten in the morning I had learned that atlases are an unreasonable shape, islands tend to be published together, and there was a time when a man could travel through a place for six weeks and consider himself qualified to explain its inhabitants forever. We ate peaches over the wastebasket because Mrs. Vale did not allow food near the books.

Inside a guide to Belgium I found a photograph of two girls standing ankle-deep in the sea. They wore identical bathing caps and solemn expressions. One held the other’s wrist, an intimate gesture quite unlike holding hands. On the back somebody had written *the day before*, without saying before what. I showed it to Mrs. Vale. She brought out a gray biscuit tin containing a pressed fern, a grocery receipt, two bus tickets, and a letter that began, *Having given the matter more thought*. The rest of the letter was missing. “Things we find,” she said, and laid the two girls face down on the fern.

I asked what would happen to the tin. Mrs. Vale said she supposed it would go into her new desk. I asked what would happen after that. She had the good sense not to tell a seventeen-year-old that almost everything in life goes into a desk and stays there. Instead she said, “What do you think ought to happen?” I proposed an exhibition. We could photograph every object and display the photographs in the entrance hall. People might recognize their property. There could be captions. We could get the newspaper interested. By the time I finished speaking I had mentally given three interviews.

“Ask about the photographs,” my father said that evening. We were sitting on the lowered tailgate eating chips. Across the square a pigeon walked into the new library with the air of a man returning a lawn mower. I thought my father meant I should ask the newspaper what size pictures it wanted. “No,” he said. “Ask if those girls want to be on a wall.” I said the girls were probably eighty by now. He tipped the last chip crumbs into his mouth. “I expect people still have preferences at eighty.” This struck me as a deliberately inconvenient thing to believe.

The next Saturday, in household science, I found a recipe for rabbit pie written on the back of a losing betting slip. In music I found the paper sleeve of a harmonica. In a thick book about grief I found a strip of four photographs from a booth. Three frames were empty except for the little pleated curtain. In the fourth, a blurred hand reached in from the side, too late to accomplish whatever it had intended. This seemed to me the best photograph anybody had ever taken. I wanted it so badly that putting it in the biscuit tin felt like an act of extravagant generosity.

Moving a library produces a peculiar kind of weather. Paper dust hangs at the height of a person’s mouth. Bare strips of wall appear in colors that have not existed elsewhere for decades. A shelf comes down and suddenly the room smells of the winter when the shelf went up: wet wool, stove soot, the ghost of somebody’s orange. With every truckload our voices grew louder, until Mrs. Vale, who had spent thirty years asking people to speak softly, began to complain of the echo. My father brought in an old quilt and hung it on the wall behind her desk.

One morning an elderly man in a navy tie climbed the stairs and asked for a book about keeping bees. Mrs. Vale explained that the books were in transit and the library would reopen in approximately two weeks. He thanked her, descended three steps, then came back and asked whether an approximation was generally longer or shorter than the thing itself. His name was Mr. Salter. A swarm had settled in his pear tree. He had no great desire to keep bees, he said, but the bees appeared to have reached their own conclusion, and his wife wanted to know whether she could hang out the washing.

My father knew which carton held the bees. This amazed me more than anything else he did that summer. We had packed eight hundred books since breakfast, yet he walked across the square, stepped around the man with the broom, and put his hand on a box marked 638–640. The book itself advised consulting an experienced beekeeper. Mrs. Vale telephoned her cousin, who came with a veil and a wooden box. That evening Mr. Salter’s wife hung out the washing. The next Saturday a pear cake arrived at the library, and Mrs. Vale ate two slices directly over an open encyclopedia.

In the third week my father hurt his back putting on a sock. He had carried six tons of books without incident; then on Tuesday morning he raised his left foot and became, in his words, a retired man. The doctor ordered rest. My father regarded rest as a substance applied externally by people who did not understand the problem. He lay on the sitting-room floor with his knees on a chair, issuing instructions to a ceiling fixture. The town offered to bring in a contractor from the city. Mrs. Vale asked for forty-eight hours. Then she called me and asked how much of my father’s work I knew.

I knew how to pack a carton and mark it. I knew where he kept the trolley, the straps, the wheel chocks, and the tin of boiled sweets he believed nobody knew about. I knew to stop when a load shifted rather than try to correct it in motion. I knew that his unbroken rule about stairs was two people, no exceptions, and that a person walking backward ought to be the one giving directions. What I did not know was how to drive the truck. “That’s all right,” said Mrs. Vale. “I drove an ambulance in London. Which side is the steering wheel on?”

We recruited two lifeguards whose pool had closed for repairs, the wicker merchant from downstairs, and Mr. Salter, who had been a railway porter and objected to the way everybody else stood. My mother came after work carrying sandwiches. We established a packing station, a staircase team, a loading team, and, at the new building, a receiving department consisting of one twelve-year-old boy who could add long columns of figures in his head but could not be persuaded that books about horses and books about horse racing belonged in different places. “Have you asked the horses?” he said when I explained it a second time.

Without having decided to, I stopped taking photographs. There was always a label to check or a sandwich to divide or a person at the foot of the stairs who needed to know whether up or down had right of way. On Thursday my father arrived in a taxi wearing slippers. He stood in the square watching Mrs. Vale reverse his truck to within an inch of the curb. Something passed across his face that I could not read. I thought he was upset that other people could do his work. Years later he told me he had been wondering how long the hand brake had made that noise.

By Friday evening the only books left were those on Mrs. Vale’s desk. They were due back from people who were dead, or had moved away, or had insisted over many years that they had returned them already. I asked why the books were there if they had never come back. Mrs. Vale looked embarrassed. “They’re replacements,” she said. She had bought them herself. Every year she made a small private adjustment between what the town owned on paper and what it owned in fact. She had never told the council because the council would have wanted to establish a procedure.

At the bottom of this pile was a book of photographs of railway stations. A pink card inside the cover showed that my father had borrowed the original in 1978. I took it home and laid it on his chest where he lay on the floor. He studied the cover. “Well,” he said, “that settles something.” He directed me to the cupboard above the water heater, where I found a canvas bag containing a folding ruler, a pair of white gloves, and the missing book. Inside were my parents’ wedding pictures. He had put them there to flatten them and had been looking for them ever since.

There were nine pictures. In one, my mother was laughing so hard that her veil had slipped over one eye. In another, my grandfather stood alone beside a table, carefully salting a tomato. My favorite showed nothing of the married couple except my mother’s elbow and the toe of my father’s shoe. The photographer had bent down to include a little girl asleep underneath three coats. Nobody knew who she was. My mother thought somebody had brought a cousin. My father thought the wedding party next door had run out of chairs. For an hour we passed this unidentified child among us as tenderly as if she might wake.

The library opened on a wet Monday. Its correct door had arrived, though the brass handles were still on their way from Denmark, so visitors entered by pulling on a loop of blue rope. There were speeches, pear cake, and a disagreement about whether the ribbon ought to be cut before or after it had been untied from the mayor’s wristwatch. My exhibition occupied one narrow wall. Instead of photographing the contents of the tin, I had photographed the pages on which things had been found: the pale fern-shaped stain, the rust outline of a paper clip, the clean rectangle left by the girls beside the sea.

I had expected people to be disappointed by what was missing. Some were. A councilman asked whether I had forgotten to put the subjects in. But a woman stood a long time before the photograph of two facing pages warped by water, then told me about leaving a novel open on her kitchen windowsill the night her eldest son was born. Rain had come in. For years afterward, she said, every time she reached a certain part of the story, the book became twice as thick. I asked if she remembered the title. “Good heavens, no. I remember the windowsill.” She measured its depth for me with her hands.

In September I left town to study photography. My father drove me to the station in the truck, which had been washed in honor of the occasion and smelled powerfully of wet rope. While we waited, he gave me the receipt for my summer wages, folded around a key to our front door. I told him I already had a key. He told me he knew, but the one I had stuck in cold weather. Neither of us mentioned that it had stuck in cold weather all my life. He had filed the new one himself. Along its teeth I could see the bright uneven country of his work.

I have that key still. It opens nothing I own. The house was sold long ago, the truck went to a market gardener, and the library has since acquired an automatic door that swishes apart at the approach of even a fairly ambitious pigeon. Sometimes, when I am looking for a battery or a safety pin, the key turns up in my hand. I think of my father at the kitchen table, drawing a file across the metal, stopping to fit it in the lock, going back for one more stroke. On the day I left, it was eighty degrees. He was thinking about January.

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want for 2500 words.
samples.result:
The first object my aunt took home from the library was a spirit level. She owned one already, but she suspected it of dishonesty. For six years the pictures in her hallway had appeared to descend gradually toward the kitchen, as though drawn by the smell of lunch. Her level said they were straight. The library level agreed. My aunt stood back, folded her arms, and considered the possibility that the house was crooked. This pleased her much more than being wrong. When she returned the level, she told the librarian what had happened. He entered something in the little notebook he kept beside the till.

“What did you write?” she asked.

“Two levels agree,” he said.

I know this because I was there, waiting to borrow a folding table. I had invited nine people to dinner on the strength of a recipe that served ten, forgetting that recipes, unlike apartments, can accommodate arbitrary numbers of guests. The librarian showed me how to pinch the brass catches without taking the skin off my thumbs. He asked when I would bring the table back. Tuesday, I said. He wrote Tuesday on a luggage tag and looped it around one leg. At home I set it up beside my own table. Together they formed a shape for which there is no word in ordinary geometry. We put the youngest guest at the seam. He spent the meal making peas roll over the boundary between public and private property.

This was in Bellwether, a town whose greatest advantage had long been its position halfway between two places people actually wanted to go. We had a handsome station, three mediocre hotels, and a clock tower built by a man who had made his fortune in buttons. When the trains stopped stopping, the station became available for other purposes. There were proposals for a restaurant, a fitness center, and a museum of buttons. The button museum came surprisingly close. Then a woman named Alma Venn died and left the town her tools, on the condition that anybody could borrow them. The station had a roof that almost worked. The tools needed somewhere to go.

At first the library occupied only the old parcels office. You could borrow a drill, a plane, a clamp, or a saw with a handle worn to the color of tea. Soon people began bringing things of their own. A wallpaper steamer arrived, then a cake tin shaped like a lamb, then a pair of binoculars in a leather case lined with purple felt. There was no committee to decide whether a lamb belonged beside a steamer. The librarian, whose name was Edwin, found shelf space for both. His test for admission was to ask the donor when somebody might want the thing. “At Easter,” the owner of the lamb tin said. Edwin accepted this. The man who brought in half a canoe could imagine no occasion for its use and had to take it home.

I became a volunteer after the dinner party. This makes me sound more civic-minded than I was. In fact I had put a hot saucepan directly on the folding table, leaving a pale ring on its dark surface, and I hoped to do enough good that nobody would mention it. On my first Saturday Edwin handed me a cloth and a small bottle of furniture polish. For two hours I attended to the ring. People came and went behind me. A girl borrowed the binoculars to watch a nest above the bakery. Somebody needed a ladder. An old man returned a mandolin and said he had learned everything he intended to learn on it. At noon Edwin brought me coffee.

“Can you still see it?” I asked.

“Certainly,” he said. “Where would you put your cup otherwise?”

I left my coffee in the ring. After that I worked the counter. I liked the moment before a borrower told me what they needed. A person coming through the parcels-office door might be about to make a wedding cake, clear a gutter, find a lost earring, or learn whether their shelves were level. Once, a boy of about twelve asked for “something to make my room different when I get back.” He was leaving that afternoon to spend a month with his father. We lent his mother some long-handled rollers. When he returned, his room was the yellow of the inside of a peach. He brought us a photograph. In the photograph he was asleep.

The oddest requests usually came from people who knew precisely what they wanted. One Thursday a woman in a green coat asked for a bell audible at a distance of two fields but not three. Her goats, she explained, grazed in the second field. In the third lived a man who had once been engaged to her sister. She wished to call the goats without summoning him. We had six bells. For half an hour she stood on the platform ringing them while Edwin walked down the abandoned track, raising one hand when he could no longer hear. She took the smallest bell but one. I never found out whether the man came. The goats did; she sent Edwin a jar of cheese.

For every such transaction there were fifty involving the pressure washer. It was enormous, red, and in almost continuous demand. Borrowers would arrive with quiet ambitions concerning a path or a flight of steps. Two days later they would bring it back on the point of exhaustion, having discovered beneath the dirt of many years an unsuspected acreage of washable town. They cleaned gates, driveways, birdbaths, the stone paws of ornamental lions. For one glorious summer Bellwether looked freshly unwrapped from the knees down. Above that height the old soot remained intact. From the windows of a passing train, had there been one slow enough, we must have appeared to be sinking gradually into a cleaner, brighter version of ourselves.

The trouble began, as trouble in small institutions often does, with a grant. A foundation had money to give away. A councilor suggested we apply. The roof still leaked over what had once been the first-class waiting room, and there was talk of acquiring a second pressure washer. I offered to write the application because I worked in an office and knew how to make a paragraph sound as if the future depended on it. The foundation wanted evidence of impact. How many people had we helped? How much money had we saved them? What measurable changes had we brought about in their lives? I went to Edwin for the notebooks.

There were seventeen. I stacked them on the folding table and opened the earliest one. It contained dates, names of objects, and brief remarks in Edwin’s narrow writing. “Saw returned sharper.” “Lady in hat says cake came out whole.” “Two levels agree.” Sometimes he had recorded a practical detail: which part of a hinge to oil, which extension lead fitted the hedge trimmer. The notebook had nothing to say about the number of people helped. It did not even distinguish between a single borrower who came in twenty times and twenty borrowers who came once. As for the money saved, some citizens had plainly spent rather more than they would have done had we never lent them anything. A free tile cutter can lead an otherwise prudent person into a complete renovation of the bathroom.

I designed a questionnaire. It had boxes for household size, employment status, and estimated retail cost of item borrowed. Edwin examined it with the expression of someone to whom a small, wet animal has been entrusted. He did not object. He put a stack beside the till and placed a sharpened pencil on top. For the next few weeks borrowers completed the forms, sometimes while kneeling awkwardly on the platform because the folding table was out. One man estimated the retail price of our melon baller at seven hundred pounds. A woman borrowing a sewing machine put “complicated” in the box for household size. Under employment status, a retired postman wrote, “My daughter keeps me busy.”

The questionnaires produced some satisfactory numbers, provided you overlooked the melon baller. Yet I began to notice what happened when I pushed a form across the counter. People who had come in talking stopped talking. They bent over the boxes, attempting to become the sort of person whose life could be written down in the space available. Then they left. I knew that the sewing machine had gone out for four days to a household of complicated dimensions. I did not know what it had sewn. More precisely, I did not know because I had stopped asking. I was busy adding up the prices of things nobody had bought. At night I dreamed of a town made entirely of receipts.

One rainy evening I found Edwin in the waiting room arranging saucepans under the leaks. We possessed a considerable range of saucepans because a hotel kitchen had closed, but on that particular evening the roof showed greater variety still. Water struck metal in several different keys. Edwin stood listening, then shifted a milk pan six inches to the left. I told him I thought the questionnaire was a mistake. He shrugged. I told him the grant might pay for a new roof. He put a stockpot under a fresh drip.

“Both can be true,” he said.

This irritated me. I wanted one thing to be true, preferably something for which I could take immediate corrective action. Instead we spent the next hour drying chairs and moving boxes of donated Christmas lights. Before I went home I asked why he had never put the notebooks into any kind of order. He seemed surprised. They were in order, he said. April came after March. The wallpaper steamer came back before it went out again. What other order had I in mind? I tried to explain that if you wanted to find all the entries about one object, you had to go through every book. He nodded.

“Otherwise,” he said, “you'd miss the rest.”

I took the notebooks home. The foundation deadline was Monday. I spent Saturday looking for entries I could use, and Sunday reading the rest.

Here is what happened to a blue enamel roasting pan over a period of eleven years. A newly married couple borrowed it for their first Christmas. Their turkey was too big, so they cooked the legs separately. A schoolteacher used it to catch water beneath a radiator until the plumber came. Somebody filled it with ice at a street party. Somebody made an ambitious pudding that Edwin described only as “contested.” For six months the pan disappeared. It came back with a note of apology and a replacement handle made of oak. The married couple borrowed it again, this time to make lasagna for a memorial lunch. There was no indication whose. On its last recorded outing, a child used it as a lake in a model village. Edwin had drawn three tiny ducks in the margin.

On Monday I submitted the application. I included our best estimate of the number of loans and a more cautious estimate of the corresponding savings. I described the condition of the roof. There was a box marked “Any other information,” with a limit of two hundred words. In it I put the history of the roasting pan. We did not get the grant. The foundation wrote that the proposal had considerable merit, which turned out to be a quality it shared with all the unsuccessful proposals. The money went to a mobile dental clinic. Even Edwin, whose coat had acquired a permanent damp patch across the shoulders, admitted that teeth were important.

We raised the money for the roof by other means, none especially picturesque. There was a direct debit scheme. The council discovered an underspend in a maintenance budget. A roofing company offered a discount if we let them put up a sign, which we did. For a while the largest lettering anywhere in the station said VALE & SONS: ASK US ABOUT SLATE. People did occasionally ask us about slate. Edwin referred them to Vale, or to either of his sons. The saucepans went back on their hooks. We kept the questionnaires, but we moved them to a side shelf and made them optional. The figures became less reliable and the stories improved.

Years later, when Edwin retired, his replacement asked me what ought to be done with the notebooks. Her name was Sara. She had worked in a public library and had strong opinions about cataloging. Within a month she had made it possible to discover whether the pressure washer was available without walking all the way to the station. This struck some borrowers as a loss; they had enjoyed the walk and the opportunity to express surprise that the washer was out. Most people appreciated the change. Sara also established, without evident difficulty, a system under which the half canoe could be accepted. An amateur theatrical company borrowed it three times. Apparently, from the audience, you see only one side of a canoe.

I suggested the notebooks be kept somewhere dry and accessible. Sara bought a glass-fronted cabinet. At the party for its unveiling, my aunt, by then nearly ninety, asked to borrow the level again. A crack had appeared above her kitchen door. She wanted to know if it was getting worse. I explained that a level could tell her whether the lintel was straight but not whether the crack was growing. For that, she should mark its ends lightly in pencil and look again after a few weeks. She listened with the patience older relatives reserve for people whose nappies they have changed.

“I know about the pencil,” she said. “I want to see if the house has straightened up.”

We went to her house together. The hallway pictures still sloped toward the kitchen. Beyond them, on the wall beside the back door, was the photograph of our dinner party all those years before. I had forgotten she took it. Everyone was looking at the camera except the boy at the seam of the tables. He had a pea poised at the top of the slope, one finger behind it, his whole attention fixed on where it might go. At the edge of the photograph, just visible past a dish of potatoes, was the pale ring left by the saucepan. I could have covered it with my thumb. My aunt fetched a pencil. I held the level while she climbed the two steps to the kitchen, and when we had finished being useful to each other, we sat down to lunch.

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want for 2500 words.
samples.result:
The first thing anybody borrowed from the Linden Street Library of Things was a ladder. The first thing anybody returned was a different ladder. We knew because ours had six steps and the one Mr. Bello brought back had seven. He stood in the doorway while we counted, his cap in his hands, looking more troubled with every number. “I’ve had yours in the garage all week,” he said. “I can’t imagine where it got the extra.” We let him take it home again. By closing time he had found ours, and we had found something to put on the sign besides our hours: PLEASE MARK YOUR OWN LADDER.

I worked Tuesdays and Thursdays, four until eight, in what had once been the baggage room of the Linden Street station. Trains still stopped upstairs, though nobody had checked a bag there since 1972. Every twenty minutes the ceiling gave a little cough of plaster. We kept the finer tools in drawers. Most of what we had came from people clearing out their parents’ houses, which meant we possessed eleven electric carving knives and no vacuum cleaner that could turn left. You got used to steering the good one in clockwise spirals, as if slowly putting a spell on the floor.

My favorite object was a yellow cake tin in the shape of a lamb. It came in two halves that fitted together at the belly. The instructions, handwritten on the back of an envelope, recommended reinforcing the neck with a stick of dry spaghetti. Even so, the lamb often lost its head. Borrowers brought in photographs: a lamb resting its chin on a bank of coconut grass, a lamb gazing backward at its own tail, a lamb whose head had been replaced with a tangerine. We kept the pictures in an album. There was no rule you had to show us what you made. People generally wanted to.

In November, a woman named Ada Pike came in to borrow a long tape measure. She was perhaps seventy, with a straight gray fringe and a green coat that buttoned crookedly. While I copied down her address, she examined the lamb album from beginning to end. At the tangerine she made a small noise of approval. Then she asked, “Do you lend anything that can make a sound?” I showed her the stud finder, which beeped, and the pressure washer, which made conversation impossible. She listened politely. “I mean a particular sound,” she said. “I’m trying to find a door.”

I thought she meant a hidden door and got the stud finder out again. In fact she knew exactly where the door was. It had been in the kitchen of the flat above Pike’s Bakery, at the corner of Bell and Eighth, until the whole building was taken down to widen the intersection. It swung both ways. When it closed, it made a click, a pause, and a second, softer click. Her brother Simon, who lived three hundred miles away, maintained that the second sound had come from their mother putting down the bread knife. Ada intended to settle the question before Christmas.

“What’s the tape for?” I asked. “I thought I’d begin with the size of the kitchen.” She had permission to measure the patch of pavement where the bakery had stood. I pictured her out there in the November dusk, feeding the yellow tongue of the tape into traffic, and offered to help after my shift. She considered this without any visible gratitude. “Have you eaten?” she asked. I had not. At eight we locked up and went to the corner, where she took two hard-boiled eggs from her pocket. Each was wrapped in a bus timetable. She had salt in a twist of paper.

The bakery had occupied less ground than either of us expected. Ada could identify one surviving reference point, an iron drain cover patterned with little raised diamonds. She had once dropped a key through it. From there we measured twelve feet toward the lights and nine toward a shop that sold mobile phones. The kitchen door, according to her calculations, had stood approximately where a blue hatchback was waiting to turn. Its driver lowered his window. “Everything all right?” he called. “You’re in my kitchen,” Ada told him. The light changed. “Lovely place,” he said, and drove away.

We spent the next Thursday testing hinges. I brought in the loose-jointed brass pair from my bathroom cupboard. Ada had found a spring hinge at a salvage yard, and Mr. Bello, who happened to be returning a wallpaper steamer, contributed the lid of his lunch box. None made anything like the right sound. The lunch box came closest, but only because Mr. Bello had left a fork inside. Ada wrote our results in a school exercise book. Her handwriting was tiny and sloped sharply uphill. “My brother thinks I’ll forget what I heard,” she said. “He’s waiting me out.”

I asked whether Simon remembered anything else about the kitchen. A great deal, apparently. He remembered the pattern on the oilcloth, green pears in white bowls. He remembered their mother dusting flour from the top of the radio with a pastry brush. He remembered a brown scorch on the ceiling where their father had tried to fry a pudding. Ada disputed the pears, which she said were quinces, and the pudding, which she said was cheese. Neither of them could explain what their father had been trying to accomplish. It struck me as a deficiency in my own life that nobody had ever tried to fry me a pudding.

Word got around. People began coming down to the baggage room with recordings of doors. We heard the padded sigh of a cinema exit, the indignant squeal of a greenhouse, the brisk clack of the little wooden gate at the public pool. A boy brought in a recording of his guinea pig shutting itself in a doll’s wardrobe. You could hear the boy’s breathing, a rustle, then his delighted whisper: “He’s done it again.” Ada listened to each contribution with the gravity of a competition judge. She never said a sound was wrong. She said it belonged somewhere else.

Soon we had so many recordings that I put them on the old computer and made a directory. I meant to label it DOOR SOUNDS, but I was interrupted by a man wanting pinking shears, and for several weeks the directory was called DO. By the time I noticed, people were asking if they could hear the Do, and the name stuck. On quiet evenings we played it with the screen turned off. The game was to guess where you were. The easiest was the fish shop: after the door banged, a voice invariably said, “Mind the step.” The hardest was the roof hatch of a canal boat in rain.

Near the end of November my father called. Our talks had grown brief since my mother’s death, partly because she had always carried the telephone from room to room and supplied us with subjects. Without her, he and I tended to exhaust the weather on both coasts in under a minute. This time, for something to say, I told him about Ada. He listened. “A swing door can knock twice if the floor’s uneven,” he said. There was a pause while we both registered the unexpected availability of a second topic. “What sort of floor did she have?” he asked. I promised to find out.

“Linoleum,” Ada said. “Red, with pale flecks. If you dropped a cherry stone you had to get down on your knees.” I relayed this to my father. The following Tuesday a parcel arrived containing a square of red linoleum, two small hinges, and a note: *Try a loose threshold strip.* He had drawn a diagram on the back of an electricity bill. I recognized his way of drawing wood, three parallel lines with a knot like a sleeping eye. As a child I had believed this was a feature of wood itself, that every board contained somewhere in its length a single closed eye.

Mr. Bello built us a frame. The boy with the guinea pig painted the door red, although nobody remembered what color the original had been. Ada hung it herself. For the threshold we used a length of brass from the station’s lost-property cupboard, which had become ours on the not unreasonable grounds that nobody was coming back after forty years to claim a threshold. The first swing produced an excellent click. The second click proved harder. We loosened screws and tightened them. We tried wedges of newspaper, felt, and a playing card. Once we produced three clicks and had to go backward.

Ada rang Simon from the library. I heard his voice for the first time, rich and impatient, coming out of her coat pocket while she propped the phone against a toolbox. “You’ve built a whole door?” he said. “Not a whole one. It’s only four feet high.” “Oh, that’s quite a normal thing to have done, then.” She swung it. On the phone there was a long silence. “That’s a door in a railway station,” Simon said finally. Ada looked furious. Then a train passed overhead, and the two of them began to laugh. They had exactly the same laugh, descending in three short notes.

After that Simon sent us things. An envelope of green cloth he thought resembled the oilcloth. A photograph of their father, bare forearms crossed, standing outside the bakery beside an enormous ornamental loaf. The loaf was shaped like a swan and wore a narrow white ribbon. On the back somebody had written *Second prize*, which made me desperately curious about first. Finally Simon sent a cassette wrapped in a clean tea towel. Its label read *A’s concert / end blank*. Ada had played the clarinet as a girl. She denied there was any reason on earth to listen to her doing so now.

We had three cassette players, all donations, none quite functional. One played slowly enough to turn a clarinet into a foghorn. One ate the first inch of tape. The third worked if you lay it upside down and held the battery cover shut. On it we heard applause, several music stands falling over, then a group of children feeling their way through a tune I almost knew. Ada identified herself immediately. “There. The one who’s early.” She was early with conviction, pulling ahead at every turn and waiting, faintly exasperated, for the rest of the band to arrive.

At the end came more applause and a man saying, close to the microphone, “Is that still going?” Then a stretch of hiss. I was reaching for the stop button when we heard crockery. There was running water and a pigeon somewhere nearby, making that repetitious inquiry pigeons never seem satisfied to have answered. A woman said, “Move your elbow, Si.” Ada sat down on the box of Christmas lights. From far away came a click, a pause, and something that might have been a second click or might have been practically anything. We played those seven seconds until the player began to smell warm.

It established nothing. Simon, listening over the phone, heard his mother set down the bread knife. Ada heard the door settling in its frame. Mr. Bello thought it was the catch on a hollow metal bin, and the guinea pig boy, whose name I had finally learned was Julius, proposed that somebody had clicked their tongue. My father reserved judgment until he could hear it on better speakers. But there was something else on the tape nobody disputed. After the sound, quite distinctly, the woman began to sing. Just six notes, followed by the same six notes again. Both Ada and Simon had forgotten she did that.

I made copies. One for Ada, one for Simon, one for the directory, though that one contained only the clicks. The singing seemed to belong upstairs in their kitchen. On our last Thursday before Christmas, Ada arrived with a paper sack of buns made from her father’s recipe. Each had a piece of dried apricot tucked into the middle. We ate them standing around the red door. Julius put a bun on either side and filmed his guinea pig pushing through. My father called, ostensibly to ask whether the brass strip had been countersunk. I let him listen to everybody chewing and telling one another not to get crumbs in the hinges.

I expected Ada to take the door home. Instead she requested a luggage label and wrote *Door, freestanding, red. Opens either way.* We put it in the catalogue between *Dolly, furniture* and *Drill, cordless*. I doubted anyone would borrow it. Within a month it had appeared in a school play, served as the dramatic entrance to a proposal of marriage, and helped a nervous rescue dog get used to passing through the flap into a garden. Each borrower adjusted it a little. By March it made no click whatsoever. I mentioned this to Ada. “Good,” she said. “I’d hate to think of the poor dog getting a fright.”

In spring I went to visit my father. On the first morning we made pancakes, using a bowl with a spout and a wooden handle polished dark by my mother’s hand. I had forgotten that she used to pour one small pancake first, for testing the pan, and that whoever happened to be in the kitchen got to eat it with their fingers. My father slid it onto my plate. Neither of us remarked on the custom. There was no particular merit in keeping it and no reason to let it go. Later we went through the house recording doors. The linen cupboard, to our surprise, sounded almost exactly like a duck.

The Do is still there, if you ever come through Linden Street with twenty minutes to spare between trains. Ask whoever is at the desk for the headphones. There are more than a hundred entries now, arranged in no useful order. Somewhere around the middle you will find seven seconds of an ordinary kitchen on a busy afternoon, long enough ago that the children who stood in it have white hair. Listen once, then again if you like. You may hear a knife touch a table. You may hear a door find its place in a frame. When I listen, what I hear most clearly is the pigeon outside the window, going on and on about whatever mattered to it that day, with no idea anybody was keeping a record.

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want for 2500 words.
samples.result:
The first thing my father asked me to do after his cataract surgery was buy him a different shower curtain. For eleven years he had believed the one in his bathroom was white. Now he could see that it was covered in pale blue dolphins wearing expressions of private satisfaction.

“I wash myself in front of those things,” he said.

I took it down. He sat on the closed toilet lid, still wearing the enormous disposable sunglasses the clinic had given him, and kept me company while I worked the rings loose. My father had been an electrician. It bothered him to watch anybody do a job from the wrong end, but the doctor had forbidden him to reach above his head, which gave me a temporary freedom I had never enjoyed as a child. I worked from the wrong end.

At the store I bought him a yellow curtain with no pictures on it. I also bought six oranges, a newspaper, and a purple pot of miniature chrysanthemums. I wanted to show him things. I had the vulgar enthusiasm of somebody who has just given a friend a good book and wants to sit there watching the friend read it.

He approved of the curtain. He said the oranges looked expensive. He spent a long time with the newspaper, not reading the articles but studying a photograph of a city councilman accepting a novelty check.

“You can see where they folded it to get it in the car,” he said.

I looked. You could.

My father lived on the eighth floor of a building occupied mostly by people who had moved in forty years earlier intending to stay until they could afford somewhere better. In the meantime, the neighborhood had become somewhere better, at least according to the price of a sandwich. Downstairs, the shop where my mother used to have keys cut now sold Japanese stationery. The owner was a nice young man who sometimes cut keys anyway because the machine had come with the lease and he had taught himself to use it.

I was staying three nights. I had made arrangements involving my dog, two coworkers, and a woman who could only come to walk the dog if her son passed his driving test. My father thought this was excessive. He had put fresh sheets on my old bed, however, and on the nightstand there was a glass of water on a saucer, the way my mother used to leave it. Under the bed was a box labeled CATHY—HORSE PERIOD. I had been interested in horses for eight months in 1989. Apparently enough material had survived to justify an archive.

On the second morning I found my father at the living room window with a pair of binoculars.

“Come here,” he said. “Tell me what that fellow is doing.”

Across the courtyard, on a balcony one floor below us, a man in a green sweater was ironing a length of pink fabric. Every few seconds a gust lifted the loose end and wrapped him in it.

“I think he’s losing,” I said.

My father handed me a spiral notebook. He had drawn the windows across from his in four rows of six. In the squares he had written little descriptions: FERN, RED LAMP, NEVER OPENS, BOY WITH TURTLE. The ironing man’s square was labeled WEATHER.

“Why weather?”

“He used to have one of those stations out there. Wind speed, rainfall, everything. I could just make out the numbers with these.”

I felt a small, professional-grade pang of daughterly concern. Was this what he did all day? I had imagined him busy with the activities elderly people in brochures are always pursuing: swimming, ceramics, laughing over salads. I had not imagined him recording the location of a fern.

“Does he know you watch him?”

“Catherine, the man is ironing on a balcony.”

This seemed fair. My father explained that the notebook had started with a practical purpose. A year earlier the lights in the opposite building had begun to flicker. Not all of them, just certain apartments. He had tried to determine whether the pattern suggested a fault in a common supply line. He called the superintendent, who thanked him politely and did nothing. Three weeks later, half the building lost power.

“You must have been pleased,” I said.

“It was February. I’m not a monster.”

He had been pleased. I could tell by the care with which he put away the binoculars.

That afternoon we went for his checkup. On the bus my father kept turning his head toward small pieces of the world I would have been willing to bet money nobody had ever wanted to see more clearly. A padlock furred with rust. A paper cup rolling under a parked van. White caulk around a black window frame, applied by a man who, in my father’s estimation, ought to have his thumbs taken away.

At the clinic the surgeon shone a light into his eye and asked him to read letters. My father read beyond the line requested. The surgeon, whose entire working life must have prepared him for men like my father, congratulated him with apparent sincerity.

On our way out, a woman near the elevators was trying to put a winter coat on a little girl. The girl had gone limp in the comprehensive way children do when they wish to transfer responsibility for their skeletons to someone else. Her mother got one arm in. The other came out. My father watched for a moment and then held his palm out to the girl. In it lay a small brass washer.

“Would you hold this for me? With that hand.”

She put her arm straight through the sleeve to take it.

“You may keep it,” he said.

In the elevator I asked him why he had a washer in his pocket.

“In case I need a washer.”

I had spent years in therapy and had never arrived at so complete an explanation of anything.

We got off the bus early to buy fish. It was just after four, and sunlight came straight down Mercer Street, getting under the awnings. My father stopped in front of a bakery. There were six cakes in the window, each iced in a different color. He leaned close to a green one decorated with sugar violets.

“Your mother would have said it tasted like a hat.”

It was the first time during my visit that either of us had mentioned her. She had been dead nearly three years. We talked about her readily enough when we had business to conduct, a name to remember or a recipe to dispute. It was harder when there was no reason. I missed the ease with which she could be mentioned by people who hadn't loved her very much.

“Did things change color for her?” he asked.

“What do you mean?”

“At the end. With the medicine.”

I had been with her more than he had during those last two weeks. He had caught some respiratory bug and been told to stay away from the ward. By the time they let him back in, she was seldom awake.

“She thought the ceiling was pink one morning,” I said. “But it might have been. There was a pink building across the street.”

“Did it bother her?”

“No. She wanted me to get the name of the paint.”

He nodded, and we went in and bought two slices of the green cake. We ate them standing at the counter. They tasted of almonds and of the refrigerator in which they had spent the night.

On my last evening, the man in the green sweater came to the door. He was younger than he looked from across the courtyard, possibly because I had mistaken concentrated exasperation for age. Up close he had freckles and the trimmed black mustache of a person whose friends had eventually stopped trying to talk him out of it.

“Leon,” he said, shaking my father’s hand. “I understand you have binoculars.”

My father looked at me. I arranged my face to communicate that although I had indeed accused him of spying, I had not undertaken to organize his victims.

Leon’s problem was a bird. It had come in through his balcony door and disappeared somewhere inside the apartment. He knew it had not gone back out because he had shut the door immediately, an action he now conceded had been strategically unsound. For two hours he had searched. Then it occurred to him that someone looking through the windows from a distance might see the top of a cupboard or a high shelf invisible from the floor. The superintendent had referred him to us.

“Did he say anything else about me?” my father asked.

“He said if I ever wanted to know when my lights were on, you’d have the paperwork.”

My father received this in silence. He fetched the binoculars. Leon went back to his apartment and turned on all his lights.

It was an extraordinary room. The pink cloth, freed from its argument with the wind, hung in long panels from the ceiling. There were trees made of wire, their branches hung with teaspoons. A yellow moon leaned against a chair. On the table stood a miniature white house, beautifully proportioned except for its door, which was tall enough to admit a giraffe.

“Theater,” said my father.

“Or a very difficult divorce.”

We took turns looking. Leon moved around below our field of vision and occasionally held up his phone with a message typed in large letters. ANYTHING? Then: FOUND SOME MONEY. Then, after a considerable interval: NOT MUCH.
