Eventually I spotted the bird. It was perched on top of the tall white door, its brown body nearly indistinguishable from the shadow it cast on the wall. As I watched, it tucked its head briefly beneath one wing. I called Leon and told him where to look.

“What kind is it?” my father asked.

“Little. Brown.”

“That narrows it down to birds.”

Leon opened the balcony door, switched off the lights, and went into another room. We sat in the dark at our end, waiting. Nothing happened. It is remarkable how quickly a person can become invested in the movements of an animal whose existence was, until very recently, none of her business. I began to have opinions about the bird’s intelligence. I wanted it to make better choices. I caught myself thinking that if it would only listen to me, it could have a wonderful life.

Beside me my father said, “I never thought to ask if she could see that building.”

For a moment I had no idea what he was talking about. Then the hospital room returned to me: the high bed, the pink brick across the way, the moons of adhesive left on the glass by notices somebody had removed.

“I don’t know if she could,” I said. “From the bed, I mean.”

“I kept telling her she had a nice view. Every time I called. I said, ‘At least you've got a nice view.’”

What I remembered most clearly about those calls was the tremendous labor of putting the phone on speaker. My mother invariably turned the volume down while trying to turn it up, then took photographs of her chin. I would finally get my father’s voice into the room and she would close her eyes and smile.

“I think she mostly liked hearing you say ‘at least,’” I told him.

“What’s that supposed to mean?”

“You said it whenever anything went wrong. At least the pipe burst over the sink. At least the car was already ugly.”

He considered this. “It was an extremely ugly car.”

Across the courtyard the bird flew straight out through the open door, so fast that all I saw was the little door of the white house rocking on its hinges.

The next morning I packed. My father gave me three oranges, the remainder of the cake, and a screwdriver with an insulated handle because he had noticed, on a visit to my house four years before, that mine was rubbish. I took the horse box out from under the bed. It contained a plastic currycomb, seventeen drawings, and a library book called *Your First Pony*. On the due-date slip, stamped in purple ink, was a Tuesday in June.

“You realize they can take the apartment,” I said.

“Not if we keep moving.”

I left the box. My father said he might want to look at the drawings now that he could see properly. This was kind of him, as the horses I drew had legs that bent in either direction according to the needs of the composition.

At the door he handed me a folded piece of pink fabric. Leon had brought it over early that morning. It was a ticket, or anyway it had the name of a play printed on it, and a date, and underneath that ADMIT TWO. My father said he had looked up the theater. It was in the basement of a former bank and seated thirty people, assuming none of them had shoulders.

“Thursday after next,” he said. “Can you manage that?”

I started to tell him about the dog and work and the intricate transportation needs of a seventeen-year-old boy to whom I was not related. Then I thought about the miniature house. I wanted to know who was going to walk through that door.

“Yes,” I said.

On the train home I peeled one of the oranges. It was dry at the stem and excellent everywhere else. The woman opposite me had fallen asleep with her cheek against the window. Each time the train rounded a curve, a spot of condensation appeared on the glass just in front of her mouth, then vanished. Farther down the carriage, two schoolboys were trying to balance a coin on the narrow edge of a seat. Neither had managed it. Neither had yet suggested stopping.

I wish I could say the world appeared sharper to me, that my father’s repaired eye had somehow corrected my own. In fact the train window was filthy. Beyond it lay a succession of warehouses distinguished chiefly by the changing names of things available wholesale. My phone had fifteen messages. The dog had eaten part of a bath mat. I had forgotten the cake.

Two Thursdays later, though, I went back. My father wore his good jacket. We sat in the last row, which was the third row. When the lights went down, the spoons in the wire trees began to tremble and made a sound so much like rain that several people looked up at the ceiling. The tall door opened. Through it came a woman carrying an ordinary wooden chair upside down over her head. Beside me my father leaned forward, delighted. For once neither of us had the slightest idea what we were looking at. We stayed to find out.

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want for 2500 words.
samples.result:
On the last Thursday of August, my mother came to the municipal pool to claim a white shirt that had been hanging in the lost and found since 1978. I was sitting at the front desk with a roll of quarters, trying to decide whether the quarters belonged to the pool or the vending machine company. After thirty-two years in municipal recreation, I could still be brought to a standstill by a question involving twelve dollars.

“Men’s shirt,” she said. “Blue stitching on the cuffs.”

“Hello to you, too.”

“I heard you on the radio.”

That morning I had given a short interview about the pool’s closing. The radio host had asked about the oldest item in the lost and found, and I had described the shirt. What I had wanted to talk about was the boiler. It had heated nearly half a million gallons of water at a time and required a man named Dennis to come in every Sunday and hit a particular valve with a wooden spoon. But the host preferred the shirt. Evidently he knew his audience.

My mother put her library books on the counter. She was eighty-one and had recently taken to reading murder mysteries set in restaurants. One of the books had a whisk on the cover, dripping an improbable amount of blood.

“Let’s see it, then,” she said.

I took her downstairs. Strictly speaking, the shirt hadn’t been in the lost and found for forty-six years. Things left in the wire basket by the entrance were washed and donated every September. The shirt had survived because somebody had put it on a hanger in the staff cupboard, where a succession of employees had reasonably assumed that it belonged to another employee. It had shared this space with lifeguard hoodies, a pair of trousers Dennis kept for emergencies, and, for most of the nineties, an expensive-looking suede jacket that turned out to belong to no one any of us had ever met.

The date was written on the shirt’s paper laundry tag. July 18, 1978. The tag had gone brown and soft as the wing of a moth.

My mother took the shirt off the hanger and turned the left cuff inside out. There were five small blue crosses in an otherwise straight line of white stitching.

“Well,” she said. “There’s a surprise.”

“Dad’s?”

“Your father had arms like a tyrannosaurus. Look at the sleeves on this.”

She held the shirt up against herself. The cuffs covered her hands. She examined the collar, then brought one shoulder up to her nose and sniffed it, an act so intimate that I looked away. Beyond the little basement window, someone in red flip-flops was walking along the pool deck. I watched the feet stop, reconsider, and take three steps backward.

“It belonged to a man named Arthur,” she said.

I waited. She folded one sleeve across the chest and then the other. My mother could fold a fitted sheet into a rectangle as neat as a slice of cheese. It had always seemed to me that this ability and her refusal to tell a story in any recognizable sequence must draw on the same finite reserve of patience.

“Was Arthur a boyfriend?”

“He was a bus conductor.”

“Those aren’t mutually exclusive.”

“He taught me to swim.”

This was interesting for a number of reasons, the first being that my mother could not swim. She had spent every family holiday at the edge of the water, holding our glasses, our watches, the paper sacks that had contained our sandwiches. When we called to her to come in, she said someone had to mind the things. There had never been any shortage of things. You could have emptied our entire house onto a beach towel and my mother would have sat beside it quite contentedly with a crossword.

“You can swim?”

“I could swim then. I imagine I still can. I can still peel an apple.”

“Why have you been telling me all my life that you can’t?”

“I have never told you any such thing.”

She was right. I could remember her saying that the water looked cold, that her hair had just been done, that she wasn’t about to leave a perfectly good wristwatch under a shoe. I could not remember her saying she couldn’t swim.

Upstairs, the front bell rang. It had been salvaged from the old grammar school, a brass dome on a wooden base, and children found it nearly impossible to ring just once. This was a single, apologetic tap: an adult with a question.

“Don’t disappear,” I told her.

“Where would I go? You’ve got my books.”

At the desk a man in cycling clothes wanted to know what would become of the starting blocks. His daughter had learned to race here, and he hoped to buy the block from lane four. I wrote down his number on the list of people who wanted pieces of the pool. By then I had requests for the clock, the brass bell, two benches, the tiled seahorse by the shallow steps, and a locker door on which a marriage proposal had been scratched in 1986. The couple were still married, although each had privately informed me that the other one wanted the locker door.

My mother came upstairs wearing Arthur’s shirt over her dress. On her it looked like the sort of thing a painter might wear to suggest that she was too busy painting to buy clothes.

“Do you have a swimsuit here?” she asked.

“For me?”

“Unless you think we can both fit in yours.”

I kept a spare in my office, black with a green stripe at the waist. I also had a clean towel and a pair of goggles with one clear lens and one lens permanently fogged by some failure of modern chemistry. She accepted the suit and the towel but declined the goggles.

“There were no goggles in 1978.”

“There were definitely goggles in 1978.”

“Not on my head, there weren’t.”

We had closed the pool to the public the previous evening. A contractor was due on Monday to begin draining it. There had been a campaign to keep it open, of course. There had been petitions and a photograph in the paper of forty people holding hands in the shallow end. I had attended six meetings at which we discussed how best to save a building most of the people present had not entered in years. The roof needed replacing. The filtration system was obsolete. In February a piece of the ceiling had fallen into lane two during the adult beginners’ class, where it floated, to everyone’s surprise, with the serene determination of a small island.

A new pool was being built across town, beside the ice rink. It would have family changing rooms, a lift, and a wide ramp into the water. People who had never been able to use our pool would be able to use that one. I approved of the new pool. I had helped choose the depth markings and argued successfully for more hooks in the showers. I had even seen the room that was to be my office, with its sensible desk and its view of three young birch trees held upright by stakes. None of this made me want to empty the old one.

While my mother changed, I walked out onto the deck and switched on the underwater lights. It was a habit from the early shift, when the first swimmers came in carrying darkness on their coats. Even in daylight the lights did something lovely to the pool. They made the water look thick enough to lift by the corner.

My mother emerged with the towel around her shoulders. The suit fitted her reasonably well. She had tied her white hair back with an elastic band she must have found in the changing room; a small yellow plastic daisy stood above her left ear.

“Which end is the deep end?” she asked.

“You said you learned here.”

“It’s been forty-six years. You might have turned it around.”

She sat on the top step. For a minute she did nothing but move her feet through the water. Then she descended the steps backward, gripping the handrail, until the water reached her waist. Her legs below the surface looked pale and slightly detached from the rest of her, like the legs of a museum statue assembled from several different statues.

I sat on the deck and took off my shoes.

“Was Arthur his first name or his last name?”

“First. His last name was Bell. He had the number twelve route, down past the gasworks.”

“Did Dad know him?”

“Everyone who took the number twelve knew him. He was forever giving you back the wrong change.”

She pushed away from the rail and floated facedown, arms and legs spread. I was halfway to my feet when she rolled onto her back. The yellow daisy came loose and drifted off toward lane three.

“I used to get the last bus home from the laundry,” she said. Her voice sounded different with her ears underwater; she spoke too loudly, as though addressing somebody on the roof. “One night a little boy got on in his pajamas. No shoes. Had the fare in his hand, mind you. Exact fare for a child.”

Arthur had asked him where he was going. The boy had said he was going to see his brother swim. His brother had won a race that afternoon, and the boy had missed it because he’d been sent to bed with an earache. He thought swimming races happened like films at the pictures. If you missed the afternoon showing, you could come back in the evening.

“Very sensible, really,” my mother said.

Arthur had got the name of the boy’s street out of him and persuaded the driver to take a detour. My mother walked the boy to his door, where his parents had not yet discovered him missing. Then she went back to the bus. Arthur was waiting for her with a white shirt folded on his knees. It was his good shirt, he explained. He wore his uniform on the bus and changed afterward to go dancing. The cuff had split. Could she mend it at the laundry?

“I said we washed things. We didn’t mend them. He said, ‘Well, could you wash the two sides together particularly hard?’”

She laughed so suddenly that water went into her mouth. She righted herself, coughing, and I passed her the towel. For a while she stood in the shallow end with the towel inexplicably draped over her head. It gave her the air of a minor biblical figure about to deliver unwelcome news.

“So I mended it. Blue thread because that was what I had. He offered me money, but I’d seen him at the pool with the little ones on Saturday mornings. I asked him to teach me instead.”

“Why?”

“Because I was tired of not knowing how.”

There were eight lessons. She came before the laundry opened, and Arthur taught her to put her face in, to breathe out, to let the water hold her. On the eighth morning she swam a length without stopping. He walked beside her on the deck in his conductor’s uniform, carrying a tin cup of tea. At the far end he set down the cup and applauded. She thought of that applause for years afterward whenever she had to do anything she was afraid to do.

“And he left his shirt here?”

“No. I brought it back that morning. Hung it in the cupboard so it wouldn’t crease. We both forgot.”

“What happened to him?”

“How should I know? They did away with conductors. You had to put your money in a machine.”

I was disappointed. I had already supplied Arthur with a number of possible futures, each more interesting than the last. He might have gone to sea. My mother might have seen him years later in another town, crossing a square with flowers under his arm. At a minimum, I felt he owed us a postcard.

My mother handed me the wet towel. “Pay attention now.”

She faced the length of the pool. The building had gone quiet around us. No ventilation fans, no voices from the changing rooms, no rubber soles squeaking on tile. Outside, a delivery truck went by playing three notes of a song through an open window, and then it, too, was gone.

She pushed off. Her stroke was an old-fashioned breaststroke, head dipping under and rising again, feet sweeping out in broad, unhurried circles. At first she swam crookedly. She touched the lane rope, corrected, and continued. I walked beside her. At the halfway mark she paused to clear her throat and waved me back when I offered a hand. The second half took longer. The water folded over her shoulders. A little wave went ahead of her and struck the wall a moment before she did.

She kept one hand on the edge and caught her breath.

“Well?” she said.

I applauded. The sound was embarrassingly big in the empty building. She gave a small bow, or as much of one as a person can give while holding on to the side of a pool.

Then she said, “I’ve been wondering whether it would fit your brother.”

“What would?”

“The shirt. He needs something decent for his interview.”

All afternoon I had been trying to understand what the shirt meant. My mother, having established that it was clean and in good condition, had already found somebody who could use it.

I fetched the steps we used for the beginners’ classes and lowered them into the deep end. She climbed out slowly. We found the yellow daisy in the filter basket, and I clipped it to the handle of her handbag while she dressed.

At the front desk she signed the lost-property ledger, the last entry on a page otherwise devoted to phones and single shoes. In the column marked *Description of Article*, she wrote *One good shirt*. Then she tucked it under her arm and went out to catch her bus.

I had intended to turn off the underwater lights and lock up. Instead I changed into the damp black suit. The lining was cold enough to make me gasp. I took a cup of tea from the office and set it at the far end of lane four. There was nobody left to mind it, but in an empty building I thought I could take the chance.

From the shallow end it looked very small, a white cup in its own blue square of tile. I slipped into the water. For some time I stood there, up to my shoulders, looking down the extraordinary distance an ordinary person could swim. Then I put my face in and went to get my tea.

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want for 2500 words.
samples.result:
The first thing I measured for the town of Bellwether was a dead man’s trousers. His widow had taken them down from the washing line and found that one leg hung lower than the other. She wanted to know whether the fault lay in the trousers, the line, or the earth beneath her feet. I was twenty-three, newly appointed deputy surveyor, and delighted to be asked a question to which there could be a definite answer. I laid the trousers on her kitchen table. The right leg was seven-eighths of an inch longer than the left.

“Thank goodness,” she said. “I put that line up myself.”

She gave me a soft-boiled egg for my trouble. I ate it standing by the sink while she folded the trousers, longer leg inside the shorter, and put them away in a drawer. I didn’t ask why she had been washing them six months after her husband’s death. In those days I thought tact consisted mostly of leaving before the next question occurred to you.

The town surveyor was a woman named Ada Pike, who kept a red cabbage on her desk. Every Monday she replaced it with a fresh one. People assumed it had some technical purpose, perhaps to do with humidity. Once I saw a visiting engineer take its temperature. The truth, which Ada disclosed only after I had worked for her a year, was that she liked red cabbage and couldn’t be trusted to remember to buy one on the way home.

Our office occupied two rooms above the municipal baths. Even in winter we worked with a window open. Steam rose through the floorboards, loosening the glue on our maps, and every few weeks a road peeled away from a hillside and curled into the air. We kept the older maps flat under bricks. On Friday afternoons the schoolchildren came swimming, and through the pipes we heard their cries of outrage and triumph. An hour later, walking home, I would see the same children soberly purchasing potatoes or holding a gate for an elderly neighbor. It interested me that both kinds of conduct could be going on in a person, separated by so little time and a change of clothes.

Most of our work concerned drains. Water will consent to go where you send it, provided you have correctly understood where it already wishes to go. I became good at understanding water. I could stand at the upper end of a street in dry weather and point to the doorstep that would be wet in November. This earned me a reputation for gloomy prophecy, although I was quite cheerful in other departments of life.

After five years Ada retired. She took the cabbage and left me everything else, including a shallow drawer marked DISPUTES, which I had never seen her open. Inside were a silver teaspoon, a packet of sunflower seeds, a photograph of a dog sitting in a pram, and a notebook. The first page of the notebook bore a question in Ada’s square handwriting: *How far is it from the station to the sea?*

Underneath were eleven different answers.

Bellwether stood on a tidal estuary, so I supposed the disagreement concerned the point at which the river became the sea. This was a favorite subject in the public house, especially among men whose wives had given them a time to be home. But several answers were much too short. One said forty yards. Another said the distance was negligible in a high wind. A third, in a child’s hand, read, *All the way there and none of the way back.*

I visited Ada at her cottage. She had been retired three days and had already painted her front door yellow.

“What’s the teaspoon for?” I asked.

“Measuring medicine. I wondered where that went.”

“And the distance from the station to the sea?”

“Oh, that.” She took the spoon from me and polished it against her sleeve. “It was going to be a present for my brother.”

I hadn’t known she had a brother.

“Leon,” she said. “He went blind at forty. Came home to live with me, and wanted to walk down to the sea by himself. I began asking people how they went. Funny business. Nobody starts from the same station, even when there’s only one.”

A porter, she explained, started from the luggage door. The woman who sold newspapers started from her stall. Children started from wherever they managed to shake off the adult who was supposed to be accompanying them. As for the sea, the fishermen placed it well beyond the harbor mouth, whereas Ada’s brother would have been satisfied with a patch of stone where he could sit and get his shoes wet.

“Did he make the walk?”

“Hundreds of times. He met a fellow who took his lunch down there every day. They went together.”

“And the present?”

“He got a cardigan. You can see I still had the better part of the work to do.”

I put the notebook away. For the next thirty years I measured Bellwether in the ordinary fashion. We extended the cemetery, replaced two bridges, and established that the bandstand was subsiding at a rate too slow to alarm the musicians but fast enough to account for the persistent migration of the bass drum. I married a history teacher named Kit. We had one daughter, Rose, who left town at eighteen to study dentistry and returned at twenty-nine with a small son and an African grey parrot. The boy was called Martin. The parrot had belonged to a dentist and could imitate, with horrible fidelity, the sound of a drill slowing to a stop.

Kit died one spring while repotting a geranium. I mention the geranium because for months afterward everyone asked me what I had done with it. Nobody liked to ask what I had done with Kit, whose ashes were in a blue biscuit tin on the mantelpiece. The geranium survived. It was not an especially handsome plant. Eventually I gave it to a jumble sale and bought it back for sixpence when I saw it still sitting there at closing time. It seemed an unnecessary second humiliation for something that had only been trying to grow.

That summer the council proposed shutting the municipal baths. The boiler needed replacing, the roof leaked, and a leisure center had opened nine miles away, featuring a machine that produced waves at regular intervals. Our estuary produced waves at irregular intervals and charged nothing, but this argument carried little weight with the committee. I was instructed to measure the building in preparation for its sale.

I began on a Monday before opening time. Without swimmers the place had an ecclesiastical look. High windows divided the light into pale shafts. At the deep end, beneath eight feet of perfectly clear water, lay a copper coin, a hairpin, and a small white object that proved, when I fetched the skimming net, to be a human tooth.

“That’ll be mine,” said the attendant from the doorway.

He was a broad, gentle fellow named Frank, with all his front teeth visibly present.

“One of the back ones,” he explained. “Temporary crown. I sneezed.”

He wrapped it in a square of lavatory paper. When I told him why I was there, he walked with me around the perimeter, holding the far end of my tape. The hall was eighty-one feet long, forty-six wide. The pool itself measured sixty by twenty-four.

“Longer than that,” Frank said.

We measured it again.

“Sixty,” I said.

“Took my Elsie a year to get across.”

His Elsie, who was now a bus driver with two daughters, had been afraid to let go of the side. Each Saturday she moved one tile farther along the wall until she reached the corner. Then she began working her way out across the width, Frank walking backward in front of her, the tips of her fingers resting on his wrists.

“Twenty-four feet,” he said. “Well, there you are.”

Upstairs, I opened the shallow drawer. The packet of sunflower seeds had split at one corner. The photograph of the dog was faded almost beyond recognition, but the notebook was sound. On a clean page I wrote: *How big are the municipal baths?*

I left the book by the entrance with a pencil on a string.

For two days nobody wrote anything. On Wednesday someone drew a naked woman, anatomically ambitious but structurally unsound. On Thursday somebody else gave her a hat. Then an entry appeared in a fine blue hand: *Exactly large enough for my husband to pretend he has not seen me swimming toward him in my new green costume.*

Her husband replied underneath: *I saw you.*

This seemed to give everyone permission. By Saturday there were six pages. A midwife wrote that the baths were the only place in town where nobody could telephone her. A boy wrote that the distance from the top diving board to the surface was materially greater on the first day of the holidays than on the last. Someone who signed himself A TAXPAYER observed that the building was roughly the size of a new boiler plus annual maintenance, neither of which grew on trees. Frank put a tick beside this. He had been nursing that boiler through cold mornings for nineteen years and felt it deserved an accurate obituary.

I had not meant the notebook to become a petition. Perhaps that was why it did not sound like one. A petition asks you to agree before you have finished reading. The notebook had room for the woman who found the changing cubicles filthy, the man who owed his marriage to an accidental exchange of towels, and the child who simply wrote, *When I go under I can hear everyone’s feet.*

The council met on the first Tuesday in September. I submitted my measurements on one sheet of paper and brought the notebook in my coat pocket. It was a warm evening. Through an open window came the smell of onions frying at the café next door. The chairman asked if anyone had anything to add. I stood up, meaning to read some entries, and became aware that nearly everyone in the room had already read them. The book had been passed from hand to hand all summer. Even the chairman had contributed a sentence about learning to float during the week his parents separated.

So I told them about the tooth.

It wasn’t an effective speech. I had no wider point to make about the tooth. It had just struck me, standing there with my hand in my pocket, that here was the last thing in the world I would have expected to find while measuring a building. Several people laughed. Frank, from the back, announced that it was back in working order. Then we voted.

The baths closed by eleven votes to eight.

I would like to report that the notebook changed the chairman’s mind, or that an anonymous benefactor purchased a boiler. What happened was that the accounts were as bad as anyone had said, the roof was worse, and the council had three schools requiring fire doors. In October the pool was drained. I watched the water go down past the depth markers, exposing a narrow green ribbon along the grout. At the very bottom the last few gallons spun furiously around the outlet, as if somebody below had finally pulled out a plug.

A furniture dealer bought the building. He put a floor over the pool and used the diving platform to display a grandfather clock. My office moved into the former magistrate’s chambers, where the maps stayed flat and the pipes made no sound at all.

In November Martin came to stay with me for a weekend. He was seven. Rose sent him with two jerseys, four pairs of socks, and detailed instructions about his reluctance to eat anything green. The parrot stayed home. On Saturday it began to rain before breakfast, and by eleven we had exhausted the resources of the house, including chopping an apple into an unbroken spiral and seeing how many pennies could be balanced on the geranium pot.

“What did Grandma sound like?” he asked.

I had expected, sooner or later, to be asked what she had been like. I had an answer prepared concerning her interest in other people and the complete inadequacy of her handwriting. I had not prepared for her voice.

“She spoke quite low,” I said.

“How low?”

I tried to demonstrate and sounded like a man introducing a boxing match. Martin was courteous enough not to laugh.

“When she was in another room,” I said, “you could tell whether she was talking to a person or an animal. She was more formal with animals.”

“What did she say to them?”

“Good afternoon, usually.”

He considered this. Rain ticked against the window. I remembered Kit singing on a bicycle, calling upstairs for a towel, reading aloud the directions on a packet of wallpaper paste as though the manufacturer had personally disappointed her. None of these recollections supplied the actual sound. I found I could remember the shape of her mouth saying my name more easily than I could hear her say it.

“Get your coat,” I told him.

We walked to the station. Under the iron canopy, rainwater rattled into the gutters. I showed him the luggage door where the porter began his journey to the sea, and the recess where the newspaper stall used to stand. We walked past the furniture shop. In the upper window the grandfather clock indicated twenty past four, although it was not yet noon.

At the harbor steps we sat with our shoes on the lowest dry stone. The tide was coming in. Beyond the harbor wall a little tugboat pushed against a barge piled high with gravel. Martin wanted to know how much gravel. I said I couldn’t tell from here. He wanted to know the depth of the channel. That I knew: fourteen feet at low water, provided the dredger had been through.

“Grandma brought me here,” he said at last.

“I expect she did.”

“She said good afternoon to that.”

He pointed. Halfway down the wall, just above the rising water, a squat iron drain projected from the stone. A flap over its mouth lifted whenever water came through, then fell shut with a conversational little clack.

I could see why she had answered it.

We stayed until the tide reached our soles. On the way home we bought a red cabbage, which Martin agreed was not technically green. We cooked it with an apple and too much vinegar. Before Rose came on Sunday, I found Ada’s notebook and wrote down the drain, the rain, the gravel barge, and what Martin remembered his grandmother saying. Then I gave him the pencil. Beneath my account, in letters bearing hard enough to mark the pages underneath, he added the one measurement I had forgotten to take: *We sat there until our feet got wet.*

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want for 2500 words.
samples.result:
The first bench I stole weighed almost nothing. It was made of two milk crates and a plank, and it stood outside a laundromat on Plover Street. I was twenty-three, employed by the city, and wearing a vest the color of a traffic cone. I took the plank first. By the time I came back for the crates, a woman had put her wet laundry in one of them. We looked at each other. I took the empty one and left.

My job title was Seasonal Streetscape Assistant. There were three of us, although the other two had been assigned to hanging baskets, a distinction I attributed to their having lied on the application about their experience with flowers. We were clearing the walking route between the train station and the new maritime museum. Someone important was coming to open it. Nobody seemed to know who. Our supervisor, Dennis, had given me a clipboard with a column marked OBSTRUCTION and another marked DISPOSITION. For the Plover Street bench I wrote “miscellaneous lumber” and “removed.” I thought disposition meant mood and was proud of having figured out otherwise without asking.

That evening, on my way home, I passed the laundromat again. An old man was sitting on the remaining crate. He had turned it upside down. Because it was low, his knees rose almost to his shoulders, giving him the vigilant posture of a grasshopper. He was eating a peach with a pocketknife, cutting off one careful yellow piece at a time.

“You took the good half,” he said.

I had changed out of my vest. “How did you know it was me?”

“I watched you do it.”

I stood there, somehow finding this explanation insufficient.

He cut another piece. “You want some?”

I said no, although it was an excellent-looking peach. Then I went back to the municipal yard, climbed through the gap beside the locked gate, and got the plank. The crate was gone. I carried the plank the eleven blocks to Plover Street, resting it on alternate shoulders. When I arrived, the man had finished his peach and acquired a newspaper. He examined the plank.

“What am I supposed to do with that?”

“I thought you wanted it back.”

“I did. You should’ve brought the other half.”

This was my introduction to Mr. Vale, who had once played clarinet in a dance band, had outlived two wives and a thoroughly unsuccessful umbrella shop, and had no particular interest in making young people feel better about themselves. I learned these things later. That night we balanced one end of the plank on the crate and the other on a stack of telephone directories from the laundromat. Mr. Vale sat down experimentally. The directories sighed but held.

“Now,” he said, moving over, “you can have some newspaper.”

I tell this story because whenever the city gives me an award, somebody says I began my career by building a bench. There is a bronze plaque to this effect in the lobby of the planning department. In fact, I began by taking one apart. The difference matters to me, though not enough to pay for a new plaque.

The next morning Dennis called me into his office. He had a photograph of the restored bench on his desk. In the photograph, taken at dawn, the telephone directories looked positively geological.

“You missed something,” he said.

“Yes.”

“Can you tell me what?”

I considered the question. Dennis was a square, sunburned man whose shirt pockets contained two pens, a thermometer, and a small comb. I had never seen him use any of these things. Through his window I could see the hanging-basket assistants loading geraniums into a truck. One of them was holding a plant by its flowers.

“People sit there,” I said.

Dennis turned the photograph around. “I mean the screw.”

A rusty screw stuck out of the plank at one end. Once he pointed it out, I could see it quite clearly.

“Go take the screw out. If it catches somebody’s trousers, we’ll hear about it until Christmas.”

“What about the bench?”

“What about it?”

“It’s on the route.”

“So is the laundromat. Don’t bring me the laundromat.”

On Friday, the important person arrived. It turned out to be a retired television presenter who had grown up locally and was famous for announcing the weather in a dinner jacket. Rain drove the ceremony indoors. An aide carried the ribbon inside and tied it between two coat stands so the presenter could cut it. Nobody walked the route. I spent the morning in the municipal yard separating usable lengths of timber from pieces too short or too rotten to keep. Dennis showed me how to knock the boards together and listen. Sound wood rang a little. Rotten wood made a noise like a person setting down a hat.

By September I had a permanent job in street maintenance. By December I had learned why the hanging baskets did so poorly on the east side of town: the watering truck was too tall to fit under the railway bridge, and nobody had wanted to put this in writing. In January I drew a map of every public seat in the central district. I did it on my lunch breaks, mostly because winter made lunch breaks long. I used blue dots for benches with backs, green for benches without, and red for places where people sat despite the apparent intentions of whoever owned the property.

The red dots were the interesting ones. There was a warm stone ledge behind the bakery. There were the broad steps of the tax office, nearly deserted except at noon, when six bicycle couriers congregated to eat elaborate lunches from glass containers. There was a low concrete cylinder outside the pharmacy that had once held a lamppost. A woman sat on it every Thursday at three, holding a violin case between her feet. She never opened the case. After several weeks of wondering, I asked her why she sat there.

“Because my bus comes at ten past.”

I made a note of this. Then, ashamed of having expected a better answer, I crossed the note out. Later I crossed out the crossing-out. It took me a surprisingly long time to understand that the bus was the better answer.

The map remained a private amusement until my mother broke her ankle. She lived on the fourth floor of a building without a lift, above a hardware shop that sold, among other things, very handsome ladders. After six weeks indoors she became difficult in inventive ways. She telephoned the radio station to dispute the pronunciation of “archipelago.” She sent back a grocery delivery because the bananas were “emotionally green.” When the doctor finally permitted her to walk to the end of the street, she dressed as though for a transatlantic crossing and told me not to hover.

Halfway down the block she needed to rest. There was nowhere to sit.

We made it to a parked car. She leaned against its bonnet while I stood in front of her, trying to look sufficiently related to excuse what we were doing. An alarm went off. Upstairs, a blind snapped open.

“Wave,” my mother said.

“What?”

“If they see an old lady waving they’ll think it’s all right.”

We waved. The blind came down. The alarm continued.

On my map the nearest bench was only a few hundred yards away. To a person at a desk, this was the same neighborhood. To my mother it might as well have been across the estuary. We got her home, one shop doorway at a time. That afternoon I spread my map out on her kitchen table and showed her all the places where a person could sit.

“You’ve done it backwards,” she said.

This was among her favorite assessments, applicable to everything from my education to the loading of a dishwasher, but on this occasion she had a point. I had mapped the seats. What she wanted to see were the gaps.

We took a ball of orange wool from her knitting basket and laid strands across the map between the places she went: the grocer, the library, her sister’s flat, the post office where the clerk knew not to offer her commemorative stamps. Wherever she judged the distance between seats too great, she tied a knot. Her unit of measurement was not the yard but the good day. On a good day she could get from the hardware shop to the crossing. On a bad day she could get as far as the ornamental pear tree, which was not even marked.

“You ought to put the tree in,” she said. “Otherwise how will you know where I mean?”

When I brought this map to Dennis, small knitted landscapes rose from the paper where the wool had buckled. He looked at it for a long while.

“Your mother do this?”

“Both of us.”

“My wife buys this color. You can never finish anything with it. You get halfway through a pullover and discover you don’t know anybody orange.”

He put the map on the wall. For a month nothing happened. Then the city received a modest grant for neighborhood improvements, and Dennis asked if I knew where we could use five benches.

We installed the first outside the hardware shop. My mother came down to supervise. She objected to its angle, its height, and the fact that the slats were likely to retain rain. Dennis handed her the small comb from his pocket and asked her to hold it while he adjusted the rear legs. She became so absorbed in the responsibility of the comb that we finished without further criticism. Years later I asked Dennis if that had been the idea.

“No,” he said. “It was digging into me.”

The second bench went by the ornamental pear tree. The third went outside the pharmacy, where the woman with the violin case continued to sit on the concrete cylinder. She preferred, she said, to face the other way. We turned the fourth bench around before we bolted it down. The fifth sat in the yard for almost a year because the residents of two neighboring streets wanted it, and neither group could bear the prospect of its being enjoyed by the other. Eventually it went to a football pitch half a mile away, where on Saturday mornings it disappeared entirely beneath a mountain of small coats.

I stayed with the city for thirty-eight years. The wool map became a survey, and the survey became a program, and the program acquired a budget large enough to attract people who said “deliverables.” We made mistakes. We put a beautiful curved seat beneath a horse chestnut tree that in autumn bombarded its occupants with military accuracy. We tried a metal design that reflected so much afternoon sunlight into a dentist’s office that patients in the chair were given sunglasses. A bench dedicated to a beloved headmistress was installed facing a blank wall, owing to a contractor’s misreading of an arrow. Her former pupils came to the unveiling and agreed that she would have preferred it that way.

Some of the best seats were accidents. When a storm brought down an elm in Parson’s Field, the crew cut the trunk into sections and left them overnight. By morning a class of schoolchildren had arranged the smaller rounds in a circle and was holding what appeared to be a trial. A boy stood in the middle, vigorously defending himself. I never learned the charge. We left the rounds there until they softened into the ground. By then the children who had put them there were tall enough to sit on the field gate and too old to be caught doing anything so childish as conducting a trial.

Mr. Vale lived to ninety-four. He got a proper bench outside the laundromat eventually, though he claimed it was less comfortable than the plank. When the laundromat closed and became a shop selling expensive soap, he continued to sit there, explaining to disappointed customers where they could go to wash their clothes. After his death his niece gave me his clarinet. I had never expressed an interest in playing it, and she had never expressed an interest in giving it to anyone who did. It was simply left over. For years it lay in its case on top of my wardrobe.

The summer after I retired, I took it to a music shop to see whether it could still be played. The young woman behind the counter fitted a new reed, tried a scale, and produced a sound so rich and companionable that for a moment I felt personally greeted. Then she gave it to me. I produced the distress call of a cabinet being dragged across a floor.

“Same instrument,” she assured me.

I began taking lessons on Wednesdays. My teacher was the woman who used to sit outside the pharmacy with the violin case. She had taught woodwinds as well as strings for forty years. The case, she told me, had generally contained her lunch, two exercise books, and a pair of indoor shoes. Her violin lived at the school. I asked why she hadn’t used an ordinary bag.

“I had a perfectly good case.”

Last week I managed, for the first time, to play an entire tune outside my own kitchen. I chose the bench on Plover Street because it seemed unlikely that Mr. Vale, wherever he was, would miss an opportunity to tell me what I was doing wrong. The soap shop had its door propped open. Across the street a delivery driver was rearranging boxes in his van. I put the case beside me, took out the clarinet, and began.

The delivery driver recognized the tune before I finished it. He whistled the last few bars from inside the van, taking the high note I had been worrying about easily, almost carelessly. I went back to the beginning. This time he came in at the right place. A woman leaving the soap shop paused to listen, and for the length of the second verse we were, by any reasonable definition, a band.

Then the driver shut his doors and left. The woman walked on. I wiped the mouthpiece, put the clarinet away, and stayed where I was for a while. It had rained earlier. Water stood in bright beads on the slats at the far end of the bench, which my mother could have told them would happen. A bus went by. From somewhere behind the soap shop came the uneven mechanical thumping of a washing machine; apparently somebody back there still had clothes to wash.

A boy in a school uniform stopped beside me. His shoelace had come undone. He lifted one foot, tried to catch the lace, and nearly fell over. I moved the clarinet case off the dry half of the bench. He sat down.

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want for 2500 words.
samples.result:
The first thing my father sold after he died was a paper bag full of paper bags. The woman who bought it counted out fifty cents in nickels and said, “Your dad would’ve let me have these for a quarter.”

“He should’ve come in today, then,” I said.

She considered this and dropped another nickel on the counter. “For the joke.”

I had taken two weeks off from my job to empty his shop. He sold things that larger stores sold in packages of eight, or no longer sold at all: individual curtain rings, rubber feet for ironing boards, the little keys that opened the glass doors of certain bookcases. His best seller, by a considerable margin, was string. There were eleven varieties, and he could tell which one a customer wanted by the distance between the hands they held up to describe it.

My plan was to sell what I could, give the rest to the theater department at the high school, and return the premises broom-clean to a landlord named Joel. Joel was converting the building into apartments. He’d shown me a drawing of a young couple drinking coffee in what had been our stockroom. They appeared delighted by the natural light. I hadn’t had the heart to tell him there wasn’t any.

On the second morning, a boy came in carrying one end of a long blue rope. The rope went out the door behind him.

“Is he here?”

“No,” I said. I’d been getting good at the next part. “My father died at the end of April.”

“I know. I meant the other one.”

There had never been another one. My father considered an employee an expensive means of losing track of your scissors.

“What do you need?” I asked.

The boy pulled on the rope, and a wooden elephant rolled over the threshold. It was about the size of a Labrador, painted a dirty cream color, with a slot in its back and ears cut from old inner tubes. An elaborate saddle had been drawn on in green felt pen. On the saddle someone had written LINDA.

“She doesn’t go right anymore,” he said.

This seemed incontestable. The left hind wheel was an inch smaller than the others. As I watched, Linda described a slow, unauthorized quarter turn and came to rest against the ice-melt display.

“Did my dad make this?”

“No. I made her. He was the other one.”

I’d forgotten how pleasant it was to be told something by a child who believed the only obstacle to your understanding was that you hadn’t yet heard the same words twice.

“Leave her here,” I said. “I’ll see what I can do.”

The boy, whose name was Max, parked Linda in the window and took the rope home. I found out later he needed it to get into his tree house.

That evening I ate dinner at the counter, a ham sandwich assembled on top of an invoice for brass washers. Outside, people kept stopping to look at the elephant. A teenage girl took a photograph of it. Two men in orange roadwork vests came in to ask what it cost. When I said it wasn’t for sale, one of them said, “Why, what’s wrong with it?” Around seven, Joel arrived with a tape measure and a yellow bakery box.

“I didn’t know what kind of cake you like,” he said, “so I got the kind I like.”

We ate slices of lemon cake off squares of waxed paper. He was measuring the windows for replacement glass. The old panes had bubbles in them, tiny ellipses in which the buildings across the street stood upside down.

“I used to do that,” Joel said, seeing me look through one. “Spent a whole summer when I was eight trying to see myself in those things. I knew I ought to be there, on account of how I was there.”

I showed him Linda. He squatted beside her with an audible series of clicks. “Well,” he said, “he tried the easy thing first.”

On the underside of the elephant, in my father’s handwriting, was a date from March, followed by the words SMALLER WHEEL NO HELP. Beside this was a printed word in green: OBVIOUSLY.

“He let the kid build it wrong,” Joel said admiringly. “Never managed to do that with you.”

It was so precise a description of my childhood that for a moment I felt Joel had opened a letter addressed to me.

I had been an able child with a reputation for clumsiness that came entirely from trying to finish things before my father could take them out of my hands. I soldered my first two wires together at thirty-six, in a community class, and was astonished to discover I could do it sitting down, at a reasonable pace, without an enraged man reaching over my shoulder. My father’s last gift to me had been a kitchen knife, hand sharpened. He’d included three pages of instructions and two adhesive bandages.

“What do you suppose is actually wrong with her?” I asked.

“Why don’t you ask the engineer?”

Max returned the following morning and we turned Linda over on a blanket. Without the dignity lent her by her upright posture, she looked like an amateur coffee table. Her belly was made from a cupboard door; you could still see the pale circle where a knob had been. The axles ran through loops of copper pipe strap, secured by an assortment of screws so varied it seemed unlikely that two of them had ever occupied the same room before.

Max demonstrated the problem. With all four wheels of equal size, Linda pulled to the right. With the smaller wheel, she pulled to the left, but only reluctantly, and the rest of the time she wouldn’t go at all.

“Where does she have to go?” I asked.

“To school. We’re collecting money for the aquarium. We get to adopt an octopus.”

“How much does an octopus cost?”

“No, it stays there. You get a letter.”

“From the octopus?”

“From Denise at the aquarium. She’s got email.”

He put a quarter into the slot in Linda’s back. It landed with a small, expensive sound.

“Can you get that out again?”

“Not yet,” he admitted.

We set about the wheels. There is a species of happiness peculiar to the first twenty minutes of a repair, before you know what a repair is going to require. We found four matching wheels in a box marked CASTER DISASTERS. We cleaned the axles with an oily rag. We drove Linda down the aisle between plumbing supplies and garden tools and she swerved right with the decisiveness of a commuter turning into his own driveway.

Max sat cross-legged on the floor. “Do we fix the elephant,” he asked, “or do we just move the school?”

We ate the rest of Joel’s cake.

By Friday the shop was half empty. A woman from the high school had taken the paint, the chain, and a brass bell loud enough to announce the end of a war. My father’s regular customers wandered through in mounting distress, rummaging among the reduced stock for objects they’d had no need of until faced with the prospect of never having them. An elderly man bought all forty-seven of our remaining sink plugs. I helped him carry them to the bus stop.

Max came by after school with a girl named Araceli, who had brought the front axle from a discarded baby carriage. She had also brought her little sister Nina, who lay down on the floor and went immediately to sleep. While Max and I wrestled the wheels off the axle, Araceli drew a diagram of Linda on the back of a receipt. She measured from corner to corner and reported that one diagonal was longer than the other.

“She’s a parallelogram,” Max said, appalled.

“Not necessarily,” said Araceli.

They were at an age when finding a use outside school for a word learned inside school was like spotting a teacher at the pool. They said *parallelogram* several more times. Nina slept through an argument about trapezoids.

We could have made the frame square. We had clamps and glue and at least a hundred metal brackets. But doing it would have meant taking off the sides, which would have meant damaging the saddle, and the saddle, it turned out, had been drawn by Nina. She could no longer be counted on to repeat the performance. Her interests had moved on to horses and cutting her own hair.

Instead, we penciled a rectangle onto the crooked belly, and remounted both axles along its short sides. I was allowed to hold the ruler. At six-fifteen we set Linda on her feet. Max gave the rope a tug. She traveled the length of the shop, passed through the open door, and rolled out onto the pavement, where three people applauded and one jumped aside.

The applause woke Nina. She came to the door rubbing a red mark on her cheek where she’d slept on the head of a carriage bolt.

“How do we get the money out?” I asked.

She reached under the elephant’s tail, turned an ordinary cupboard catch, and opened the door that formed its belly. A quarter fell out.

Max stared at her. “Since when?”

Nina shrugged. You could see what sort of life she led among people continually surprised by the existence of things she’d known for ages.

That should have been the end of Linda as far as I was concerned. The children took her away, and the following day I found a green message written under the counter where Max had sat to eat his cake. GOOD LEMON. I unscrewed the board and kept it. I realize how this sounds. I had discarded six boxes of my father’s personal papers without reading any of them, and here I was going to the trouble of extracting four painted-over screws to preserve a restaurant review.

On my last Wednesday I made it into the narrow cupboard behind the till. My father had kept his coat there even in summer, along with a spare pair of shoes in case he got his feet wet. On the top shelf was a red biscuit tin. I stood on the counter to reach it and spent a while up there looking down. From that height I could see the path worn pale in the linoleum, a branching channel from counter to shelves to door. There was an island in it where the column of my father’s stool had stood. I had spent years supposing he hardly moved.

The tin held no biscuits. It was full of photographs of things I had made.

Here was the birdhouse with the steep orange roof that I remembered painting and did not remember building, because he had built it. Here was the pair of stilts on which I had broken a toe. Here was the lampshade decorated with squares of photographic negative, an idea that had seemed beautiful to me until we turned on the lamp and projected fragments of our dentist’s retirement party across the kitchen ceiling.

Beneath these I found things I had forgotten making because he had not been involved, or so I’d thought: a shirt sewn from two pillowcases, a table with a cracked tile top, a mobile of forks suspended from a colander. He’d photographed these where they stood, on washing lines or in corners of rooms I recognized with a physical jolt. In a picture of a yellow bookshelf in my first apartment, I could see a bit of my own elbow, raised against the flash.

I turned that one over. On the back he’d written NO FIXINGS INTO WALL? ASK.

It made me laugh. I was glad he hadn’t been secretly altogether different. It would have been a nuisance, at my age, to have to acquire an entirely new set of grievances.

Joel came in while I was still sitting on the floor. I showed him the photographs. He looked at each one for longer than politeness required, then selected the picture of the lamp.

“I was at that party,” he said. “See the woman with the melon? First wife.”

I gave it to him. He went away holding it at arm’s length, looking for people he knew among the patches of light.

On the final morning I swept the shop from back to front. A surprising quantity of what looked like the floor was actually dirt, and a surprising quantity of what looked like dirt was the floor. I was working on the distinction with a putty knife when I heard wheels outside. Max and Araceli had brought Linda back. She wore a blue paper rosette and had acquired, at the back of her head, a pair of immense eyelashes.

“Wrong end,” Nina informed me, pointing.

The lashes were a tail.

They’d raised eighty-three dollars. Denise had sent a photograph of the octopus pushing the lid off a jar, and Max had printed it out and taped it to the saddle. Its name was Pickle. It had one white sucker among the pink ones. Araceli said this was how the staff knew which octopus it was, although there was currently only one.

“Do you want her?” Max asked me.

“Linda?”

“We’re doing birds next. Birds don’t need anything this big.”

I thought of the train home, of the narrow stairs to my apartment, of my wife’s quite reasonable request that I bring back nothing that had feet. Strictly speaking, I could have made a case for wheels. I looked at the crooked saddle and the cupboard catch and the green word *obviously*, invisible now against the ground.

“No,” I said. “But I’d like a picture.”

We stood Linda in the doorway. Nina sat on her back. Araceli held the rope, and Max, after much consideration, stood behind her with his hands in his pockets, in the attitude of a man whose employers have asked him to pose beside a satisfactory bridge. I took two photographs in case somebody blinked.

“Get in,” Max said. “We can do the timer.”

In the picture we finally kept, I am still hurrying into place. My face is blurred and my mouth is open because I am telling Nina not to lean back quite so far. She is leaning back quite far. Nobody has fallen yet.

I had a copy printed for the red tin. On the back I wrote the children’s names, the date, and the amount they’d raised, as accurately as I could remember it. Then I added one detail a person wouldn’t know from looking, the sort of thing my father would have wanted on record in case anybody should one day be foolish enough to take the assembly apart.

THE FRAME IS CROOKED, I wrote. THE WHEELS ARE STRAIGHT.

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want for 2500 words.
samples.result:
The first thing we found when we emptied the town clock was a teaspoon. It lay in the dust beneath the pendulum, bowl upward, holding three dead flies and a bead of rainwater. My brother thought the spoon might be valuable. He had the disposition of a man who could find a fortune in a sock drawer, although in practice he usually found socks. I wiped the handle with my thumb. PROPERTY OF ST. ANNE’S HOSPITAL, it said. The hospital had been demolished when we were children. For some reason this made the spoon seem less like treasure and more like something we ought to give back.

We were in the clock tower because our father had left us a job. He had maintained the clock for thirty-seven years, first as a municipal employee and then, after his position was eliminated, as a man with a key nobody had asked him to return. His will was otherwise straightforward. The house was to be sold, the money divided. My brother could have the car if he wanted it, which he didn’t. I could have the piano if I wanted it, which I didn’t either. In the envelope with the will was a penciled note: *Take my things out of the clock before they send anybody up there.* That sounded like our father. Even in death, he expected the authorities to arrive a little late and make a mess.

There were four flights of stairs. On the first landing someone had painted a blue rectangle on the wall. On the second was a window overlooking the flat roof of the bakery, where a woman in a white apron sat in a folding chair eating an orange. I had bought bread from her that morning. Until then I had supposed that the people behind bakery counters spent their breaks eating pastries. It seemed almost an act of disloyalty to find her peeling fruit. She raised one orange hand to us. My brother waved back with the teaspoon.

On the fourth flight we had to turn sideways. Neither of us was as narrow as we remembered. Tom climbed ahead, carrying a box of black rubbish bags tucked into his belt. He had taken two days off from teaching geography and had made a schedule for the house, the bank, the undertaker, and the clock. According to his schedule we would finish the clock by eleven and have coffee at eleven fifteen. I admired this hopeful document. At home I had a nine-year-old daughter whose missing left shoe could defeat an entire morning. Tom had no children, although he had once kept a terrier that needed insulin twice a day. We each regarded the other as unacquainted with hardship.

The clock room was smaller than a bedroom and much colder than the stairs. Light came through the four translucent faces, giving everything the bluish pallor of skimmed milk. Between the mechanism and the wall our father had fitted a chair, a shelf of paperbacks, and a folding table no wider than a coffin lid. There was a kettle but no obvious supply of water. There was a framed photograph of an elderly woman in a bathing cap. Neither of us knew her. Tom turned it over. *June, first across, 1978.* We put it in the box marked KEEP, which had been meant for tools.

At first the sorting went quickly. Dried pens went into a bag. A good wool blanket went into the box. We threw away four cracked mugs and kept one uncracked mug, then took out one of the cracked ones because it had a picture of a badger wearing spectacles. We had drunk cocoa from it as children. Tom held it by the handle while I turned the base to read the maker’s name, an arrangement so familiar that for a second I expected our mother to tell us not to fight. We wrapped the badger in the blanket. The uncracked mug suddenly seemed presumptuous. We left it on the table.

Behind the shelf was a cupboard painted the same dirty cream as the wall. It opened with the little brass key our father had worn on a cord under his shirt. I had supposed this key gave access to the mechanism itself, or perhaps to a private compartment in which he kept the more disappointing details of his finances. Instead we found exercise books. There were thirty-one of them, the cheap kind with multiplication tables on the back. Each had a year written on its cover. Tom opened the earliest and read aloud: “January third. Wind east. Mrs. Vale’s awning lost one stripe.” He looked at me. “How does an awning lose one stripe?”

The next entry said the river had risen to the white stone. Then: “Boy with red case waits through two buses.” Then: “At twelve eighteen, all pigeons lifted from south roof except one.” Page after page contained these small reports. No verdicts followed them. The boy might have been waiting for a third bus, or postponing an unpleasant music lesson, or simply enjoying his possession of a red case. Our father declined to say. At intervals he recorded the clock’s behavior: gaining in dry weather, losing after frost. There were stretches of blank pages. In March of one year he wrote only, “Cannot see bakery. Scaffolding.” I calculated the year. It was the March our mother died.

I had imagined bereavement making him diligent. That was the version I had told people: after our mother died, Dad threw himself into the clock. It was a phrase that required no further conversation, which was mostly why I liked it. Now I pictured him sitting in his chair, trying to look past a plank. Perhaps the scaffolding really had been the important thing that March. The bakery roof would vanish, the woman with the orange would have nowhere to sit, and the view he knew would be temporarily unavailable. Grief might consist partly of being unable to endure another alteration, however ordinary, in the arrangement of the world.

Tom had found his own name. “Thomas crosses square carrying model volcano. Considerable leakage.” He remembered the volcano. Its wet papier-mâché base had given way outside the chemist, leaving a trail of brown paste like something produced by an enormous dog. He had earned a poor mark for presentation but a good one for understanding the movement of the continental plates. “I never knew he saw that,” Tom said. He read the entry again, this time silently. Then he closed the book with one finger between the pages and asked whether I thought we ought to keep all thirty-one.

I said yes too quickly. By then I had begun to want an entry for myself. I could think of plenty of occasions on which I had crossed the square in a state worth recording. Once I had marched through wearing a wedding dress made from old curtains, collecting money for the school theater. Once I had slapped a boy beside the fountain, immediately regretted it, and kissed him on the same cheek. I had even gone into labor outside the bank, though admittedly this had looked less dramatic from the pavement than it had felt from within. Surely somewhere I had caught the eye of the man who noticed one pigeon remaining on a roof.

We took the books downstairs in two loads. On the way back up, we stopped at the bakery window. The woman had finished her orange and was shaking the peel into a plastic pail. Tom tapped the glass and held up the photograph of the swimmer. She leaned forward, squinted, and pointed at herself. Then she pointed down. We met her in the alley beside the bins, where an extractor fan blew warm, yeasty air against our ankles. Her name was June. In 1978 she had been the first person to swim across the reservoir after it was filled. The distance was not remarkable, she said, but the water was very cold.

Why did our father have her photograph? June looked puzzled by the question. He had taken it. He had also lent her the bathing cap, although it had belonged to our mother and was too tight. For years afterward, every time it rained hard, he had gone into the bakery to ask whether she fancied another crossing. “It wasn’t especially funny the first time,” she said, “but by the twentieth it got quite good.” She accepted the photograph. In exchange she gave us two buns stuck together at the edge and insisted this counted as one bun for purposes of payment, which in any case she refused.

We ate sitting on the lowest stair. It was nearly noon. Tom took out his schedule, crossed out coffee, and wrote *bun*. This struck us both as funnier than it was. A little sugar fell onto his trousers. He rubbed it in, producing a dark smear, exactly as our father would have done. I nearly told him so, but people had been saying such things to us all week. You stand like him. You’ve got his hands. As if our father, having lost the use of his own body, had distributed a few surviving gestures among the relatives. For the moment I let Tom have his trousers to himself.

Our last discovery was under the chair: a shallow drawer containing envelopes addressed but never sealed. Inside each was a photograph of the square. Snow had softened the fountain into a white mushroom. A delivery van stood on three wheels while two men studied the fourth, which had come to rest outside the florist. In another, hundreds of paper lanterns hovered just above the crowd at the summer fair, before the council prohibited their release. The addresses belonged to people in the pictures. Some envelopes bore only a description: *Lady with yellow gloves.* *Twins, probably from station road.* Here, apparently, was a second job our father had not quite managed to leave us in writing.

I wanted to deliver them. Tom wanted to finish the room. We compromised by finishing the room while I complained about it. The kettle, disconnected from its base, contained a handful of washers. The paperbacks were mostly detective novels with their final pages turned down, a system of marking completion that seemed unnecessarily conclusive. We carried the chair to the landing, failed to make the turn, and carried it back. Eventually we took off one arm with a screwdriver. At half past two the clock room stood empty except for the mechanism, the folding table, and that sound a recently emptied room has, as if a conversation next door has just become audible.

Before we left I stood where the chair had been. Through a narrow clear pane beneath the western dial I could see a slice of the square. It wasn’t much of a view. The fountain basin was hidden. The bank entrance lay behind a stone numeral. Most of the pavement outside the chemist fell below the window ledge. You saw people for perhaps six strides; then you lost them. I had thought of my father looking down like a minor god, acquainted with everyone’s comings and goings. In fact, he had spent thirty-seven years watching people emerge from behind a four and disappear beneath a five.

That evening, at his kitchen table, I searched the books. I wish I could say I came upon a single beautiful sentence that settled some uncertainty between us. What I found was “Clara, new coat?” Three years later: “Clara and friend go east with ladder.” I had no memory of the ladder. My coat had been secondhand, green with horn buttons, bought with money from my first Saturday job. He had said nothing about it at the time. There were other Claras in town, and it was possible the one with the ladder was not me. I copied both entries onto the back of an electricity bill and put it in my purse.

Over the next month Tom and I delivered most of the photographs. The man whose van had lost a wheel was still in business. He displayed the picture in his shop under a sign saying that standards had improved. The twins turned out to be cousins. The lady with yellow gloves had died, but her husband wanted the envelope as well as the photograph because he had forgotten the exact shade and liked seeing the word *yellow* in somebody else’s handwriting. A few people showed no interest. One woman asked why our father had been photographing her husband outside a betting shop. We admitted we didn’t know. She kept the picture anyway.

We gave the books to the town library. The librarian found room for them beside the parish maps. They were not cataloged as diaries because, she said, a diary generally gives some account of its author. She entered them as weather records, which seemed fair enough. You could discover when the river froze, which spring the swifts returned late, and how often rain erased the far side of the square. On the shelf label there was space for a formal title. Tom suggested *Observations from the Clock Tower*. I preferred *Considerable Leakage*. In the end the librarian wrote our father’s name and the dates, leaving the contents to surprise whoever happened to look.

The council installed an electric motor that autumn. The hands still crept forward with the same hesitant motion, but the clock became almost perfectly accurate. People complained. They had grown used to making private adjustments, subtracting two minutes in September and allowing an extra minute to catch the early bus in June. For a while everyone arrived slightly ahead of time. Then the novelty wore off. The bakery put two tables on its roof and got permission to serve coffee there in fine weather. From the table nearest the parapet you could see the little clear pane beneath the western dial, dark now, and surprisingly high.

I still have the hospital teaspoon. It lives in our sugar jar, where its narrow bowl is useful for breaking up lumps. One morning my daughter asked why it had writing on it. I told her about the hospital, the pendulum, her grandfather, and the three dead flies. She listened with the strained courtesy children offer when a simple question has gone badly wrong. Then she asked what I had supposed was the most unimportant question in the whole affair: how had rainwater got into the clock? I didn’t know. The roof had looked sound. Perhaps the bead of water had been condensation. Perhaps my wet sleeve had brushed the spoon when I bent down to pick it up. I said we could go and look the next time it rained.

She considered this. Outside, a bus went by with no passengers. Across the street a man in bedroom slippers dragged a blue suitcase to the curb and sat on it to wait. My daughter put two slices of apple on her toast, then removed one and ate it separately. “We don’t have to,” she said, kindly releasing me from my promise. She took her plate to the sink. At the door she paused, went back for the teaspoon, and held it up to the gray morning light. “Those flies must have been thirsty,” she said, and put it away.

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want for 2500 words.
samples.result:
The first thing Ruth learned about drawing a map of a town was that nobody agreed on where the middle was. The mayor put it at the courthouse. The children put it at the pool. Her father, who had delivered milk for forty years and still thought of streets in terms of who took what, put it at the old Bell house, where he used to finish one crate and start another. “Though that was before the twins went off milk,” he told her, as if this were a complication she ought to take into account.

Ruth had been hired to make a map for the backs of the new bus shelters. There were to be six shelters, each with a bench, a little roof, and a panel three feet wide. The town had previously erected shelters without benches on the theory that benches encouraged loitering. Then someone on the council had asked what waiting for a bus was if not loitering with a destination. This person lost the next election, though probably for other reasons. The benches, once approved, survived him. They were being made in a shop normally devoted to kitchen cabinets and would have unusually fine dovetail joints.

The assignment came to Ruth because she could draw, knew the town, and had submitted the lowest bid. She had submitted the lowest bid because she had forgotten to include the cost of her own time. When she discovered this, she considered withdrawing. Instead she bought a pleasingly expensive pencil, on the grounds that an enterprise already ruined financially might as well be enjoyable. It was dark green, with a brass cap. Every morning she sharpened it over the kitchen sink. Every evening she washed a little gray crescent off the side of her hand.

The town engineer gave her a digital file containing every legal road, parcel, easement, and drain. For two days Ruth tried to turn this into something useful. The file knew that the pharmacy occupied 0.18 acres but not that its entrance was around the corner from its sign. It knew the exact curve of the river but had neglected the fact that one could not see the river from River Street. A visitor following the file might reasonably spend an afternoon looking for water behind the tire shop. Ruth closed her computer, put on her coat, and went out to be a stranger.

Being a stranger in a place where you grew up requires discipline. At the first intersection a man called, “Your dad got his gutters done?” and she had to admit that he had. Outside the bakery she smelled hot nutmeg and immediately knew that it was Thursday. Nevertheless she tried. She got off the bus at each proposed shelter and chose a modest destination: a toilet, a cup of coffee, the library, the river. She wrote down the first moment she had to make a decision and what, if anything, the town supplied to help her make it.

There was a sign for the library, but in summer it would be covered in leaves. There was a sign for the hospital, which had closed. The only public toilet marked on the engineer’s file was in a building that now sold clarinets. The man who sold clarinets said people still came in asking, sometimes urgently, and he generally let them use his. “But please,” he said, when she explained the map, “don’t make it official.” She promised. He gave her the names of two places with better plumbing and less expensive merchandise between the door and the facilities.

At the fourth shelter she met a woman carrying a birthday cake in a transparent box. It was a sheet cake with blue icing and the words GOOD LUCK DENNIS. Ruth asked her the best way to the river. “With this?” the woman said, lifting the cake a fraction of an inch. It had not occurred to Ruth that there might be a cake route and a non-cake route. There was, however, a long flight of steps beside the church and a gentler route past the bowling alley. The woman recommended the latter. “Dennis is retiring,” she added. “It’s not his birthday.”

By Friday Ruth had a notebook full of details and no idea which belonged on a map. The most visible landmark on the east side was a fibreglass rooster left over from a restaurant that had burned down. It stood twelve feet high on a steel pole, presiding over a vacant lot. Nobody could tell her whether it would remain there. The least visible landmark was the historical society, housed behind smoked glass in a building indistinguishable from a small insurance office, which in fact it also was. On Tuesdays one could insure a boat or read the diary of the town’s first dentist.

Her father invited her to supper. He made fried potatoes and eggs in the iron pan he had once threatened to leave exclusively to whichever of his children learned to clean it properly. Ruth was an only child, but this had not diminished the threat. After eating, she spread her drafts across the table. He studied them with the attention he usually reserved for the instructions on seed packets. Finally he put one blunt finger on the blank space behind the school. “Where’s the cut?” he asked. She knew at once what he meant. She had used it every day for eleven years.

The cut was a footpath between two gardens, screened by a laurel hedge. It connected the schoolyard to the street behind it and shortened the walk home for half the children in town. It had no legal standing. On the engineer’s map, anyone attempting to take it would apparently have to pass through a breakfast room. “I can’t put somebody’s garden on a public map,” Ruth said.
