Her father conceded this. “Funny, though,” he said, “to leave out the bit everybody knows.” Then he gathered up the plates, and she heard him running hot water over the pan, in violation of his own instructions.

On Saturday she went to see the cut. She had not used it since leaving school, and it was narrower than she remembered, though she herself was considerably wider. Someone had laid flat stones in the mud. Someone had tied a strip of yellow cloth around a low branch. Halfway along the hedge there was a wooden gate she had never noticed. It opened while she was looking at it, and a person in slippers came out carrying a bowl of vegetable peelings. They stood face to face in the intimate green gloom, equally surprised, like people who had opened the same cupboard from opposite sides.

The person introduced himself as Martin. It was his hedge, his compost heap, and partly his path; the other half belonged to his sister next door. He had no objection to children using it. He did object to bicycles, mainly on account of the blind bend. He had once been knocked into a gooseberry bush by a boy delivering newspapers and had received neither an apology nor, that morning, a newspaper. When Ruth asked about the map, he thought for a while. “I like hearing them in the morning,” he said. “I don’t particularly want to hear everybody else.”

She left the cut off. But the conversation changed the way she understood the blank parts of her drawing. She had been treating a blank as a failure to find out what was there. Sometimes it meant she had found out quite precisely. She omitted the clarinet shop’s toilet. She omitted the low wall where young people went in the evenings to practice kissing, a place she knew about firsthand and had no intention of inspecting for accuracy. She omitted an excellent pear tree that hung over a fence. A map that gave away all the pears would soon be a map of an ordinary tree.

At the first public review, the council chamber smelled of floor polish and wet wool. Ruth pinned her draft to a noticeboard. She had marked the bus routes in strong colors and the walking routes in gray. The river was blue, which nobody contested, though in person it was almost always brown. The rooster appeared as a small black silhouette. A council member asked why a defunct chicken restaurant deserved recognition when several thriving restaurants did not. “Because you can see the chicken from the bridge,” Ruth said. The council member, whose brother owned a thriving restaurant, wrote something down.

Then a girl in the back raised her hand. “Where am I?” she asked. Ruth began to explain that a red dot would indicate the location of each individual shelter. “No,” the girl said patiently. “Where am I now?” They were in the council chamber, of course, but the approach to it was through an annex, across a glazed passage, and up a staircase in what looked, from outside, like another building. Ruth walked over to her own drawing. For a few dismal seconds she could not work it out. The girl’s mother tried to hush her. “No, that’s a good question,” Ruth said.

That night Ruth cut up the draft. Her first map had been a picture of the town with directions laid over it. The second began with six pieces of paper and six sentences. From here you can see the clock. From here you can see the church steps. From here, on a clear day, you can see the water tower, but on any day you can see the laundromat with its enormous orange door. She began each drawing with what a person would see on looking up. Only then did she add the things that person might be looking for.

The new maps did not all face north. At the station shelter the top of the map was east, because that was the way you faced when you stood in front of it. At the pool it was south. She gave each one a conspicuous compass arrow and expected complaints. The engineer surprised her by approving. He had spent a year designing instrument panels for agricultural machinery and knew the trouble a person could get into when a diagram made him turn left in order to go right. “Especially with a beet harvester,” he said, and for a moment seemed to be remembering something expensive.

She marked the steps. She marked every crossing where the curb had been lowered and every crossing where it had not. She timed the walks herself, then went back with her father, who was slower going uphill and much quicker on the level, particularly if he thought somebody was timing him. At the hill above the river they stopped at a bench neither of them had noticed before. It faced not the view but a brick wall warmed by the afternoon sun. They sat there without speaking. On the map Ruth put a small symbol for a seat. She left the wall to explain itself.

In late March the maps went to the printer. The following morning, a truck with a crane arrived at the vacant lot and removed the rooster. Ruth happened to be buying onions across the street. She came outside in time to see it rise above the rooftops, its absurd yellow feet dangling over the town. For a few seconds it achieved the distinction, rare among either roosters or restaurants, of actual flight. Then it settled onto a flatbed. The driver fastened a strap across its breast. “Where’s it going?” Ruth called. “My sister’s,” he called back, as if this settled the geographical question.

She phoned the printer. Too late. All six panels had been printed, sealed, and packed. Ruth went home and lay down on the kitchen floor, a habit she had acquired during a difficult period in her twenties and retained for administrative emergencies. From down there she could see a lentil under the stove and a cobweb joining two chair legs. The town had stayed still just long enough for her to draw it incorrectly. After a while her father let himself in, stepped over her to put milk in the fridge, and asked if she had tried drawing something else where the rooster used to be.

What she drew, on six small pieces of weatherproof adhesive vinyl, was the roofline of the bridge. It was not tall or funny or beloved of children. It did, however, seem likely to remain attached to its foundations. She applied the patches before the panels were installed. On the proofs she kept for herself, the rooster remained. Years later these would give rise to an argument about which edition of the maps was the first, a question of considerable interest to precisely three people, one of whom had once been the little girl in the council chamber.

On opening day there were speeches beside the station shelter. The cabinetmaker ran his thumb along the front edge of the bench. The mayor thanked a regional transportation fund by its full legal name. While he spoke, an actual bus arrived, and the people who needed it had to excuse themselves through the crowd gathered to celebrate its existence. Ruth stood at the back with her father. Across the road a man got off carrying a small suitcase. He waited for a gap in traffic, crossed, and stood in front of the new map. Ruth watched him look at it, look up, and look at it again.

He came over to her. For a terrible moment she expected him to ask which way to the river, or where the library was, or why the town possessed so many curiously dispersed facilities for clarinet players. Instead he pointed to the blank white strip below the map, where the printer had left just enough room for future timetable changes. “Do you have a pen?” he asked. His sister was collecting him, he explained, but he wanted a cup of tea. Ruth handed him her green pencil. On the back of an envelope he wrote GONE TO BAKERY and tucked it into the frame.

A breeze lifted the envelope. Her father caught it, folded it once, and wedged it more firmly into the gap. The mayor finished speaking. People applauded and began testing the bench. Ruth and her father stayed there while the others went off, watching in case the note blew away again. Ten minutes later a woman came hurrying from the station car park. She read the envelope, smiled, and set off in the right direction.

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want for 2500 words.
samples.result:
The first thing my mother bought after she went deaf was a piano. It was an upright, painted a dreadful green, with a cigarette burn on middle C. Three men delivered it on a Wednesday afternoon. By turning it sideways and removing our front door, they got it as far as the bend in the hall, where it stuck. Mother considered this a perfectly good place for a piano. For the next eleven years, anyone coming into our house had to go through the kitchen or be very thin.

She had never played. Before she lost her hearing, her principal interest in music had been getting the people upstairs to turn theirs down. I thought the purchase was an act of defiance, the sort of thing one read about in magazines at the dentist. I told people so. In fact, as she later explained, she had seen it in the window of the hospice shop, and green was her favorite color. I have spent much of my life discovering how often I mistook my mother for a more literary person.

A piano tuner came the following Saturday. He had a little leather bag and a name, Mr. Vale, that suited his profession so well I suspected he had chosen it. He played a scale, opened the top, and took out a teaspoon, two marbles, and an envelope addressed to a woman in Leeds. Then he wrote on his pad: HOW GOOD DO YOU WANT IT?

Mother wrote back: HOW GOOD CAN YOU GET IT FOR FORTY POUNDS?

He took off his coat.

That afternoon was the first time I noticed the hall had a voice of its own. The picture glass buzzed at one pitch; at another, the brass letter flap lifted a little and fell. When Mr. Vale played a low G, the radiator in the upstairs bathroom answered. I was thirteen, and had recently learned in school that everything was made of atoms. This had struck me as unlikely, especially in the case of things like radiators, which were plainly made of radiator. Now I could almost believe it. The whole house seemed loosely assembled and available for comment.

Mother stood with her hand against the side of the piano. When he finished, she paid him forty pounds and gave him the teaspoon. He declined the marbles. The envelope, which was unsealed, contained a recipe for dripping cake and a newspaper clipping about a tortoise that had returned to its owners after six years. Mother posted it. She disliked unfinished business and had complete faith in the ability of the postal service to find a woman in Leeds in possession of a tortoise.

I began playing because there was no other comfortable way to make a telephone call. Our telephone sat on a little shelf above the piano stool, and conversations with my friend Kit tended to involve long pauses while he ate. During these intervals I picked out advertisements and football chants. One evening I managed the first eight notes of the theme from a detective series. Mother, coming in with the washing, stopped, put down the basket, and signed, *Again.*

We were both beginners at signing. For a while our conversations had the quality of telegrams sent during a natural disaster. *Milk gone. Man Thursday. Aunt angry but alive.* Still, *again* was clear enough. I played the eight notes. She set a hand on the piano and tapped the rhythm with her other hand. Then she went upstairs and returned with a fat blue book she had bought for fifty pence along with the instrument. Its title was *The Happy Pianist*. The child on the cover wore a bow tie and had the fixed expression of a boy whose parents were standing just outside the photograph.

My first proper tune was “Lightly Row.” I played it for three weeks. Kit stopped ringing. The people upstairs, in a surprising reversal of our previous relationship, began to knock on the floor. Mother loved it. She liked to stand in the bend of the hall with her shoulder against the wood, eyes shut, while I played the same sixteen bars. I tried playing something else once, to see if she could tell. She opened one eye and signed, *Wrong boat.*

By winter she had discovered that other people liked the piano too. The postman could do a little boogie-woogie. Our neighbor Mrs. Preece knew precisely one Chopin prelude, which she performed at great speed, as if trying to get through a level crossing before the gates came down. A plumber called out to fix the bathroom tap played a hymn so slowly and beautifully that Mother paid his invoice without noticing he had charged us for two visits. It was not a salon. Nobody wore a scarf indoors or discussed Vienna. People came to the kitchen door on some other business and stayed for a cup of tea and a go on the green piano.

Then my cousin Ruth arrived with her cello. She was seventeen, serious, and six feet tall in her stockinged feet. She had been studying a piece by Bach and wanted to know how it sounded outside her bedroom. The answer, at least in our hall, was enormous. The first low note seemed to travel up through the soles of my shoes and rearrange the contents of my pockets. Mother, halfway down the stairs, sat on a step. Ruth played for perhaps four minutes. For once nobody hurried to put the kettle on afterward.

Mother signed something I didn’t know. She had been taking classes on Tuesday evenings and had lately overtaken me.

“What?” I said, forgetting.

She spelled it out on her fingers. *F-L-O-O-R.*

We spent the next hour moving Ruth and her chair about. The effect was strongest on the third stair and weakest by the kitchen door. With her endpin on a particular scuff in the boards, Ruth could make the little bones in Mother’s ankle tickle. Shift the chair six inches and the sensation disappeared. Mother got the chalk and marked the spot. Then she marked the best places to sit. By the time Ruth put her cello away, the hall looked like the scene of a complicated but rather polite murder.

The following Tuesday, Mother brought two friends home from class. The week after, there were five. Some were deaf, some heard perfectly well, and one, a bus driver called Alan, had simply seen a crowd going down our side passage and followed it on the assumption that something was for sale. Ruth played Bach. I played “Lightly Row,” then, under pressure, the detective theme. Alan turned out to have a rich bass voice. He sang “Ol’ Man River” with his palm flat against the upright and forgot most of the words. Nobody minded. The last bus went without him.

An arrangement developed. On the first Tuesday of each month, at seven in the evening, anybody could come and anybody could play, provided they helped with the chairs. We borrowed stacking chairs from the Baptist church and returned them by Thursday, when the Baptists required them for biscuits and an examination of conscience. Kit came back. His father knew somebody with a double bass. Someone else brought a bass drum, an experiment we did not repeat. Mother bought a big roll of lining paper and taped a length to the hall wall. People drew maps of where they felt things: a shiver at the elbow, a flutter under a heel, a buzz in the bridge of the nose. Mrs. Preece drew an excellent nose.

For a while I believed our evenings had solved deafness. This was the kind of conclusion available to a boy who could hear and had solved very little else. I wrote an essay about it at school. My English teacher entered it for a prize offered by the local paper; it won, and a reporter came round to take a photograph of Mother at the piano. He wanted her to look toward the window with an expression of quiet triumph. Mother wanted to know whether he had moved the bins, because it was collection day. The resulting photograph showed a woman apparently gazing toward a brighter future. She was, in reality, watching a refuse lorry reverse over her begonias.

The headline said MUSIC RESTORES A MOTHER’S LOST WORLD. She read it at breakfast with a piece of toast in one hand. I had expected tears. She turned the page and checked the price of a secondhand camping stove.

Later, as I was getting my things for school, she caught my sleeve.

*Nice essay,* she signed. *Whose mother?*

Mine, obviously. I pointed at her.

She shook her head. *Your mother hates that song about the river.*

This was news to me. She went on: *Your mother likes the people. And the green. Write about the green next time.*

At school they gave me a book token and clapped in assembly. I bought a novel about a boy who escaped to sea and did not mention the prize again. For several years afterward I considered the whole affair a lesson about journalism. It took me longer to understand that she had also been telling me something useful about asking a person a question before writing down the answer.

When I left home, the Tuesdays went on without me. I went to university, learned to cook three dishes, fell in love with a woman who considered all three of them soup, and moved into her flat. On my visits home the lining paper gradually filled. A child drew purple feet beside the skirting board. Someone wrote, near the light switch, *Trumpet here, provided Dennis faces the lavatory.* New people appeared in photographs. Alan retired from the buses. Mrs. Preece slowed down, which improved her Chopin considerably. Mother’s signing grew quick and full of jokes I often needed explaining. It was an odd experience to become the least articulate person in the house where I had learned to speak.

One November she slipped outside the chemist’s and broke her hip. She recovered well, according to the surgeon, who did not live in a house with a piano filling its hall. The occupational therapist took one look at the arrangement and said the upright had to go. There was now a walking frame to consider, and whatever its other virtues, a walking frame could not breathe in.

I came home on a Friday to organize matters. Mother had placed an advertisement offering the piano free to anyone who could collect it. There had been fourteen calls, thirteen of them asking if she delivered. The fourteenth was from a woman who wanted it for a pub but wondered if it came in black.

“We could take it apart,” I said.

We were sitting in the kitchen, where she could see my mouth. She signed, *And put it together where?*

This was the difficulty. My flat was on the fourth floor. Ruth lived in Brussels. The Baptist church had two pianos already, one beyond repair and one, according to the minister, beyond forgiveness.

On Saturday morning Mr. Vale came. His leather bag was the same, but he now wore two hearing aids and his eyebrows had become extravagantly long. He removed the front panel and studied the action. He pressed the burned middle C. It gave a serviceable plonk.

“Still got my tuning,” he said.

“Is that good?”

“No. That was eleven years ago.”

He and Mother conferred in writing, as before. I made tea. By the time I came back an agreement had been reached. The soundboard was cracked, the hammers were worn, and the piano had no great future as an instrument. He would take the action for spare parts. A woodworker he knew might find a use for the rest.

I was furious. This took me by surprise. I had spent half my adolescence complaining about having to come in through the kitchen. Yet there I stood, aged twenty-four, prepared to pick a fight with an elderly piano tuner over the integrity of a piece of furniture nobody wanted.

Mother watched my face. *You want it?*

I nodded.

*Where?*

I had no answer.

She went on, *I don’t mind being deaf. I mind being unable to get to my own front door.*

So on Monday the piano came apart. Once the action was out, it looked less like an instrument and more like a cupboard in which someone had unwisely stored a harp. Mr. Vale’s friend took the case. Two men carried the iron frame out to their van. For the first time in eleven years, daylight from the little window above the front door reached the kitchen wall. There was a clean rectangle on the floor surrounded by a dark tide of dirt. We found thirty-seven pence, a bus ticket, and one of the marbles.

That Tuesday was the first Tuesday of the month. I thought people might stay away, but at half past six Alan came through the front door carrying a folding table. Kit followed with a pot of stew. Mrs. Preece brought six little custard tarts, one of which she ate as she was taking off her coat. The chairs arrived from the church. No one had arranged any music. We ate, and afterward Mother dealt cards. By nine she had taken most of Mr. Vale’s small change. The third stair was still a good place to sit, especially if you wanted to see everybody’s hand.

Years later, after Mother died, I helped clear the house. The lining paper came down in brittle strips. I kept the bit with the nose. In the cupboard under the sink I found the blue book, its pages swollen from a leak, the unhappy boy still in his bow tie. I sat on the bare third stair and tried to remember “Lightly Row.” My fingers could do it on my knee, although I could not have sung it for money.

Outside, someone lifted the letter flap and called my name. It was a young woman from three doors down, holding a little green stool. Her grandfather, the woodworker, had made it from the side of the piano. She thought I might want it.

It is in my kitchen now. My daughter stands on it to wash strawberries or inspect whatever is frying. If you turn it over, you can see along one edge a narrow strip of darker green, the paint that never saw daylight. Sometimes people ask why I keep such a battered thing. I used to tell them the long version, with the cello and the chalk marks and the note that made the radiator sing. These days I usually give them my mother’s answer. It’s a good color.

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want for 2500 words.
samples.result:
The first thing anyone told me about the town clock was that it had four faces and kept three times. The face above the pharmacy was right. The one looking down the hill toward the boatyard was seven minutes slow. The two that faced the residential streets were both eleven minutes fast, an arrangement that had sent two generations of children running to school with toast in their hands. When I asked which face the clockmaker used, the woman at the bakery said, “He has a watch.” She slid my change across the counter and went back to cutting a wedding cake into slices small enough to fit through the door of a refrigerator.

I had come to Bellwether to empty my uncle’s apartment. He had lived above a shop that sold good shoes, by which its owner meant shoes you could complain about in person for twenty years. My uncle had owned six pairs, all brown. The shoes were still there, arranged under his bed according to some distinction finer than color, and each contained a folded paper bag. He had saved paper bags, rubber bands, lengths of green string, and the little pencils banks used to give away. He had not saved the letters my mother wrote him. At least I never found them, though I opened every book he owned and shook it gently by the spine.

On the second morning I found an envelope marked RENT, containing eight hundred dollars, and another marked TAX, containing a recipe for gingerbread. Inside a biscuit tin was a photograph of my uncle at about thirty, standing beside a woman whose face had been rubbed white by somebody’s thumb. I called my mother to ask who the woman was. “That’s a bad print,” she said. “It came out like that. Her name was Irene and she could put her whole fist in her mouth.” This was so unlike the answer I had prepared myself to receive that I sat down on the bare mattress and laughed until I had to blow my nose.

My mother had been ill for some time. Her illness made speech expensive, and she spent it according to principles of her own. She would not tell a doctor where it hurt if she had already told a nurse, but she would telephone me to say that a bird had just flown through her kitchen carrying what looked like a ravioli. I had fallen into the habit of finishing her sentences. Sometimes I finished them wrong and she let it go. That was worse than being corrected. Before hanging up that morning, I asked whether she wanted anything of her brother’s. After a long time she said, “The yellow bowl, if there’s room.”

There was room. The problem was that there were eleven yellow bowls. I put them on the windowsill in order of size. Two were plastic, one was wood painted the color of a lemon, and one was an old mixing bowl with a spout and a hairline crack that divided its interior like a river on a map. The others were ordinary cereal bowls in several shades of institutional custard. I photographed the lineup and sent it to my mother, who had owned her phone for nine years without once looking at a photograph on it. Then I went downstairs to see the man who sold good shoes.

His name was Pavel. He was fitting a small boy for sandals while the boy’s father tried to interest him in a model decorated with sharks. The boy wanted silver sandals with a buckle shaped like a flower. Pavel set both pairs on the floor and asked him which he would rather look at all summer. That settled it. After they left, I asked Pavel if he knew which yellow bowl my mother might remember. He said my uncle used to take one to the public gardens on Thursdays. “What did he take in it?” I asked. “An expectation of soup,” Pavel said. “Sometimes a spoon.”

I had not known my uncle went to the public gardens. My picture of his life had been assembled from holiday visits, during which he occupied the end of our sofa and made a single highball last an afternoon. If asked what he had been doing, he always said, “Keeping out of the papers.” He gave me a fountain pen for my sixteenth birthday, despite the fact that I was fourteen and left-handed. Now he was dead and had apparently spent Thursdays among people who understood the significance of a particular bowl. I wrapped the cracked one in a towel and took it to the gardens.

They were smaller than their name suggested. A hedge enclosed six flower beds, a drinking fountain, three benches, and a patch of gravel on which an elderly woman was trying to teach a terrier to walk backward. The dog plainly knew how but objected to doing it for nothing. Whenever she showed him a piece of cheese, he reversed smartly. Whenever she concealed it in her fist, he sat down and examined the sky. I watched for a while before asking about the soup. “That finished years ago,” she said. “Before the fountain, even. What a nuisance you didn’t come then.”

She came over to inspect the bowl. “Not that one. That one’s for beating eggs.” She told me to ask at the library for a man named Robin, who had done the washing up. “Nobody remembers dishes like the person who washes them,” she said. I thanked her. As I left, the dog walked backward the length of the gravel without being prompted, a performance of great precision that his owner missed because she was bending down to tie her shoe. He looked at me. I very nearly applauded, but there are things you can spoil by letting on that you have seen them.

Robin turned out to be the librarian, a youngish man with a beautiful red beard and the alarming habit of lowering his voice while you were still speaking, so that you felt yourself getting louder and louder by comparison. He remembered my uncle perfectly. “He brought the bread,” he whispered. “Never soup. The soup was Mrs. Alvarez. He brought rolls in a yellow wooden bowl with a napkin over them.” I described the lemon-colored bowl. He nodded. “Had a little foot on it. Wobbled. We always put a folded bus timetable underneath.” Here, at last, was a detail I could test.

Back at the apartment I set the wooden bowl on the kitchen table. It did wobble. A crescent of pale wood showed where its foot had been worn down on one side. For a moment the whole undertaking seemed wonderfully straightforward. A question had been asked, the proper witnesses consulted, and an answer obtained. I called my mother. “I found the bowl,” I said. “The wooden one you wanted.” There was silence at her end, followed by the small hollow knock of her handset striking her earring. “Wooden?” she said finally. “What on earth would I want with a wooden bowl?”

I carried all eleven bowls home. They filled most of the trunk, wrapped in shirts I had intended to donate. My mother lived three hours inland, in a flat that smelled of hand cream and the orange peel she dried on the radiators. I brought the bowls up four at a time. By the third trip she had recognized what I was doing and begun to laugh. It was not a generous laugh. “Did it never occur to you,” she said, taking a breath halfway through, “that if I asked for an apple you needn’t cut down the tree?”

She pointed to the smallest plastic bowl. It was the ugliest by a comfortable margin, with a melted place on its lip and a picture of a duck almost entirely scoured away. “That’s the fellow.” She turned it over. On the bottom, in letters faint as the veins on her hand, somebody had scratched an M. I had taken it for the maker’s mark, though it would have been a remarkably modest manufacturer who put his initial on a product with a bent pin. My mother’s name was Margaret. She took the bowl into her lap and rubbed the M once with her finger.

I made tea. I made enough noise making it to give her time to decide whether she wanted to tell me anything. Outside, a man on a ladder was taking down the electric stars the council had strung across the street in December. It was April. One star refused to come loose. The man got down, moved the ladder six inches, climbed up, and tried again. My mother watched this with interest. “He wants to turn it the other way,” she said. Below him, a woman in an orange vest made the same suggestion by rotating her finger in the air.

“It was a boat,” my mother said. I looked at the bowl. “Well, obviously it was a bowl. We used it as a boat. There was a gutter outside the house where we lived before your grandfather got the job at the laundry. When it rained, the water went all the way down to the corner. We put things in the boat to see if they could make the voyage.” A button made it. A lump of sugar did not, though the boat arrived intact. A beetle they selected as captain opened its wings and resigned almost immediately. My uncle used to run ahead to keep the vessel out of the drain.

I asked how old they had been. My mother considered. “Old enough to know better than to take a bowl outside. Not old enough to have anything else worth taking.” She thought it had been lost when they moved. Then, years later, at my uncle’s apartment, she had seen it under the sink holding a bar of soap. She had meant to ask for it but had not wanted him to think she objected to his using it for soap. “And after that,” she said, “whenever I remembered the bowl, I wasn’t there, and whenever I was there, I didn’t remember the bowl.”

That evening it rained. Water ticked against the metal sill. The streetlights came on and made the pavement look recently varnished. I cooked a meal of potatoes and eggs, and we ate it watching a television programme in which strangers assessed the value of a silver teapot. My mother thought they were all wrong, including the man who had brought it in. During the advertisements she asked what I meant to do with the other bowls. I said I would take them to a charity shop. “Except the wooden one,” she said. “That fellow at the library might like it. You could ask.”

I slept on her sofa. In the early morning I heard her moving around the kitchen, opening a drawer, waiting, closing it, opening another. I found her in her dressing gown with the duck bowl on the counter and an assortment of possible passengers laid out beside it: a cork, a walnut, a paper clip, a blue glass bead, and a small brown coin that had outlasted the government that issued it. She looked embarrassed. I moved the washing up out of the sink and put the plug in. “We’ll need weather,” I said, and turned on the cold tap.

The empty bowl sat high in the water. With the walnut aboard, it listed slightly. The cork was disqualified on the grounds that it was itself a boat. The bead rolled around the bottom in a way that would have been unpleasant for anyone obliged to share a cabin with it. Last of all we put in the coin. This was a mistake, not because of its weight but because my mother tried to adjust its position with the back of a teaspoon. The bowl tipped, took water over its melted lip, and sank with a decisiveness it had never shown in the conduct of its daily duties.

For a second neither of us moved. Then my mother began to laugh again, this time so hard that she had to lean against me. I was aware of her shoulder blade through the thin cloth, the almost frightening lightness of her, and also of the fact that my left sock was getting wet. The sink had overflowed. I shut off the tap. We used three towels and the mat from the bathroom to mop the floor. The blue bead vanished beneath the refrigerator, where, unless someone has since had a reason to move the refrigerator, it remains aboard a different and much slower vessel.

I took the wooden bowl back to Bellwether. Robin did want it, though not for the reason I had imagined. The library had been looking for something in which to put the slips of paper on which children wrote suggestions for new books. Within a week the bowl held requests for books about sharks, ghosts, horses, and how to get rich, as well as one folded note that read simply NO MORE FROGS. Robin wedged a bus timetable under the foot. I kept the cracked mixing bowl for myself. It proved no good for eggs, which found the crack immediately, but served very well for onions.

There were still things to do at the apartment. I gave the suits to somebody who knew a tailor. Pavel took the shoes back without asking for the receipts. In the biscuit tin, behind the damaged photograph of Irene, I found a second print in which her face had come out clear. She was looking away from the camera at something beyond my uncle’s shoulder. He, however, was looking straight into the lens, with a delicious expression I had never seen him wear in life: the look of a man who has just said something outrageous and is waiting to discover whether he has got away with it.

On my last afternoon I sat in the bakery with coffee and a slice of the same kind of cake I had seen on my first morning. From my chair I could see two faces of the town clock at once. It was twenty past three on one and thirteen past on the other. A girl on a bicycle coasted down the hill toward the boatyard, both feet off the pedals. Below her, a man was pulling a tarpaulin over a boat. For a little while nobody needed me to decide what to keep, and I took my time with the cake.

Then my mother called. She wanted the gingerbread recipe. I said I had it somewhere and began describing the envelopes, the pencilled labels, the peculiar system her brother had apparently devised for his accounts. “Yes,” she said when I paused. “I was the one who put it there. Your grandmother was coming over and I didn’t want her to take it back.” I started to ask why she hadn’t just copied it. Instead I ate the last forkful of cake and waited. Across the square the minute hand above the pharmacy moved forward. “Turn the paper over,” my mother said. “There’s a better recipe on the back.”

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want for 2500 words.
samples.result:
The first thing I learned about repairing clocks was that people will forgive a clock for stopping, but they take it personally when a clock is wrong. A stopped clock is furniture. You can put a vase in front of it and get on with your life. A clock that loses four minutes between breakfast and lunch makes a fool of you in front of the dentist. This was my father’s theory, and for forty years he tested it from a narrow shop between a bakery and a place that sold nothing but lampshades. I inherited the shop. The theory came free.

On a wet Thursday in November, a woman brought me a clock that had never told the time. She carried it against her stomach with both arms, the way you carry a child who has fallen asleep somewhere inconvenient. Its case was walnut, its glass was cloudy, and instead of numbers around the dial it had the names of twelve streets. The single hand pointed to Bell Lane. There was a keyhole beneath the dial and a shallow drawer at the bottom. Someone had scratched a multiplication problem into the lid of the drawer: seven times eight equals fifty-four.

“I know,” the woman said when she saw me looking. “It’s fifty-six. I was under considerable pressure.” She introduced herself as June Vale. Her father had made the clock, she said, and she wanted it working by Saturday. When I asked what it did, she looked surprised, as if this were the one question a clock repairer ought to be qualified to answer. Then she turned the case around. Pasted to the back was a yellowed photograph of a man in shirtsleeves standing beside an enormous oven. Behind him, barely visible at the edge of the photograph, hung the clock.

It had belonged to a pie shop. Every Saturday, June explained, her father sent a boy out on a bicycle with a tray of pies. There were twelve stops on his route. Before the boy left, her father wound the mechanism and set the hand to the first street. As the morning progressed, the hand advanced from street to street, so anyone coming into the shop could see where the pies were supposed to be. “Where they actually were,” June said, “depended on the boy. One had a sweetheart on Mercer Road. Mercer Road was a very lucky place to live.”

I lifted the case onto my bench. “And you’re opening the shop again?” I asked. She said no. The building had been converted into flats years ago. Nobody in her family baked professionally anymore. She herself had spent thirty-eight years in insurance, where the most interesting thing that ever happened was a pigeon getting into a meeting about pigeons. On Saturday she was having lunch with the boy who had ridden the bicycle. His name was Arthur. They had been married for fifty-one years, divorced for six, and had recently discovered that they could manage lunch. She wanted to bring him something other than a bottle of wine.

Once June left, I removed the back. Inside was an ordinary spring-driven movement connected to a remarkably unordinary brass wheel. Its rim had been cut into twelve unequal steps. A feeler rested against the rim, and a long lever ran from the feeler to the hand. The wheel turned steadily; the hand did not. It would sit on one street for nine minutes, jump to the next, stay there for fourteen, then jump again. Somebody had measured the bicycle journey, including the time it took to make change and argue about whether a meat pie contained enough meat. Those intervals were the teeth of the thing.

The immediate fault was obvious. The lever had slipped from its pivot and fallen sideways, jamming the wheel. The underlying fault was less obliging. The hole in the lever had worn oval from years of use, and somebody had tried to fix the resulting wobble with a piece of folded paper. I eased the paper out with tweezers. It was a betting slip dated half a century earlier. The horse was called Municipal Pride. Judging from the subsequent career of the slip, I supposed the horse had not won, but as a professional I try not to offer opinions outside my field.

By Friday afternoon I had bushed the hole, polished the pivot, cleaned the movement and set the clock running. Bell Lane lasted eleven minutes. Orchard Street lasted eight. Mercer Road, disappointingly, lasted no longer than any reasonable commercial stop. At the end of its circuit the hand reached Foundry Square, where it stayed while the mechanism continued to tick. I waited twenty minutes. Then I saw a second lever beneath the drawer. When I pulled the drawer open, the hand swung neatly back to Bell Lane and a bell rang once. The sound was small and impatient, like a spoon striking the side of a boiled egg.

I called June. “The boy was meant to put his money in the drawer,” I said. “It resets the route.” There was silence at her end. Then she asked me to do it again. I held the telephone near the case, opened the drawer, and let her hear the bell. After a moment she said, “I thought it was the door.” All through her childhood, she explained, she had remembered that sound as the shop door opening. She had even described it to her own children: their grandfather’s shop, the flour on the floorboards, the little bell that rang when a customer came in.

“Apparently I’ve been letting a great many imaginary customers in,” she said. I told her that was better than turning real ones away, which was the sort of remark my father used to make when presented with any emotion more complicated than satisfaction with a repair. She paid over the telephone and arranged to collect the clock on Saturday morning. That should have been the end of my involvement. But at ten the next day she arrived in a green coat, took one look at the bright face behind the cleaned glass, and asked whether I owned a bicycle.

There are questions to which the technically correct answer is a serious tactical error. I owned a delivery bicycle with a wooden box over the front wheel. My father had bought it in the seventies to collect mantel clocks from elderly customers; I used it mainly to transport sacks of cat litter for a cat who regarded commerce, effort and me with equal suspicion. June wanted the clock delivered to Foundry Square at noon. She would meet me there with Arthur. “I’d carry it,” she said, flexing her fingers, “but I needed help getting my coat on today, and I resent what that suggests.”

At a quarter to twelve I wrapped the clock in a blanket, settled it in the box and set off. It had rained overnight. The asphalt was dark, the sky was suddenly blue, and every parked car looked freshly purchased. I took Bell Lane because it seemed appropriate. It was scarcely a lane anymore; the old cottages had gone, replaced by a medical centre and a supermarket with an ambitious selection of olives. At the junction I turned into Orchard Street, then Mercer Road. There was a housing estate where the foundry had stood, but the square at its gates remained.

June was sitting on a bench outside a café. Beside her was a tall, narrow man in a cap, feeding small pieces of toast to a dog under the table. It was not his dog. Its owner, at the next table, was absorbed in a crossword and appeared unaware that her terrier had entered into a separate catering arrangement. When I pulled up, the man stood and put his hand on the wooden box. “You’ve got the weight too far forward,” he said. June looked at me. “Imagine,” she said, “how restful it was to be married to an expert.”

Arthur recognised the clock before I had entirely uncovered it. He did not react as I expected. He frowned, put on his glasses and examined the lower left corner of the case. “There used to be a burn here,” he said. There still was. Under the polish it looked like a thumbprint. He explained that June’s father had once set down a hot tray against the clock and sworn the boy to secrecy. “You told me it was lightning,” June said. Arthur considered this. “I was probably hoping you’d find me interesting.” She took off one glove and touched the burn with her finger.

I set the hand to Bell Lane and explained the repair. Arthur listened politely until I described the unequal steps on the brass wheel. Then he interrupted. “You think those were the stops?” I said I did. June said everybody knew that was what they were. Arthur shook his head. “If I’d done the route in that order, I’d have crossed the tram tracks six times. With gravy pies? You wouldn’t.” He borrowed the crossword woman’s pencil and drew his route on a paper napkin. Bell, Mercer, Foundry, Orchard. After that, nothing matched the dial until the final two streets.

June looked genuinely put out. “I spent my childhood telling people where to find you.” Arthur said he was sorry to hear it. “But why did Dad make the blessed thing if it didn’t tell anybody where you were?” The terrier rested its chin on Arthur’s shoe. A bus drew up on the far side of the square and lowered itself with a sigh. I could hear the clock ticking inside its case. It occurred to me that I had cleaned the wheel without looking closely at its underside. Old makers often signed their work where nobody but the next repairer would see it.

With June’s permission I took the back off again. I had a screwdriver in my jacket; I generally do. I turned the wheel slowly and angled my phone camera beneath it, using the screen as a mirror. There was writing there, but no signature. In fine black ink, along the inner edge of the brass, someone had written quantities: two dozen, one dozen, eighteen, two dozen. Beside each quantity was a letter. June read them aloud. “B, O, M, C.” Then she stopped. “Beef,” she said. “Onion. Mutton. Cheese.” Arthur leaned over my shoulder. “C was chicken. You couldn’t give the cheese ones away.”

The clock had timed the oven. Each step was a batch, and each batch had been named for the street whose shop or canteen had ordered it. The pies on Arthur’s bicycle were a different business altogether: individual pies sold from a tray to people on their doorsteps. Over the years June had put the two operations together in her head, a sensible economy from a child’s point of view. Her father had let her explain the clock to customers because it kept her busy and because, as Arthur delicately put it, correcting his daughter had never been among the man’s preferred recreations.

“What about the money drawer?” I asked. I confess I had grown attached to my own part of the explanation. Arthur pulled it open. It was barely two inches deep, and two narrow ridges ran along the bottom. He said it had held the wooden peel handles while the peels themselves stood upright beside the oven. At the end of the morning June’s father took out the shorter peel to fetch the last tray from the top oven. The drawer rang. Tomorrow’s first batch came round on the dial. No boy, no money, no triumphant return. Just chicken pies coming out of the heat.

June ordered three coffees and asked the waitress to bring whatever kind of pie they had. It was apple. We sat on the bench and ate it out of little cardboard dishes while the clock moved from Bell Lane to Orchard Street. I felt vaguely ashamed of how readily I had believed the first account, though it had been a good account and had explained everything I knew at the time. June seemed less troubled. “That’s two things I’ve got wrong about one little bell,” she said. “I ought to go through the rest of my childhood before I start repeating it to anybody.”

Arthur scraped the last of the cream from his dish. “You didn’t get the sound wrong.” He said this without looking at her, in the tone of a man pointing out that a window had been left open. She set down her spoon. For a while we watched the terrier’s owner fill in the squares of her crossword. Finally June said, “I thought you rode slowly on Mercer Road because you had a girl there.” Arthur admitted he had ridden slowly on Mercer Road. The cobbles were terrible. He had liked a girl on Bell Lane, but she had generally been occupied explaining a clock.

I left them there with the clock on the table and the napkin map folded under one foot of it to make it stand level. On the ride back, I tried Arthur’s route. It was better than mine. You went downhill on the long streets, climbed on the short ones, and crossed the old tram tracks only once, at something close to a right angle. The rails were gone, but the patched seams in the road remained. I had ridden over those seams for years without wondering why they curved so gently or why a row of shops should follow a curve when all the houses behind them stood straight.

On Monday an envelope came through the shop door. Inside was the photograph from the back of the clock, with a note asking if I could have a copy made before I pasted it in place again. June wanted one for Arthur. Looking at it under my bench lamp, I noticed a small striped shape beneath the oven. It might have been a cat. It might have been a folded cloth. A week earlier I would have decided it was a cat and, given another day, could probably have told you its name. I took the photograph to the print shop and asked for three copies.

The third hangs over my bench. Customers sometimes ask if the man in the picture is my father. I say no, he baked pies. If they ask about the clock, I tell them how its wheel worked. Occasionally somebody can follow the whole business from the unequal steps to the twelve names on the dial, and then we have the rare pleasure of understanding a thing together. Mostly they say, “Fancy that,” and hand me a watch that belonged to an uncle. I write down the uncle’s name along with the fault. It costs nothing, and people like to see it on the ticket.

Last month June came in with a kitchen timer shaped like a lemon. It had cost less, new, than the price of opening it, which I told her. She knew. Arthur had dropped it into a pot of soup, and now it ran for nine minutes regardless of where you set it. “Nine is fine for eggs,” she said. “We’re worried about everything else.” I found a grain of rice lodged against the spring. While I worked, she sat by the window doing a crossword in pencil. When the timer rang, she glanced up. “Soup,” she said, and for once I knew the whole history of a sound.

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want for 2500 words.
samples.result:
The first thing we lent from the dresser was the drawer itself. A woman named Eileen needed something shallow and reasonably square to carry a cake on two buses. The cake was for her former husband, who had married a diabetic and apparently no longer got what Eileen considered a proper birthday. We lined the drawer with a clean pillowcase. It stuck on the left, and you had to lift it slightly to get it out. I demonstrated this even though, once she had the drawer in her hands, it was information of no conceivable use to her. I was new at the job.

The dresser stood in the lobby of the Marlowe Street baths, which hadn't been baths for thirty years. The city still owned the building and heated it just enough to keep the pipes from bursting. Upstairs there was a rehearsal room, a tax preparation service, and, on Thursdays, a man who repaired accordions. Downstairs there was me. My job title was Building Attendant II. Nobody could identify Building Attendant I. I had a mop, a desk, and a view of the laundromat across the street, where somebody had painted the word WASH backwards on the inside of the window, with the result that it read backwards from outside as well. It takes real conviction to make that particular mistake with an S.

Eileen returned the drawer on Monday. There was a piece of cake in it for me, wrapped in foil, and a square of hardboard cut to fit the bottom. “That wood bows,” she said. “You want to watch that with anything damp.” I thanked her. It was a yellow cake with chocolate icing, the kind I like. She stood at my desk while I ate it, not in expectation of praise, as I first thought, but because she wanted the foil back. It was an unusually good piece of foil, the heavy kind that retains the shape of the thing it has covered. She folded it into quarters and put it in her purse.

By Friday two people had come in asking about the cake carrier. I said what we had was a drawer. One of them said, yes, that was what she meant. She took it to a school supper and brought it back full of teaspoons. She had intended to borrow a few from the supper and had forgotten when to stop. We put the spoons in the top right drawer. By the end of the month the dresser also contained a bicycle pump, a set of pastry cutters shaped like the states of the Union east of the Mississippi, and a pair of binoculars with one working eye. I made a sign: THINGS YOU CAN BORROW. It was meant to distinguish the dresser from my desk. It didn't. My stapler went to a wedding and came back with a pale pink ribbon tied around its middle.

I began keeping records after the bicycle pump disappeared. This was not because I thought keeping records would get it back. We knew exactly where it was. Mr. Diaz had taken it to his brother in Syracuse, experienced a crisis in his marriage, and decided to remain in Syracuse, where he had always been happier. His wife came in especially to tell me this. “Write it down,” she said. “Otherwise whenever you see me you're going to think: bicycle pump.” She was right. Once I wrote it down I was free to think about other things when I saw her, like whether she was doing all right. She was. The brother, it turned out, had a wife of whom she was extremely fond, and they now had long, expensive telephone conversations without either of their husbands interrupting. The pump was ultimately returned by mail at a cost greater than the price of two new pumps.

My records consisted of a composition book with three columns: Object, Name, Expected Back. The third column was the most interesting. Almost nobody could tell you with confidence when they would be finished with a level. They had a shelf to put up, certainly. They had the shelf, the brackets, and the little bag of screws. What they didn't have was any information about the person they would be on Sunday afternoon. Would that person want to put up a shelf? Would that person feel strongly enough about the shelf to move the sofa? Under Expected Back people wrote things like “Sunday unless Ron visits” or “before the baby.” One man, borrowing an extension cord, wrote “when the hedge is beautiful.” He brought it back the next morning. He had quite a small hedge, but he had been right to be ambitious for it.

For a while I became overinterested in the enterprise. I went to yard sales on Saturdays looking for things people might need only once. A melon baller. A pipe wrench. A small, ferocious brush designed to remove pills from sweaters. I spent my own money, not much individually but rather a lot when considered as a sum. These things were almost never borrowed. What people wanted, apparently, were the things other people had already needed and could no longer justify keeping. A plaster foot on which to display a single shoe. A roll of black cloth for photographing an engagement ring you wanted to sell without telling the person who had given it to you. A tape recorder with a button that had to be held down by a thumb or a piece of folded cardboard. People came in for these things with the calm certainty of shoppers who had consulted a catalogue.

“Do you have one of those stools for playing the cello?” a boy asked me one afternoon.

I said I didn't think there was a special stool for playing the cello.

“There is if your feet don't reach the floor.”

We tried him on several chairs. In the end he took the accordion repairman's lunch stool, which had a round seat covered in red vinyl and legs that unscrewed for transport. I left a note for the repairman. The following Thursday he ate his sandwich sitting on the stairs and told me that he preferred it. From the stairs he could see the sky through the high windows above the lobby doors. “I never know what kind of day it is in here,” he said. “All day I hear people letting the air out of things.”

I wish I could tell you I made friends with him. In a story about a public building, two people who spend years under the same roof ought eventually to learn something surprising about each other. But we mostly discussed whether the toilet on the second floor was running again. Once, after a heavy snow, he put a hand on my shoulder to steady himself while he took off his boots. I remember the substantial weight of that hand. I don't remember his first name. I remember the boy because his mother sent me a photograph of him at a recital, sitting very straight on the red stool. Behind him a girl with a violin was looking down into her sleeve, plainly wondering how far up it she could get her hand without attracting the attention of an adult. Quite far, on the evidence.

The trouble began when the city decided the baths were in use. Of course the city had known about us all along. It paid my salary and the gas bill, and once a year a patient woman came to count the fire extinguishers. But in a substantial binder downtown the building had been classified as Underutilized, which meant we were allowed to go about our affairs in peace. Then somebody from the newspaper photographed Eileen carrying the cake drawer down the steps. You could see the painted tiles around the entrance, blue fish blowing blue bubbles, each bubble with a little white crescent to indicate the play of light on water. The photograph ran on a page about neighborhood life. The mayor's deputy recognized the tiles from his childhood swimming lessons. He came to visit with four other people, all of whom had excellent coats. By spring we had been reclassified as a Community Resource.

There followed an interval in which I spent a good deal of time on the telephone explaining the dresser. Was it a tool library? No, although we had tools. Were borrowers members? Of what? Were the items sanitized? I wiped them, if that was what was meant. Could we provide figures for the previous fiscal year? I could, but they would include a woman who had borrowed the same six teaspoons every Wednesday for nine months rather than face the fact that her bridge club was permanent and she needed more spoons. I didn't know if that was one transaction or thirty-nine. The young man on the telephone said it depended on what picture we wanted to paint. I looked across the street. Someone had scraped the W and the A off the laundromat window. For the time being the establishment was called SH, backwards, a request for quiet issued chiefly to people on their way out.

Perhaps you think I'm going to say that the city ruined the dresser. It didn't. The city bought us a handsome steel cabinet with adjustable shelves and a lock that worked. We had needed a lock since a toddler discovered the pastry cutters and tried to swallow Rhode Island. The young man on the telephone turned out to be good at his job. He found a category of municipal property that covered objects recovered from city drains, and under that heading we were able to lend things without requiring proof of residence. He came over on his lunch hour to show me how to fill out the form. He also borrowed a long-handled mirror to see where his cat went when she got behind the refrigerator. He returned it the same afternoon. “There's a whole second cat back there,” he said. He looked tired but pleased, the way people look when a mystery turns out to have been real.

What nearly ruined the dresser was my knee. I had been having trouble with it on the stairs, particularly going down, and then one day I stepped off a curb carrying a grocery bag full of oranges. I didn't fall spectacularly. I sat rather neatly on the curb as if I had decided to wait there for a parade. An orange rolled out of the bag. A man crossing the street changed direction to retrieve it, and for some reason the sight of him changing direction made me understand that I had hurt myself seriously. Before he reached me I was crying hard enough to frighten him. He put the orange in my lap. “I can get the others,” he said, although the others were still in the bag. There are moments when everybody present would be grateful for a straightforward job.

I was gone eleven weeks. The city sent a substitute who knew boilers and had worked in a much bigger building. His name was Len. He found the composition book and did his best with it, but he had the temperament of a man who had kept a large building warm by taking small irregularities seriously. If a person wrote Tuesday in the third column, Len expected to see that person on Tuesday. On Wednesday he telephoned. He did not scold or threaten. He merely said, “We had you down for yesterday,” which proved far more effective. The shelves filled up. The steel cabinet filled up. Things that had been gone so long I had forgotten we possessed them reappeared, including the plaster foot, now wearing a sock someone had knitted to keep it from getting chipped. When I returned, the lobby looked like a shop on the morning before it opens for business, everything arranged and not a soul in sight.

Len had done one thing I would never have thought of. On wet days he put a chair just inside the entrance so people could sit down to close their umbrellas and take off their overshoes. It was the most popular service the building had ever offered. Shoppers stopped to rearrange their bags on it. Children knelt on it to watch for the bus. A courier sat there every afternoon at four to eat a pear. “Nobody borrows anything anymore,” I complained to Eileen. She had come by to inspect my knee, which she regarded as belonging to the neighborhood and having been entrusted, perhaps unwisely, to me. She pointed at the courier. “He's borrowing the chair.” I said that wasn't the same. “Well, don't tell him,” she said. “He's got juice all down his front. He's having a bad enough time.”

The spoons went out again first. Then the level. Somebody took the sweater brush. I kept the record book but stopped asking for dates. Len moved to a new swimming pool out near the airport, where he discovered a faulty valve in his first week and saved the city, according to a letter he sent me, “a not inconsiderable amount of water.” I liked hearing from him. My knee got better up to a point and then decided that point suited it. I kept a cane under the desk. The laundromat hired a sign painter, who put gold letters on the glass, properly facing out. It was called Viola's. In all those years I hadn't known that. I went across one day to see if there was a Viola. There was, and she had been wondering for some time whether we could use a serviceable iron with a very short cord.

Not long before I retired, a young woman came in with the cake drawer. I hadn't seen it in years. One corner had been reinforced with a strip of tin, and the hardboard Eileen had cut was stained in overlapping circles, like a map of islands drawn by someone who had heard about islands but never seen one. The woman set it on my desk. “My grandmother said you'd know where this goes.” For a moment I couldn't think what she meant. Then I went over to the dresser, where we kept the forms now, and pulled out the box of envelopes that occupied the empty space. The drawer went halfway in and stopped. I lifted it slightly. It slid the rest of the way with a soft wooden knock. The young woman asked if that was all. I said yes, and she went out to catch her bus.

All afternoon I kept opening it. I put in the spare pencils, took them out, tried it with the envelopes, decided against them. At five I left it empty and locked up. Across the street Viola was ironing a white shirt in the window, turning the sleeve around the narrow board a little at a time. She raised the iron when she saw me, just an inch or two, cord permitting. I raised my cane. Then she went back to the sleeve, and I went home.

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want for 2500 words.
samples.result:
The first street my father forgot was the one named after his mother. He was looking at the crossword when he said, “What was that little street behind the button factory? The one where you could buy a rabbit on Saturday.” I said, “Florence Street.” He filled in something quite different—MARTEN, probably, or SABLE—and went on drinking his tea. It was only later, on the bus home, that I remembered Florence Street had never been an official name. His mother had lived there, and his father, who delivered coal, had written FLORENCE on the route card. The name had stuck among the drivers.

This seemed to me a thing worth putting down. I was working at the city library then, in the room where people brought questions that had defeated the main desk. Most were soluble. A man wanted the result of a bicycle race held in 1958; a woman needed to know whether the previous owner of her house had died in it, because her new boyfriend refused to sleep upstairs. We had newspapers, directories, tax rolls, and a telephone with a cord long enough to let me reach the window. What we did not have was any way of finding Florence Street.

I began with a sheet of good paper from the supply cupboard. Across the top I printed NAMES NOT ON THE MAP. Under that I wrote Florence Street in pencil, leaving room for corrections, and ruled columns for location, dates of use, and source. My father, when I showed him, objected to being called a source. “Makes me sound like plumbing,” he said. He also objected to the position of the street. I had it running behind the button factory. It ran beside the factory, he said. Behind the factory was where you bought the rabbit. I rubbed a hole in the paper getting this right.

For a fortnight Florence Street stood alone. Then a girl came in asking for directions to the Piano Steps. She was meeting somebody there at four. The main desk had sent her upstairs on the theory that I understood young people, being thirty-six and the only member of staff with a bicycle helmet. I did not know the steps, but I knew to ask what you could see from them. “Your feet, I suppose,” she said. We looked together at satellite photographs until she recognized a blue awning. The Piano Steps were eleven shallow stairs outside the magistrates’ court. A skateboard descending them played a scale of sorts.

“Is that what everybody calls them?” I asked. She considered. “Everybody who’s meeting me today.” This struck me as a useful minimum qualification for a place-name. I added it to the sheet. By spring I had thirty entries and a drawer of index cards. There was the Cold Seat, a granite sill outside a bakery, occupied each morning by whichever delivery driver arrived too early. There was Little Wednesday, a market that took place on Friday but had been founded by traders expelled from the larger Wednesday market for a dispute involving the sale of socks. Nobody agreed on the nature of the dispute.

I put a notice beside the library doors: WHAT DO YOU CALL A PLACE THAT THE MAP CALLS SOMETHING ELSE? Beneath it I hung a canvas pocket for replies. The pocket had once held children’s mittens, and one mitten remained in it all through the project, a green one with a white thumb. The first week brought us seven names, two complaints about parking, a recipe for liver dumplings, and a note in an envelope marked PRIVATE. The note said, “I call the seat by the canal Arthur’s seat because that is where Arthur told me. Please don’t put it in anything.” I didn’t.

The surprise was how quickly the names became verbs. People did not say they were going to the Long Way, a passage between two apartment blocks. They said they would “long-way it,” which meant walking through the passage slowly enough to finish a conversation before going indoors. To “take the brass” meant to cross a hotel lobby as a shortcut, and was named for a polished handrail that the hotel had removed in 1981. My favorite was “to get Septembered.” In the park, one chestnut stood in a draught between tall buildings and dropped its leaves weeks before its neighbors. To get Septembered was to be caught under it on the wrong afternoon.

By then my father had begun losing other words. He could not summon *colander*, so he brought me the thing itself, shook it irritably, and said, “The opposite of an umbrella.” Yet he could give directions through a demolished district in exquisite detail. Turn left, he would say, at the tobacconist’s ugly dog. If the dog is indoors, look for the patch of bare earth where he usually lies. Once, driving him to an appointment, I missed our turning because I was listening to his account of a shortcut over a railway footbridge. The footbridge had come down before I was born. We arrived twelve minutes late.

I wanted to record him. He agreed on the condition that I come for lunch and bring something better than soup. I bought two pork pies, a bag of pears, and a small digital recorder whose instruction booklet was longer than any story I expected him to tell. We sat at his kitchen table. I pressed the red button. My father straightened his back and said, in the voice he used for insurance claims, “The district in question was principally residential, although light industrial concerns were also represented.” We endured six minutes of this. Then the recorder’s batteries failed, and he told me about the horse that went upstairs.

It was a coal horse, patient as furniture, and a boy had led it up three flights of stairs in a half-built tenement on a bet. Horses, according to my father, would climb a staircase readily enough but took a dim view of coming down. A crowd gathered. Somebody sent for a butcher; somebody more sensible sent for the boy’s mother. She removed her apron, tied it over the horse’s eyes, and backed the animal down one step at a time while describing, for all three floors to hear, the future that awaited her son. Thereafter the tenement was known as Horse Heaven. Or perhaps, my father said, that was a pub.

I found no horse in the newspapers. I did find an advertisement for a public house called the Horse and Seven, which gave me the unpleasant sensation of watching a conjurer expose another conjurer’s trick. Had the pub produced the horse? Had the horse improved the name of the pub? I wrote both possibilities on a card. When I told my father, he shrugged. “You think people went there for the spelling?” he said. He had a point, though not one that would satisfy the head librarian, who had lately begun talking about an exhibition and used the word *verified* with increasing frequency.

The head librarian was called Bina Roy. She had once removed a pigeon from the reading room using only a wastebasket and a folded copy of the financial pages, and I trusted her judgment in most matters. She examined the cards on my desk. “How many people need to say a name before we print it?” she asked. I said two, then remembered the girl and the Piano Steps. “Two who know each other, or two who don’t?” Bina asked. I said I saw the difficulty. “Good,” she said. “If you didn’t see it, I’d give the wall space to the watercolors of local bridges.”

We decided against making one big map. A dot on a map looks so confident, and a boundary looks more confident still. The Cold Seat occupied four feet of stone; Little Wednesday occupied a different stretch of pavement depending on the weather and the mood of the licensing inspector. Instead, we set out a row of school desks and put a neighborhood on each one. Visitors could open the lids and find photographs, street plans, scraps of testimony, and cards with space for amendments. On the wall we hung blank paper. Bina supplied pencils, tied on lengths of string long enough for a person to disagree at some distance.

The exhibition opened on a wet Thursday. For the first hour nobody came except a man who regularly slept in the genealogy section and had mistaken the rearranged furniture for an improvement in his accommodations. Then the rain got heavier, a bus broke down outside, and we acquired an audience of nineteen damp strangers. A nurse in blue trousers identified the Cold Seat at once. Her father called it the Widow’s Shelf. A boy said it was known at his school as the Bum Fridge. All three names made perfect sense to the people who used them. All three parties were faintly offended by the others.

Within a week we had our first serious quarrel. Two sisters disagreed about the location of a place called the Orchard, where neither remembered a single tree. One drew a square around a row of garages. The other crossed it out and drew a square around a playing field. Their pencils snapped. I brought fresh ones. Eventually they established that their family had moved house in 1974 and their mother, who did not think children needed an unlimited supply of nouns, had called the open ground behind both houses the Orchard. The sisters sat down on the floor and laughed until one had to ask the way to the lavatory.

Not all the corrections were welcome. A former factory foreman took exception to our card for the Queen’s Entrance, a gap in a fence used by women working the early shift. They made the gap, he said, to avoid having their time cards checked. One of the women came back the next day and wrote, “We made it because the proper gate was half a mile round and we had feet.” Underneath, in smaller writing, she added, “He used it too.” I left all three statements together. The foreman returned on Saturday, read the addition, and stood for some time with a pencil in his hand. He put it back unused.

My father declined four invitations before agreeing to visit. He wore his good jacket and brought the recorder, now fitted with new batteries, because he had misunderstood the nature of an opening and thought he might be required to make a speech. At the Florence Street desk he read his card twice. “Who told you this?” he asked. “You did.” He looked pleased, then doubtful. “Did I tell you about the rabbits?” I said he had. He leaned closer. “It wasn’t rabbits every Saturday. Sometimes it was pigeons.” He took a pencil and added this information in his neat capital letters. Then he crossed out SOMETIMES and wrote USUALLY.

We went downstairs for tea. In the café he asked whether I remembered his mother. I did, a little: a solid woman in a brown cardigan who kept sugar in a jar labeled RICE. Beyond that I had mostly photographs. He said she had hated the street where they lived. The factory windows overlooked her kitchen, and in summer the men would shout down suggestions about whatever she was cooking. Once she carried a pot of stew upstairs, paid a penny to enter the factory canteen as a visitor, and set it down in front of the loudest man. “There,” she said. “Finish it yourself.”

I asked why nobody had told me that before. My father turned his teaspoon over and licked it, a habit I had fought through several decades and abruptly lost the wish to correct. “You never wanted to know where she lived before,” he said. I protested that I had always wanted to know about the family. “That’s different. If you ask about the family, people tell you who married whom. Ask about a kitchen and you hear what went on in it.” He wrapped two biscuits in a paper napkin for later. We took the lift upstairs so he could add the stew to the card.

The exhibition stayed up for three months. A publisher offered to make a book if we would settle on the hundred most authentic names, which was like asking for the hundred wettest spoonfuls in a bath. We declined. A bus driver proposed recording the unofficial stops on his route, and that we did. You can still hear him in the local collection, announcing each stop in his official voice and then again as he would to a passenger carrying shopping: “Municipal Recreation Facility. That’s the Baths, love.” The pool had been filled in for twenty years, but apparently nobody ever asked to get off at the Municipal Recreation Facility.

My father moved into a smaller flat that autumn. Sorting his things, we found the original coal route cards in a biscuit tin under a stack of instruction manuals for appliances he no longer owned. There was FLORENCE, in my grandfather’s sloping hand, between GAS LANE and SHORT CUT IF DRY. On the reverse was a list of weights and prices, a drawing of a woman’s shoe, and the words NO CREDIT TO MAN WITH FERRET. My father claimed not to remember the man, the ferret, or the circumstances of the prohibition. I suspect that on this occasion at least he was keeping something to himself.

The cards are in the library now, in an acid-free box that cost more than my grandfather earned on a good day. On Friday afternoons I take the box to my father’s flat, and we choose a route. We do not try to travel it. We sit by the window with the card between us and see how far the conversation goes. Sometimes he remembers a turning and nothing beyond it. Sometimes we spend the whole hour outside one house. Last week he looked at SHORT CUT IF DRY and said, “Never was, though,” and we abandoned the route in favor of a game of cribbage.

People still leave things in the canvas pocket. The other morning I found a note in a young hand: “The place behind the library where my dad lets go of the bike is called by us the place behind the library where my dad lets go of the bike. Sorry it is long.” I took the note upstairs and made a card for it. For location I wrote *east service yard*. For dates of use I wrote *this spring*. Under source, a heading I had never got around to changing, I copied the words *by us*. Then I went to the window. It was nearly closing time. Out in the yard a man was running with one hand extended, a perfectly unnecessary hand, while ahead of him a child on a yellow bicycle rounded the bins and rode on.

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want for 2500 words.
samples.result:
The first sound I recorded for the town of Bellwether was my own stomach. I was standing in the empty council chamber, wearing headphones and holding a microphone toward the ceiling, when a large animal appeared to wake up somewhere under the floor. I tore off the headphones. The room was quiet. I put them back on. The animal gave a long, considered reply.

“Have you had lunch?” asked June Vale, the town clerk.

I admitted I had not.

“Well,” she said, “before we preserve anything for posterity, let’s get you a sandwich.”

The town had received a modest arts grant to make a sound map. Visitors would be able to touch a spot on a screen and hear what happened there: water passing beneath the iron bridge, shoes on the wooden stairs of the library, the high school band practicing behind the gym. I was twenty-six, recently graduated, and the owner of a microphone expensive enough to make people assume I knew how to use it. June hired me for six weeks. The sandwich, she made clear, would come out of her own pocket.

I began with the obvious things. I recorded the noon whistle at the paper mill and the courthouse clock striking four. The clock struck five times, which I noted on the file. At the bakery I captured the slap of dough against a floured bench. At the swimming pool I lowered a waterproof microphone into the deep end and discovered a world of distant knocks and enormous, velvety booms. A little girl asked what I was doing. When I told her, she put her face in the water and shouted, “My name is Frances!”

For several days I went around with the proprietary happiness of a person gathering mushrooms. Other people walked past a drainpipe; I could take it home. I acquired the freight elevator at Lutz Furniture, the pedestrian signal on Elm, the squeaking pivot of the playground horse. I had a folder called BELLS and another called BIRDS and a third, increasingly important folder called PROBABLY BIRDS. In the evenings I sat in my rented room above the pharmacy, listening to Bellwether while Bellwether itself went on outside.

June reviewed my progress on Friday afternoons. She listened without closing her eyes, the way some people taste soup. Her office contained thirty years of council minutes, a rubber plant of exceptional width, and one photograph of a young man in swimming trunks standing beside a canoe. I assumed he was somebody she had lost. On our second Friday he came in wearing a parcel company uniform, took eleven dollars from her purse with permission, and called her Mom.

“These are nice,” June said after he left. “But why have you got the lid of the blue mailbox?”

“It makes a good noise.”
