“It does. But nobody here would know it from the lid of a mailbox in Ohio.”

This struck me as a provincial objection to an international standard of hinge. I tried to explain that the map was a portrait, that a portrait required ordinary features as well as distinguishing ones. June ate three peanuts and folded the top of the packet down.

“Go see Mr. Saye,” she said. “Ask him about the applause.”

Mr. Saye lived in a narrow house behind the former picture palace, which had been divided into a carpet showroom and a chapel. He was ninety-one. His daughter led me through a kitchen full of cooling pies to the back porch, where he sat shelling peas into a stainless steel bowl. I set the microphone on the table. He looked at it and began dropping the peas one at a time from a greater height.

“I used to run the films,” he said. “Is that what you’re after?”

I asked about the applause.

“Oh, that wasn’t for the films. That was for Leonard.”

Leonard, it turned out, had driven the last bus from the railway station. On Saturday nights the feature ended at ten forty-five and the bus was due to leave at ten fifty. The theater doors opened onto a side street; the stop stood around the corner on Market. If the credits ran long, somebody would telephone the station and ask the dispatcher to tell Leonard to wait. Leonard always waited. When the doors opened, the audience could see the rear of his bus reflected in the dark window of the jeweler’s shop opposite. If they saw it there, they applauded.

“People clapped for a reflection?” I asked.

“They clapped for the bus. The reflection was how they knew they had one.”

“Did Leonard hear them?”

“He said he could. I think he liked to say he could.”

I asked whether any recording existed. Mr. Saye laughed. “Who’d stand in a doorway holding a tape recorder when he had five minutes to catch a bus?”

That night I labeled the file SAYE, ARTHUR—RECOLLECTION OF APPLAUSE. It was twenty-three minutes long. Near the end, his daughter came out and said the pies were ready. He told her I was from the radio. She said in that case I ought to know his name was Albert.

My project changed after that. At the grocery store I put up a card asking, “What did Bellwether used to sound like?” Replies arrived on the answering machine in June’s office. A woman remembered the milkman carrying empty bottles between his fingers, four in each hand. A retired teacher imitated the particular cough that had passed through assembly whenever the headmaster said “character.” Three callers mentioned a dog named Admiral who sang along with the ice cream van. One of them was prepared to sing both parts.

I still made field recordings, but more often I sat at kitchen tables while somebody tried to put a vanished noise into words. A loom had sounded like a drawer of cutlery falling down stairs, except regular. The old dentist’s drill had been green. Yes, green was a color, the man understood that, but the sound had been green as well. A skating pond made a noise on cold nights like a whale calling through a keyhole. I had never heard a whale or listened through a keyhole. Nevertheless I felt I knew exactly what she meant.

There were disputes. The founders’ parade had begun with a cannon, unless it had begun with a bass drum struck behind the war memorial, unless it had begun, as one indignant letter maintained, with a prayer. The bird outside the post office that said “Peter, Peter” had said “Teacher, teacher” and had lived outside the bank. I stopped trying to settle these matters. On the map I placed three small dots at the parade ground. I drew the line at putting a bird in two places, then remembered that birds could fly.

By the fifth week I had gathered so much material that the map took a full minute to load. June found me at midnight in the council chamber, cutting the silences out of a recording of a woman describing her father coming home from work. First there had been his bicycle bell at the corner, she said. Then the gate. Then nothing for a while, because he always stopped to pull a weed or two. Then his key missing the lock.

“Why did he ring the bell at the corner?” I had asked.

“So we’d put the kettle on.”

June sat down beside me. On my screen, the woman’s voice appeared as a blue thicket broken by level stretches of pale gray.

“You took out the weeding,” June said.

“She wasn’t talking.”

“I know. She was waiting for him to get to the door.”

I put it back. We listened to twelve seconds of an old woman’s refrigerator, a truck passing in the street, and a small click that might have been her wedding ring touching the table. Then the key missed the lock.

“Do you have one?” I asked June.

“A refrigerator?”

“A sound you remember.”

She considered. “My sister could whistle with a blade of grass. She held it between her thumbs.”

“What did it sound like?”

“Terrible. That was the attraction.”

“Could we record you talking about it?”

“No need,” she said. “She lives in Dayton. I can ask her to do it.”

The next morning an audio message arrived from an Ohio number. There was some negotiation with a lawn mower, a long inhalation, and a blast so piercing that a dog began barking several yards away. Then two women laughed, one in my headphones and one at the desk across the room. June pressed the heels of her hands against her eyes. “She’s still got it,” she said.

The public unveiling was scheduled for the last Sunday in August. The hardware store lent us a projector. The chapel lent us fifty folding chairs, each bearing on its underside a small paper label that read CHAPEL, as if an unmarked folding chair might be readily mistaken for private property. We hung a sheet on the wall of the council chamber. At three o’clock June opened the doors, and sixty-eight people came in out of the heat.

I had prepared remarks about acoustic ecology. Looking at the audience, which included Frances from the swimming pool wearing a dress patterned with lemons, I abandoned them. I explained how the map worked. I clicked the iron bridge. Water rushed through the chamber, followed by the hollow tire music of a car crossing overhead. People turned toward the windows. Outside there wasn’t a cloud in the sky.

Then I let the audience choose. We heard the paper mill and Admiral and the underwater declaration of Frances, who received the afternoon’s first round of applause. We listened to Mr. Saye shell peas, though he had stayed home because Sundays were for his family. When I played the clock striking four, the audience counted aloud to five. Somebody called for the dentist. Somebody else called, with feeling, for absolutely anything but the dentist.

About forty minutes in, a boy in the front row pointed to a dot at the edge of the screen. It lay well beyond the town boundary, in a pale empty region where the map software had found nothing worth labeling.

“What’s out there?” he asked.

I knew the dot. During my first week I had driven north to record the railway crossing at Harker’s Field. I had waited an hour without a train. The dot was supposed to be hidden; I had put it on the map as a reminder to go back.

“Nothing much,” I said. “I was waiting for a train that didn’t come.”

“Let’s hear it,” said the boy.

People settled back into their chairs. I clicked.

At first the room filled with a soft continuous shushing. Wind moved through the dry grass beside the track. An insect ticked somewhere close to the microphone. From very far off came two notes of machinery reversing. I stood beside the projector, suddenly conscious of charging the public money to listen to a ditch.

Then, behind me, a man said, “Lapwing.”

Another voice said, “No, that’s the gate on the Ullman place.”

“My God,” a woman whispered. “That is the gate.”

The noise came again: a thin rise, a pause, a thin fall. Perhaps it was a bird. Perhaps somebody a quarter mile away had spent that hot afternoon carrying things through a gate. A minute went by. The recording contained my shoe shifting on gravel, my sleeve brushing the microphone stand. Nobody asked me to skip ahead.

I let it play for four minutes. In the fourth, we heard an approaching engine. It grew louder, passed, and faded. A man near the back took off his cap.

“Anthony,” he said.

Several people turned.

“That’s my brother’s truck. Listen when he changes gear. He’s got that loose bit on the exhaust.”

I dragged the cursor back. The engine approached again. As the driver shifted, a brief metallic jangle rose out of the growl.

“Could be any truck,” said a woman beside him.

“Could be,” he agreed, perfectly happy.

Afterward, while we folded chairs, I asked whether his brother had died. He looked startled. “Anthony? He’s at the lake. Why?”

I said I had misunderstood.

“He owes me a ladder,” the man added, as though this might help me get the story straight.

My contract ended on Tuesday. I packed my headphones and microphone, said goodbye to the pharmacist downstairs, and carried my suitcase to the bus stop on Market. Across the road, the jeweler’s window reflected a white delivery van and half a cloud. June came to see me off. She brought two egg sandwiches wrapped in waxed paper, one for the journey and one against the possibility, never yet disproved, that a young person might be hungry again later.

I asked what she would do with the map. She said the schools wanted a copy. The library would keep the original files. There was enough money left to buy a recorder that people could borrow with a library card.

“Are you going to keep adding things?” I asked.

“If people bring them in.”

The bus rounded the corner. Its brakes gave a descending sigh. For six weeks I had been training myself to hear such noises as potential possessions. My hand went to the side pocket of my bag before I remembered I had packed the microphone under my clothes.

June noticed. “You’ll have to remember that one.”

What I remember now, years later, is not the brakes. I remember the waxed paper warming through against my palm. I remember that the driver had a little electric fan clipped to his dashboard and that its blue blades turned so slowly I doubted they could move any air. I remember June stepping back from the curb, already looking toward the council offices, where there was work to do that had nothing to do with me. As the bus pulled away, I looked into the jeweler’s window and saw my own bus traveling there, full of people going in the same direction at precisely the same speed.

There might have been applause. Of course there wasn’t. But I understood, at last, the practical arrangement: how the people coming out of the picture palace could see, without hurrying yet, that they had time. I hoped they had used a little of it. I hoped somebody had stood under the marquee to finish telling a joke, and somebody else had pretended not to hear the end, so that on the ride home there would be a reason to tell it again.

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want for 2500 words.
samples.result:
The summer the river went low, my father and I found a staircase in it. Eleven limestone steps came down from the weeds on the north bank and ended on a landing about the size of a kitchen table. Beyond the landing there was mud, and beyond the mud the diminished river hurried along, looking embarrassed to be caught so far from either shore. My father sat down on the bottom step and took off his shoes. He was seventy-three. His feet, which I had not seen in years, were unexpectedly elegant, like a pair of white gloves laid aside after a dance.

“This is where your aunt learned to swim,” he said.

I thought he meant his sister June, who had been dead for twenty years, but he meant my mother’s sister Evelyn, who was alive and living above a pharmacy in Toledo. This surprised me. I had never imagined that the families knew each other before my parents married. In my mind they had entered the church through opposite doors, fully assembled for the occasion. When I said so, my father laughed. “Who do you think introduced us?” He picked up a flat stone and rubbed the mud from it with his thumb. “Evie was my girl first.”

There are disclosures for which one wishes to be sitting somewhere more dignified than on a stump with a sandwich in one’s mouth. I swallowed. My father sailed the stone over the mud. It struck the water once and vanished. He looked at his hand as though it had disobeyed him. Then he put on his shoes and asked if I wanted to see where the bathhouse had stood. I said yes, although what I wanted was a complete account of his romantic history, beginning with kindergarten and accompanied, if possible, by dated photographs. We climbed the steps. The bathhouse had become a clump of sumac.

That evening I telephoned Evelyn. She answered on the first ring and said, “If this is about the peaches, I don’t want any.” An enterprising neighbor had been selling subscriptions to a fruit delivery service. I assured her that I had no peaches and told her about the stairs. I could hear a television in the background and the metallic knocking of her spoon against a cup. When I repeated what my father had said, the spoon stopped. “His girl?” she said. Then, unexpectedly, she began to laugh. “Oh, honey. He paid me a quarter a week to let him tell people that.”

My father had been shy, she explained, and a boy who already had a girl could go to a dance without having to ask anybody. The arrangement suited Evelyn because she wanted to dance and he was willing to learn the steps in her parents’ garage. I asked if my mother had known. “Who do you think set the price?” Evelyn said. Apparently my mother, at sixteen, had been a gifted negotiator. The quarters went into a blue jar, and by the end of the summer the sisters had bought a secondhand tennis racket. They took turns playing with it against the wall of the Methodist church.

I lived four hours from my father and had come home to help him sell his house. This had been my idea sufficiently long ago that we could both pretend it was his. He had fallen in March while carrying a basket of laundry upstairs. Nothing broke, but for two hours he sat on the landing with a wet towel under his head, waiting for his legs to become trustworthy. By July we had found an apartment with an elevator, a narrow balcony, and a view of the high school baseball field. All that remained was the small matter of deciding what constituted a life and what could go to Goodwill.

My father approached this question by sorting screws. He owned eight coffee cans of them, all thoroughly intermingled with washers, bent nails, foreign coins, and the little metal keys once used to open tins of sardines. Each morning he poured one can onto the workbench. Each afternoon I came down to find the screws organized by length and the contents of the rest of the house undisturbed. I made trips to the donation center. I filled out change-of-address forms. On Thursday I sold the dining room table to a woman who raised miniature horses. When I returned, my father had started sorting the washers.

The river walk had been an attempt to get us both out of the house before one of us said something accurate and unkind. It worked so well that we went again the next day. Overnight the water had retreated another yard. Downstream of the staircase, a row of wooden posts leaned out of the mud. My father remembered a floating dock anchored there, a concession stand that sold orange soda, and a lifeguard called Mr. Bell who could whistle through a gap in his front teeth. He remembered the smell of hot rope. He could not remember what year the place closed.

We began taking a notebook. I drew a crude map and he corrected it. The concession stand had been farther east. The bathhouse had faced the road, not the water. A little footbridge had crossed the creek, although the creek now ran through a concrete pipe beneath the parking lot of a store that sold mattresses. At home I called Evelyn, who supplied amendments. Mr. Bell had not been a lifeguard; he had sold the soda. The lifeguard was his brother, also Mr. Bell. Neither had whistled. That was a woman named Dot who came down on her lunch break to swim exactly twelve lengths between the dock and a buoy.

“Why twelve?” I asked.

“Because she had a job,” Evelyn said.

On Saturday she arrived by bus with a canvas overnight bag and the tennis racket. She was eighty-one, six years older than my father, and had dyed her hair a red so emphatic it made everything near her look a little underexposed. The racket was in a wooden press, its handle wrapped in unraveling green tape. She handed it to me as one might hand over a subpoena. “There,” she said. “Now you don’t have to take his word for anything.” My father, behind her, was already carrying her bag upstairs to the room where he had fallen.

At breakfast they quarreled about a song. My father claimed the loudspeaker at the swimming hole had played “Goodnight, Irene” every evening at closing time. Evelyn said there had been no loudspeaker. My father asked how anyone had known when to leave. “It got dark, Leonard.” He buttered his toast all the way into the corners. She watched with the satisfaction of someone who had once found a habit annoying and was delighted to discover it still available to annoy her. I began to understand that I had brought together two people who could do for each other something I could not do for either of them.

At the river Evelyn stood on the landing for a long time. Then she pointed to a spot in the mud and said, “My glasses are out there.” She had lost them diving off the dock the summer she turned seventeen. For the rest of August she had done without, because her family could not afford another pair until September. “Everything was beautiful,” she said. “You should have seen the boys.” My father sat on the step and laughed until he coughed. A heron lifted out of the reeds across the river, its legs hanging down behind it like two lengths of loose black thread.

I don’t know whose idea it was to look. Probably mine. I had spent the week throwing away useful things and was susceptible to the prospect of recovering a useless one. We bought rubber boots at the hardware store and borrowed a long-handled rake from the man next door. Evelyn directed operations from the landing. The dock, she said, had been much longer than the posts suggested, except when she thought it might have been shorter. My father worked a few feet from shore, lifting objects with the rake while I rinsed them in a bucket. We found a green bottle, a padlock, three marbles, and the porcelain arm of a doll.

By afternoon we had attracted two children and a man walking a terrier. The children were brothers, nine and eleven, or possibly eleven and nine; each revised the other’s testimony. They found a spoon almost immediately. The man identified our green bottle as a bottle and stayed an hour. Nobody found the glasses. What we found instead was a strip of brass with four screw holes and a word engraved on it: MABEL. It was scarcely longer than my finger. My father cleaned the lettering with a grass stem. “Well,” he said, with great contentment. “Here’s something I don’t know anything about.”

This interested him more than all the things he did remember. At supper he proposed that Mabel had been a boat. Evelyn proposed a dog. I suggested a suitcase, and we spent a pleasant half hour disputing the likelihood that anyone would attach a brass plate to luggage. The next morning my father took the strip to the public library. He returned with photocopies of newspaper advertisements, a history of local rowing clubs, and the librarian, who had come to buy our refrigerator. She gave us forty dollars and told us that in the twenties there had been a small ferry upstream.

For three days Mabel was a ferry. We imagined her cable humming underwater, her deck crowded with bicycles and berry pickers. Then the librarian called to report that the ferry had been named City of Auburn and had operated twenty miles away on an entirely different river. Mabel became a horse for a while, on the strength of a photograph in which a brass plate gleamed on a leather harness. She became a cash register, a park bench, and a machine for pressing shirts. The children returned with their mother and made a forceful case for a pirate. My father, to his credit, asked them what evidence would help us decide.

Meanwhile the house grew empty. Rooms acquired echoes peculiar to their dimensions. A handclap in the front bedroom sounded thin and official; in the pantry it came back soft, as if someone on the other side of the wall had clapped politely in return. Without the dining room table we ate off our knees on the porch. Without the refrigerator we bought small quantities of food and finished them. Evelyn slept on a folding cot and pronounced it better than the guest bed, an opinion she might profitably have offered thirty years earlier. We kept the brass plate on the kitchen windowsill beside a tomato ripening in the sun.

One night my father told us that after my mother died, he had gone for nearly a month without buying salt. The shaker was empty. He would sit down to an egg or a bowl of soup, remember, and eat it anyway. The next time he went to the store he would buy milk, bread, apples, a newspaper, everything but salt. It had frightened him more than forgetting a name or missing an appointment. Buying salt was such a small part of what my mother had done that he had never thought of it as something anybody did. He had believed, apparently, in a world in which salt occurred naturally on tables.

Evelyn said my mother had once forgotten to put sugar in a wedding cake. This was news to both of us. It had been the first wedding cake she ever made for money, and she realized her mistake only after the layers were cooling on the counter. There was no time to begin again. So the sisters pierced the cake all over with knitting needles and poured sweetened lemon juice into the holes. The bride’s mother called a week later to ask for the recipe. For years afterward my mother had made the cake that way on purpose. It was the one I chose for my own wedding.

I had always understood the knitting needles to be an example of my mother’s precision. I could see her at the counter, placing the holes at careful intervals, wiping each needle on a folded cloth. It pleased me to imagine the original occasion: the two sisters in a hot kitchen, the cake already wrong, the clock advancing, someone rummaging through a basket of yarn. I wished I had known that version of the recipe when my marriage ended. I had spent a good deal of time then trying to locate the exact moment at which I should have begun again.

The rain came on a Wednesday. It began in the night and woke everyone, not because it was loud but because the gutters, after weeks of disuse, were full of hard little seedpods that rattled like teeth in a cup. At first light we drove to the river. The landing was under water. By noon the lowest three steps had disappeared, and by evening only the top one showed through the flattened weeds. The river carried sticks, foam, a yellow bucket, and great revolving patches of leaves. My father stood under my umbrella. “Well, that saves us looking for those glasses,” he said.

Moving day was clear. The brothers came over to help and accepted the marbles as payment. Evelyn took the racket back to Toledo, having established whatever point she meant to establish by bringing it. We left the screws in their labeled jars for the new owner, a young electrician who seemed almost unnaturally grateful to have them. At the apartment my father placed his chair by the balcony door. From there he could watch the baseball team practice turning double plays. He disliked the shortstop’s habit of patting the ball into his glove before he threw it and looked forward to disliking it for the rest of the season.

I found Mabel in my shirt pocket that evening. My father had slipped her there while we were carrying boxes. I called to ask what he wanted me to do with her. “You’ve got a door, haven’t you?” he said. I owned several, but I knew the one he meant. My study had been a bedroom before the divorce, then a room where I stored things I hadn’t decided whether to keep. Lately I had put a desk in it. I held the brass strip against the wood at eye level. It fit nicely between two old nail holes. All it needed was four small screws.

I could have bought them at the hardware store on the corner. Instead, the next Sunday I drove four hours and knocked on the door of a young electrician who was eating his lunch. He knew the jar at once. He shook four screws into my palm and added a fifth in case I dropped one. Then I went to my father’s apartment, where we sat on the balcony and watched the shortstop. He still patted the ball before throwing it. Even I could see it cost him time. But the first baseman held out his glove, and the ball got there.

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want for 1000 words.
samples.result:
The first time I helped inventory the lost property at the swimming pool, I expected to find goggles. We had goggles enough to furnish a small, many-eyed army. What I did not expect was a brass doorknob, heavy as an apple, with a square spindle sticking out of it. I turned it in my hand. Somewhere, I thought, a person had gone swimming with the means of entering a room in one pocket and had come home without it.

“People bring their problems here,” said Jean, who had worked the front desk for thirty years. “Sometimes the problems have hardware.”

The pool occupied the ground floor of a municipal building. Above us, people applied for permits to widen driveways or keep chickens. Below us, in a blue room with bad acoustics, children learned the useful distinction between floating and standing on somebody else. I was nineteen. My job consisted of selling tickets, mopping, and explaining that the clock over the deep end was seven minutes fast, while the clock in the lobby was not slow but stopped. In the absence of reliable public time, swimmers consulted their stomachs and usually went home at noon.

Every August we emptied the cupboard.

Jean had a system. Anything washable went through the laundry. Anything valuable went into the safe upstairs. Anything with a name prompted a search of the telephone directory, unless the name was Speedo, a confusion I suffered once and was not permitted to forget. The rest we spread across three folding tables for a week. Then a church collected the clothes, the goggles went into a lending basket, and the stranger objects awaited a ruling from Jean.

The doorknob presented a difficulty. “You can't give somebody half a door,” she said. She set it beside the till while she considered.

For the next few days, everybody who bought a ticket touched it. Some tried the turn with a wrist, some with fingertips. A small boy held it to his mouth and announced a train to Glasgow. An elderly man said it was the sort his grandmother had polished every Thursday. He demonstrated her technique on his shirtfront, then asked for his usual locker, number twelve.

What surprised me was how little curiosity anybody expressed about the missing door. The knob had ceased to be evidence of a loss. It was a thing to do while Jean counted out your change.

On Wednesday a girl came in alone carrying a plastic carrier bag. She was twelve, perhaps, with the ferocious politeness of a child conducting adult business. “I understand,” she said, “that you have clothes.”

I showed her the tables. She inspected two sweaters, read their labels, and folded them better than I had. From the bag she produced a green cardigan with wooden buttons.

“My father took this one,” she said. “His is almost exactly the same.”

We found his under a towel. It was almost exactly the same. She examined the cuffs before accepting it as the correct one.

“How can you tell?” I asked.

“He keeps a pencil in his sleeve.”

There was, indeed, a short pencil between the folds of wool. She slid it back into place. At the desk she paused, put her hand on the brass knob, and made the familiar turning motion.

“We've got one like that,” she said.

Jean looked up. “One like it, or a door that needs it?”

“A drawer,” said the girl. “My dad makes scenery. We've got a whole drawer of those.”

She left with her father's cardigan. Jean watched the glass door ease shut behind her.

“A drawer,” Jean repeated, annoyed at having spent four days picturing a door.

At the end of the week, we still had the knob. We also had a single brown shoe, a paperback atlas, and a biscuit tin containing seventeen birthday candles shaped like the number six. Jean awarded the atlas to the lifeguard, who wanted to cycle through France. She kept the shoe another month on the grounds that its partner was unlikely to be useful on its own. The candles went upstairs to the permits office. Someone there was turning sixty-six in October and expressed satisfaction at having spares.

“What about this?” I asked.

“Put it in the drawer.”

It stayed there until winter. One wet afternoon a pipe burst above the lobby ceiling. We closed the pool and moved the desk away from the drip. Behind it was a narrow cupboard I had never noticed, its door painted the exact tired cream of the wall. Where its handle should have been was a square hole.

Jean and I looked at each other. I opened the drawer. She fitted the spindle. It turned.

I would like to report that we found something marvelous. We found floor tiles, six of them, left by whoever had laid the lobby floor. There was also a dead spider and a penciled measurement on the plaster. The knob was almost certainly not the original. Its spindle was too long, and when Jean released it, the brass sagged. But it had opened the cupboard. We stood for a moment regarding our inheritance of tiles.

Then Jean took one out. For years the tile just inside the entrance had rocked underfoot, making a noise like a spoon set down sharply. The following Tuesday a man from maintenance replaced it. Afterward the regulars kept stepping on that spot twice, once expecting the sound, once checking its absence.

I went away to college in September. I don't know what became of the knob. What I remember is the old man from locker twelve coming in out of the rain, stamping his feet, and pausing on the repaired tile. He took one careful step backward. He looked down. Then he looked over at Jean, who was doing the crossword.

“You fixed my note,” he said.

“Your what?”

He tapped the tile with his heel. “Used to be an F.”

Jean reached into the till and handed him his key. “You'll have to hum it yourself.”

The first thing my father did after he retired was take the numbers off our house. They were brass, and he wanted to polish them. He set them on newspaper on the kitchen table, where, detached from the brick, they looked less like an address than a disappointing hand of cards: a one, a four, another one. By noon he had made one of the ones shine. By evening he had discovered that the four was not brass at all. Somebody, years before we bought the place, had painted a cheap metal four to match its more distinguished neighbors.

This pleased him enormously. He carried the four around in his shirt pocket for several days, taking it out whenever conversation approached a natural lull. The woman at the pharmacy heard about it. So did a boy collecting money for the school orchestra. My father had spent forty years as a municipal accountant, a profession that had taught him to appreciate discrepancies and had seldom permitted him to enjoy them. Here was a discrepancy with no injured party, no missing receipt, no need for a meeting on Thursday. He stripped the paint and found a handsome gray metal underneath.

My mother wanted the numbers back up. People were beginning to miss the house. A parcel of bath towels went to the neighbors, and a man coming to inspect the furnace drove past twice before calling from the corner. My father agreed that something must be done. What he did was buy a narrow plank of cedar. On this he intended to mount the numbers, setting the gray four a little higher than the brass ones. He showed me a pencil drawing. The effect he was after, he explained, was of a tall child walking between two short parents.

I was thirty-eight then and in a hurry that had already lasted fifteen years. I had come over to borrow a stepladder. Standing in the garage with one hand on its aluminum rail, I suggested that he could simply screw the numbers back into their original holes. He considered this proposal as seriously as he would have considered a revised estimate for resurfacing a road. Then he said, “Well, yes, if the point was to finish.” I laughed because I thought he was making fun of himself. He looked mildly surprised, and I took the ladder home on my car.

For the next month the cedar plank occupied two sawhorses in the garage. My father beveled its edges, disliked the bevel, and made the plank narrower in the course of removing it. He tried three finishes on scraps. When I visited, he was generally sitting on an upturned bucket, studying some part of the operation that did not, to my eye, reward sustained study. Meanwhile my mother wrote 141 on an index card and taped it inside the front window. The card curled in the sun. From the road it resembled a small hand beckoning a driver to come closer.

One Saturday, while we were having coffee, the boy from the orchestra came back. He was selling grapefruit this time. His name was Leon, he played viola, and he wanted to know how the four was coming along. My father took him to the garage. Through the kitchen window I could see them bending over the plank, their heads at nearly the same height because my father had begun to stoop and Leon had not yet begun to grow. My mother bought six grapefruit. “I don’t even like grapefruit,” she said, putting the receipt in the drawer with the scissors.

Leon suggested blue. This was a serious interruption. Until then my father had been working within the range of colors that wood might reasonably be persuaded to become: honey, tobacco, the brown of tea left standing. Blue introduced the question of the front door, which was green, and the shutters, which were black. It also raised the possibility that the plank did not have to look like wood. They spent the afternoon mixing leftover house paint in a yogurt container. At five Leon went home with a blue thumbnail and my father went in to lie down before supper.

The finished sign was nothing special. I think this is important. The blue dried darker than either of them expected. The four, raised half an inch above the ones, looked like a four that somebody had put on crooked. There were two visible screw heads, although my father dabbed them with paint. He installed it crooked, too, then corrected it, leaving a small pale wound in the brick. My mother took down the index card. The furnace man found us on his first try the following autumn, an achievement for which he received considerably more praise than he could understand.

I have the sign now, in a box with a meat thermometer, some photographs, and the key to a car nobody in the family owns. I could put it on my own house, but my number is sixty, and even my father would have admitted that this presents difficulties. Sometimes I take it out when I am looking for something else. The back is more interesting than the front. There are six pencil marks where he considered placing the four. There is a blue whorl left by a thumb. A cedar shaving is caught beneath the head of a screw.

Last week I finally returned the stepladder. Not to my father, of course, but to Leon, who bought the house with his husband and keeps finding things my father left unfinished. We stood in the garage deciding where the ladder ought to go. It would fit beside the door if we moved a hook; it would fit behind the workbench if we shortened a shelf. Leon got a tape measure. His husband brought out three chairs and a plate of sliced pears. After a while we folded the ladder and laid it on the floor, where it was in nobody’s way that afternoon.

The most useful object in our apartment building was a brown chair that nobody wanted. It stood on the half landing between the second and third floors, directly beneath a window painted shut since at least the invention of margarine. The chair had a split in its vinyl seat. In summer the edges of the split pinched bare thighs, a fact every child in the building learned once and remembered forever. On the underside, in blue ballpoint, someone had written DENNIS. Nobody knew whether Dennis had owned the chair or merely been the last person willing to crawl under it.

On Tuesday evenings Mrs. Vale sat there halfway up with her groceries. She could manage the stairs or she could manage a conversation, but not both, so if you met her climbing you had to wait for the chair before telling her anything interesting. This gave the news a pleasing ceremonial quality. You carried it beside her, along with the bag containing the tins, while she gripped the rail and concentrated. Then she would sit, arrange her skirt over her knees, and say, “Well?” Even the announcement that the corner shop had run out of eggs felt worth the climb.

One February morning the chair disappeared. In its place was a rectangle of cleaner linoleum and a single blue thread. Somebody taped a note to the window: WHERE IS CHAIR? The missing article made the question sound urgent and international, as though embassies had already been notified. By lunchtime a second hand had added WHICH CHAIR? This was generally considered a poor joke, although my father maintained for years that it was a legitimate request for information. There were, he pointed out, millions of chairs. My mother asked how many of them he thought ordinarily lived outside our front door.

For three days people offered substitutes. A scarlet footstool appeared first, too low for Mrs. Vale to rise from without assistance. Next came a folding garden chair that closed around its occupant with the brisk discretion of a dentist drawing a curtain. Someone contributed a piano bench; someone else took it back to practice scales. Meanwhile the notes multiplied. One tenant blamed the landlord, another blamed teenagers, and a third proposed buying a replacement together. Under this proposal Mr. Levin wrote that he would happily contribute provided the new chair was not brown. We discovered strong feelings about municipal orange.

I was eleven and eager to investigate. My friend Ada had a magnifying glass, which we carried conspicuously despite finding nothing small enough to require it. We knocked on every door and asked when the resident had last seen the chair. Answers varied from yesterday to eighteen months ago. A man on the fourth floor said he had never seen it, then described it accurately enough to make himself our principal suspect. Ada suggested a trap. I suggested biscuits. We went downstairs to her kitchen and ate six ginger biscuits while discussing whether the police were allowed to have favorites.

On Saturday we found the chair in the laundry room. It was upside down on a blanket beside the boiler, with its four feet pointing toward a row of drying socks. Mr. Okafor from the ground floor was kneeling over it, easing tiny brass tacks out of the seat with a screwdriver. He had seen the split grow wider, he explained, and had taken the chair downstairs to mend it. Why hadn't he left a note? He looked honestly surprised. He had expected to finish before breakfast. Then the wood beneath the vinyl had turned out to be rotten too.

He showed us the old seat board. It came apart between his fingers like wet cardboard. The new one was cut from a cupboard door his sister had left in his cellar after remodeling her kitchen. One side was painted a brilliant yellow. This would face downward, he said, so nobody would know. Ada and I exchanged a glance. Here was precisely the kind of information that justified an investigation. We helped stretch green fabric across the seat, pulling opposite corners until our knuckles paled, while he drove in the tacks. The fabric had once been his good winter coat.

We carried the chair upstairs that afternoon. Mrs. Vale tried it first, although it was not Tuesday and she had no groceries. She settled herself, shifted experimentally, and pronounced the seat half an inch too high. Mr. Okafor said he could shorten the legs. She said he would do no such thing; she was making an observation, not lodging a complaint. Several people came out to admire the work. Mr. Levin liked the green. My father examined the window notes and admitted that, under the circumstances, WHICH CHAIR? had probably been an unnecessary question. Nobody claimed responsibility for writing it.

Years later, visiting my parents, I found a boy lying on his back beneath the chair. His shoes stuck out across the landing. For one absurd second I thought he was repairing a complicated piece of machinery, perhaps draining its oil. Then he wriggled free and asked me if I knew about the yellow. I told him I did. He looked disappointed, so I asked if he knew about Dennis. Within seconds he was back underneath, inspecting the rails. I waited with my shopping bag against my ankle until he emerged, dusty and triumphant, having found all six faded letters.

I almost told him everything: the cupboard door, the coat, the notes, the ginger biscuits. Instead I sat down. I had forgotten how much easier it was to talk to somebody on that landing when neither person was trying to get somewhere else. The boy had a theory that Dennis was a carpenter who signed all his work in secret. Why in secret? Because otherwise, he explained patiently, people would keep asking him to make things. Upstairs my mother opened her door and called to see what was keeping me. “News,” I called back, and stayed to hear the rest.

The first thing my aunt did when she bought the old cinema was sit in every seat. There were two hundred and sixteen of them, red velvet gone brown at the shoulders, and she gave each one the length of a song on her portable radio. This took most of a week. When I asked what she was listening for, she said she was looking. From the back corner, the emergency light floated in the middle of the screen like a small green moon. From the front row, a tall person could see the rafters. She wrote these things down.

I was seventeen that summer and employed to remove chewing gum. My equipment consisted of a paint scraper, a bucket, and an apron advertising a brand of vermouth. Under seat F12, I found a silver ring caught in a hard pink wad. My aunt washed it and put it at the ticket window beside a sign saying FOUND SOMETHING? LOOK HERE. I suggested that the first word should be LOST. She considered this, then turned the sign over and wrote RING. This was typical of her. She would accept a correction without necessarily accepting the solution that came with it.

The cinema had been closed eleven years. Nobody in town had asked for it to open again. People wished my aunt luck in the tone they used for somebody setting out to walk a very considerable distance in unsuitable shoes. The hardware merchant offered her a discount on light bulbs but declined to advertise before the feature. My father, her brother, brought round a casserole and checked the fire doors. A girl from my chemistry class came in to ask whether we were hiring. When I showed her the scraper, she remembered an appointment and left me to my work.

On opening night we showed a comedy about two musicians who inherit a horse. Six people came, including my father, who paid full price and bought almonds although he disliked them. I watched from the aisle. The strange thing about six people laughing in a room built for hundreds is that you can hear them decide. One woman began with a surprised bark, a man joined in, and soon the others took the risk. Toward the end, when the horse entered a courtroom wearing the judge’s hat, all six laughed at once. Upstairs, my aunt let out a whistle.

She never made much money on the films. What saved her was the rain. That October it rained for nineteen days, flooding the basement room where the municipal choir rehearsed. Its director asked to borrow the cinema on Tuesday evening. Forty singers arrived carrying folding stands, wet coats, and the smell of peppermint. I had stayed late to balance the till. From behind the ticket window I heard them trying to find a note together. At first they sounded like furniture being moved upstairs. Then the note settled, and the loose coins in their little wooden trays began to tremble.

After that came a dance teacher whose studio ceiling had fallen in, then a retired surveyor who wanted to explain the geology of the valley to anyone willing to listen. He brought an astonishing number of rocks. The youngest person in his audience was eight and the oldest was ninety, and both wanted to know whether our hill might ever become a volcano. The surveyor said no. The child looked disappointed. The old man looked disappointed too. My aunt sold thirty cups of tea and found a striped mitten, which she placed beside the ring under a new sign: THINGS.

By Christmas the sign had become inaccurate again. There were so many things that my aunt had moved them into a glass cabinet, while the sign remained at the window, pointing at me. Inside were three spectacles cases, a tin of cinnamon sweets, one shoe with a buckle, and a photograph of a young sailor standing beside a donkey. People began to stop by just to inspect the cabinet. Sometimes they recognized an object. More often they recognized a category of misfortune. “I’m always doing that,” they would say, touching their own glasses or glancing down to check their shoes.

I left for college the following September. By then the cinema had acquired a piano, a license to serve soup, and a regular Thursday audience for films selected by drawing titles from a hat. My aunt wrote letters on the backs of unused tickets. They were short letters. A visiting cellist had broken a string. Someone had claimed the mitten. The surveyor had got married to the choir director, which struck me as news deserving rather more space than the mitten. When I told her so, she sent another ticket: “He wore blue. She wore yellow. We had enough spoons.”

Years later, after she died, I came home to help my father clear her flat. We found the notebook from that first week, its pages ruled into columns for seat, sightline, noise, and comfort. Some entries were practical: loose bolt, torn cushion, draught from door. Others were harder to interpret. At H9 she had written, “Good place to receive bad news.” At C4: “Bring somebody here who has forgotten how big a face is.” The final entry, for the narrow seat beside the rear exit, said simply, “Nobody can see you from here, but you can still hear them laugh.”

That evening I took the notebook to the cinema. A different woman ran it now. She was showing a film about an astronaut returning to Earth, and the lobby smelled of soup. I bought a ticket and found the narrow seat by the exit. Halfway through, the astronaut dropped a bag of oranges in a supermarket. They rolled everywhere, bright against the dull floor, and people on all sides of me began to laugh. I sat there until the last orange stopped rolling. Then I opened the notebook on my knee and added, underneath my aunt’s entry, “Yes, you can.”

**The Drawer Beside the Stove**

On the morning we emptied my mother's kitchen, my sister claimed the good saucepan, my brother took the blue mixing bowl, and I asked for the drawer beside the stove. I meant its contents, but my brother had already fetched a screwdriver. For a moment the three of us stood considering whether the drawer itself might come in handy. This was how our mother had raised us: before a thing went into the rubbish, somebody had to imagine a reasonably convincing future for it. My brother put the screwdriver away. We found a biscuit tin and tipped the drawer into it.

At home I spread everything on the table. There were fourteen birthday candles, three of them burned down to little pastel commas. There was a key with a paper label reading BACK, although my mother had lived in four houses since she started labeling keys. There were elastic bands gone rigid in the shapes of the vegetables they had once embraced. Under a square of sandpaper lay a photograph of my father holding an enormous fish. Someone had written on the back, in handwriting I did not recognize, “Actually quite small.” I rang my sister. She said the handwriting was mine.

The prize, if that is the word, was a little wooden bird with a red beak and a steel clip underneath. I remembered it perched on a bag of flour, then on the curtains when the catch broke, then briefly on the collar of our elderly spaniel, who accepted decoration as he accepted weather. I clipped it to my shirt while I sorted. An hour later the postman delivered a parcel and glanced at my chest with such careful courtesy that I signed for it without explaining. For the rest of the afternoon I felt oddly well dressed in the bird.

My mother had never called it a junk drawer. It was simply where you looked. If a spectacle screw fell into the carpet, you looked there for the magnifying glass. If a child announced over breakfast that school required a model volcano by nine, you looked there for a cork. The fact that neither item was usually present did not diminish the authority of the place. Looking bought a minute in which panic could settle into ingenuity. Often you emerged with something quite different and an idea that would never have occurred to a person in possession of the proper equipment.

I used to think this habit belonged to an era of shortages. My mother rinsed foil, saved string, and cut the blank halves off letters before throwing them away. Yet she could be gloriously wasteful. She bought raspberries in February. She once took a taxi thirty miles because a friend on the telephone sounded a little flat. What she disliked was not expenditure but premature conclusions. A torn envelope had finished carrying a letter; whether it had finished being useful was another question. A friend who said she was perfectly fine might still like somebody to arrive with cake and raspberries.

Near the bottom of the tin I found a brass fitting like a thimble with ambitions. It had threads inside, two holes in its side, and a patch of green paint. I sent a picture to the family chat. My brother suggested part of a lamp. My sister said pressure cooker, then immediately withdrew the suggestion on grounds that she did not want responsibility for what happened next. My niece, who was seven, said it was a hat for a frog. Nobody improved on that. I put it on the windowsill, where the late sun filled its two holes with light.

For several months the biscuit tin remained in my hallway. I intended to reduce its contents to essentials, by which I meant objects I could explain to another adult without embarrassment. Then my neighbor knocked. Her grandson was visiting, the battery cover on his toy train would not stay shut, and did I happen to have one of those absurdly tiny screwdrivers? I did not. What I had was a narrow strip of thin blue ribbon. We tied it around the engine, made a bow over the boiler, and sent the train circling under the table in magnificent if implausible steam.

After that I moved the tin to the kitchen. It began to collect things my mother had never touched: a spare button from my winter coat, a token for a swimming locker, the smooth white stone my niece entrusted to me while she learned to cartwheel. I worried briefly about mixing the old collection with the new. Then I remembered my mother shaking fresh breadcrumbs into a jar that already contained breadcrumbs. Nobody in our house had ever made a solemn distinction between Tuesday's toast and Friday's. The jar was for crumbs. The drawer, I decided, had been for whatever came next.

Last week my sister came to supper. While I drained potatoes, she opened the tin in search of a candle for the table. She found the little pink stubs and laughed, then set one upright in a clementine peel. We ate by its meager light for perhaps forty seconds before the wick drowned. For those seconds we could see each other perfectly well; it was the potatoes that vanished into shadow. My sister reached across and took my hand. Then she switched on the light and said they needed salt. They did. I had forgotten it entirely, as I often do.

When she left, I washed the plates, dried the bird where a splash of gravy had reached its tail, and clipped it onto the open bag of coffee. Tomorrow I may clear out the brittle bands. They snap at a touch now, and even my mother would concede that a band incapable of stretching has retired from the trade. The brass fitting stays. This summer I am taking my niece down to the pond behind the library, where frogs sit among the reeds with their handsome heads quite bare. We have no intention of interfering. We merely wish to compare sizes.

samples.result:
On Saturday mornings, my father used to turn the kitchen clock to face the wall. He did this after breakfast, with the dishes still on the table and the last pancake cooling in the pan. He never announced it. One moment we lived in a house where it was nine fifteen; the next we lived in a house where a small round clock was studying the wallpaper. My mother wore a watch, of course. The oven had a green digital display. Nobody was being fooled. Still, something happened when he turned that clock around. We stopped asking what came next.

What came next, usually, was washing up. My sister washed and I dried, an arrangement based on the fact that she considered my washing inadequate and I considered her drying nonexistent. She would lift a plate from the water and hold it out without looking, confident that my hand would be there. For years I thought this was an ordinary way to do dishes. Only later, sharing apartments with people who set each object carefully in a rack, did I understand that we had worked out a little piece of choreography. Even now, handed a wet plate, I turn left.

Behind our house was a strip of land too narrow for a garden and too shady for grass. My father called it the orchard because a single pear tree grew there. The pears were terrible. They had a hard, gritty band around the core, and their skins went from green to brown without passing through any state you would willingly eat. Every autumn he picked them. Every autumn my mother set three in a bowl on the table. Visitors admired them. We accepted the compliments with the smooth, collective dishonesty of a family whose decorative fruit could break a tooth.

One Saturday, a branch came down. There had been no storm. We were inside arguing about whether a particular sheet of newspaper was old enough to put under a paint tin when we heard a crack, followed by the unmistakable sound of several dozen pears landing on the shed. Outside, the branch lay across the roof like an arm thrown over the back of a couch. A squirrel ran along it, stopped at the broken end, and looked down. For one absurd second we all waited for the squirrel to offer an assessment. Then my father went for the ladder.

The job took most of the morning. My father cut the branch into lengths while my sister steadied the ladder and I gathered pears in a bucket. My mother, who had objected to the pear tree on practical grounds for twenty years, stood in the doorway defending it against an accusation nobody had made. “It held on a long time,” she said. A neighbor came over with a better saw. Another brought coffee. By noon we had seven people in the yard, two ladders, three opinions about pruning, and enough wood to heat a room we did not actually have.

Among the fallen pears was one that had split cleanly in half. A wasp settled on it. I crouched to watch, mostly because somebody was about to suggest that I sweep the shed roof. The wasp worked at the flesh with such patient concentration that I began to feel we had judged the pears by an unnecessarily narrow standard. Here was a customer, after all. Here was genuine enthusiasm. When I told my mother, she said that if the wasp wanted the rest of them, it was welcome to bring a truck. She kept the split pear on the fence.

I remember that morning better than I remember my graduation. This seems unfair to everyone who rented a gown, drove through traffic, or sat on a folding chair waiting for my surname to arrive. I remember being happy at graduation. I remember a blister on my heel. But I cannot tell you what the sky looked like. On the morning the branch fell, the sky was white at the edges and blue directly overhead. The neighbor with the saw had shaving cream under one ear. My sister drank coffee from a measuring cup because we had run out of mugs.

For a while I tried to manufacture mornings like that. I invited friends over without an agenda, which meant that the absence of an agenda became the agenda, and I spent the afternoon anxiously checking whether everyone was being spontaneous. I bought pears from a market. They were delicious, which spoiled the effect. Eventually I understood that nobody in our yard had set out to make a memory. A branch had fallen. It needed moving. The coffee was not symbolic; the people holding the ladder wanted coffee. Whatever lasted had entered by a side door while we were carrying wood.

Last winter, my sister called while I was making supper. She had found the kitchen clock in a box of things our parents no longer wanted. Did I want it? I asked whether it worked. She said it lost eleven minutes a day. We agreed that this was a considerable professional failing in a clock, although perhaps consistent with its upbringing. A week later it arrived wrapped in an old dish towel. There was a pale rectangle on the back where a price sticker had been. I put in a battery and hung it beside the kitchen window, facing in.

It tells an increasingly improbable time. Yesterday I ate lunch at half past six. I could have it repaired, but its position is useful: from the stove, I can see the clock and, just beyond it, the apartment building opposite. Around dusk, a man there waters a row of plants with a blue jug. He takes each pot to the sink and lets it drain before returning it to the sill. I have no idea who he is. Sometimes, waiting for water to boil, I watch him finish. Then I salt the water, reach for the pasta, and make dinner.

On the last Thursday of every month, the library in Bellweather lent out a room. The room was upstairs, twelve feet square, with a window over the bus stop and a radiator that knocked even in June. Anyone could book it for forty minutes. You could bring in whatever you needed, provided you took it away afterward. For years the reservation sheet had hung beside the copier, under a photograph of the town's first snowplow. Few people noticed it. Those who did generally assumed the room was for meetings. It was, sometimes. But a meeting was not required.

Ruth discovered this at sixty-three, six weeks after retiring from the bakery. She had gone to the library to copy the warranty for her refrigerator. While the machine warmed itself, she read the sheet. At ten on the previous Thursday, somebody named Dennis had written “accordion.” At eleven, two sisters had put “discussion of Dad.” The noon appointment said simply “floor.” Ruth asked the librarian what that meant. “I believe he wanted to lie down,” the librarian said. “At home he has a dog who takes that as an invitation.” Ruth booked the next available slot and wrote “table.”

She owned a perfectly good table. What she lacked was a table at which nothing had happened yet. At her kitchen table she had paid bills, peeled apples, signed school forms, and listened while her husband explained why he wanted to leave. The table had outlasted the marriage by nineteen years. One end still bore a pale ring from the pot of tea she had made that afternoon, because apparently even the end of a marriage required tea. She liked the table. She just wanted, for forty minutes, another one. She hadn't decided what to do with it.

On Thursday she brought a grocery bag containing an orange, a pencil, a packet of envelopes, and a blue saucer. The librarian unlocked the room. The table inside was gray laminate, faintly sticky at one corner. Ruth set the orange on the saucer. Outside, a boy at the bus stop tried to balance a skateboard on its nose. He nearly succeeded several times, and each failure seemed to interest him as much as the attempt. She watched until his bus arrived. Then she turned over an envelope and drew the orange. It looked like a potato in a shallow boat.

She drew it again. This time she noticed that the orange was not round. Its weight had settled toward the bottom, and the little green mark where the stem had been was well off center. She had handled thousands of oranges at the bakery. In December she could grate the zest from sixty before the first batch of morning rolls came out. She knew how hard to press without reaching the bitter white underneath. Yet if anybody had asked her that morning where an orange kept its widest part, she would have had to guess. This struck her as funny.

At the end of forty minutes she had seven drawings and an appointment for the following month. She ate the orange on the walk home. The day was cold enough to sting the thin places beside her fingernails when the juice ran into them. At home she put the drawings in the drawer with the refrigerator warranty. She did not buy a sketchbook. Buying the proper equipment seemed likely to attract the attention of some inner supervisor who would want to know her intentions, her schedule, and whether she had considered doing something useful with the finished work.

In February she brought a whisk. It was a poor choice for a beginner, all those wires disappearing behind one another, but she had liked it in the shop because the handle was yellow. In March she brought her left shoe and spent most of the session trying to loosen a knot before realizing she could draw the knot. In April the room was closed: a pipe had burst. She sat on the library steps and drew the key to her house. A little girl stopped to watch. “You missed a tooth,” the girl said. Ruth looked. She had.

In May, Dennis was coming out as she arrived. He carried his accordion in a case lined with red velvet and had the exhausted good humor of someone who had just moved a wardrobe upstairs. Ruth asked what he had played. “The same eight bars I played in January,” he said. “Any better?” she asked. “Oh, considerably louder.” He held the door for her. On the table lay a black button from his coat. Ruth called after him, but he had reached the stairs. She drew the button, then left it at the desk in an envelope marked Dennis.

By autumn the drawer no longer closed easily. One evening Ruth took the envelopes out and spread them across her kitchen table. There was the whisk, more tangled on paper than in life. There was the key with its corrected tooth. There were two attempts at a pear her neighbor had grown, a bent teaspoon, a pinecone, and the clasp of her mother's old purse. She shifted them around to make room for supper. The orange she liked best was the first one. That little boat of a saucer seemed quite seaworthy. She propped it against the salt.

The next morning, while her toast darkened, she drew the salt shaker on the back of an electricity bill. Halfway through, the toaster clicked and startled her into making a long stray line. She buttered her toast, sat down again, and gave the salt shaker a companion at the far end of the line: a small, improbable dog on a lead. It was the first thing she had drawn that wasn't there. She gave the dog a fine curled tail. Then, because there was room on the table and the light was good, she put in the person walking it.

The first thing I repaired for money was a clock that had nothing wrong with it. I was twelve. Mrs. Alvarez brought it across the landing wrapped in a dish towel, though it was an ordinary plastic kitchen clock with a picture of a rooster on its face. She said it lost ten minutes every morning. I put it on my desk, watched it through lunch, and reported that it kept excellent time. She gave me two dollars anyway. Years later I learned that her husband had been turning it back so she would sit with him a little longer over coffee.

My father repaired shoes in a narrow shop below our apartment. He disliked the word *cobbler*, which customers used with an air of having remembered the name of a rare bird. “Shoe repair is fine,” he would say. He let me keep a drawer under the counter for the small appliances people brought after Mrs. Alvarez recommended me. Most needed batteries. One radio needed its volume knob pushed firmly back onto the stem. My father watched me return it to a delighted cabdriver and said, “You know, there are jobs where they pay you even when you don’t get lucky.”

The shop smelled of leather, rubber, and the orange my father peeled at three each afternoon. He took the skin off in one piece and laid it on the radiator in winter. He could recognize certain customers by the sound of their approach. There was a school principal who landed hard on the outside of his right heel, and a florist whose wooden clogs announced her from halfway down the block. When the florist came in wearing sneakers one Saturday, my father looked genuinely startled, as if a person he knew had climbed in through a window.

I did not take over the business. I went away to study accounting, married a woman who taught swimming, and became competent at a number of things that would have bored my father senseless. He sold the shop when his fingers grew too stiff for stitching. For his retirement party we ordered a cake in the shape of a boot. The bakery made it bright blue, a color he had never once been asked to put on a shoe. He ate the heel standing up in the kitchen, still wearing the paper napkin my daughter had tucked into his collar.

After he died, my mother asked me to sort his tools. She wanted the cupboard for towels. I had imagined this as an afternoon of solemn decisions, but most of the cupboard contained dried tubes of glue and receipts from a supplier in Ohio. In a tobacco tin I found brass eyelets, three foreign coins, and a photograph of myself at twelve behind his counter. On the back he had written, in the block capitals he used on claim tickets, RADIO DEPARTMENT. I put the photograph in my pocket and threw away the glue. The tools went home with me in a grocery bag.

They stayed in the bag for almost four years. Then one wet evening my daughter came over with a loose strap on her sandal. She was twenty and had recently discovered that her parents owned various things she preferred not to buy. She had come for tape. Instead I got out the bag. We spread everything across the dining table: awls, pincers, a little hammer polished dark where his thumb had rested. I knew what each tool was called. To my considerable embarrassment, I had almost no idea what to do with any of them.

My daughter found a shoe repairer near the bus station. We took the sandal there the next morning. The man behind the counter examined the strap and asked whether she wanted the stitching to match. The original thread was yellow. He had brown, black, and a fierce pink left over from a dance costume. She chose pink and paid to have the sound strap restitched to match it. While we waited, I told him about my father’s shop. He asked what machine my father had used. I described its green paint and the noise it made. “That narrows it down to all of them,” he said.

I had expected the tools to make me sad. What bothered me instead was the loss of all those answers. For years I could have asked my father why he wet a piece of leather before stretching it, or what he listened for when he tapped a sole. I had been present for so much of the work that I mistook proximity for instruction. Yet I could remember, with useless precision, how he answered the telephone: “Yes, shoes,” as though settling an argument begun before the caller was born. My daughter still answers my calls that way when she is in a good mood.

The repairer bought most of the tools. I kept the hammer because it fit my hand, and because a hammer, unlike a curved needle, stood some chance of earning its keep in our house. A month later I used it to hang a shelf in the laundry room. The shelf sloped slightly toward the door. My wife set a marble on it to demonstrate the problem, and we watched the marble gather speed and drop neatly into a basket of clean socks. For a while we kept a marble beside the detergent so visitors could see the trick.

Last Sunday my daughter brought her little boy over for breakfast. He found the marble in a saucer of loose change. I carried him into the laundry room, cleared a space between the detergent and a box of clothespins, and showed him where to set it down. Each time it dropped he demanded another turn. From the kitchen my daughter called that our coffee was getting cold. I could hear her scraping the last of the good jam onto her toast. “Coming,” I called. The boy held out his hand. I fished the marble out of the socks and gave it back.

The first thing Mara repaired for the town was a bench that nobody remembered buying. It stood outside the post office, facing a brick wall. Someone had painted it green around the bolts, leaving six rusty circles like the rings left by tiny cups. When her father was alive, he used to sit there after collecting his pension, even in rain. Asked what he was looking at, he would say, “Nothing yet.” She had taken this for one of his jokes. Now, kneeling on his folded coat to undo the bolts, she found that the wall was rather good company.

There were things to see if you stayed low. At the foot of the wall grew a fern no longer than her thumb. A child's handwriting, scratched into the lowest brick, announced that ANDY CAN. Higher up, a pale rectangle showed where a notice had protected the surface from thirty years of weather. Mara was trying to decide what Andy could do when the postmaster came outside with two mugs. He set one on the pavement. “Council finally sent somebody?” he asked. “No,” she said. “Mind if I tell people they did? I've written them four letters about that bolt.”

She took the boards home in a shopping trolley. In her kitchen she laid them across two chairs and sanded until the room smelled of pencil shavings. Her father had taught her to run an old stocking along finished wood; if it caught, there was still work to do. Lacking a stocking, she sacrificed one of her sheer black socks. It snagged so often that by bedtime it resembled a small fishing net. She ate her supper standing at the sink because the chairs were occupied, and discovered she could watch the moon rise in the bowl of a spoon.

On Thursday she put the bench together again. On Friday a woman telephoned about a gate. On Saturday somebody left a toaster outside her door with an envelope containing three pounds and an apology for the crumbs. Mara returned the toaster unopened. She knew wood and hinges, and she understood the sort of plumbing that misbehaved in plain sight, but electricity seemed to her a private agreement between clever people and lightning. She kept the envelope, though, having noticed on its back a recipe for seed cake. In place of the money she left a slice wrapped in greaseproof paper.

By the end of summer she had mended a dozen gates, two cupboards, a puppet theatre and the long drawer beneath the map case in the library. The drawer was her favorite. Every time the librarian opened it, the river on the oldest map acquired another crease. Mara planed a whisper from each runner and rubbed the wood with the stub of a birthday candle. Afterward the river slid into daylight without a sound. The librarian stood there opening and closing it until a boy at the reading table looked up and asked if she needed him to fetch somebody.

People began asking Mara what she meant to do with herself, as though she had spent these months on a railway platform waiting for her life to arrive. She could not explain that she liked seeing where things wore out. A cupboard door usually sagged on the side nearest the stove, because that was where a cook reached for salt. The puppet theatre had lost a strip of velvet exactly where the dragon rested his chin between appearances. Wear gave you a picture of the person who wasn't there. Sometimes, of course, all it gave you was a loose screw.

In October the council sent a truck to collect the bench. Mara happened to be buying stamps. Through the post office window she saw two men in orange jackets studying the bolts with an attention that felt almost affectionate. She went out holding a sheet of seabirds, each worth the price of a letter. The younger man showed her his work order. The bench was on a list of street furniture to be replaced. Its replacement, already in the truck, was black, made of recycled plastic and shaped so rain would run straight off. “Sensible,” Mara admitted, surprising them both.

They let her have the old one, but there was nowhere in her kitchen for a bench, and her garden was a passage wide enough for one determined bicycle. For a week it stood in the postmaster's garage beside a broken rowing machine. Then Andy, who turned out to be a retired midwife named Andrea, suggested the ferry landing. “I used to sit on the ground there,” she said. “These days I can get down all right, but getting up creates a public spectacle.” They borrowed the library van and carried the bench down to the water on a Sunday.

It faced the estuary now. There were cormorants on the pilings and a red buoy that leaned sideways at the turn of the tide, as if listening for an answer under the water. Mara tried out each end of the seat. The view was certainly better, but she missed the fern, and she wondered who would notice when frost finally loosened that scratched brick. Andrea sat down beside her, bringing the smell of peppermints. For a while neither spoke. Across the channel someone was hanging white sheets on a line; the wind filled them one by one, like square sails.

“What was it you could do?” Mara asked at last. Andrea considered. She said there had been a boy, perhaps, or a spelling test. Possibly she had only wanted to scratch something into a wall and had been interrupted before she finished. “Andy can what?” Mara said. “Well, precisely.” The ferry came in, lowering its ramp onto the wet concrete. A cyclist rolled ashore with yellow flowers sticking out of his pannier. Andrea moved her bag so he could sit between them. He did, and for the next ten minutes all three watched the empty boat go back for somebody.
