The lost and found at the municipal pool lived in a shopping cart with one bad wheel. By August it held enough towels to dry a small wedding party, though no wedding party would have chosen that combination of colors. There were goggles with only one lens, a paperback swollen to the thickness of a dictionary, and the left half of a pair of bright green flippers. I was seventeen. My job, among other duties, was to wheel the cart out each morning and let people look for what they had lost.

People approached the cart differently depending on what they were missing. A person who had lost a towel went through the pile with brisk, businesslike movements. A person who had lost a wedding ring stood a few feet away and asked permission to come closer. Children generally recognized their possessions by some detail invisible to adults. A boy once picked a plain white sock out of a mass of plain white socks and said, with complete certainty, “This is the one that hurts.” His mother accepted this as proof, and so did I.

My favorite claim involved a blue plastic bowl. It sat in the cart for three weeks, nested inside a sun hat. Then one afternoon a woman spotted it from the deep end. She climbed the ladder, crossed the concrete dripping wet, and lifted the bowl above her head. “I knew it,” she called to her husband. He was eating pretzels on a folding chair. Without looking up, he said, “I never said you didn’t bring it.” An entire marriage passed between those two sentences, and then she went back in the water.

At closing time on the last Sunday of the season, we sorted the cart. Anything still useful went to a charity shop. Everything else went into black bags. I found this an unpleasant task, particularly when a thing had been carefully labeled. There was a tiny red sweatshirt with DANIEL written inside the collar in permanent marker. Whoever had written the name had gone over the D twice. I put the sweatshirt in the charity box and turned it so the collar would not show. I could not have said whom I was sparing.

Years later, while helping my father move, I opened a kitchen drawer and found six cheese graters. He lived alone and, owing to an old injury to his thumb, bought his cheese already grated. I lined the graters up on the counter. Two were identical. One was the little rotary kind you see in restaurants. Another resembled a steel washboard made for a doll. My father examined the collection with interest, as if the graters had assembled there on their own to hear an announcement. “Your aunt gave me that one,” he said.

I asked which ones he wanted to keep. This was the wrong question, although it took us an hour to discover why. He chose the rotary grater, then changed his mind because it was hard to clean. He chose the washboard, then remembered that it scraped his knuckles. Finally he wrapped all six in newspaper. At his new apartment, there was no drawer deep enough for the parcel. It spent two nights on the kitchen table, taking up the place where he liked to set his elbow while doing the crossword.

On the third morning, he rang to ask whether I wanted a cheese grater. I owned one already, but I went over. He had unwrapped them and was feeding the packing paper through the rotary model. Short gray ribbons fell into his lap. “This one was your mother’s idea of a good present,” he said. “She liked the handle.” He turned it a few more times. I had forgotten the particular squeak it made, and then, hearing it, remembered being eight and waiting for spaghetti. I took that one. He gave the others away.

I have used it perhaps four times. It really is hard to clean. A little crescent of Parmesan gets wedged behind the drum, where the bristles of the dish brush cannot reach. Sometimes I think I ought to mount it on the wall as a piece of family history, but that would make it solemn, and nobody in my family ever experienced a solemn moment with that grater. Mostly it lives beside the potato masher. When I need the masher, I move the grater. This strikes me as about the right amount of ceremony.

Last winter I left a wool scarf on a train. It was charcoal gray, a color selected, apparently, to match the upholstery of every commuter railway in the country. I filled out an online form. Under “distinguishing features,” I wrote that one end had a small burn from a spark at a bonfire. The form also wanted an estimated value. I entered twelve dollars. There was no field for the fact that it was exactly the right length to wind twice around my neck without leaving ends that dipped into soup.

A week later, a clerk called. They had three gray scarves, she said, but none with a burn. Was I sure about the burn? I was. She sounded disappointed. Then she asked me to hold on. I heard a drawer open and close, followed by the hollow bump of a receiver being set down on a counter. When she came back, she said, “I was looking for a hole. You mean the bit where the wool’s gone shiny?” Yes, I said, that was precisely what I meant. “Well,” she said, pleased, “you could have said shiny.”

I picked it up on Friday. The clerk had threaded a paper tag through the fringe and written my surname on it, going over the first letter twice where her pen had failed. I unwound the string and handed her back the tag. Outside, the weather had turned unexpectedly mild. I carried the scarf home in my hand, stopping once at a crossing to check that I still had it, although all the way from the station I had been rubbing the shiny patch between my finger and thumb.

The first thing we lent was a ladder. It belonged to my father, who had painted it yellow after backing the car over its predecessor in the dark. When Mrs. Vale wanted to clean her gutters, she walked into our hardware shop and asked what a ladder cost. Dad told her. She stood quite still for a moment, looking at the notes in her purse. Then he said, “Actually, what you want costs nothing. You only need to be eight feet taller for half an hour.” He took her round the back and showed her how to work the stiff hinge.

By the time I inherited the shop, the lending book occupied an entire drawer. My father had recorded names, dates, and objects in green ink, reserving red for observations. Beside a drain snake: returned exceptionally clean. Beside a wallpaper steamer: ask after baby. I could follow the arrival of that baby through subsequent loans: a hacksaw, a spirit level, a staple gun. Then, four years later, the same family borrowed a posthole digger. I knew the house. On summer evenings I passed a small wooden gate there, bright blue, with a latch set well beyond the reach of a curious child.

I wanted to make the system efficient. This was partly because I had studied accounting and partly because the drawer stuck whenever it rained. I made a spreadsheet with columns for condition, replacement value, and expected return. The red observations presented a problem. There was nowhere sensible to put “tell him pears are ripe.” For a while I kept an additional column called Notes, but once you give something a heading you feel obliged to put something under it. Soon every transaction ended with me staring at a blank rectangle, trying to think of something noteworthy about a perfectly ordinary man.

One Thursday, a woman came in to borrow the long measuring tape. She had silver paint on one ear and carried a paper bag fragrant with warm bread. “How long?” I asked, meaning the loan. “That's what I mean to find out,” she said. Her name was Rosa. She was measuring the old cinema screen, which had been rolled up behind the stage since the roof began leaking in 1998. Somebody had bought the building to convert it into flats. Rosa had permission to take whatever she could carry away before the contractors arrived. She thought the screen might make curtains.

It did not make curtains. Unrolled, the material was too stiff to gather and too stained to leave flat. But the reverse was a lovely even gray, and Rosa, who painted scenery for amateur plays, recognized a sky when she saw one. She laid it across the cinema floor and painted the view from the hill above town. There were the allotments, the river, the train depot with its three crooked chimneys. Near the bottom, scarcely larger than a postage stamp, stood our shop. She painted the yellow ladder leaning against the brick, although we kept it indoors by then.

We hung the painting on the shop wall in September. It covered forty years of screw holes and made the place feel strangely open, as though a customer choosing sandpaper might step backward into the river. People began coming in to find their houses. Some complained. The butcher said his awning had never been green. A girl in a school blazer looked for her grandmother's bungalow and discovered that an enormous painted oak stood in the way. She brought her grandmother the next afternoon. “Good,” the old woman said, examining the tree. “I always thought we needed a bit of privacy.”

That winter the river came up through the cellar. Nothing dramatic happened. There were no rescues, no boats in the high street, just six inches of brown water and a smell that suggested another six inches on the way. I carried stock upstairs until my arms shook. At closing time Rosa appeared with the butcher, the girl, her grandmother, and seven people whose names I knew chiefly from the spreadsheet. Nobody mentioned the lending book. They took shelving apart, shifted cartons, and constructed an improbable tower of plastic buckets. The grandmother sat at the till and sold two torches for cash.

My father's drawer swelled shut. By the time I got it open, the bottom pages of the lending book had knitted themselves into a single soft block. Rosa spread the book beneath a fan. We spent an evening separating the leaves with the little steel spatulas used for mixing paint. Some entries survived intact. Others left green ghosts on the pages facing them, as if each transaction had been quietly conducted twice. A red instruction concerning somebody's dog came away on my thumb. We never established what my father had wanted done about the dog, or even whose it was.

In spring I put a table beneath the painting. On it I left the rescued book, a packet of pencils, and a box of index cards. The spreadsheet stayed. It was useful to know who had the pipe wrench, especially when somebody else was standing ankle deep in water. The cards were for anything the spreadsheet couldn't accommodate. For weeks nobody touched them. Then someone wrote that the wallpaper steamer whistled just before it was ready. Someone else drew a diagram of the ladder hinge. A third person left a recipe for pear cake, specifying that bruised fruit was perfectly acceptable.

Yesterday a boy wanted the ladder. His kite was caught in the painted oak, he explained, pointing over my shoulder. For one peculiar second I looked at the wall for the kite. Then I understood: the real tree was behind his grandmother's bungalow, and he had no better way of giving me directions. We wheeled the ladder down together. He steadied it while I climbed. From the top I could see, beyond the leaves, the river flashing between roofs. The boy asked what was taking so long. “Nothing,” I said, and stayed there another moment before passing his kite down to him.

When my grandfather died, I inherited a drawer. This was not the result of any formal arrangement. My cousins had taken the good tools, my sister wanted the kitchen table, and somebody had found a buyer for the piano. The drawer was sticking out of a workbench destined for the dump. I pulled it free because I recognized its handle: a brass fish, screwed on upside down, with one bright eye where years of thumbs had polished it. I meant to keep the handle. Somehow, on the drive home, the rest of the drawer acquired a claim on me as well.

Its inventory was disappointing. There were seven keys, none labeled; a tobacco tin full of washers; three green marbles; a photograph of a dog I could not identify; and an envelope containing the instructions for a pressure cooker. Underneath everything lay a neatly folded paper bag. My grandfather had written GOOD BAG on it in blue pencil. This struck me as so perfectly characteristic that I called my sister to tell her. She laughed, then went quiet. Finally she said, “Was it the kind with handles?” It was. “Those are good,” she said, and we both laughed harder than before.

For months the drawer sat on my washing machine. Whenever the spin cycle started, the keys shuffled around in the tinny, purposeful way of people taking their seats before a meeting. I had the idea that I ought to make something of its contents, perhaps a framed arrangement with the photograph at the center. The trouble was the dog. What if it belonged to a neighbor he disliked? What if the photograph had come with a secondhand wallet? A memorial ought not to give pride of place to a completely incidental dachshund. At least, that was my thinking that winter.

In March, my downstairs neighbor knocked to ask whether I had a washer. She held up a bolt between finger and thumb, as delicately as if she were offering a cricket to a bird. Her name was Salma. We had lived in the same building for four years and previously exchanged only packages and information about the bins. I brought out the tobacco tin. On the landing, we tipped its contents into my palm and poked through them. One washer fit. She went downstairs to finish fixing a stool, and I went back inside feeling oddly proud of my grandfather.

After that I stopped trying to decide what the drawer meant. I used the paper bag to carry some pears to my sister. She gave it back at Christmas, full of books for my daughter, who was then six and suspicious of any story in which an animal learned a lesson. The green marbles went into a game of her invention. Its rules occupied several pages, though in practice victory went to whoever could roll a marble under the refrigerator. Retrieving one required a yardstick, a flashlight, and an adult prepared to lie flat on a floor that needed sweeping.

The keys were harder. A key implies an answer somewhere, a particular arrangement of metal waiting to consent. Throwing one away seemed less like discarding an object than refusing a small appointment. I tried them in the surviving furniture, including my sister's table, which had a shallow drawer nobody remembered seeing open. No luck. My daughter suggested trying them on doors around the neighborhood. I explained why people might object to this research. She proposed asking first, which was reasonable, and would have been an interesting way to meet people, but I lacked the necessary courage. We kept the keys.

Years later, at a family picnic, I showed my aunt the photograph. She recognized the dog immediately. “That's the one that bit him,” she said. Apparently my grandfather had been delivering groceries after school when a dachshund shot out from beneath a porch and attached itself to his trouser cuff. The owner paid for the trousers. Why the photograph? My aunt shrugged. “Maybe he liked the dog.” Then she turned it over and noticed something I had missed: four faint gray corners, the residue of paste. The picture had once belonged to an album. That was all we learned.

I like knowing about the bite. I like even better that the story stops where it does. My grandfather, who in my memory is always old, gets to be a boy on a porch, furious about his trousers or frightened or trying not to laugh. No one now can say which. There is a courtesy in leaving him there with his private reaction, rather than furnishing him with the one that makes the best anecdote. I put the photograph back in the drawer. By then the drawer had a place on a shelf beside our front door, at hip height.

It holds different things now: bicycle lights, stamps, a mitten awaiting its partner. The pressure cooker instructions went to a woman who bought the same model at a church sale and was looking for the manual. She sent me a postcard afterward, reporting success with lentils. Two keys remain. The others hang from a mobile my daughter made in school; in summer, a breeze from the open window makes them tap softly together. Salma's stool is still in service, although the seat has been painted yellow. I know because last week I sat on it while she cut my hair.

Yesterday the brass fish came loose. I fetched a screwdriver and considered turning it right side up at last. With the screws out, I could see the pale shape its body had sheltered, a little fish of fresh wood swimming in the darker grain. Turn the handle over and the tail would stick out below it like a stray pencil mark. I set it back the way it was. Today my daughter pulled the drawer open for a stamp. Her thumb landed on the bright eye. She shut it with her knee and went out to post her letter before lunch.

The first sound I gave the museum was the squeak of my father's kitchen drawer. You had to lift it a little to get past the swollen part of the frame, and the squeak came just before it gave way. On the recording you can hear the spoons shift as the drawer opens. Then you hear my father say, with genuine irritation, “Well, are you going to get one or not?” He thought I wanted a spoon. I did take one, eventually, and ate a yogurt I hadn't wanted because explaining seemed like more trouble than eating a yogurt.

The museum occupied two rooms above a shoe repair shop. Its director, Ada, had been a court stenographer and still tended to watch people's mouths when they spoke. She accepted recordings on the condition that the donor could identify the sound and had permission from anyone whose voice appeared. My father signed his form on the back of a gas bill. Under the question about public access, he wrote, “Anybody who wants to hear a drawer is welcome to come over and fix the other three.” Ada filed the bill intact. She considered the offer part of the accession.

For three years I worked there on Saturdays. My favorite job was writing the labels. A boy brought us the whir of the little fan inside his mother's artificial leg; a gardener brought hail falling into an empty wheelbarrow. The difficulty was saying enough to make a person put on the headphones without telling them what to hear. I wrote that the hail sounded like a pocketful of change being flung at a tollbooth. Ada crossed it out. “Now nobody gets to hear hail,” she said. I changed the label to the date, the street, and the size of the stones.

We had regulars. A bus driver spent his lunch breaks listening to washing machines, distinguishing brands with an accuracy that frankly upset him. Two sisters came after school to play each other recordings at random and invent terrible explanations. A steam radiator became a horse learning to type. A loose shutter was a giant trying to get comfortable in a cinema seat. Ada, usually strict about noise in the listening room, let them laugh. Once I caught her trying to imitate the typing horse downstairs while the shoemaker fitted a new heel to her boot. He guessed woodpecker with hiccups.

Our most requested recording contained almost nothing. It came from a woman named Elena who had set her phone on a windowsill during the last evening before a road opened behind her house. There was a bird at the beginning, six minutes of leaves moving, then somebody far away dropping what might have been a tray. Visitors listened all the way through. They often removed the headphones slowly, as though the room outside had acquired a different pressure. One man complained that he could hear traffic over the leaves. He was hearing the street below us through an open window.

That autumn the shoemaker retired. The landlord offered us the downstairs at a rent we couldn't possibly pay, then leased the whole building to a dentist who needed somewhere to put an X-ray machine. Ada announced the closure on a postcard. She refused to call it a farewell celebration because, she said, she had already bought biscuits for the annual meeting and didn't see why the same biscuits should suddenly signify something else. Forty people came. The bus driver brought a cake shaped like a washing machine, with a single red sock revolving behind a door of clear boiled sugar.

We had arranged for the library to take the collection. The librarian arrived with padded crates, an inventory, and her small daughter, who occupied herself by crawling under the refreshment table. Halfway through packing, the girl asked why we were putting all the noises in boxes when there were plenty still happening. From under the table she could hear things we couldn't: the papery grind of cake crumbs beneath our shoes, the soft thump of a knee against a hanging coat. We got down beside her. For a minute there were seven adults kneeling on a floor that badly needed sweeping.

My father came late, carrying the drawer. He had finally got around to planing its sides and thought we might want the original object, although the original sound was gone. Without the cabinet it looked forlorn, a shallow wooden boat built by somebody with only the vaguest idea of water. Ada turned it over. On the underside, in pencil, my mother had written a telephone number. None of us recognized it. My father read it aloud twice and suddenly remembered: a woman who used to deliver eggs on Thursdays, driving a blue van with one green door.

We used the drawer to carry the leftover cups downstairs. Outside, my father held it while I unlocked the car. A spoon slid across the bottom at precisely the pitch of the spoon in the recording, and we both looked down, surprised to find that some portion of the exhibit had escaped. He laughed. I hadn't recorded his laugh for the museum. It had never seemed to qualify; he laughed every day, sometimes at jokes so poor that preserving the evidence would have been unkind. I nearly reached for my phone. Instead I took the drawer so he could get in.

At home he put it back in the cabinet. It ran beautifully. We stood opening and closing it for the pleasure of a job well done, the spoons traveling half an inch each way. After a while he filled the kettle. I found two cups and the biscuits Ada had wrapped for us in a paper napkin. From the kitchen table I could see the pale stripe his plane had left along the wood. He put the milk between us, sat down, and asked what the girls had called that horse. This time, when he tried the sound, I guessed it on the first go.

When the library took the clock down, everybody discovered that it had been six minutes fast. For thirty years people had glanced at it, shut their books, and reached the bus stop with time to spare. Children had been collected punctually. A man named Dennis had finished the crossword every Thursday at what he understood to be a respectable hour. The clock went away on a Monday, leaving a pale circle above the returns desk. On Tuesday, Dennis missed his bus. He came back inside and asked the librarian what she proposed to do about it.

The librarian was my mother. She proposed that Dennis sit down for twelve minutes, which was how long it would be until the next bus. He said that wasn't the point. She said she knew it wasn't the point, but it was raining. Dennis sat down. My mother went back to covering a new atlas in clear plastic, pressing the bubbles toward the edges with the side of her thumb. She could do this beautifully. At home she couldn't put a fitted sheet on a mattress without ending up on the mattress herself, kneeling inside the sheet.

I was fourteen that summer and spent my afternoons at the library because our apartment was being painted. This was the official explanation. The painters finished in June. I kept coming through August, carrying the same paperback in my pocket so that no one could accuse me of wanting company. I liked the hour before closing, when the light climbed the opposite wall and illuminated, shelf by shelf, subjects that otherwise received little attention: municipal drainage, indoor ferns, the history of buttons. For three days in July, buttons enjoyed a radiance usually reserved for saints.

The missing clock began to attract suggestions. A woman who taught arithmetic offered a poster of the multiplication tables. Someone brought in a watercolor of a boat. A small boy suggested a window, and when my mother explained that the other side of the wall was the staff toilet, he considered this new information and suggested a much smaller window, high up. My mother wrote every proposal on an index card. She didn't have to. There was no committee. She simply felt that an idea ought to have somewhere to go after its owner went home.

In the second week of August, Dennis arrived with a paper bag. From it he took a kitchen clock shaped like a fried egg. The yolk was the face; the hands were a knife and fork. His sister had given it to him years before, he said, and he had never found quite the right place for it. My mother put a battery in. The fork advanced with a noise like a fingernail tapping glass. We stood listening. “Perhaps,” Dennis said eventually, “the children's room.” My mother said the children had done nothing to deserve it.

What I remember best is how hard he laughed. Dennis was a narrow, formal man who wore a tie even in weather that made the glue soften in the book spines. His laugh was enormous and quite unsuitable for him. It came out once, startling us all, and then again because we had been startled. My mother had to put down her scissors. A woman emerged from the reading room to see what had happened, and Dennis, trying to explain, held the egg over his head as though it were an item recovered from a shipwreck.

By September the original clock was back. A repairman positioned a ladder beneath the pale circle and asked my mother to tell him when the face was level. Dennis supervised from the newspaper table. I watched from the doorway, already late for school and willing to be later. Once the clock was up, the repairman set it by his watch. Dennis looked at my mother. My mother looked at Dennis. Neither said anything until the repairman had folded his ladder, collected his receipt, and carried his box of tools out into the bright morning.

Then my mother fetched the little wooden stool she used for the top shelves. She climbed onto it, took the clock down, and handed it to Dennis. He moved the minute hand forward six marks. It was a solemn operation. When he gave it back, she polished a thumbprint from the glass with her sleeve. “There,” she said. I asked whether this wasn't rather a peculiar thing for a library to do. Weren't libraries meant to give people accurate information? “Certainly,” my mother said. “The correct time is available at the bus stop.”

Years later, after she retired, I asked her about the cards. We were clearing out a drawer full of rubber bands, expired coupons, and keys to doors nobody could identify. I thought we might find the suggestions bundled together. I wanted the one about the little window. My mother had no idea what I meant. She remembered Dennis, of course. She remembered the egg. But the cards had gone the way of most paper in a building devoted to preserving it: into a bin on an ordinary afternoon, without ceremony or any suspicion of future demand.

Last winter I went back. The library has new carpets and outlets at every table. Above the returns desk hangs a screen announcing classes, tax assistance, a meeting for people learning to mend their clothes. In one corner the screen gives the time, exactly right. I took down a book about buttons and sat until the light failed. Then I put on my coat and walked to the bus stop. A woman there asked if the number nine had gone. I looked down the road. It was beginning to rain, and through the library windows I could see a young man wrestling a sheet of plastic over a large book. “Not yet,” I said. We had six minutes. I nearly told her the whole thing. Instead I held my umbrella a little higher, and she stepped underneath.

samples.result:
My father kept a drawer of things that belonged to places he no longer lived. There was a brass key to the apartment above the bakery, a white porcelain knob from the bathroom in Dayton, and a blue plastic pool pass stamped SUMMER 1986. He could tell you what each thing was, but not why he had kept it. Asked directly, he would turn the object over as if the answer might be printed on the back. Then he would offer you coffee. By the time the coffee was ready, you generally had the decency to ask him about something else.

When he moved into a smaller place, the drawer came to me, contents and all. It was easier to pull it out of the old desk than to find another box. I set it on my passenger seat and put the seat belt around it, an act that would have amused him if he had seen it. At the first red light, the porcelain knob rolled forward and struck the brass key. The sound was exactly the sound of his kitchen when he was looking for scissors, and for a moment I nearly asked him what he was trying to open.

At home I sorted everything onto the dining table. Beneath a packet of picture hooks lay a photograph of a woman standing beside a horse. The woman wore a dark skirt and enormous rubber boots. The horse had its eyes closed. On the back, in my father's narrow handwriting, someone had been identified only as “the fool.” I called him. Naturally I expected a story about an old girlfriend, possibly one who had left him for a man with a better horse. “That's your aunt Ruth,” he said. “And that's not a horse. Look at the ears on him, for heaven's sake.”

I had never met Ruth. She lived in Oregon and sent a Christmas card most years, always signed in green ink, always arriving in January. In family conversation she was described as independent, a word spoken with admiration by my father and considerable precision by my mother. I found her number and called before I could invent a reason not to. “I have a picture of you with a mule,” I said after introducing myself. “Well, that narrows it down to about twenty years,” she said. In the background somebody on television was enthusiastically estimating the value of an antique clock.

I described the boots. “Oh,” she said, and turned off the television. The boots belonged to her father. She had borrowed them because the field was flooded and because, at sixteen, she believed that any problem involving mud could be solved by taller boots. The mule was called Leonard. He had walked through a gap in the fence, crossed the road, and planted himself in the shallow water of a baseball diamond. There was to be a game that afternoon. Her father had sent her to fetch him. “Why you?” I asked. “Because I was the one who wanted the damn mule.”

She remembered the baseball coach standing on the pitcher's mound, the only dry spot, holding a clipboard over his head against the rain. She remembered the team sitting in the dugout eating sunflower seeds. Nobody offered to help. Sixteen boys watched her walk into water nearly up to her knees and take Leonard by the halter. He would not budge. She pushed his chest. She pulled his ears. Then one of the boys, a quiet kid whose name she had forgotten, came out of the dugout carrying a paper cup. He let Leonard smell the seeds and walked slowly toward the road.

“My brother took that picture when we got home,” Ruth said. “I was so mad I could hardly see. He said if I stood still he'd give me a quarter. A quarter was something then.” I asked which of them my father had meant by the inscription. “Himself, probably. He gave me the money before he checked whether there was film in the camera.” But there had been film, I pointed out. “Yes,” she said. “And now you have a picture. Isn't it funny how a thing can go right and you remember it as a thing that nearly went wrong?”

We talked for another hour. She wanted to know about my work, whether my father's new windows opened easily, whether I had inherited the family tendency to sneeze in bright sunlight. Before hanging up, she asked me to send her the photograph. I made a good scan, the kind in which every blade of grass looks more purposeful than grass has ever looked in person. I put the original in an envelope between two pieces of cardboard. On the back of one piece I wrote down the story of Leonard and the baseball team, including the boy with the sunflower seeds.

A week later my father called. Ruth had called him. They had argued about the mule. He maintained that Leonard had been collected from a football field; she had asked him how many football fields he knew with a pitcher's mound. He had conceded the point. Then they had argued about the quarter. “It was fifty cents,” he told me. “I remember because I wanted two comic books, and after I paid her I couldn't buy either one.” He sounded pleased. In the new apartment his voice had sometimes acquired the careful brightness of a person speaking to a visiting nurse. Not that afternoon.

The drawer is under my bed now. The pool pass is still in it. So is the key, which I tried once in my own front door out of idle curiosity. It went halfway in and stopped. Yesterday Ruth sent me a postcard showing the Oregon coast beneath a sky of improbable orange. No greeting, no signature, just a line in green ink: “The boy was Walter Pike.” I phoned her and asked how she had remembered. “I didn't,” she said. “He sells eggs on Thursdays at the market. I took the picture along.”

On my first morning at the lost property office, a man came looking for a cake. He had left it on the number six bus, in a white box tied with string. It was his daughter's birthday. The driver had already brought it in, but I was new enough to insist on proof. What kind of cake? I asked. He considered this. “Disappointing,” he said. “I tried to make a horse.” We opened the box together. The animal had sunk in the middle and appeared to be kneeling in prayer. I handed it over. He thanked me without meeting my eyes.

Most things that arrived at our counter had suffered some small indignity. Umbrellas turned inside out. A violin case bore the tread of a remarkably narrow bicycle tire. Someone had used a paperback dictionary to mop up coffee; from P onward the language was inaccessible. My colleague June taught me to record these injuries without guessing at their causes. Write “brown stain,” she said, not “coffee.” Write “cover detached,” not “badly loved.” I had never written “badly loved,” but apparently someone once had. June had worked there for thirty years and retained a precise memory of every interesting mistake except her own.

In November we received a wooden drawer. Nothing else, just one kitchen drawer, painted yellow, with a porcelain knob and a sheet of green paper lining the bottom. It came off the last train on a Thursday night. I entered it under Furniture, which until then had consisted entirely of folding chairs. For several days we discussed the person who had lost it. June thought a cabinetmaker was matching paint. The cleaner thought somebody had been evicted in stages. My own theory involved a magician, though I could not say what particular trick required a drawer that stuck slightly when pushed.

People began leaving things in it. A delivery driver put his pen there while he signed for a parcel, then went away without it. June dropped in a brass button she found beside the lift. I contributed three rubber bands and a key to a padlock we no longer owned. By December, without anybody intending it, the drawer had resumed its occupation. If you needed string, a safety pin, or a coin from a country that had since adopted the euro, there was only one sensible place to look. We stopped thinking of it as lost property. It was simply the drawer.

Then a woman arrived with a photograph of a kitchen. I recognized the yellow paint before she spoke. In the photograph a boy stood on a chair rolling pastry, his sleeves pushed up unevenly. Behind him, at hip height, there was a dark rectangular gap. “My brother,” the woman said, pointing to the boy. “I took this the day before they pulled the house down.” She had meant to keep one thing from the kitchen and had chosen the drawer because their father had made it. On the way home she changed trains twice. Somewhere she had set it down.

I fetched it from under the counter. We had acquired rather a lot of things by then. As I tipped them onto my blotter, out came a candle shaped like a seven, two curtain hooks, a dog whistle, and a folded recipe for onion soup in June's handwriting. The woman laughed. “That's about right,” she said. She ran her thumb along the inside edge and showed me a shallow notch. As children they had closed the drawer on a length of wool leading down the hall, to see whether their sleeping father would notice when his kitchen began to unravel.

“Did he?” I asked. “Of course. We were pulling a drawer across the floor.” She tucked it beneath her arm. There should have been a satisfying noise when the office door closed behind her, but the pneumatic hinge had been adjusted that morning, and she left us in perfect silence. For the rest of the afternoon we worked around the little heap on my desk. Twice I reached underneath the counter for the drawer. June put the curtain hooks in her pocket. At five she unfolded the recipe and discovered it was not onion soup after all, but instructions for descaling a kettle.

I thought of buying another drawer. There was a furniture shop near my flat that sold salvaged fittings, and on Saturday I went in. The owner showed me six. One was walnut, with dovetailed corners so fine they resembled a diagram explaining the idea of precision to beginners. Another smelled of cloves. I slid them in and out of their cabinets while the owner stood by, politely enduring the least consequential decision of his working week. Finally he asked what dimensions I needed. I admitted that I had nothing to fit the drawer into. “Ah,” he said. “Much greater choice, then.”

I went home empty-handed. On Monday the heap was gone. June had used the rubber bands to bundle some timetables, given the whistle to a crossing guard, and put the birthday candle in an envelope marked SEVEN, OR POSSIBLY SEVENTY IF YOU HAVE A ZERO. The pen had been claimed by the delivery driver, who said it was the only pen in the city that worked in the rain. I asked about the useless key. June pointed to the violin case with the bicycle mark. Its owner was coming at lunchtime, and one of the catches needed persuading from underneath.

Years later, what I remember best about that office is how often a person, reunited with a possession, immediately put it to work. A scarf went around a neck. A watch was wound and consulted. The violinist took out her bow, tightened it, and played four notes before she even signed the form. They were not especially lovely notes. She was listening for damage, and so were we. The last note wavered, steadied, then filled the little room where June and I stood holding our breath, each of us, for once, quite certain what the other had been hoping to hear.

The first thing my father did after retiring was move the kitchen clock six inches to the left. It had hung above the telephone for thirty years, but the telephone was gone, and from his new chair at the table he could see only half its face behind the lampshade. He measured the distance, made a pencil mark, and fetched his drill. At lunch my mother came home and said, “Who moved the clock?” She had not yet put down her bag. This struck him as an extraordinary tribute to the precision with which she observed the world.

What she had actually noticed was the pale circle on the wall. Everywhere else, the yellow paint had deepened under successive summers of frying onions, boiling peaches, and occasionally setting a dish towel on fire. Behind the clock was a patch of innocent lemon. My father proposed washing the wall. My mother proposed putting the clock back. They compromised by doing nothing for eleven years. Whenever I visited, I meant to ask whether the circle bothered them anymore. Whenever I left, I remembered that I had forgotten to ask. Eventually the circle became the thing I looked for when I came in.

My parents sold the house in February. The woman who bought it was a piano teacher named June, who asked if she might keep the curtains until she could afford new ones. My mother left her the curtains, the rods, a stepladder, and a note explaining which neighbors would lend her what. Mr. Bello had a long extension cord. The twins next door owned a wheelbarrow, although you had to inflate the tire. Nobody had a decent posthole digger. The note ran to three pages and did not mention that the upstairs bathroom door could lock itself in damp weather.

I went back in April for a box of records we had overlooked in the attic. June answered in stocking feet, holding a spoon. Somewhere beyond her a child was playing the same four notes over and over, with a long investigative pause between the third and fourth. She led me through the kitchen. Both circles were still there: the pale one and, six inches to its left, the cleaner ring left by the clock when my father took it down. June had drawn two black dots and a smile inside the first. Inside the second she had drawn a frown.

“Reviews,” she said, lifting the spoon toward the piano. The child landed hard on a fifth note, an event so unexpected that we stood still to hear what he would do about it. He played it again, softly. Then he began working his way backward, trying to find the four notes by which he had arrived. June waited until he found them before calling out, “Good, Milo. Now come have some soup.” I had assumed the spoon was for conducting. This is one difficulty with returning to a familiar house: you expect everything new in it to require an explanation.

In the attic I found the records beneath a quilt that did not belong to us. June had already begun storing things up there. A carton marked CHRISTMAS contained, as far as I could see through the open flaps, a single red mitten and an astonishing quantity of wire. Beside it stood a plaster foot, larger than an ordinary foot, with each toenail painted blue. I wanted badly to know its history and understood that I no longer possessed the right to shout down the stairs and ask. I took the records and left the foot to its private business.

At their apartment my father was setting up the turntable. He had chosen the place partly because its living room accommodated his speakers at what he considered the correct distance from one another. This left my mother very little choice about where to put the sofa, but in exchange she had an entire small bedroom for sewing. For years she had cut patterns on the dining table, clearing everything away before supper. Now she could leave a sleeve unfinished on Tuesday and find it precisely as unfinished on Friday. Nothing about retirement, she told me, had equaled this particular luxury.

We played a recording of a clarinet concerto. Halfway through, my father got up and moved the right speaker an inch. My mother looked up from the cuff she was hemming. “Better,” she said. I could hear no difference. Then a delivery truck outside reversed, contributing three evenly spaced beeps in a key surprisingly hospitable to the orchestra. My father laughed so hard he had to lift the needle. We ate sandwiches. For dessert my mother produced two pears, which she divided among the three of us by a system whose fairness she defended before anybody had thought to object.

I told them about the faces June had drawn on the kitchen wall. My mother immediately wanted to know which face was smiling, the original position or the revised one. My father said this was not a competition. When I told them it was the original position, he said that a piano teacher was hardly the person to consult about the placement of a clock. He went to the window with his plate and stood eating the last sliver of pear. Across the street, someone had hung bright green curtains in a room otherwise empty except for a bicycle.

Before I left, I noticed their clock on the sill beside his elbow. There were no holes in the apartment walls yet. “Where will you put that?” I asked. He turned it around so the face pointed out the window. We considered the arrangement. From our side all you could see was a battery compartment and a little brass wheel. My mother joined us. Across the street a young man came into the room with the green curtains, unlocked his bicycle from the radiator, and glanced our way. My father raised his hand. The young man checked his wrist and waved.

The first thing I learned at the town's lost property office was never to shake an umbrella indoors. The second was that a person who has lost an umbrella cannot remember its color, but can describe with perfect accuracy the sound it makes when opened. “Like someone sitting on a biscuit tin,” said a woman on my first morning. We had thirty umbrellas. I opened six before she nodded. Outside, the sun was shining. She carried her umbrella home under her arm with the grave satisfaction of a musician who has just got a difficult instrument back in tune.

My job was supposed to last a summer. I was nineteen, saving for a room in a city where nobody would know which primary school I had attended. The office occupied the old station buffet. Behind my desk, a tiled sign still offered TEA AND A SLICE for a price no longer possible in any currency. Trains stopped there four times a day. Between them, I accessioned scarves, spectacles, shopping bags, single gloves, and an alarming number of dentures. My supervisor, Len, insisted that dentures be recorded as “one set, partial” rather than “several teeth.” He had standards.

In July somebody handed in a door. It was narrow and blue, with a brass hook on one side and a penciled ladder of children's heights on the other. The finder had seen it lying beside the bicycle racks. Len and I stood it against the wall. Neither of us could imagine how to lose a door. You might forget that you had brought your gloves; surely you would remember walking down the street behind a broad sheet of wood, unable to see anything except your shoes and the occasional terrified pigeon escaping from underneath.

The local paper ran a photograph. For scale, the photographer asked me to stand beside the door, which made me look like a contestant on a quiz show with exceptionally poor prizes. Within days we had visitors. A carpenter identified the wood as pine. A retired teacher recognized the handwriting beside the height marks, then put on her glasses and withdrew her claim. Two little boys asked permission to measure themselves. Soon there were fresh pencil lines labeled Robin and Tim, and I had technically violated the rule against altering an article in custody.

Len pretended not to notice. He had begun eating his sandwiches beside the door, sitting on an upturned crate, reading yesterday's racing results. One afternoon I found him with his thumbnail resting on a notch halfway up the frame. “My sister used to cheat,” he said. “She'd draw herself taller after we'd gone to bed.” I asked whether his parents had minded. “Minded? They thought she'd developed a remarkable capacity to grow on Thursdays.” He finished his sandwich. It contained cucumber sliced almost transparent, the way his wife had liked it. She had died in February.

By August the door had acquired a reputation quite independent of its owner. People brought visiting cousins to see it. A girl with a red fringe made a careful drawing of its hinges. Someone left a pot of geraniums at its foot, as if the rest of the house might materialize if properly encouraged. I started to dread the arrival of anyone who looked purposeful. I liked our office better with the door in it. This struck me as an unprofessional feeling, particularly since the whole point of the office was to give everything back.

Its owner arrived on a wet Tuesday, wheeling a bicycle with one pedal missing. She was about forty, in painty trousers, and she laughed when she saw the geraniums. The door had come from her father's pantry. She had been taking it to the tip on a borrowed trailer when the strap worked loose. By the time she noticed, she was three miles away and late for a dental appointment. “I thought, well, somebody'll make use of it,” she said. “I didn't expect quite this.” She touched the line labeled Tim. “He's tall for seven.”

I fetched the release form. Under distinguishing features, she wrote a small burn behind the hook. We checked. There it was, a brown crescent, caused by her brother trying to dry a sock with a candle in 1978. He had blamed their mother for buying flammable socks. Len laughed so hard he had to take off his glasses. The woman signed, folded her copy into a pocket, and regarded the door with some dismay. We regarded her bicycle. The afternoon train came and went. Rain rattled against the glass roof over the empty platform.

In the end she took only the brass hook. Len found a screwdriver, and she held out her hand for the screws, two dull little things that had spent half a century in the dark. She said she would put the hook beside her kitchen sink for tea towels. The door stayed. When the office closed three years later, it became a tabletop in the station café. I know because I went back last April and ate a buttered bun with my elbows resting somewhere between Robin and Tim.

I live in the city now. Last week I put a hook beside my own sink, a cheap one from the hardware shop, fixed slightly crooked because the drill met something stubborn in the wall. My daughter hangs her apron there. This morning I caught her standing on a chair, trying to get it down without asking for help. I nearly told her she had grown. Instead I fetched a pencil and stood her against the pantry door. She insisted on keeping her shoes on. After some negotiation, we wrote that detail down too. One day somebody looking at that mark will want to know whether the half inch belonged to the child or to the shoes. I see no reason to leave the matter to chance.

samples.result:
When the city replaced the crossing signal outside my apartment, I lost the sound by which I knew it was Sunday. The old signal made a dry, wooden knocking. On weekdays it disappeared under buses and conversation, but on Sunday mornings, with the windows open, I could hear it from bed. Six knocks, a pause, then six more. I had never once thought, What a lovely sound. Mostly I thought nothing at all. Then one morning the signal spoke in a crisp recorded voice, and I sat up as if somebody had come into my room.

A few days later I borrowed a recorder from my sister. She used it for interviews and kept it in a case with a tiny fur cover for the microphone. The cover made the whole apparatus look like a sleeping mouse. I told her I wanted to record things around the neighborhood before they vanished. “Which things?” she asked. This was an excellent question for which I had made no provision. I took the recorder home and put it by the door, where for a week it accumulated receipts.

My first recording was of the gate at the public pool. In winter the pool was empty, but a groundskeeper still came through every morning. The gate had a rising squeal followed by a lavish metallic crash, an operatic arrangement for a man arriving to skim leaves out of a hole. I asked if he minded opening it twice. He looked at the recorder, considered the request, and said, “You ought to get the one at the tennis courts.” It turned out he had opinions about six or seven gates. We spent his break on a tour.

After that I began asking people what they would miss hearing. They almost always answered a different question first. They named a sound they hated: the refrigerator at work, a reversing truck, the upstairs neighbor who seemed to own one boot and one marble. Given another minute, though, they would usually come up with something exact. A pharmacist liked the click of the little drawer where she kept her lunch money. A boy at the bakery nominated the pop of the paper bag when his father snapped it open. His father had never noticed that he did it.

There were practical difficulties. A recording of rain on the library skylight was chiefly a recording of my coat sleeve moving against a chair. The fishmonger’s shutter, magnificent in person, sounded on playback like somebody dropping a spoon. And certain sounds refused to occur in the presence of equipment. The bakery boy’s father, called upon to perform his bag trick, tore three bags in succession. His son laughed so hard he had to sit on a sack of flour. I got that part, with permission, and labeled the file BAGS, UNSUCCESSFUL.

By midsummer I had eighty recordings and no idea what to do with them. My sister needed her recorder back. I copied the files onto my computer, where their little blue icons lined up with the melancholy tidiness of chairs after a meeting. Now and then I played one for a guest. Usually I had to explain what the guest was about to hear, and afterward explain why it had sounded better on the day. I discovered that “Wait, here comes the good part” is a difficult promise to keep when the good part is a drain.

In August the library let me set up a listening table at its street fair. I brought headphones, a laptop, and a handwritten menu. Nobody stopped until I crossed out LOCAL SOUND ARCHIVE and wrote GUESS THAT NOISE. Within ten minutes there was a queue. People mistook the pool gate for a delivery truck and the delivery truck for distant thunder. A little girl correctly identified the library’s book return from a single thump. She explained that hardbacks went down flat, whereas paperbacks sometimes turned over on the way. The librarian tested this later. She was right.

Late in the afternoon an elderly man put on the headphones and listened to the tennis court gate four times. He had played there with his wife, he told me, every Thursday for nearly thirty years. I braced for the gravity of what might follow. Instead he said, “She cheated on the lines,” with such fresh indignation that I laughed. He took off the headphones. “You can ask her. She’s over there buying a hot dog.” She came back with mustard on her thumb and denied everything. Neither of them thought the gate sounded particularly familiar.

I had imagined the recordings as small containers into which a piece of the neighborhood could be sealed. At the fair they served more like handles: people took hold of one and went somewhere I couldn’t have predicted. The lunch drawer reminded a woman of the cash box at her first job. The rain that was mostly my sleeve reminded two brothers of camping in a tent neither had liked. Even a wrong guess could be wonderfully specific. No, that wasn’t a train coupling in the freight yard, but now I wanted to hear the train.

I still go out collecting occasionally, using my phone now, which is perfectly adequate if I remember to stand still. Last Sunday I finally recorded the new crossing signal. While I was waiting for it to speak, a pigeon landed on the metal sign above the button. Its claws made a brief scattering noise, like someone setting down a handful of rice. Then a cyclist called good morning to a woman he evidently mistook for somebody else, and she called good morning back. The light changed. The voice gave its plain instruction. Listening at home, I found I’d missed the first word because I had been saying good morning too. I left the recording as it was.

The first thing my father got wrong about our town was the smell. He had built the railway station down to the wire basket beside the ticket window, and the wire basket contained three twists of paper, each no bigger than a flea. But the whole station smelled of the glue he used on it. The real one smelled of floor wax, wet coats, and the orange my mother always peeled on the platform, digging her thumbnail in to get the first piece started.

I mentioned this when I was nine. My father held out a paintbrush.

“Show me how to paint a smell.”

I took this as a genuine assignment and spent most of Saturday rubbing orange peel on the station roof. For years afterward, one corner of the roof was darker than the rest. Visitors assumed it was water damage, skillfully rendered. My father accepted their compliments.

The town occupied two doors laid flat across four trestles in our basement. You had to duck beneath the doors and come up through a hole to reach the municipal swimming pool. This meant that anybody repairing the diving board appeared, from the perspective of the railway passengers, to be an enormous disembodied head rising behind the Methodist church. My mother liked to go down there when my father had company and slowly emerge, eating an apple.

He had rules. Nothing went into the town until he had seen it himself. No building could be included merely because it would be interesting to make. No person could appear twice, which became a problem when the postman, already permanently stationed outside the bakery, was elected mayor. My father left the mayor’s chair empty. He said the man still had his rounds.

By the time I left home, the model was sixteen years out of date. The cinema was showing a picture nobody remembered. Our old blue car stood outside a house we had sold. In actual life the council had filled in the swimming pool after a crack opened along its bottom and proved too expensive to fix. In the basement, a girl in a yellow bathing cap was forever deciding whether to jump.

My father died in February, when the ground was too hard for my mother to do much in the garden and the days were too short for her to want to do much else. I stayed for a fortnight. We cleared his wardrobe, canceled his appointments, and ate food brought by women who had all somehow agreed that what had happened called for grated cheese. Neither of us mentioned the town until the night before I was due to leave.

“I’d like my basement back,” she said.

I had imagined the model going to a museum. It turned out that museums had basements of their own, already full of things people had imagined going to museums. The library offered to take the station, but only if we could put it in a case. The school wanted the whole town until somebody measured the classroom door. Finally my mother put a notice in the paper: MODEL TOWN TO BE DISMANTLED. RESIDENTS MAY COLLECT THEIR PREMISES SATURDAY, TEN TO FOUR.

I extended my stay. I wanted to see who came.

The baker came first. He was a young man who had bought the business the previous summer and had never met my father. He turned the little building over and discovered, penciled underneath, the date of its completion and the words *rear gutter doubtful*. He promised to check. Two sisters arrived for the same house and, after a brief conference on the stairs, decided that the elder would keep it and the younger would have the cinema, where she had once been sick into the elder’s handbag.

All morning people carried buildings up into the daylight. Empty rectangles of green paint appeared where houses had stood. A man in a good suit asked for the bus shelter. He had waited there every evening for three years while courting his wife, who lived in the next town. My mother wrapped it in a square of tissue as carefully as if it were a piece of wedding cake.

At half past three, a woman I didn’t know came down the steps sideways, favoring one knee. She stood for a long time beside the pool.

“I worked the desk there,” she said. “Seventeen summers. People think it was a nice cool job, but that little office was an oven.”

She pointed out the open window my father had given the office, and the matchstick propping it up.

“That’s right,” she said, pleased. “Otherwise it fell on your fingers.”

We couldn’t lift the pool. It had been set into the door itself, a shallow rectangle carved out with a chisel and painted an improbable Mediterranean blue. I offered her the girl on the diving board. Instead she chose the office window, which came away easily, matchstick and all. She put it in the coin compartment of her purse.

By four there was hardly anything left. My mother took the Methodist church, not out of any religious feeling but because, she said, she had always enjoyed the view from behind it. I took the station. We unscrewed the trestles and leaned the doors against the wall. Underneath them the concrete floor was clean and pale except for four little rust rings and one ancient apple sticker.

The station sits on my kitchen shelf now, between the cookbooks and a cup of foreign coins. Last winter my daughter asked about the dark patch on the roof. I told her about her grandfather, his rules, and the Saturday I spent trying to paint a smell. She listened with the serious attention children reserve for accounts of adults doing something foolish.

“Did it work?” she asked.

I took down the station. Quite solemnly, we put our noses to the roof. There was dust, certainly, and the dry, faint sweetness of old cardboard. My daughter shook her head. But I could smell that orange.

samples.result:
The first thing I bought for my apartment was a table that would not fit through the door. I had measured the wall where it would stand and the space between the radiator and the window. I had even measured my knees while sitting down. The door, which I used twice every day, had escaped my attention. For forty minutes the table stood on the landing like a large animal declining to enter a trailer. My neighbor came home with groceries, considered the situation, and said, “Have you tried taking the legs off?” We became friends, although not immediately on equal terms.

His name was Martin. He owned tools in the casual way other people own teaspoons. If you needed something to grip a pipe without scratching it, he went into his kitchen and returned with exactly that. His kitchen drawers contained very little cutlery. Once, eating soup at his place, I asked for a second spoon, and he handed me a measuring spoon marked one tablespoon. It worked perfectly well, except that I became unpleasantly aware of how much soup I was eating. Martin finished first and rinsed his bowl. “Twenty-three,” I told him. He nodded as if this confirmed his estimate.

After we got the table inside, I spent a week trying to decide what to put on it. In the furniture shop it had held a blue jug, three lemons, and a book about Portugal. At home it held my keys, a gas bill, and the small wrench Martin had forgotten. I bought lemons. Within a few days I had used one for fish and one for tea, and the remaining lemon looked less like a decision than an oversight. The jug never materialized. The wrench stayed. It was the one thing on the table that visitors consistently picked up.

My sister came over to help me paint. We covered the table with newspaper and set the open tin in the middle. Halfway through the afternoon she sat down, still holding her brush, to tell me that she was thinking of leaving her job. She had been thinking about it for months. While she talked, a drop of green paint traveled down the handle, crossed her knuckle, and landed beyond the edge of the newspaper. Neither of us noticed until later. She apologized and tried to lift it with a fingernail. I said to leave it. She left the job in June.

I would like to say that, whenever I saw the green mark, I thought of her courage. Usually I thought it was a pea. Several times I tried to brush it onto the floor. Objects are unreliable custodians of the meanings we assign them. They keep the evidence and decline to supply the story. Someone buying that table secondhand might reasonably conclude that its former owner painted carelessly or ate vegetables without enthusiasm. They would never guess that my sister had stood beside it, wiping her hands on her trousers, practicing what she would say to her boss on Monday morning.

In winter Martin started coming downstairs on Thursdays to do the crossword. His apartment was warmer, but mine had the better light. We made rules. No looking anything up before eight. No writing an answer unless you could explain it. Proper names were exempt from the second rule because neither of us could explain why we knew the names of racehorses. We ate toast over the puzzle and accumulated crumbs in the fold. Now and then a clue defeated us for weeks afterward. We could remember the question exactly but not the number of letters, which made further thought essentially useless.

One Thursday he brought down a letter from his daughter. She wanted him to move closer to her. There was a flat available near the station, with a lift and a small balcony. We examined the photographs on his phone. The balcony faced a brick wall, but if you leaned out, his daughter had written, you could see a chestnut tree. Martin enlarged the photograph until the supposed tree dissolved into green squares. “Could be anybody’s tree,” he said. We did the crossword. At half past eight he said he had already paid the deposit. I put the kettle on again.

When he moved, he gave me the contents of one kitchen drawer. There were pliers, washers, two screwdrivers, and a little brass key that he could not identify. I offered him his wrench back. He seemed surprised to see it. “That’s yours,” he said, with the mild impatience of a man correcting an error in arithmetic. I put it with the other tools. They filled the drawer in my kitchen where I had been keeping takeaway menus. For months afterward I opened it expecting the number of a curry house and encountered instead the means to tighten a tap.

Several years later, when I moved out, my sister helped me carry the table downstairs. We took the legs off first. On the underside, written in pencil, was a name neither of us recognized, followed by a date some thirty years before I bought it. Beside the name someone had drawn a fish with surprisingly human teeth. My sister took a photograph. I wondered who had drawn it and whether the person signing the table had approved. Then we heard the van driver sounding his horn, and the fish went facedown against a blanket, keeping its expression to itself.

The table stands in my kitchen now. On Thursday evenings Martin sometimes calls with a clue. His daughter has bought him a book of difficult puzzles, and he suspects the compiler of making mistakes. While we talk, I clear a space among the envelopes and cups and write his suggestions on whatever comes to hand. Last week the answer was “wobble.” I sat back, pleased, and felt the table shift under my elbow. One leg needed tightening. I knew which drawer to open. Martin waited on the line while I knelt beneath the table, eye to eye with the fish.

samples.result:
The first thing anyone noticed about the new clock in Bellweather Station was that it had no hands. The second thing, which took considerably longer to notice, was that people still looked up at it when they hurried through the doors. They would raise their chins, register the blank white circle, and consult a wrist or a telephone instead. By then they had usually stopped walking. This produced a small, persistent traffic jam beneath the clock, exactly where the architect had drawn a cluster of leisurely figures admiring his proposed improvements to the station. He considered this a vindication.

Mara sold coffee from the kiosk opposite platform three. From six until eleven each morning she watched the confusion, and because people assumed that anyone behind a counter knew how the world worked, she answered questions. No, the clock was not broken. Yes, it had been installed that way. No, she did not know what it meant. A brass plaque was supposed to explain the artwork, but the plaque had been delayed. “Probably coming by train,” said a customer in a green coat. He liked his joke so much that he came back the next morning to tell it again.

On Thursday a little girl asked Mara what time she would give the clock if she could choose. Mara was steaming milk and wanted to say something quick, but the question slipped past the busy part of her mind. “Four twenty,” she said. At four twenty, when she was ten, her father used to knock off work at the bakery and bring home whatever had failed to sell. There might be an apricot tart, or there might be six plain rolls and the solemn responsibility of deciding which one to eat first. She had not thought about that in years.

The girl chose midnight, which she had never seen. Her mother chose half past seven on a Sunday morning, provided nobody needed anything. The man in the green coat, overhearing, said he would take the minute before a horse race whose result he already knew. Mara wrote their answers on the cardboard sleeve of a cup. She could not have said why. Business was slow, the pen was handy, and it seemed discourteous to let three perfectly serviceable times disappear. She set the cup beside the till with a handwritten label: TIMES AVAILABLE FOR THE CLOCK. By noon it was full.

People wrote on receipts, ticket stubs, and the margins of a property brochure somebody had abandoned. One person wanted the instant the bath reached the correct temperature. Another specified nine minutes after the birth of his son, when a nurse finally thought to offer him a chair. Somebody wrote “Tuesday,” crossed it out, and wrote “a better Tuesday.” Mara liked the answers that made little sense to anyone but their authors. “Behind the garage, still light.” “When the soup had barley in it.” She emptied the cup into an old biscuit tin and put it back beside the till.

When the plaque arrived, it explained that the absence of hands challenged the tyranny of scheduled movement. A railway employee fixed it to the wall, checked his watch, and ran for the eight fourteen. Most passengers ignored the plaque. A few read it and looked annoyed. The cup was another matter. People began arriving with their answers already written. Some asked to draw out a stranger’s time in exchange for their own. Mara allowed this, reasoning that she had never formally undertaken to provide archival services. Soon passengers were carrying bits of other people’s afternoons to offices all over town.

One wet morning, the man in the green coat drew a square of yellow paper. He read it twice. “The last time I lifted my daughter,” he said. “Not the last time ever. The last time before she got too big.” He folded the paper and slipped it into his breast pocket. For once he had no joke. Mara gave him his coffee, and he went to stand beneath the clock. Through the window she saw him make a call. She could not hear what he said, though she saw him laugh and then hold the phone away to listen.

Winter came. The station roof leaked into a bucket whose position had to be adjusted according to the wind. A timetable change made everyone furious for a week and grateful for a month. Mara’s father moved to a smaller flat, and on her day off she helped him sort his kitchen. In the back of a drawer they found the scalloped metal cutter he had used for apricot tarts. He wanted to throw it away. She wanted to keep it. Neither expected the other to care, and their surprise became an argument that ended, rather pleasantly, in making pastry.

They ate the tarts standing up because the chairs were stacked in the hall. The pastry was tough. Her father blamed the flour, then the oven, then the general decline of apricots. Mara noticed that he had powdered sugar on one eyebrow. Outside, a delivery lorry reversed in a series of mournful beeps. She thought of the cup at work and understood the appeal of writing down an hour you wished to visit again. What surprised her was how little the hour itself seemed to know about being precious. It went on making crumbs and dirty dishes like any other.

On Monday she opened the kiosk at six. The blank clock glowed faintly in the early dark, and the first train brought a smell of wet wool and cold metal into the station. Before the queue formed, Mara took a till receipt and turned it over. She tried to remember when the tarts had come out of the oven. Three, perhaps, or a quarter past. In the end she wrote, “While the chairs were in the hall.” She folded the receipt once and put it in the cup. A woman bought tea, drew Mara’s slip, and carried it downstairs toward the arriving train.

samples.result:
The summer my mother retired, she began returning things. Not purchases, which she had always returned with the receipt folded neatly around the offending button or cracked lid, but objects that had lived in our house for decades. A blue casserole went to Mrs. Vale across town. A pair of binoculars went to a man who had moved to Oregon. From the linen closet came a yellow towel with MARTIN written on its hem. Nobody remembered Martin. My mother washed the towel, pressed it, and laid it on the dining room table as if expecting him to arrive before lunch.

I was staying with her while my apartment building acquired new plumbing and, according to increasingly optimistic notices, a water supply. Every morning over coffee I received an assignment. Find out whether the Vale daughter still taught piano. See what postage to Oregon would cost. Look through the school photographs for a boy called Martin, possibly a swimmer. I asked what had brought this on. She tipped the sugar bowl toward herself, although she took her coffee black, and studied the small white slope inside. “I have spent thirty years,” she said, “looking around this place for a decent screwdriver.”

This seemed less an explanation than a fresh assignment. Nevertheless, the work agreed with me. Calling strangers with good news is a pleasure ordinarily reserved for people who award grants. The binoculars, it turned out, had belonged to a birdwatcher who was now nearly blind. His granddaughter wrote to say that he wanted them anyway. Mrs. Vale received her casserole without emotion but sent back six peaches in a paper sack, each peach wrapped separately in a page from the sporting section. We ate them standing at the sink. Juice ran down our wrists. The home team had lost again.

By August the dining room held only the towel. We had identified three Martins, none of whom wanted it. One explained at considerable length that his family had always used green towels because his mother believed yellow attracted wasps. Another offered to take it if we were in a bind. The third had been dead since February; his husband answered my letter in a careful hand, enclosing a photograph of Martin at the beach. He was a slight man wearing enormous sunglasses, and over his shoulder, blurred but unmistakable, hung a white hotel towel with a narrow stripe of blue.

“Maybe Martin was the brand,” I suggested. My mother looked insulted. She knew the difference between a manufacturer's label and a name written by a parent, she said. Manufacturers did not go back over the M when the ink ran thin. I picked up the hem. She was right. That awkward first mountain had been climbed twice. I thought of somebody bending over a kitchen counter before camp, already late for work, holding the cloth taut with one hand. Perhaps a child had stood beside that person eating cereal. Perhaps he had said, Nobody's going to steal my stupid towel.

That afternoon the plumber called. There was water in my kitchen again, though for the moment hot came from both taps. I packed my books and carried them downstairs. In the garage my mother was sitting on an overturned bucket, dismantling a wooden box that had once held Christmas ornaments. Beside her lay a screwdriver with a handsome amber handle. “Where did that come from?” I asked. “Hardware store,” she said. “Four dollars.” She passed me the lid of the box. On the underside, in her own handwriting, was a list of gifts from the year I had turned nine.

Among the usual entries, socks and puzzles and a book about whales, was one item I could not account for: a front door key. At nine I had been too young to come home alone. My mother reminded me that I used to go outside after supper and ring the bell, sometimes a dozen times in an evening. I liked the sound, but more than that I liked the ceremony of being admitted. Eventually she had given me a key so she could finish a meal. Had it worked? She laughed. “You unlocked the door and rang the bell anyway.”

I took the lid upstairs. In the empty dining room the late light had found a flaw in the windowpane and projected a little crooked rainbow onto the wall. I folded the yellow towel around the lid to keep its splintered edge from catching on my clothes. My mother came in as I was leaving. For a moment I expected an objection. Instead she tucked a loose corner under my arm. “Give me a call when you get there,” she said, although my apartment was twelve minutes away and she could practically see the roof of it from her porch.

The apartment smelled of plaster. I opened the windows, set the box lid on a shelf, and carried the towel to the bathroom. There was a small puddle under the sink. I got down on my knees and dried the floor, working the towel around the pipe and into the narrow dusty space behind the pedestal. When I stood up, a streak of rust crossed the yellow cotton. I felt unexpectedly ashamed, as though I had put a wedding dress to work polishing silver. Then another drop gathered on the pipe. I spread the towel underneath and called my mother.

She answered on the first ring. In the background I could hear the radio playing the shipping forecast, a program she enjoyed despite living nowhere near navigable water. I told her about the leak and the rust. “Well,” she said, “it was never much good for drying yourself. Too thin.” Outside, somebody was trying to parallel park a truck, and a stranger on the pavement had stopped to guide him. A little more, the stranger said, come on, you've got room. I sat on the bathroom floor and watched the yellow darken, listening to my mother's weather for distant boats.
