samples.result:
The first thing anyone put on the empty shelf was a lemon. It sat in the middle of the board, bright as a headlamp, with a little green leaf still attached. The shelf was in the laundry room of my building, above the table where we folded our clothes. Until that morning it had held three iron scorch marks and nothing else. Nobody knew who had installed it or what it was for. The lemon suggested an answer. By evening it was gone, and in its place someone had left a paperback dictionary with the word *rhubarb* underlined in blue.

I lived on the fourth floor then, in an apartment so narrow that opening the oven door meant leaving the kitchen. I was recently divorced and had developed opinions about things that didn't warrant opinions: the correct thickness of toast, the best hour to buy groceries, which of the two dryers was more nearly honest about how long a minute lasted. The shelf interested me because it was a development. On Tuesday there had been no shelf business. On Wednesday there was a dictionary. I looked up *rhubarb*. Besides the plant, it could mean a noisy argument, especially in baseball.

Within a month the shelf had acquired a clientele. A woman from six took a green glass pitcher and returned with four good teaspoons tied together with yarn. Somebody contributed a jigsaw puzzle in a biscuit tin. On the lid they had written, “Almost certainly boats.” I took it upstairs. It was boats, except for eleven pieces of an entirely different puzzle, apparently a close view of a horse. I spent a slow Sunday fitting the horse pieces together. What emerged was one patient brown eye and enough of a white fence to give the animal somewhere definite to be.

The first disagreement concerned a printer. It was enormous, gray, and heavy enough to bow the board. A note said WORKS, which somebody amended to WORKS IF YOU HAVE THE CABLE, which somebody else amended to WHAT CABLE. For a week we did our folding beneath this exchange. Finally Mr. Bell from the ground floor brought down a cable from his private collection of cables, a collection his wife had been disparaging for thirty years. The printer printed a test page of astonishing beauty: magenta squares, yellow ladders, a whole small city of cyan windows. Mrs. Bell took it upstairs to frame.

Around Christmas I found a red wool mitten on the shelf. Not a pair. A single mitten, left hand, child-sized, with a black button sewn near the wrist. I knew that mitten. My mother had knitted dozens like it, always with a button so the pair could be fastened together by a loop of elastic. For a second I entertained the magnificent impossibility that one of mine had crossed forty years and two state lines to meet me in a basement. Then I turned it over. The thumb was beautifully shaped. My mother had never gotten the hang of thumbs.

I made a sign: “Who knitted the red mitten? I'd like to learn.” The following evening there was a reply beneath mine, in small severe capitals: “THURSDAY. BRING WOOL. NOT THAT FURRY STUFF.” This was how I met Agnes, who lived directly below me and knew me chiefly as a set of footsteps followed occasionally by a dropped shoe. She was eighty-one. She had made the mitten to test a pattern and left it downstairs because throwing away a perfectly good mitten struck her as wasteful, even if the number of cold children with exactly one hand was admittedly limited.

We sat at the folding table while my shirts went around behind glass. Agnes taught by making me look rather than listen. When I asked where the needle went, she held up her own work, waited, and let me find the opening. My first mitten would have fit a reasonably ambitious turnip. My second fit my hand provided I kept my thumb pressed flat against my palm. Agnes said this represented progress for me, if not for the thumb. By March I had a pair I could wear outside. They were gray, warm, and conspicuously the work of somebody learning.

What surprised me was how little the building changed. We did not become a family. People still abandoned wet clothes in the washers. Someone continued to cook fish on Friday nights in a manner that seemed to involve the entire ventilation system. Agnes and I sometimes rode the elevator without speaking, perfectly content to watch the numbers descend. But when a parcel for me was delivered to her apartment, she knew which door was mine. When her kitchen light failed, I knew where she kept the stepladder. These were modest adjustments. They made the place easier to live in.

I moved out two summers later. On my last morning I carried a box of possible offerings down to the laundry room: two mysteries, a corkscrew shaped like a trout, the biscuit tin of boats. The shelf was full. I stood considering my options until a boy came in with his father and spotted the tin in my arms. “Is that for taking?” he asked. I said it was, with one qualification. There was a horse in the harbor. He accepted this news without concern. In fact, he said, tipping the pieces until they rattled, that was probably why the boats had come.

My new building has washing machines in every apartment. For months I did my laundry in luxurious privacy, reading on the sofa while my socks tumbled dry. Then one Saturday I bought too many peaches. I carried three into the hall in a cereal bowl and set it on the deep sill beside the stairs. There was no sign; I hadn't thought to make one. By supper two peaches were gone. By morning the bowl was empty, washed, and back on the sill. Someone had tucked beneath it a square of paper, folded once. Inside was a drawing of a peach pit, exactly to scale.

samples.result:
At the public library in my old neighborhood, there was a drawer marked MAPS THAT NO LONGER HELP. Nobody knew who had written the label. It was not an official category. The official categories were much less interesting. Inside lay a bus map from before the river bridge, a plan of a department store that had become apartments, and a walking guide to trees, several of which had evidently walked away. On rainy afternoons I would open the drawer and choose somewhere impossible to go. This was cheaper than traveling and, in certain respects, required a better pair of shoes.

One Saturday I selected the department store. Its directory promised notions, linens, a portrait studio, and a restaurant called the Copper Pear. I wanted especially to find notions. As a child I had imagined these were thoughts available for purchase, arranged by price and usefulness. A mild suspicion might cost a nickel. A conviction would come wrapped in brown paper. Even after I learned that notions meant buttons and thread, the word retained its original merchandise for me. I copied the floor plan onto the back of an envelope and set off in a drizzle fine enough to wear indoors.

The building stood on Alder Street. Its new entrance occupied the old display window, so that everyone arriving home briefly became something for sale. A man in green slippers was collecting his mail. I explained my errand, expecting embarrassment to end it. Instead he examined my envelope and said, “My kitchen is hosiery.” He sounded pleased. He introduced himself as Leon and offered to show me upstairs. We rode an elevator whose brass indicator still swept a little arc above the door, although the needle now pointed steadily between two and three, maintaining a private opinion about our actual altitude.

Leon's apartment smelled of toast. Hosiery had excellent light. Through a tall window I could see the wet roofs of buses pausing at the intersection and, farther off, a woman on a balcony squeezing rainwater from a yellow cushion. Leon set the envelope on his table. His late wife, he said, had worked in the portrait studio when they were young. She disliked photographing babies but had a gift for husbands. She asked them to calculate seventeen times six. In the instant after they found the answer, each wore a look of modest accomplishment that his family recognized as happiness.

Did he have a portrait she had taken? He did, but it was not of him. From a shelf he brought down a photograph of a pear on a white plate. The fruit had one leaf, withered at the edges, and a bruise shaped like Australia, assuming Australia had suffered some coastal erosion. His wife had taken it on her last afternoon at the store. The restaurant was already closed. Someone had left the pear by the register, perhaps as payment, perhaps because there are only so many objects a person can carry out of a life in one trip.

We drank tea. I asked whether he remembered where the notions counter had been. Without looking at my envelope he pointed directly down. “Mrs. Vale,” he said. “She does alterations. You'll appreciate that.” We found her door propped open with a dictionary, the heavy kind that used to settle disputes by the sheer sound of landing on a table. Inside, a boy stood on a stool while Mrs. Vale pinned his trousers. His socks displayed small, disreputable frogs. He was going to a wedding, he informed us, but was not himself getting married. He wished to make that distinction clear.

When he stepped down, Mrs. Vale considered the floor plan. She had indeed arranged her sewing machine almost exactly where the old notions counter had stood. This struck me as a marvelous coincidence until she explained that both positions were beside the only convenient electrical outlet. I liked the explanation better. A coincidence closes neatly, like a clasp. An outlet opens onto a whole history of practical decisions: someone needed light there, someone drilled through plaster, someone else, decades later, refused to spend good money on an extension cord. The boy practiced walking solemnly. His frogs rose and fell. 

By then the rain had stopped. I thanked them both and went outside, where sunlight shone on a puddle full of scaffolding. I still had an hour before the library closed. On the envelope I drew Leon's table, the elevator needle, the dictionary, and two frogs, one noticeably more competent than the other. Then I crossed the street to see the building from a distance. In a third-floor window a man in green slippers raised one hand. From below, the gesture looked like a shopkeeper turning a sign from CLOSED to OPEN, or possibly the other way around.

Back at the library, the woman at the desk supplied a fresh envelope because mine had developed a tea ring across the linens department. I decided to keep the ring. She watched me tuck my drawing behind the directory and asked whether I had found what I wanted. I said yes, although in fact I had not known what I wanted until a few minutes earlier. I had wanted the past to be somewhere other than behind me. Upstairs from a sewing machine seemed a perfectly satisfactory arrangement. The librarian shut the drawer gently with her hip.

Years later, when the library moved, I went to the sale of its old furniture. The map cabinet was gone. I bought a small oak stool instead, an awkward thing to carry home on a crowded bus. A little girl asked what it was for. I was about to say reaching high shelves, but she had already put her toy rabbit on it. The rabbit sat upright in the aisle, facing forward, the only passenger with a seat perfectly suited to its legs. We rode that way for six stops. When the girl got off, she thanked me for bringing the rabbit's chair.

At closing time, the librarian tipped the book-return bin and heard something roll. It was a lemon, a good one, heavy for its size. She set it on the desk and finished checking in the books.

There was a place in the lost-property drawer for keys, and a place for glasses, and a large and frankly optimistic place for single gloves. There was no place for a lemon. She left it by the date stamp.

At nine the next morning a small boy came in with his father.

“Did you get it?” he asked.

“The lemon?”

He nodded, relieved. His father put a hand on his shoulder. “Tell her why, Cal.”

Cal studied the carpet. “You said I could bring back anything I took out.”

“And you took out a lemon?”

“From the tree in the courtyard.”

She had wondered about that tree. In six years she had seen it produce exactly one lemon, high on a branch above the bench. Apparently all it had needed was another week and a boy with a father tall enough to lift him.

“You can keep it,” she said. “Fruit works differently from books.”

Cal picked up the lemon. It filled both his hands. “What about the seeds?”

“Those you can bring back.”

He did, on Thursday, in an envelope marked LEMON PARTS. By then she had found a pot.

Today I’m thinking about a repair I saw on a library book. Someone had torn the corner off a page, taking the last few letters of six lines with it. A librarian, I assume, had cut a piece of paper to fit the gap, taped it on, and written the missing letters in blue ink. The handwriting was small and rather upright. For half a page the novelist had a collaborator.

What I liked best was the word “nevertheless.” The tear had gone straight through it, so that “never” was printed and “theless” was in blue. It’s an ungainly word to begin with, and the repair made you feel every joint in it. I must have spent a full minute looking at that word in a novel whose title I’ve since forgotten.

Somebody had to find another copy to get those letters right. I picture the two books open side by side on a desk, the good one held flat with an elbow while the librarian tried a pen on a scrap to make sure it wouldn’t bleed. Maybe it was nearly closing time. Maybe somebody was waiting to take the book home.

I hope they noticed “nevertheless.” I also hope they were so caught up in the story that they didn’t.

The best thing I ever saw in a museum was a small boy explaining a revolving door to his grandfather. They hadn’t bought tickets yet. As far as the boy was concerned, they were already at the exhibit.

“You have to keep walking,” he said.

His grandfather, who had probably been through several thousand revolving doors, gave it a look of reasonable doubt. “Even when I get outside?”

The boy considered this. “No. Outside you can do what you want.”

They went around twice. On the second revolution the grandfather raised a hand to the woman at the ticket desk, as if passing her on a riverboat. She raised hers back.

I spent the next hour looking at Roman glass. There was a little blue cup I liked very much, repaired from three pieces, with a thumbnail-sized chip missing from the rim. The label said it had been used for drinking. Usually that kind of information slides right off me, but that morning I could picture somebody owning it: turning the chipped side away from a guest, filling it a little short of the top.

On my way out I took the revolving door around twice. The woman at the desk was on the phone by then. She waved anyway.

“No, I mean that’s what I use the mint for.” She pinched off a sprig. “The sock’s pink.”

I liked her for not trying to cheer me up.

“Yes.”

The man who answered thought for a moment. “Kitchen ones or sewing ones?”

I hadn’t known there would be a question. “Let’s start with the kitchen ones,” I said.

“Glue?” I said.

“No. It’s big, and this is a small shop.”

Her reply came while I was eating the pear. *That was our antenna. We were listening for whales.*

I had no memory of the whales at all. I called her to find out whether we’d heard any.

I waited. I had brought in my father’s watch, which had started losing about four minutes a day. At first this hadn’t bothered me. Then I missed a train by just enough time to see a woman in a blue coat settle into the window seat I would have chosen.

The watchmaker came back carrying two coffees. He set one on the counter in front of me.

“How did you know somebody would be waiting?”

“I didn’t,” he said. “That one’s for later.”

He opened the watch and bent over it. I drank nothing. From the back room came a single, extravagant cuckoo, though it was twenty past eleven by my phone.

“My dad used to set it five minutes fast,” I said.

“Want me to do that?”

I almost said yes. Then I remembered my father in the hall, patting his pockets for his keys, calling to my mother that they had plenty of time because his watch was five minutes fast. She had already been sitting in the car for ten.

“No,” I said. “Just make it right.”

When I came back on Friday, the watch was ready. The watchmaker set it to the second and buckled it around my wrist. I caught my train with time to spare. The window seat was taken, but the one across from it was free, and it turned out there was a river on that side.

**On Lending Tools**

I lent a neighbor a drill and immediately needed it. This was surprising, since I had owned the drill for six years and used it twice. But as soon as it crossed the hall, I noticed a shelf that could go up. I even held the shelf against the wall for a while, enjoying the rare pleasure of being prevented from doing something I had no intention of doing.

My neighbor brought the drill back on Sunday. She had used it to put a handrail beside her bathtub. “Come try it,” she said.

“My dad’s visiting,” she said. “He won’t ask for help getting out.”

We stood there for a moment looking at the rail. It was exactly where your hand wanted it to be.

The shelf is still behind my sofa. A month later, when the man downstairs asked if anyone had a drill, I brought it down before I could think of anything else that needed doing.

My neighbor Mara keeps a drawer of things that have lost their partners: one brass earring, three dice from different games, a blue mitten small enough for a doll. When I asked what she planned to do with them, she looked surprised. “Nothing yet,” she said, as if yet were a perfectly respectable length of time.

Last winter the power failed during supper. Our building emptied into the hallway, where somebody had lit a camping lantern. The children got restless. Mara went upstairs and came back with her drawer.

She set the objects on a tea towel and invited us to invent a museum. The mitten, according to a boy on the second floor, belonged to a mouse who delivered ice. The earring was a handle from a door in the moon. A bent teaspoon had been bent deliberately by a queen who disliked soup.

The next summer I went home for a visit. Dad met my train wearing shorts I had never seen before. His shins, which I may also never have seen before, were brown and surprisingly battered.

We walked through the square. The town had put flower boxes beneath the clock tower. The hands still said 2:18.

“Do you miss it?” I asked.

“Oh, parts of it.”

“Which parts?”

He thought about that. “About halfway up there’s a window. In winter you could see straight into the bakery. They’d be turning the loaves out. Always liked that.”

I had imagined him missing the great brass mechanism, the privilege of setting the town in motion. Instead he missed a window. It struck me that I knew very little about what he had been doing all those years.

At the pool he introduced me to the woman in the silver cap. Her name was June. She had been married once to a bassoonist and could hold her breath for two lengths. My father could swim six lengths by then, though he changed strokes three or four times and once simply stood up.

“Come on,” he said.

I told him I hadn’t brought a suit.

“That’s what I used to say,” he said, and went back in.

I sat in the gallery while the afternoon lanes filled. June was teaching a small boy to put his face in the water. My father swam to the deep end and rolled onto his back. He wasn’t especially graceful. His chin stuck out and his toes emerged at irregular intervals. From above he looked a little like a man being carried away on an invisible stretcher.

Then he opened one eye, caught me watching, and splashed me with astonishing accuracy.

My father lived another twelve years. When people here remember him they generally mention the clock, and that’s fair enough. Thirty-one years is a long time to keep anything going. But when I want to hear his voice, I think of that phone call, of the little silence after I asked if he had floated on his back, and of a pencil scratching on paper at the other end of the line: a man of sixty-eight, alone in his kitchen, making a note to try the other way.

When the city took down the clock at Mercer and Ninth, they left its shadow on the wall: a pale circle above the pharmacy, with four little squares where the brackets had been. For thirty years I had looked up at that clock on my way to work. The morning it was gone, I looked at the circle and thought, quite distinctly, *I have plenty of time.*

I was late, of course.

The clock had always run seven minutes fast. This was useful to people who didn’t know it and useless to people who did. My father, who repaired watches in a shop across the street, considered it a personal insult. Once a week he wrote down the discrepancy on a postcard and mailed it to the Department of Public Works. After he died, I found a bundle of replies in his desk. The first twelve were form letters. The thirteenth said, in blue ink, “Dear Mr. Vale, I walk past it too. I know. Yours, Denise.”

There were no more postcards after that. Instead, there were Christmas cards from Denise.

I inherited the shop. Not the skill, unfortunately, just the lease and many shallow drawers full of screws small enough to inhale. I tried keeping it open. People came in with stopped watches, and I changed their batteries. If that didn’t work, I gave them directions to a man in Queens. Gradually the watch business became a key-cutting business, because the machine came with instructions and the instructions were good. My father’s name stayed on the window: VALE, HOROLOGIST. Below it I taped a sheet of paper that said KEYS $4.

The afternoon the clock disappeared, a woman came in carrying its minute hand.

It was nearly as long as her arm, black on one side and a startling clean white on the other.

“Denise?” I said.

“His daughter?” she said.

We shook hands across the counter. She had retired from Public Works years ago, but a friend on the crew had called her when they took the clock down. The housing was cracked. The motor had burned out. She had asked for the hand and, having obtained it, discovered she did not particularly want a large piece of municipal property in her apartment.

“I thought your father might like it,” she said, and then shut her eyes. “Listen to me. I went to his funeral.”

“He’d have hated it,” I said.

“Yes,” she said happily. “He would.”

We tried it in several places. Horizontal above the door, it looked like a direction nobody should follow. Upright beside the register, it looked like a sword. Finally Denise laid it on the floor to free her hands while she put her scarf back on. A customer stepped over it, collected two brass keys, stepped over it again, then came back from the sidewalk.

“Is that the minute hand?” he asked.

Soon there were six people in the shop. One remembered the clock being slow, not fast. Another insisted it had once had a second hand. A delivery driver said he’d spent a whole summer eating lunch beneath it and had never noticed it at all. Denise sat on the stool behind the counter and listened with the serene expression of a woman to whom none of these complaints could any longer be officially addressed.

At closing time, she bought a key.

“What for?” I asked.

“My front door.”

“I mean, do you need one?”

“Eventually,” she said.

After she left, I swept the floor. I turned off the lights. In the window, my father’s gold letters floated backward over the dark street. Across the way, the pale circle was still visible above the pharmacy. They would paint it soon, I thought, or the weather would darken it until nobody could find the edge.

I picked up the minute hand. At its base was a square hole, and the hole, by a coincidence my father could have expressed to three decimal places, fitted over the square spindle of the old awning crank.

I slid it on. It held.

In the morning I stood outside the shop and turned the minute hand. High above me, the striped canvas unrolled for the first time in years. Dust fell. Two dry leaves and a green plastic dinosaur dropped onto the pavement. The awning was faded almost to pink, except for the last foot, which had been rolled tight against the wall and was still a magnificent red.

At nine, Denise came by on her way to buy bread. She stood under the awning and looked up at the red stripe.

“Was that always there?”

“The color was.”

She considered this. Then she took the dinosaur, which she said her grandson would like, and went on down the street.

It rained that afternoon. People stopped beneath the awning to close umbrellas, open umbrellas, search for bus fare, finish phone calls. A boy waited there for his mother. A woman put down her groceries and divided the weight more evenly between two bags. Nobody came in for a key until nearly five.

I had the door propped open. I could hear the rain hitting the canvas, a good sound, surprisingly loud. When the woman with the groceries had finished rearranging them, she stayed another minute with her hands empty. I stayed where I was. Neither of us looked up.

At the library where I worked when I was nineteen, we kept a drawer full of things people had used as bookmarks and then forgotten. The rule was that anything worth more than five dollars went to the front desk. This required the evening staff, none of whom earned much more than five dollars an hour, to make certain judgments about the world.

A photograph of a horse: drawer. Two tickets to a baseball game: front desk until the game was over, then drawer. A five-dollar bill: the subject of a surprisingly bitter meeting.

My favorite was a shopping list written on the back of an envelope.

*Milk  
Batteries  
Something for Dennis*

For months I wondered what Dennis got. I pictured him as a difficult uncle who came to supper every Thursday and brought his own stool because the dining chairs hurt his back. Something for Dennis might be marzipan. It might be a magazine about trains. The person making the list had known exactly what kind of thing would do, which seemed to me an enviable degree of intimacy.

At nineteen I was bad at buying presents. I bought people things I wanted them to like. For my mother, who read mysteries in the bath, I bought a thick biography of a Russian poet. For my friend Ben, who liked working on cars, I bought a jazz record because I’d recently discovered jazz and believed the discovery might be transferable.

One rainy night a woman came in ten minutes before closing and asked whether we had found a photograph of a horse.

I got the drawer. She went through the photographs—we had accumulated several horses by then—and selected one of a brown mare standing beside a wire fence. On the back, in a child’s handwriting, was the word *June*.

“Is that the horse’s name?” I asked.

“No,” she said. “That’s when we saw it.”

She put it into her wallet behind a picture of two boys in identical striped shirts. I wanted to ask why this particular horse, glimpsed in June, mattered enough to come downtown in the rain. But she had already thanked me and gone, and my manager was trying to get the vacuum cleaner to surrender a shoelace.

Years later, helping my mother move, I found the Russian poet in a box marked BATHROOM. The bottom inch of the book had swollen to twice its proper size. A receipt marked her place about halfway through.

“You read this?”

“Some. His wife’s having a terrible time.”

Between us on the floor lay three rubber ducks, a tin of buttons, and the little green clock that had sat on the toilet tank all my life. We were supposed to be sorting. Instead I opened the book at the receipt and my mother told me about the wife. She had to keep moving the family from one damp apartment to another. She had sold a good coat. Nobody ever seemed to mind the children except her.

“Does it say what became of her?” my mother asked.

I looked in the index and turned to the last page where the wife appeared. She had outlived the poet by thirty-one years. For twelve of them she’d run a hotel on the Black Sea.

“A hotel!” my mother said. “I’d have read that book.”

We stopped for lunch. Down the street there was a place selling sandwiches wrapped in white paper, and while we waited at the counter my mother noticed a rack of detective novels for a dollar apiece. She chose one with a drowned baronet on the cover. I paid for it along with the sandwiches.

Back at the house, she took her sandwich upstairs. A few minutes later I heard the taps running. We still had most of the bathroom to pack, but I took the supper plates out of their cupboard and began wrapping them instead.

By four, the baronet’s daughter had confessed to moving the body, the poet was in a box with the bathroom scales, and I had packed everything we needed to eat supper except two forks and a gravy boat. My mother stood in the kitchen doorway with her hair wet.

“Did you keep the receipt for lunch?” she asked. “I need something to hold my place.”

When my mother sold the house, my brother wanted to take the pencil marks off the kitchen doorframe. He arrived with a pry bar wrapped in a beach towel.

“You can’t just remove part of the house,” I said.

“It’s trim, Annie. They sell it by the foot.”

What they did not sell by the foot was the afternoon I overtook him. I was eleven and he was fourteen. Our father measured us twice because Paul had begun to cry. On the wood beside my name, Dad had written, in his fussy all-capitals, VERIFIED.

The buyers were coming at noon for the keys. It was ten-thirty. Our mother sat at the kitchen table eating an orange over the sink, or as nearly over the sink as a person could manage without getting out of her chair.

“Ask them,” she said.

Paul considered this a failure of imagination. He had brought matching trim. He had brought white paint in a jam jar. He had even brought the tiny brush from his daughter’s watercolor set, its handle printed with yellow ducks.

“By the time they get here,” he said, “there won’t be anything to ask.”

He worked the flat end of the bar under the wood. The first nail came free with a squeak. Behind the strip was a narrow band of green wallpaper, a color so vigorous and unpleasant that all three of us said, “Oh,” and leaned closer.

“Your grandmother picked that,” Mom said.

“I thought Grandma had taste.”

“She did. She liked that.”

Paul eased out the second nail. Halfway up the frame, the wood split lengthwise. He stopped. A sliver stood out from the wall, bearing the top half of an E.

Mom put down her orange.

“I used to cheat,” she said.

Paul kept one hand on the bar. “At what?”

“When he measured you. I’d put my thumb under the book.”

“Which of us?”

“Whoever was having a bad year.”

Outside, the scrub jay that had spent the morning dismantling a patio cushion flew past the window with a long white thread in its beak.

“Eleven was a pretty bad year for me,” I said.

“It was,” she agreed.

“Fourteen was no picnic,” Paul said.

“You had the drums.”

“I was bad at the drums.”

“You didn’t know that then.”

He started laughing, which made the pry bar wobble, which made me grab the loose end of the trim. For a moment the two of us stood there holding it to the wall.

“I’ve got nowhere to put this,” he said.

Neither did I. My apartment doors were metal. Paul’s wife had spent two years renovating their house to look as little like the house we grew up in as money allowed.

Mom took the duck brush out of his pocket. “Put it back.”

We put it back. Paul tapped the nails in with the heel of his hand as far as they would go, then fetched his hammer. I fitted the splinter into place. Mom painted a thin white seam along the crack. She had a steadier hand than either of us, though lately she had asked me to write her checks.

At noon the buyers came: two women and a little boy in a red coat, too warm for the weather. While the adults dealt with keys and the garage code, he stood in the kitchen examining the pencil marks. Then he backed up to the frame, heels together, chin lifted. He did it so naturally I looked around for a pencil.

My mother already had one.

“May I?” she asked the women. They nodded. She found a paperback in her handbag and rested it on his head. He held himself very still.

“What’s your name, sweetheart?”

“Daniel.”

She drew the line and wrote DANIEL beside it, then handed his mothers the pencil. Paul carried her handbag to the car. I took the bag of oranges. We were halfway down the front walk when I thought to ask.

“Did you give him the thumb?”

Mom looked back. Through the kitchen window we could see Daniel jumping, trying to touch the top of the door.

“First day in a new house,” she said. “Absolutely.”

At nine on Tuesday morning, a woman came into the municipal archives and asked to hear the lake.

“I don’t mean waves,” she said. “I mean when it froze.”

I was alone at the desk. My supervisor had gone to the dentist and left me three things to do, none of which involved the lake. I asked the woman what year.

“Any winter before they built the road.”

This was a sensible distinction. The road ran along the eastern shore, and even at night you could hear the trucks changing gears on the hill.

I found six recordings under LAKE, all made by the same person, Martin Bell, who had taught physics at the high school. Five were on cassette. The sixth was a reel of quarter-inch tape in a biscuit tin. On the lid, in red pencil, he had written: *Cold enough at last.*

The woman took off her gloves finger by finger. She had a little crescent of blue paint on one thumbnail.

“Is he family?” I asked.

“Who?”

“Mr. Bell.”

“No. Is that important?”

It wasn’t. I had wanted a story to go with the request, preferably one that would justify not doing the three things on my list. I went downstairs for the reel-to-reel player.

We listened in the map room. At first there was a rush of wind, then a zipper going up or down, then a man saying, quite distinctly, “Damn the button.” After that, nothing for so long that I reached toward the machine.

The woman caught my sleeve.

A low note had begun. It slid upward and broke into three quick knocks. From what sounded like a great distance came a thinner answering note. Then the whole lake went off at once: a boom, a shiver of high notes, and a noise exactly like someone shaking a sheet of metal at the back of a school play.

The woman laughed.

“Sorry,” she said. “I’d made it much more dignified in my head.”

We listened to the rest. Mr. Bell stamped his feet. A dog barked. The ice made a few experimental chirps, as if embarrassed by its earlier performance. At the very end, a child said, “Can we go in now?” and Mr. Bell said, “We could have gone in ages ago. I thought *you* wanted to stay.”

There was a click.

The woman put both gloves back on.

“Did that help?” I asked.

“Oh, yes. It’s the water heater.”

She explained that she had recently moved into a flat above a bakery. Every morning at four, something woke her. For weeks she had lain there trying to place the sound. Yesterday she had remembered standing on the shore in her yellow boots, listening to the ice. She’d had the daft idea that perhaps the sound had followed her somehow, all the way to a second-floor flat on King Street.

“But that’s not it,” she said. “Not even close. I’ll speak to the landlord.”

After she left, I rewound the reel. The tin had a catalogue number on the bottom, and I looked it up in the old accession book. There was Mr. Bell’s address, the date of donation, the speed at which to play the tape. Under DESCRIPTION someone had typed *Thermal contraction of freshwater ice. Intermittent surface fracturing. Some extraneous noise.*

For the first time that morning, I did one of the things my supervisor had left me: I updated a catalogue entry.

I kept the ice and the fracturing. I kept the speed. In place of the last sentence I wrote: *Also audible: wind, clothing, footsteps, dog. At end, brief conversation between recordist and child about whose idea it was to remain outdoors.*

It took up more space. There was room.

The shortest item in the lost-property ledger was a tooth.

I found the entry in my second week at the municipal swimming pool, while looking for a man’s missing glasses. The ledger went back to 1983. In those days the staff had written in green fountain pen. *One tooth, bottom of deep end*, someone had recorded, then, in the column headed CLAIMED BY: *Boy who lost it.*

I liked the confidence of that. No demand for a description.

By the time I worked there, we had a clear plastic bin for goggles, a wire basket for towels, and a little safe for anything worth more than twenty pounds. Wedding rings lived in the safe beside a single hearing aid and an envelope containing forty Canadian dollars. The glasses were on the man’s head. He discovered them himself and asked me, quite seriously, not to put the incident in the book.

Most people knew exactly what they’d lost. One woman could describe her daughter’s swimsuit down to a loose thread under the left arm, though the daughter, standing beside her in a towel, maintained that she had never seen the swimsuit before. But every Thursday an older man in a shirt buttoned to the throat would ask whether anything had turned up.

“What sort of thing?” I asked the first time.

“Oh, I’ll know it.”

I let him look through the goggles. He took his time.

His name was Leonard. He didn’t swim. His wife had swum there for thirty years, he told me, and had once come home wearing somebody else’s shoes. Same make, same colour, half a size larger. She’d been delighted. “At last,” she’d said, “these bloody things are breaking in.”

I assumed his wife had died. This was because I was twenty and assumed anyone mentioned in the past tense was dead. In fact she’d taken up bowling.

“She likes a sport where she can keep her glasses on,” he said.

“Is she missing something?”

“Almost certainly.”

By October I had worked out that Leonard came on Thursdays because the number six bus changed drivers outside the pool. His daughter drove the morning route. She had seven minutes between getting off the bus and getting into the van that took her back to the depot. Sometimes he brought her a sandwich. Sometimes they stood smoking together under the NO SMOKING sign, carefully dropping their ash into his empty sandwich box. Looking through lost property was what he did if he arrived early.

One Thursday he found what he was looking for.

It was a small blue mitten, stiff with dried pool water, with a white rabbit knitted into the back. He turned it over. A name tape had been sewn inside the cuff.

“Good Lord,” he said. “I sewed that in.”

The name was Ruth Bell. His daughter’s name. She’d worn the mittens as a child, he said, and hadn’t they been a nuisance, because the rabbits meant there was a right and a wrong one, unlike a sensible pair of mittens?

I was already constructing the story. The mitten had spent thirty years behind a radiator. A workman had dislodged it. It had come back to the man who sewed the tape into its cuff. I could see the photograph in the local paper: Leonard holding up the mitten, me beside him for some reason.

Then his daughter came in.

“There it is,” she said. “Where was it?”

“You wore this when you were little.”

“Yes, Dad. And now Maisie wears it. Where was it?”

I checked the ledger. “Ladies’ changing room. Tuesday.”

“Thanks. She’s been going to school with a sock on her hand.”

Leonard seemed as disappointed as I was. He gave her the mitten and the sandwich. They went outside to smoke.

At closing time I entered Ruth’s name in the CLAIMED BY column. There were faint squares on the page where a previous receptionist had used the ledger as a mat for doing the football pools. Upstairs, the last swimmers were collecting their children. You could tell which families had found all their belongings by the rhythm of their footsteps on the metal stairs: a quick descent for the ones who had everything; a stop, a small argument, and a single furious pair of feet going back up for the ones who hadn’t.

I worked at the pool for another two years. The Canadian dollars were never claimed. Neither was the hearing aid, though its battery lasted long enough to give a thin, indignant whistle whenever I opened the safe. Leonard still came in on Thursdays. Once, when his daughter’s route changed, he waited forty minutes before admitting she might not be coming.

I made him a cup of tea. We sat behind the desk, leafing through the old ledger. He was the one who noticed that on the line below the tooth, in the same green ink, somebody had written: *Sixpence, bottom of deep end.*

“Fair exchange,” he said.

The first time my mother forgot how to make rice, she called me and pretended she was conducting a survey.

“How much water do you use for one cup?”

“One and a half cups. Why?”

“And do you wash it?”

“You taught me to wash it.”

“I know what I taught you. I’m asking what you do.”

I could hear the pencil. For some reason that was what frightened me: she was writing it down.

“Depends who’s coming over,” I said. “If it’s just me, sometimes I don’t bother.”

“You should bother just for you.”

She hung up before I could ask her anything.

That Christmas I bought her a rice cooker. She already owned a rice cooker, as I discovered when I opened the cupboard to put mine away. The old one was a wedding present, cream-colored, with a little orange lever. It had made approximately half of my body. I had forgotten it existed.

“Well,” my mother said, watching me kneel on the kitchen floor between the two machines. “Runs in the family.”

We laughed much harder than the joke deserved. Neither of us wanted to be the first to stop.

By spring she had notes everywhere. Some were practical: GLASSES, KEYS, TUESDAY BINS. Others seemed to be addressed to a difficult employee. PLEASE FINISH ONE JOB BEFORE BEGINNING ANOTHER. There was a note on the back door saying CAT, although we had not owned a cat for eleven years.

“What am I supposed to do about the cat?” I asked.

“Oh, nothing. That one’s old.”

I reached to peel it off.

“Leave it,” she said. “I like thinking for half a second I have a cat.”

I left it.

One Sunday in June I found her at the table with a stack of index cards, trying to write down the things nobody else in the family knew. Where her father’s watch had gone. Which cousin still owed her forty dollars. The name of the woman in the photograph everybody thought was Aunt Lorna, including, when she was alive, Aunt Lorna.

“Is there anything you want to know?” she asked.

There were enormous things I wanted to know. Had she been happy with my father? Had she wanted another life? Which of the many things I had said to hurt her had actually hurt? But she had uncapped her pen and was waiting, and what came out was, “What did you put in the eggs at the beach?”

When I was nine we had rented a cottage for a week. It rained every day. My father got a fishhook through the pad of his thumb without having caught, or even seen, a fish. But the scrambled eggs my mother made on the last morning were so good that for years afterward my brother and I asked for beach eggs. She could never make them again.

She set down the pen. “I used the pan after the doughnuts.”

“What doughnuts?”

“You were asleep. Your father and I used to buy those plain doughnuts and fry them in butter. If you children had known, we’d have had to buy six. We could afford two.”

“All these years you let us think it was some kind of spice.”

“I forgot about the doughnuts.”

“But you remember now?”

“Apparently.”

I got up and looked in her bread bin. There were no doughnuts. We drove to the supermarket.

At home she cut one in half around its equator and set both halves facedown in a buttered frying pan. When the cut sides were brown we ate them standing at the counter. Then she cracked four eggs into the pan. I started to reach for the milk.

“Absolutely not,” she said.

We ate the eggs with the little forks she usually saved for company. They were fine. Faintly sweet in places. Not what I remembered.

“Well?” she asked.

I considered lying. “I think maybe you had to be nine.”

“And damp,” she said.

Afterward I washed up while she sat at the table and made out a card. I assumed she was writing down the recipe. When I went to put it in the box, I saw what she had written.

*June 12. Ellen came over. We had the doughnuts first this time, together.*

I read it twice. Until then I had thought of the cards as a way of getting things out of the house before the roof came down. It hadn’t occurred to me that she was still moving things in.

There were three doughnuts left in the bag. I put two in the freezer and took one home. On Monday morning I fried it before work. I used too much butter, which turned out to be a fairly minor error in the scheme of things. I ate both halves off a saucer with my little finger through the hole where the cup was meant to sit.

Then I washed the saucer. I was running late. I washed it just for me.

When the city put a bench at the top of Mercer Hill, my father wrote to complain that it faced the wrong way. He had a point. In one direction you could see the harbor, the grain elevators, and, on a clear day, the white scar on Dunley Island where a hotel had slid into the sea. In the other direction you could see the back of a pharmacy. The bench faced the pharmacy.

He enclosed a photograph and a self-addressed envelope. Three weeks later a woman from Public Works called to say the bench had been turned around.

“Just like that?” he asked.

“Four bolts,” she said.

He was delighted. For years he had voted, attended meetings, signed petitions. Here was a photograph he had taken on a Wednesday producing, by the following month, a change in the physical arrangement of the world. He walked up Mercer Hill to inspect it. An old woman was sitting on the bench backward, her shoes planted in the flower bed, her arms folded across the backrest.

“Better view on this side,” he said, pointing.

“I know what the harbor looks like.”

He stood there a moment. The pharmacy had blue bins, a drainpipe, and a steel door with a square of wired glass.

“What are you looking at, then?”

“My son comes out at three.”

It was ten to three. My father sat beside her, facing the harbor. A tug pushed two barges past the elevators. He tried to decide whether to tell her he was responsible for the bench. Before he could make up his mind, the steel door opened and a man in a white coat came out carrying a banana and a paperback. He saw the woman, held up the banana in greeting, and sat on an overturned crate to read.

“Doesn’t he come over?” my father asked.

“He’s on his break,” she said, as if this were an odd question, which it was.

My father told this story often. Depending on his audience, it demonstrated either that the city was unusually responsive or that a person ought to mind his business. When he told it to children, he made the banana a different fruit each time. My niece once interrupted to say that nobody held up a bowl of cherries in one hand while carrying an open book in the other, and he conceded the point.

Years later, after he died, my brother and I went up Mercer Hill. We were supposed to be choosing a place to scatter his ashes, a task for which he had left instructions of magnificent uselessness: *Somewhere outdoors.*

The bench was gone. In its place stood a metal cabinet marked TRAFFIC SIGNAL CONTROL. The pharmacy was now a dance school. Through the wired glass we could see a red cardigan hanging on a hook.

My brother set the cardboard box on the cabinet and bent to tie his shoe. Immediately a voice behind us said, “You can’t leave that there.”

It belonged to a little girl in a black leotard, holding the steel door open with her hip.

“We’re not leaving it,” I said.

“Because people put drinks there and then they blow over and the straws go down the drain.”

“Do they?”

She pointed. There were indeed several striped straws behind the grate.

My brother picked up the box. “What should people do?”

“Hold their drinks.”

The door shut. We stood looking at the spot where she had been, and then my brother began to laugh. He had our father’s laugh, which started so quietly you often mistook it for a cough and offered him water just as he got going.

We took the ashes down to the harbor. At low tide there was a little beach beside the ferry slip, and we waited there for a family to finish collecting shells. My brother rolled his trousers to the knee. I held his belt while he waded out, because the stones were slick and because neither of us wanted to explain to our mother that we had dropped Dad in with the packaging.

It went fine. Some ashes floated; most sank. A ferry backed out of its slip with a shudder that traveled through the soles of my feet. My brother came ashore and dried his legs with his socks, thereby creating a problem he had not anticipated.

On the walk home he stopped at the pharmacy on King Street to buy another pair. I waited outside with the empty box. After a while the automatic doors parted and he emerged, wearing his new socks and carrying, in addition to the old ones, two bottles of water and a banana.

I’m aware that the banana is a bit much. If I were making this up I’d give him chewing gum, or nothing at all. But he came through those doors, saw me on the curb, and raised that banana over his head, and for once in my life I was looking exactly the right way.

The first thing I learned to mend was the left knee of a pair of green trousers. My mother showed me how to slip a piece of cardboard down the leg so I wouldn’t sew the front to the back. I remember this because I took the cardboard out too soon and sewed the front to the back. For a minute I thought I might still wear them. I was nine. I put my foot in and got as far as the knee.

My mother was on the phone with the gas company. She watched me hop twice, then pointed at the seam ripper without interrupting the account number she was reading aloud.

I’ve kept a piece of cardboard in my sewing tin ever since. The current one is cut from a box of lasagne sheets. Most of what I mend now belongs to my daughter, who wears through her clothes in surprising places. Last winter she brought me a coat with the pocket hanging off on the inside. The outer cloth was untouched. Whatever had happened to it had happened in private.

“What do you keep in here?”

“Just my things.”

I put my hand through the tear. Down in the lining, along the hem, I found three stones, a pound coin, a blue pencil worn to the length of my thumb and a folded note so soft at the creases that it felt like a piece of flannel.

“Do you want this?” I asked.

She snatched it, which answered that. I handed over the pencil and the coin. The stones she said I could throw away.

They were nothing special. Not even good for skimming. I set them on the table, and while I was sewing the pocket she picked one up and rubbed its grey face with a wet finger.

“This one goes purple.”

It did, a little. We watched it dry. Then she wet it again.

My mother used to turn out our pockets into a chipped saucer on top of the washing machine. At the end of the week, anything we hadn’t claimed was hers. This was mostly an incentive to collect our change. But once I found her at the kitchen sink washing a horse chestnut I’d forgotten. It had been in the saucer for months. The shine had gone out of it and the skin was puckered. She polished it with the tea towel and put it in the pocket of her dressing gown.

Years later, when she moved into a flat, we cleared out the house together. I found that dressing gown on a hook behind the bathroom door and reached straight into the pocket. There was a tissue in there, and the little metal key for bleeding the radiators.

“What are you looking for?” she asked.

I told her.

“Oh, love,” she said. “I’ve had about six dressing gowns since that one.”

I don’t know why I’d expected to find the chestnut. I’d thrown away whole sets of furniture in the meantime.

When I finished the coat, my daughter tested the pocket with her fist. She put the pencil back, and the coin, and the folded note. She carried the purple stone upstairs. The other two stayed on the table until supper, when I scooped them up with the crumbs and put them in the bin.

A week later she asked for them.

“I thought you didn’t want them.”

“I didn’t then.”

This struck me as such a reasonable account of being alive that I went outside in my slippers and opened the wheelie bin. Unfortunately it had been emptied that morning. There was nothing at the bottom but a sticker from an apple.

We went looking for replacements. It was nearly dark, and the gravel beside our building was the wrong kind altogether, sharp little chips of yellow. We walked as far as the chemist’s, where a tree had lifted a square of pavement and exposed a pocket of earth. My daughter crouched there and worked a stone loose with her pencil.

“Here,” she said.

I held out my hand. It was brown, flat on one side. I waited while she looked for another, but she had already stood up.

“Is one enough?”

“That one’s yours.”

I almost asked what I was supposed to do with it. Then I put it in my pocket, where there happened to be a hole. We heard it hit the pavement.

My daughter looked at me. I looked at her. She laughed so hard she had to lean against the chemist’s window, and the woman inside, halfway through lowering the blind, stopped to see what was funny.

At home I fetched the lasagne cardboard and my daughter chose some thread. She wanted yellow, though the coat was black. I showed her how to knot the end and how to push the needle away from the hand holding the cloth. Her stitches went in several directions. I had to stop myself from pulling them out and starting again.

When she was done, I tried the stone. It held.

There’s a yellow pucker just below my hip now. From the outside you can see exactly where the pocket ends.

At nine on Monday morning, the council hired me to remove a doorway from the town hall.

“The whole wall?” I asked.

“Just the doorway,” said Mrs. Vale. “People keep going through it.”

This seemed to me the strongest argument in the doorway’s favor, but I had recently become self-employed and was learning which thoughts belonged on an invoice.

The doorway connected the records office to a narrow courtyard. It had no door, only two iron hinges painted so many times they resembled small white fists. On the other side stood a bench, a drain, and a pear tree. The pears were hard and yellow and, according to a handwritten notice, not for eating.

I set down my toolbox. A man in a bicycle helmet came through carrying a mug.

“Morning,” he said.

“Morning. Where are you headed?”

“Accounts.”

“Is Accounts out here?”

“No,” he said, and sat on the bench.

By eleven I’d counted seventeen crossings. A woman from Licensing came out to practice saying something under her breath. A boy delivered an envelope to the records clerk and took the long way back past the tree. Two cleaners met in the courtyard and exchanged shoes. I waited for an explanation. None came.

Mrs. Vale appeared at noon. “How are we getting on?”

“I’m trying to understand the scope of the work.”

“Brick it up.”

“People seem to like it.”

“They do. Unfortunately, the plans say there’s a wall here. The insurer has noticed.”

“Could you change the plans?”

She rubbed the bridge of her nose. “You must be new to contracting.”

That evening, at home, I told my daughter about the doorway. She was eight and sorting a tin of buttons into families according to rules she would not disclose.

“Where will the people go instead?” she asked.

“Back to work, I suppose.”

“No, I mean the ones who need to go through.”

I explained that nobody needed to go through. The courtyard led nowhere. There was another entrance by the bins for anyone who needed access to the drain or the tree.

She considered this. “Maybe nowhere is where they need to go.”

Then she held up a green button with a chip missing from one edge. “This one’s a grandfather.”

On Tuesday I brought bricks. The man in the bicycle helmet helped me unload them.

“Bit of a shame,” he said.

“What do you do out there?”

“Drink my tea.”

“Couldn’t you drink it at your desk?”

“I could drink it in the bath. But then I’d be a man who drinks office tea in the bath.”

We carried the bricks in silence after that.

I laid the first course before lunch. People stepped over it. By two, they had to lift their knees. By four, the woman from Licensing stood on one side and finished her sentence on the other.

“What was it you needed to say?” I asked.

“‘I won’t be available on Saturdays.’”

“Did it help?”

“I’ve got Saturday off.”

On Wednesday, the wall reached my waist. The cleaners came, looked at it, and exchanged shoes across the top.

“All right,” I said. “I’ve got to ask.”

One of them pointed down. She wore a black orthopedic boot on her left foot. The other wore an identical boot on her right. They had bought one expensive pair of shoes between them and took turns wearing the new one on the foot that could wear it.

“We’re breaking them in for our sister’s wedding,” one said.

“We’re both hoping to be better by June,” said the other.

On Thursday, I finished. I raked the joints, swept the floor, and painted the plaster on the office side a pale municipal cream. Unless you knew where to look, you would never suspect there had been a way through.

Mrs. Vale signed the invoice.

I went outside by the bins to collect my tools. From the courtyard, the new brickwork looked raw and rather handsome. The pear tree dropped a pear. It hit the bench with a wooden knock.

I picked it up and took a bite. It was like biting a table.

“Needs cooking,” said Mrs. Vale behind me.

“What about the notice?”

“I put that up after the clerk cracked a crown.”

She had brought a shopping bag. Together we gathered the pears that came away easily. She said she poached them with lemon peel and packed them into jars. Every December she gave the jars to people she had annoyed during the year.

“Do you have enough pears?” I asked.

“Not remotely.”

The council paid me in thirty days. A month after that, Mrs. Vale called again.

“We need a bench,” she said.

“For the courtyard?”

“For the corridor. Outside Records.”

I built it in oak, long enough for three people who knew one another or two who didn’t. The man in the bicycle helmet sat down before I’d packed away my drill. He set his mug beside him. Someone had drawn a small, convincing pear on it in green ink.

By winter, the cream paint above the bench had acquired a dark patch where people rested their heads. The woman from Licensing brought in a cushion. One of the cleaners left a wedding photograph on the windowsill: both sisters standing in silver shoes, their arms around a third woman laughing so hard her veil had slipped over one eye.

And in December a jar appeared on my doorstep. The pears inside were almost transparent. Tied around the lid was a note from Mrs. Vale.

*For the inconvenience.*

My daughter and I ate them warm, over toast. She fished the last strip of lemon peel from the syrup and held it up to the light.

“What’s that bit for?” she asked.

I thought of the bench, the doorway, the courtyard on the other side.

“Try it,” I said.

When my father retired, he started putting the wrong things in the little free library at the end of our street. First a tin of buttons, then two good hinges in a sandwich bag. My mother made him go back for the hinges.

“It says library, Martin.”

“Somebody might be looking for hinges.”

“Not there.”

He went back after supper. The hinges were gone.

For several days he bore this vindication quietly. Then a note appeared inside the library, folded around a short pencil: *If the person who left the hinges has any more, I could use one for the other side.*

My father had twenty or thirty hinges in the garage. He took them all down to the library in a biscuit tin and waited on the bench across the street. At lunchtime my mother brought him a cheese sandwich. At three she brought him his hat. At five a girl of about twelve came by on a bicycle, opened the tin, and began comparing hinges against something she had drawn on her wrist.

“Center to center,” my father called.

She looked around.

“The screw holes. It’s easier to measure from one center to the other.”

“I traced it,” she said, holding up her arm. There, in blue ink, was the outline of a hinge, complete with three solemn dots.

“Even better,” he admitted.

She was building a cupboard for her little brother, who had begun collecting stones and needed somewhere to put them. Their mother had said that if she found one more stone in the washing machine she was moving to a hotel.

“How many stones?” my father asked.

The girl considered. “Do you mean good ones?”

He came home delighted. Here was a person, he said, who understood the importance of asking what was actually being counted.

I visited that weekend. On Saturday morning he took me to see the cupboard. The girl had installed it against the fence in her backyard, low enough for her brother to reach. It was painted a violent orange. The door hung a little crooked, and on the front, in green marker, someone had written MUSEAM.

My father and I stood outside the gate while the boy, who was perhaps five, showed us the collection. There was a white stone with a hole in it. There was a piece of brick. There was a lump of asphalt with a yellow stripe, which had once been part of a road and was therefore, he explained, the only stone in the museum that knew where anything was.

“And this one?” I asked. It was a plain gray pebble in the middle of the shelf.

“That one’s just holding my place.”

“For what?”

He shrugged. Apparently I had asked the sort of question adults ask when they have never run a museum.

On the walk home, my father stopped twice to examine the ground. The second time he picked up a small green marble, clouded and chipped.

“Do you think he’d want this?”

“You can ask him.”

“No,” he said after a moment. “I think I want it.”

He put it in his pocket.

For the rest of his life, which was another eleven years, that marble sat in the shallow wooden dish beside his bed, among the practical things he took off or put on each day: watch, glasses, wedding ring when his knuckles swelled. After he died, my mother tipped the contents of the dish into my hands so she could dust under it. I recognized the marble by touch before I looked down.

“I wondered where that came from,” she said.

I told her about the orange cupboard and the piece of road. I told her about the girl with the hinge drawn on her wrist. My mother sat down on the edge of the bed, still holding the dust cloth.

“He never told me that part.”

I nearly said, *I thought he told you everything.* Instead I asked which part.

“The wrist,” she said. “I’d have liked that.”

She took the marble out of my palm and held it up to the window. In the light it was not quite green. There was blue in it, and a twist of white glass so fine you could lose it by turning the marble a fraction.

“Look at that,” she said, and handed it back.

We went on passing it between us for a while, each finding something the other had missed.

The first customer of the municipal umbrella library was a woman who wanted to return an umbrella.

“We haven’t opened yet,” I said.

“I can see that. You’re standing on the sign.”

I stepped off the vinyl banner. She laid the umbrella on the counter. It was a good one: black cotton, wooden shaft, a handle curved to fit a hand considerably larger than hers. On a brass band someone had engraved CITY OF BELLWETHER, followed by the number 6.

I had spent eleven months getting approval to start an umbrella library. I had given two presentations, revised a budget four times, and learned the fire rating of a bucket. Our umbrellas were yellow polyester. They said BORROW ME in a typeface chosen by committee.

“Where did you get this?” I asked.

“From here,” she said. “Although you had a different desk.”

She was eighty or thereabouts. She took off one glove with her teeth and pointed to a spot near the radiator.

“The desk was there. You left a shilling.”

“As a deposit?”

“No, as a little present for the desk. Of course as a deposit.”

I found a chair for her and went downstairs to Records, where Malcolm was eating an egg with a spoon.

“Did we used to lend umbrellas?”

“Probably.”

“Is there a way to know?”

He considered this an interesting question, although he had worked in Records for thirty years. He finished his egg. Then he got a stepladder.

The ledger was filed under Street Amenities, between Salt Bins and Urinals. Beginning in October 1931, the city had owned twelve umbrellas. By June 1932 it owned nine. By 1938 it owned four, one of which had been damaged by a horse. The entries stopped in September 1939.

Number 6 had been borrowed on a Tuesday by an A. Vale, of 14 Foundry Lane.

I carried the ledger upstairs. “Are you A. Vale?”

“That was my father.”

She ran her finger over the signature. The V was very deep; you could feel it through the page.

“He pressed hard,” she said. “Even his shopping lists looked legally binding.”

“Would you like a copy?”

“No. I have enough of his writing. I’d like my shilling.”

There are occasions for explaining that a currency has been decimalized, that a debt may be subject to statutory limitation, and that an umbrella bought for perhaps eight shillings has spent the better part of a century in private use. Looking at her, I understood that she had come prepared for all three arguments and would enjoy them more than I would.

I opened my purse and gave her five pence.

She put it in her glove. “Thank you.”

“Did he ever say why he didn’t bring it back?”

“He took it up to the hospital. My mother was having me. It was fine weather when we came home, so it went in the stand.”

“For eighty-six years?”

“Not continuously. We did go out.”

At ten o’clock the mayor arrived to cut the ribbon. He admired Number 6. The photographer liked it better than the yellow ones, which reflected an unflattering light onto the mayor’s chin. We took the photograph with the old umbrella open above us. In the paper the next day, the caption described me as the founder of a new civic tradition.

I thought about writing in. Instead I took the ledger back down to Malcolm and asked if we could keep using it. There were more than two hundred blank pages.

“You’ll need a form to remove it from Records,” he said.

“Where are the forms?”

He pointed to a cupboard behind me. Inside were ruled pads, purple pencils, three empty egg cups, and a little tin marked UMBRELLA DEPOSITS. There was one shilling in it.

I gave Malcolm five pence for the shilling. He eyed the coin, then my hand, then the tin.

“I don’t think that’s how that works,” he said.

“It was upstairs.”

Foundry Lane no longer existed, but the woman had written her telephone number on the receipt. I rang and explained what I had found.

“Oh, lovely,” she said. “I wondered if you’d look.”

“Would you like me to post it?”

“Good heavens, no. It’ll cost you a pound.”

She came the following Tuesday. It was raining hard enough to bounce grit against the glass doors. I gave her the shilling. She held it close to her face to read the date, then placed it on the counter and asked for Number 6.

“You don’t need a deposit anymore,” I said.

“I know. But where else am I going to spend it?”

I turned the ledger around. In the space beneath her father’s name, she signed her own. Same V.

The first time my father came to visit me in the city, he brought a pear tree on the bus.

It was February. The tree was a stick with roots wrapped in a feed sack, and the driver had made him buy it a seat. My father considered this a reasonable policy. What bothered him was that the driver had charged the adult fare.

“It’s two years old,” he said.

I lived on the fourth floor. He knew this. He had helped me carry the mattress up the stairs, pausing at each landing to examine some feature of the building that urgently required his attention. A loose hinge. An interesting tile. By the time we reached my apartment, he had discovered eleven things and admitted to none of the pauses.

“Where am I supposed to put a tree?”

He went to the window and looked down. Behind the building was a rectangle of dirt where tenants locked their bicycles to an iron fence.

“There,” he said.

“That belongs to everybody.”

“Good,” he said, taking off his coat. “I only brought one.”

We borrowed a shovel from the superintendent. Six people came outside to tell us why the tree would die. Not enough sun. Too much sun reflected off the windows. Bad soil. Salt. Someone called Dennis, whom I had never met despite living directly above him for three years, said the neighborhood had once been a button factory and the ground was probably buttons all the way down.

My father listened. Then he asked Dennis to hold the tree straight.

By evening it was planted. Dennis contributed two broom handles for stakes. The superintendent found a length of green hose to protect the bark from the ties. A woman on the first floor filled a saucepan at her kitchen sink and passed it through the window. Afterward, everybody went back inside. For several weeks the pear tree looked precisely as dead as predicted.

My father went home. March came. One morning, as I wheeled my bicycle past the tree, I noticed that the tip of a branch had split open. Inside was a green so bright it seemed unlikely to have been there all winter.

I called him.

“Leaves?” he said.

“One, possibly.”

“Don’t fuss with it.”

“I wasn’t going to fuss with it.”

“You called me at six in the morning.”

For three years the tree produced leaves, shade in an amount sufficient for one small cat, and no pears. People began to refer to the courtyard as the garden. The bicycles migrated to the other end. Somebody put out a chair. Then somebody put out a better chair, and the first chair became a table.

In the fourth spring there were blossoms. By July there were nine pears. We counted them independently and often. Dennis made a sign that said PLEASE ALLOW FRUIT TO RIPEN, which was the first indication that anyone in the building believed we would recognize a ripe pear if we saw one.

In August my father fell in his kitchen. He recovered, though he started buying milk in smaller cartons. I went home on weekends and did little jobs badly enough that he had to sit nearby and advise me. When I asked how you knew a pear was ready, he explained that you lifted it gently in your palm. If the stem let go, it was time.

“Don’t pull,” he said. “You’ll get the wrong answer.”

I returned to the city on a Sunday night and found the branches empty.

There had been a storm. Seven pears lay bruised on the ground. One had vanished. The last sat on the windowsill of the first-floor apartment beside a note: I SAVED THE GOOD ONE.

I took the seven upstairs. Cut away the bruises, peeled what remained, put it all in a pot. It cooked down to a single jar of pale, uneven sauce. The following Friday I carried it home on the bus.

My father ate some on toast. He chewed thoughtfully, although there was nothing in it that needed chewing.

“Well?” I said.

“You could have picked them a week earlier.”

“You said the stem had to let go.”

“It did let go.”

“There was a storm.”

He considered this. “That complicates the test.”

He ate another piece of toast. Outside, the afternoon bus went by, empty except for the driver. In the kitchen drawer were rubber bands, batteries, a loose brass screw, and every twist tie that had entered the house since 1987. My father scraped the jar carefully with the edge of his knife.

“What kind of pear did you say it was?” I asked.

“Comice.”

“Is that a good kind?”

He tipped the jar toward the light to see if he had missed any.

“I’d plant it again,” he said.

The key cutter at the hardware store had been listening to the same baseball game for thirty-one years.

It was the game his daughter had pitched in July of 1994. He had called it into a tape recorder from the bleachers, ostensibly for his wife, who was working a double. Over the years the recording had migrated from cassette to CD to a little blue rectangle his grandson had loaded for him. The sound had not improved in transit.

“Does she win?” I asked.

“I should hope so by now,” he said.

He was cutting me a key to my mother’s house. She had taken to locking herself out when she went to get the paper. I’d suggested a combination box, but she didn’t like the idea of her rabbits knowing the code. This was a joke. Lately I had developed the bad habit of taking a moment to decide.

On the recording, someone hit a foul ball. The key cutter’s younger voice said, “That’s coming this way,” followed by a dreadful clatter.

“Got you?” I asked.

“Lemonade.”

He ran a wire brush over the new key. I asked him if his daughter still played.

“Debbie? Lord, no. She sells industrial carpeting. That’s her on the wall.”

In the photograph a woman about my age stood beside a tremendous roll of gray carpet, giving the camera two thumbs up.

“Hospital in Akron,” he said. “Whole building.”

Then he held up a finger, and we listened. There was the ordinary hiss of wind against a microphone, a bat pinging somewhere on another diamond, the younger man saying he thought the count was two and one. Just behind his voice, a woman said, “Here, give me that. You’re missing her.”

The sound changed. The wind went away. For several seconds you could hear the hollow knock of a ball landing in a glove.

“My wife,” he said. “Got somebody to cover the end of her shift.”

“So she saw the game.”

“Most of it.”

He put both keys on the counter. I couldn’t tell which one I had come in with until I saw the little fan of brass dust beside the new one.

At my mother’s house I tried the copy. It worked if I pulled the door toward me, which was also true of the original. I found her in the kitchen with the newspaper spread open to the crossword.

“Four letters,” she said. “A kind of nut.”

“Pecan.”

“Count on your fingers, honey.”

I sat down. The kettle was beginning to make its preliminary noises. Outside, one of the rabbits was eating the parsley she had planted expressly for herself and, in actual practice, entirely for the rabbits.

“Cola,” I said.

She counted the squares with the end of her pencil. “Cola nut. Well, look at you.”

I put the spare key on the table.

“What’s that for?”

“In case you lock yourself out.”

“Not much use to me in here, is it?”

I picked it up again.

She filled in a few more answers while I made the tea. I told her about the man in the hardware store. I told her about the lemonade and the hospital carpeting and the moment the woman took the microphone. My mother listened with her pencil resting in the crease of the paper.

“Did the girl win?” she asked.

“I think so.”

“You didn’t stay to find out?”

“My key was done.”

She considered this a poor excuse. We drank our tea. After a while she got up to fetch the biscuit tin, and I noticed she wasn’t limping anymore. I couldn’t remember when she had stopped. For months I had watched that bad knee of hers every time she crossed a room, and then one day, apparently, I had quit watching.

“Oatmeal or ginger?” she asked.

“Ginger.”

“Good. The oatmeal are gone.”

I put the key on my ring, between my own front door key and the little useless one for a bicycle stolen in 2008. My mother folded the crossword back to expose the clues she hadn’t done. I could have stayed and helped, except that helping my mother with a crossword required sitting quietly until she had answered all the questions herself.

I stayed. She had twelve across wrong, but it worked itself out.
