**The Hall**

At nine on Tuesday, Ronnie pulled the folded chairs away from the wall of St. Anne’s hall to count them. Seventy-three. The insurance form said seventy-four. He went round again, this time touching each cold metal back with his finger. Seventy-three.

He was selling the hall to a man who wanted to store bathrooms in it. Not to install them; just to keep them there between manufacture and delivery. The man had shown him photographs of the crates, as if Ronnie might be won over by a particularly handsome crate.

On the stage, behind the maroon curtain, he found a blue wool glove, a Nativity sheep with one roller skate screwed to its underside, and a cake tin marked BERYL, but no chair.

He took the sheep down. If you gave it a push along the hall floor, it went straight for a bit and then made a long, stately turn to the left.

He was doing this for the third time when his sister came in.

“Busy?” said Jean.

“Trying to work out how they did the shepherds.”

“Fishing line. I was a shepherd. We had to pull them in by hand. What are you looking for?”

He told her.

“Dad took it.”

“When?”

“When Mum came home from hospital. He put it on the landing so she could have a sit halfway up.”

That would have been twenty-six years ago. Ronnie remembered his mother going up the stairs with her handbag over her arm, although there was nowhere inside the house she could possibly need her purse. He remembered the chair, too, now that Jean mentioned it. He had sat there the morning of the funeral to put on his shoes.

“Where did it go after?” he said.

Jean shrugged. “Where did the rest of it go?”

They had cleared the house in a weekend. They had been proud of this at the time. On Sunday evening they had eaten fish and chips on the front step, having disposed of both table and chairs before either of them got hungry.

Jean picked up the cake tin. “Beryl’s still about.”

“She won’t want that back.”

“Won’t she?”

“She sent a cake in it in about 1983.”

“All the more reason. Long time to be down a tin.”

Ronnie went back to the insurance form. There was a box for *quantity* and another for *condition*. He put 73 in the first and, after some thought, *capable of seating 73* in the second. Jean had found a length of electrical flex and was attaching it to the sheep.

“Give us a hand,” she said.

He stood the sheep on the stage while she went behind the curtain with the flex. On her signal he let go. The sheep rolled backwards into the curtain and fell over with a sound like cutlery going into a drawer.

“You’ve tied it to the wrong end,” he said.

“I know which end of a sheep is which, Ronnie.”

The hall door opened. A woman in a navy coat stood looking at them. Behind her were a young man with a clipboard and an older man carrying a laser measure. Ronnie had forgotten about the survey.

“Are we all right to come in?” the woman said.

“Certainly.” He picked up the sheep.

“Oh,” said the older man. “I made that.”

He turned it over in Ronnie’s hands. “That was my skate. My other one went under the donkey. You needed two for the donkey, so our Pam had to give one up as well. She was furious. She’d only just learned to go backwards.”

The woman in the navy coat took out her phone. “Let me get a picture for Pam.”

They stood the sheep on the floor. The woman crouched. Jean, still holding the flex, gave it a gentle tug, and the sheep sailed out of the photograph.

“Just a picture of the parquet now,” the woman said.

“Send her that first,” said the older man. “Tell her the bugger’s got away.”

While they measured the storeroom, Ronnie and Jean carried the chairs out to the furniture charity’s van. At the end there was a clean oblong on the wall, lighter than the paint around it. Ronnie ran his palm over it. The difference in colour gave him the unreasonable expectation that the two patches would feel different, too.

Jean put the tin under her arm. “I’ll go round to Beryl’s.”

“What if she doesn’t remember it?”

“Then she’ll have a tin.”

The surveyors came out of the storeroom discussing the width of the fire doors. The older man stopped beside the sheep, his laser measure clipped to his belt.

“Could I have it when you’re done?”

“We’re done,” Ronnie said.

The man carried it out under one arm, its stiff white legs pointing ahead of him.

Ronnie sat on the edge of the stage to finish the form. Through the open door he could see Jean at the bus stop with her tin, and the surveyor wedging the sheep into the back seat of a small green car. It was too tall to stand upright. He laid it on its side and pulled the seat belt across its middle.

The form asked whether any items remained unaccounted for. Ronnie put the tip of his pen in the square marked YES. Then he thought of his mother on the landing, opening her handbag perhaps to find a peppermint, having a few minutes to herself while everybody downstairs took care not to call up and ask if she was all right.

He moved his pen to the other square.

At closing time, June counted the library’s umbrellas. There were eleven in the barrel by the door, which was peculiar because it had not rained in forty-three days.

One was clear plastic with a yellow duck for a handle. One was black and large enough to shelter a card game. The rest were the sort of umbrellas people bought in a hurry and abandoned without quite deciding to abandon them.

June made a sign.

**PLEASE TAKE HOME YOUR UMBRELLA**

The next morning there were twelve.

“It sounds like you’re giving them away,” said Owen, the security guard.

“If I were giving them away, there would be fewer.”

“Not necessarily. People like to help.”

She changed the sign.

**THESE UMBRELLAS BELONG TO SOMEONE**

By Friday there were sixteen.

June had worked at the library for twenty-eight years. She knew what happened to a public institution that admitted it had room for something. A woman had once asked whether the library could use a globe. June had said yes. For the next decade, anyone in the county who discovered that Yugoslavia no longer existed brought June a globe.

She took down the sign. She moved the barrel behind her desk.

At four, a boy came in carrying a folded umbrella.

“No,” June said.

The boy stopped.

“I mean, hello.”

“Hello. I’m returning this.”

“Did you check it out?”

“No. I took it yesterday.”

“Why?”

He looked at her with the patient concern children reserve for adults who have forgotten the properties of ordinary objects.

“For the shade.”

Outside, the pavement shone white. Across the street, a man waiting for the bus stood in the narrow shadow of the bus-stop pole.

“What’s your name?” June asked.

“Eli.”

“Well, thank you for bringing it back, Eli.”

“My grandmother says you’re supposed to bring two back if you have an extra. That way the next person gets one.”

June looked at the barrel.

“Is that something your grandmother started?”

“I don’t know. She’s only lived here eighty years.”

After he left, June carried the barrel back to the door.

For a while she tried to discover who had begun it. Owen thought it was the crossing guard. The crossing guard credited the woman at the bakery, who said she had gotten the idea from seeing the umbrellas at the library.

“But they had to come from somewhere,” June said.

The baker considered this. “Most things do.”

In August the heat broke. It happened at 2:17 on a Thursday, while June was helping a man print a photograph of a chair he intended to buy. There was a tremendous crack overhead, and the windows went gray.

Everyone in the library went quiet. Even the printer stopped, though it often did.

Then came the rain, hard and slanting, flattening the marigolds in the planters. People gathered at the glass doors. Several held out their phones to record what rain looked like.

The man with the chair photograph said, “Would you look at that.”

June rolled the barrel forward.

For ten minutes she handed out umbrellas. The yellow duck went to a woman in blue scrubs. Two teenagers shared the enormous black one. Owen took a narrow green umbrella and walked an elderly patron to her car, holding it so carefully over her that he returned wet from one ear to the opposite ankle.

At last there was one umbrella left. It was an ugly thing, brown with orange diamonds, one rib bent outward like a questioning finger.

June opened it.

On the inside, written in faded permanent marker, was her own name.

She remembered it at once. Her father had written her name there because she was always losing things. He had chosen the umbrella, too. She had been sixteen and mortified by it. As soon as she could afford another, she had bought a small navy one with a bamboo handle.

Her father had been dead nineteen years.

June stood beneath the brown canopy in the library entrance. Above her, the letters of her name had bled into the fabric. The J had a strong horizontal stroke across the top, an extravagance her father permitted himself nowhere else except on birthday envelopes.

“Find something?” Owen asked.

“My umbrella.”

“You ought to take it home.”

She almost did. Instead she sat at the desk with it open beside her until closing, occasionally reaching out to touch the bent rib.

The next morning she brought in the sewing tin from her kitchen. With a length of strong thread, she fastened the fabric to the rib. Then she put the umbrella in the barrel.

She made one final sign.

**UMBRELLAS**

The first thing my father did when he retired was move the kitchen clock eleven inches to the left.

“It was fine where it was,” my mother said.

“It was behind the door.”

“Only when the door was open.”

He considered this a decisive point in his favor. She considered it a description of how doors work.

When I came home that weekend, the clock was off the wall altogether. It lay faceup on the table, ticking beneath a dish towel. My parents were out buying peaches. In the clock’s old spot was a pale circle where twenty-three years of cooking had failed to reach the paint. In the new spot was a small, unexpectedly violent hole.

I lifted the towel. Taped to the back of the clock was a photograph.

My mother, maybe thirty, stood barefoot on an unfamiliar lawn. She wore red shorts. There was a baby on her hip and a hose in her hand, and she was watering a little boy who stood quite solemnly in a galvanized tub. On the back, in my father’s block capitals, someone had written: JULY. THE POOL.

I was the little boy. The baby was my sister. The lawn was unfamiliar because it had become a driveway before I was old enough to remember it.

When my parents returned, I showed them the photograph.

“Oh,” my mother said. “My good shorts.”

My father put the peaches in a colander. “I wondered where that went.”

“Why was it on the clock?”

“It kept slipping.”

“The clock?”

“The photograph. It was tucked into the frame of the mirror in the hall. Every time anybody shut the front door, down it went. I got tired of picking it up.”

“So you taped it somewhere nobody would ever see it?”

He turned on the faucet. “Well, you saw it.”

We ate the peaches standing at the sink. They were ripe enough that sitting down with one would have required planning. My mother studied the photograph again. She couldn’t remember who had taken it. My father suggested Uncle Ray, but Uncle Ray had worked Saturdays.

“How do you know it was a Saturday?” I asked.

“Because that was the day we washed the dog.”

There was no dog in the photograph.

“He’d gotten out of the tub,” she explained. “That’s why you were allowed in it.”

For years, when I thought of my childhood, I thought of the things my parents had arranged for me: swimming lessons, birthday parties, the miserable educational stop at a salt mine on the way to the coast. I had never given much thought to being permitted, on a hot morning, to stand in the water a dog had finished with.

“Did I like it?”

“You wanted a turn with the hose,” my mother said. “You always liked the job better.”

She handed me the photograph. I put it in my wallet, where, over the next several months, it acquired a white crease through the lawn.

We hung the clock in its original spot. My father patched the other hole. He used a paint sample from the basement labeled KITCHEN, which turned out to mean the kitchen as it had looked two kitchens ago. The result was a neat green square on a yellow wall.

“There,” he said, with the peculiar satisfaction of a man who has made a problem smaller and more definite.

My mother looked at the square. Then she opened the kitchen door all the way.

From where we stood, you couldn’t see it.

On the day the town removed the pay phone outside the pharmacy, Mrs. Vale came down with a kitchen chair and asked the workmen to wait until noon.

“Are you expecting a call?” one asked.

“No,” she said. “I’m making one.”

She settled into the chair. The younger workman went to get coffee. The older one, whose knees had lately begun issuing opinions about everything, sat on the curb.

At eleven, the pharmacist brought out a second chair. At eleven fifteen, a boy on a bicycle stopped to ask what had happened.

“Nothing yet,” said Mrs. Vale.

The boy stayed. He was thirteen, an age at which nothing happening elsewhere can be a compelling reason to remain where nothing is happening here.

By noon there were nine people on the pavement, including the mail carrier, who had meant only to deliver an envelope and had somehow accepted half a cheese sandwich. Mrs. Vale stood, took a folded slip from her pocket, and dialed.

Everyone tried very hard not to listen.

“Hello, Arthur,” she said. “It’s me.”

The younger workman examined the lettering on his coffee cup.

“No, nothing’s wrong. They’re taking out the phone on Mercer Street.”

A bus went by.

“Yes, that one.”

She smiled.

“Well, I remember it differently. I remember you had the umbrella.”

The pharmacist went inside. Two people checked their watches. The boy leaned his bicycle against the wall.

“I know,” Mrs. Vale said. “But I wanted to tell you from here.”

She listened for quite a long time. Then she said goodbye, put the receiver back, and thanked the workmen. The mail carrier took the kitchen chair and walked her home.

The boy lingered while the men unbolted the phone.

“Who’s Arthur?”

“No idea,” said the older man. “Get hold of that washer before it goes down the drain.”

The boy put his shoe over it.

That evening, at supper, he told his mother the whole thing, including the parts he had not heard. Arthur was a sailor. There had been a tremendous storm. Mrs. Vale had waited under the pharmacy awning with a red suitcase. The umbrella, which Arthur certainly had, had blown inside out at the precise moment he proposed.

“You made that up,” his mother said.

“Some of it.”

“Which part?”

He thought about it. “The color of the suitcase.”

In fact, Arthur was Mrs. Vale’s younger brother. Forty years earlier, on that corner, they had called their father to tell him they had backed his car into a pear tree. There had been no suitcase. There had been an umbrella, although neither of them had been carrying it. It had lain on the rear shelf of the car and shot forward on impact, striking Arthur neatly on the back of the head.

What Mrs. Vale had wanted to tell him from there was that she had finally remembered what their father said after the long silence on the line.

Not *Are you hurt?* as Arthur insisted.

Not *How bad is the car?* as she had maintained for years.

He had said, with genuine concern, *Was it our pear tree or somebody else’s?*

When she told Arthur, he laughed so hard she had to hold the receiver away from her ear. Then he began to cry. He had been having a difficult winter. She knew about some of it.

They spoke again on Sunday, from their ordinary phones, and the conversation was mostly about whether Arthur’s landlord was obliged to replace his oven. When a repairman finally came, he had to wedge the oven door shut with his knee to get it to heat. Arthur felt vindicated. He called his sister to say so.

The pay phone went to a municipal warehouse. An election poster covered the bolt holes for a while; eventually the pharmacy owner filled them in. The boy kept the washer in the little tray beneath his bicycle seat, where it traveled hundreds of miles without being needed for anything.

In spring, Mrs. Vale took the train to visit Arthur. They bought pears at the supermarket because that seemed funny, though by the time the pears ripened she had gone home. He ate one standing at the sink in his kitchen. It was an excellent pear, and juice ran down his wrist into his sleeve.

He nearly called to tell her. He stopped because it was late, then because he could already hear what she would say: *What did you expect, eating it like that?*

He called anyway.

She answered on the seventh ring. “I was in the bath.”

“I’ll let you go.”

“Well, you might as well tell me. I’m out now.”

My father kept the spare key to his house in a plastic rock. Not under a plastic rock, as most people do. The rock itself opened on a hinge. It was the only rock in the flower bed, and on the bottom, in raised letters, it said ROCK.

“Nobody ever turns over a rock to see what it’s called,” he said.

After he died, I went to the house to let in the appraiser. I was early. I retrieved the key, opened the door, and put the rock on the kitchen table, where it looked considerably less like a rock.

The appraiser was a young woman named June. She had a green clipboard and wore little blue covers over her shoes. My father would have liked the covers. He would have asked for a pair and saved them for an occasion that never came.

“Anything unusual I should know about the property?” she asked.

“The hall light works from the switch marked porch. The switch marked hall doesn’t do anything. The porch light is automatic, but only if you leave the switch marked disposal on.”

She waited.

“The disposal is normal,” I said.

We went from room to room. June measured the windows. I had known those windows my whole life and had never once wondered how wide they were. Thirty-six inches in the bedroom where I grew up. Twenty-eight over the sink. June drew the house in pencil on graph paper. In a matter of minutes she had got it small enough to fit under her hand.

In the basement, above the workbench, my father had screwed jam-jar lids to a shelf so that the jars hung beneath it. He had sorted the contents by a system I’d always meant to ask about. One jar contained a wing nut, a foreign coin, and a yellow button shaped like a duck.

June stopped at the stairs.

“Was there a door here?”

There were hinge marks on the jamb. I had forgotten the door entirely until she asked. Then I remembered the sound it made: a soft knock followed by a second, harder knock, because it never caught the first time.

“There was,” I said. “He took it off when my mother got sick. So he could hear her call from upstairs.”

June wrote something down. I wanted to see what. Probably *no door*.

When we came back to the kitchen, a boy was visible through the window. He was standing in the flower bed, looking at the bare oval of dirt where the rock had been.

I opened the window.

“Can I help you?”

“Is Frank here?”

“No,” I said. “I’m his daughter.”

He considered this information. “The tall one?”

“The only one.”

He shrugged, as though this did not strictly contradict what he had said. He was about nine. There was a deflated basketball under his arm, buckled inward like an old cheek.

“He lets me use the pump.”

I knew the pump. It stood behind the basement door that wasn’t there anymore. I brought it up. The boy fitted the needle into the ball, and I worked the handle. After every stroke he pressed the leather with both thumbs.

“Good,” he said at last.

“Did you come over a lot?”

“Only when it got flat.”

“How often was that?”

He looked down at the ball. “It’s got a hole.”

He bounced it once on the path. We listened. A thin whistle rose from somewhere near the black seam.

“Frank tried tape,” he said. “But then it bounced funny.”

I told him he could keep the pump.

“Where would I put it?”

“At your house, I guess.”

He clearly thought this was a poor solution to an arrangement that had worked perfectly well until my arrival. Still, he took it. He walked down the path with the ball under one arm and the pump under the other, the hose trailing in the dust.

June was sitting at the kitchen table, turning the plastic rock over in her hands.

“I’ve never seen one that opens,” she said.

“The hinge sticks.”

She pressed it shut. The little click made the kitchen briefly sound occupied in the old way: somebody finishing one small job before beginning another.

A month later, the house sold to a couple with a baby. I left them a sheet of instructions about the lights. I took the jar with the duck button. The rest went more or less where things go.

That winter, at my apartment, I got an envelope with no return address. Inside was a school photograph of the boy, dressed in a white shirt against a blue background. On the back, in careful block letters, he had written his name, ELI, and beneath it: *For Frank’s tall daughter.*

There was also a strip of black rubber, curved at one edge, with a tiny hole in it.

I held it up to the kitchen light. The hole was so small I had to move it back and forth before the light came through. I took down the jar, unscrewed the lid, and put the rubber inside with the wing nut, the coin, and the button.

I have a theory about the system now.

My grandmother kept a list on the refrigerator of things people had borrowed. When somebody returned something, she drew a line through it but left it on the list. By the time my mother and I came to empty her apartment, nearly everything had a line through it. Three entries remained:

Dean — six folding chairs  
Ruth — blue suitcase  
Calvin — the good ladder

“We haven’t got room for six folding chairs,” my mother said.

She was on the kitchen floor, trying to separate two roasting pans that had spent several decades becoming one roasting pan. I put the list in my pocket. It gave me something to do besides decide which of my grandmother’s possessions deserved to survive her, a job for which I had discovered I was both unqualified and, in my mother’s opinion, too slow.

Dean lived downstairs. He opened the door in his socks and listened while I explained about the chairs.

“Well, where shall we start?” he said.

I thought this was a peculiar answer. Then he showed me.

One chair was by his front door so he could sit to put his shoes on. Two stood at the kitchen table. A fourth held a geranium in the sunny bit of the bedroom. The fifth was in the hall cupboard, and the sixth was with a man named Paul who played the accordion at the Saturday farmers’ market.

“Does he sit on it to play?”

“No, he puts the case on it. Bad back. People throw money in.”

I told Dean I wasn’t there to collect the chairs. This hadn’t been entirely true when I rang his bell, but it was by the time I left.

Ruth had moved to Manitoba. Her sister gave me a phone number and warned me about the time difference, which I got wrong in the other direction and ended up calling her during lunch.

“Oh, that suitcase,” Ruth said. “Has she told you what happened?”

I sat on the bare floor where my grandmother’s bed had been. There was a pale rectangle on the wallpaper and, at shoulder height, a little brown teardrop where she used to lean her head to read.

Ruth had borrowed the suitcase for a train trip. On the way home, one of the catches sprang open and her underwear fell out in the dining car. A boy of about eight calmly picked up a pair of her underpants with the salad tongs.

“He was trying to be polite,” Ruth said. “That was the worst of it. You couldn’t get cross with him.”

She’d bought a strap to hold the suitcase shut. My grandmother had refused to take it back.

“She said it had learned to travel and it would be a shame to stop it now.”

“Did she really say that?”

“No. She said, ‘What do I want with a busted suitcase?’ But I’ve told the story a few times.”

Calvin, it turned out, was dead. His son answered the phone.

“Aluminum ladder? Red paint on the bottom step?”

I said I didn’t know.

“Creaks on the third rung?”

Again, I didn’t know.

He seemed reluctant to let me claim a ladder on the strength of such inadequate credentials. I explained that my grandmother had died too, that nobody wanted the ladder, that I was just going down a list.

“Oh,” he said. “I’ve got one of those.”

I asked what was on it.

“A guy named Dean has Dad’s socket set.”

Downstairs, Dean received this news without enthusiasm.

“He owed me forty dollars,” he said.

“Well, he’s dead.”

“That’s going to complicate things.”

He looked in the hall cupboard, behind the fifth chair. No socket set. We tried the bedroom closet and the cabinet under the sink. Finally he remembered he’d given it to my grandmother, whose kitchen tap once made a hammering noise so loud you could hear it in his apartment.

Upstairs, my mother had progressed to the drawer beneath the oven. She had found seventeen baking sheets and was furious with all of them. I opened the cabinet under the sink. Behind a bottle of ammonia and a paper bag full of paper bags was a green tin box.

Every socket was there. There was also a piece of masking tape inside the lid, in my grandmother’s handwriting:

Calvin’s. Dean owes him an apology.

I read this to Dean over the phone.

“That’s her interpretation,” he said.

Calvin’s son came that evening. He brought the ladder despite my protests, because it had been on his truck for three days and he wanted the space. My mother, who by then had remembered the light fixture in the hall, unfolded it without a word.

When she stepped on the third rung, it creaked.

“There you go,” I said to Calvin’s son.

He smiled for the first time. Then he held the ladder steady while my mother unscrewed the glass shade and tipped thirty years of dead moths into my cupped hands.

My grandmother kept a drawer full of things that could turn into other things. A margarine tub could turn into a button tin. A button could turn into a wheel for a toy truck. A birthday card could turn into a bookmark, provided you cut around the part where somebody had written something nice.

“That part stays,” she said, as if there were municipal regulations.

In one corner of the drawer sat a little brass key. It was too small for a door and too plain for a diary. On rainy afternoons my brother and I tried it in everything: the clock, the desk, the battered green suitcase in the hall closet. It never fit. When we asked what it opened, our grandmother always said, “Nothing here.”

This struck us as an excellent answer. Nothing *here*. We drew maps.

Years later, after she died, my brother and I stood in her kitchen with three cardboard boxes. He lived across the country by then. We had both developed strong opinions about estate paperwork and weak opinions about almost everything that used to interest us.

He opened the drawer.

“Oh,” he said.

There were the buttons. There were the rubber bands around a cardboard tube. There was a bookmark cut from a card I had given her when I was nine. My handwriting said, *I hope you live to be a hunderd.*

She had cut around that part.

My brother found the key under a packet of snaps. He held it up by the round end, and for a second he was eight again—not younger in the face, exactly, but more willing to let his face show what he thought.

“Nothing here,” he said.

We laughed. Then he took out his phone and photographed it beside a quarter. He posted the picture to a forum for people who identify mysterious objects. By lunchtime a retired locksmith in Ohio had answered: standard replacement key for a cheap suitcase lock, widely sold from the 1950s onward. Probably several million like it.

We fetched the battered green suitcase from the hall closet. The key didn’t fit.

It was absurd how pleased we were.

We ate crackers over the sink because the plates were already packed. Outside, a boy on a bicycle kept attempting to ride up the curb without using his hands. Each time he failed, he looked around to see whether anyone had noticed. We became very interested in the crackers whenever he looked our way.

“What do you want to do with it?” my brother asked.

I knew he meant the house. There was a valuation scheduled for Friday. One of the gutters needed replacing. Neither of us could afford to keep it, and neither of us wanted to be the first to say so.

“The key?” I asked.

He glanced at me. “Sure. The key.”

In the end he took it home. I took the bookmark. We sold the house that autumn to a couple who painted the front door yellow. For a while I drove past now and then, though it wasn’t on my way to anywhere. Then one day it was on my way to somewhere, and I drove past without looking.

Last month my brother mailed me a photograph. His daughter was sitting cross-legged on the floor, surrounded by drawings. In the middle of one drawing was a mountain with an enormous keyhole in its side. There was a boat at the foot of the mountain and, in the boat, three figures wearing crowns. One of the crowns was unmistakably a colander.

On the back he had written: *She asked what it opens.*

I called him.

“You told her?”

“Of course.”

Through the phone I could hear my niece objecting to something. A moment later she came on the line herself.

“Dad says it doesn’t open anything here,” she told me. “But he hasn’t tried the garage.”

I nearly told her about the locksmith in Ohio. I could already hear myself explaining how suitcase locks used to be made. Instead I asked, “What’s in the garage?”

There was a small, scornful silence of the kind only a six-year-old can manage.

“I don’t know,” she said. “That’s why we have to go look.”

My mother kept a cigarette lighter in the kitchen drawer for thirty years without knowing how to smoke. It was a good lighter, brushed silver, with a dent in one corner. On one side somebody had engraved the name GORDON. Nobody in our family was named Gordon.

When I was nine, I asked her who he was.

“A man who had a lighter,” she said.

This was the sort of answer my mother considered complete. I went to my father, who said Gordon had been her first husband and a professional ballroom dancer. My father was washing a roasting pan at the time. He had to stop and sit down when I asked what had killed Gordon.

“The tango,” he managed.

For years I believed some portion of this. Not the tango, obviously, but the existence of a first husband. I pictured a thin man in evening clothes coming downstairs in our house, stepping over the spot where the carpet tack had worked loose.

The truth came out when we were packing my mother’s kitchen for her move to a smaller place. By then my father had been dead six years. I found the lighter under a layer of rubber bands that had gone brittle and stuck to the wood.

“Poor Gordon,” I said.

My mother looked up from wrapping a casserole dish. “Oh, for heaven’s sake. He installed the boiler.”

She told me he had left his lighter on the basement windowsill. She’d called the company, but Gordon had already gone to another job. They said they would tell him. A week later she called again. After that it seemed foolish to keep calling, but wrong to throw it out.

“Besides,” she said, “it was handy on birthdays.”

I turned the little wheel with my thumb. A spark jumped, startling us both.

In the new apartment there was one kitchen drawer narrow enough for cutlery, so everything else had to justify itself. We spent a pleasant, quarrelsome afternoon deciding what a person needed. Two corkscrews, she maintained, on the grounds that one was bad. I suggested keeping only the good one. She said you couldn’t tell which was bad until you used it. A glass lemon squeezer survived because she liked the weight. The electric knife went because neither of us could remember a meal improved by its participation.

At the end there was a shoebox of disputed objects. I took it home.

Last November, during a power cut, I went looking for matches and found Gordon’s lighter instead. It sparked but wouldn’t light. My daughter, who is twelve and has never seen anybody do anything as interesting as repair a small mechanical object, watched me take out the insert. Inside was a wad of pale cotton, dry as lint.

“What does it run on?” she asked.

“Lighter fluid.”

“Do we have lighter fluid?”

“No.”

We sat in the dark for a while. Across the street, a neighbor’s windows glowed an enviable gold. My daughter tried the wheel and got a spark on her third attempt. For that fraction of a second I could see the tip of her nose and her front teeth. She had the intent, slightly cross expression my father used to wear when threading a needle.

“Who’s Gordon?” she asked.

I nearly told her about the ballroom dancer. The shape of the joke was still there, waiting for someone to step into it. Instead I told her about the boiler man, the windowsill, her grandmother’s two phone calls.

“He must have wanted it,” she said. “It has his name.”

“Probably.”

“Maybe he’s still looking.”

I considered the odds. Gordon had installed our boiler in 1982. If he’d been young then, he might now be about my mother’s age. Perhaps there was a Gordon somewhere with a narrow kitchen drawer and no use at all for a lighter. Perhaps he had given up smoking the very day he lost it, and all the good years since were thanks to a basement windowsill in our old house.

My daughter set it on the table.

“You should get some fluid,” she said.

The lights came back before bedtime. The refrigerator shuddered into life, the oven clock began insisting it was noon, and upstairs a radio resumed a sentence it had started forty minutes earlier. I put the lighter beside my keys so I would remember.

It’s there now. On Saturday, if I think of it, I’ll take it to the hardware store. There’s a man behind the counter who knows what to do with things. He once spent fifteen minutes finding me a screw worth eleven cents. I expect he’ll open the lighter, test the wheel, and tell me whether the wick needs trimming. He may ask who Gordon is.

I have an answer ready.

At the clock repair shop, the clocks did not agree. One said ten past four, one said twenty to seven, and a little brass clock shaped like a carriage had been insisting on midnight since March. Customers often pointed this out.

“Yes,” said Mr. Vale. “Imagine the noise otherwise.”

I worked there the summer I was seventeen. My official duties were polishing glass, answering the telephone, and taking down the names of people who called a pendulum “the dangly bit.” My unofficial duty was to climb the ladder whenever Mr. Vale wanted something from a high shelf. He could climb perfectly well. He just felt that youth ought to have some practical application.

One Thursday a woman brought in a kitchen clock the color of a boiled sweet. It had a crack across the number eight and a smear of white paint on its rim.

“It loses eleven minutes a day,” she said.

“When did that start?” I asked, pencil poised.

“Nineteen eighty-six.”

I looked up.

“My husband used to set it every morning,” she explained. “Now I do it, and I’d rather not.”

Mr. Vale took the clock to his bench. The woman had hardly gone before he opened the back and showed me a small plastic movement of the sort that cost less to replace than to repair.

“Five minutes,” I said, pleased with my diagnosis.

“Probably.”

But he spent the afternoon cleaning the case. With a wooden pick he worked the grime from the little channel around the glass. He polished the minute hand. He left the paint alone.

“How did you know she wanted that left on?”

“I didn’t. Easier to take it off later than put it back.”

The woman returned on Saturday. Mr. Vale fitted a battery and let her watch the second hand make a circuit. She paid him, tucked the clock under her arm, and went out. Through the window we saw her stop beside the bus shelter. She took the clock out again. For a moment she held it to her ear, an absurd gesture on a road full of diesel engines. Then the bus came and she got on.

“Do you suppose she wanted it to lose the eleven minutes?” I asked.

“She asked for it fixed.”

“Yes, but do you suppose?”

Mr. Vale handed me the polish. “I suppose that window’s filthy.”

For years afterward I told this story as evidence of his profound understanding of grief. Then I got older and began to suspect he had simply wanted the window cleaned. It was a west-facing window above a busy road. By four in the afternoon every fingerprint shone like the print on a police record.

Last month my daughter brought me a lamp from her first apartment. The switch had gone bad. While I was replacing it, I noticed that someone had written a telephone number in blue ink on the underside of the base. Seven digits, no area code. Beside it was a name I couldn’t quite make out: Dot, perhaps, or Pat.

I had a cloth in my hand. A little alcohol would probably have fetched the ink right off.

“Do you want this number?” I called.

“What number?”

My father kept a drawer in the kitchen for objects that had lost their partners. A battery cover, a screw with blue paint in its threads, the plastic foot of a chair. He called it the meantime drawer.

“Put it there in the meantime.”

The meantime lasted thirty-seven years.

After he died, my sister and I emptied the house in three days because that was how long we could both be away from work. By the second afternoon we had become very good at it. Keep, sell, donate, tip. We could do a cupboard in nine minutes. We argued only once, about a yellow mixing bowl, and discovered halfway through the argument that neither of us wanted it.

Then we got to the drawer.

My sister picked up a small brass key.

“Anything?”

“Not that I know of.”

She put it in the tip box. I took it out.

“What are you going to do,” she asked, “walk around the world trying locks?”

I put it back.

At the bottom of the drawer, beneath a little snowdrift of pencil shavings, was a white ceramic knob painted with a strawberry. I knew it at once. It had come off the cabinet in the bathroom of our old flat, the one we left when I was seven. The strawberry had seventeen seeds. I knew because I used to count them while my mother washed my hair in the sink.

I said this to my sister.

“She washed your hair in the sink?”

“Didn’t she wash yours?”

“She made me sit in the bath and put a flannel over my eyes.”

For a moment we were offended on behalf of our younger selves, though it wasn’t clear which of us had received the preferable treatment.

“I hated the sink,” I said. “The edge hurt my neck.”

“The flannel smelled.”

My sister wanted to see the knob. She turned it over in her palm, then put it in her pocket.

“You don’t even remember it,” I said.

“I remember the flannel now.”

We finished the kitchen. A man arrived for the table and took the legs off in the hall. Outside, it began to rain on a box of books we had meant to bring in. My sister made us sandwiches on the counter because there was nowhere left to sit.

Six months later I visited her. She had fitted the strawberry knob to the cupboard beneath her bathroom sink. It looked ridiculous there. The bathroom was all slate and chrome, and the strawberry was fat and cheerful, with a green cap that leaned to one side.

Her little boy came in while I was washing my hands.

“That’s from Grandad,” he said.

“Sort of.”

“He made it.”

“He didn’t make it.”

“He grew it?”

“No. He kept it.”

This satisfied him. He opened the cupboard to show me where the toilet paper lived, a matter of some pride to him because replacing the roll was his job. Then he shut it and counted the seeds on the strawberry, touching each one with a damp finger.

He got eighteen.

I nearly corrected him. Instead I crouched beside him and counted too.

There were eighteen. One was tucked up under the green cap, no bigger than the point of a pin. I must have missed it every time.

On the first Monday of every month, my father took the forks out of the kitchen drawer and counted them. There were supposed to be twelve. If there were eleven, he went looking: under the sofa, behind the radiator, in the patch of yard where my sister and I had once tried to grow a fork tree. If there were thirteen, he looked genuinely troubled. A missing fork could be found. An extra fork meant somebody else, somewhere, was looking.

I thought this was how adults spent their Mondays. It was a surprise to marry a man who had no idea how many forks he owned.

“Enough,” he said.

“For what?”

He looked at the two plates on the table. “For tonight.”

We had been married nine years when my father moved in with us. He brought two suitcases, a radio, and a pillowcase tied at the neck with orange string. Inside were his forks. Eleven.

“One to go,” he said.

By then his fingers had stiffened. He could still count the forks, but he couldn't always separate them. My son Leo helped, lining them up on a dish towel. When they were finished, my father told him about the fork tree. I was doing the washing-up. I heard the exact moment my son began to believe in it: his chair scraped back.

“Where did you plant it?”

“Beside the garage.”

“Did you water it?”

“For a while. Then your mother got interested in roller skates.”

This was unfair. I had watered that fork well into November.

Leo considered the matter for several days. On Saturday he asked if we might go to the old house and dig it up. I explained that the house belonged to another family now. You couldn't just go into somebody's garden with a shovel.

“You could ask,” he said.

Which was true, though much of adulthood, in my experience, consisted of arranging your life so you didn't have to.

I wrote a note. A woman named Janet called me. She had been meaning to take out the bed beside the garage anyway. Sunday would be fine. Did we want to stay for tea?

My father wore a tie. Leo took a spoon for digging, on the theory that the shovel might damage the roots. My husband came along because, he said, there was no possible way he was missing this.

The garage was smaller than I remembered. Janet lent us a kneeling pad and showed us where a gas pipe ran. We found a green marble, a roofing nail, and the little white wheel from a toy ambulance. After half an hour Leo sat back on his heels, streaked with mud.

“Maybe somebody picked it,” he said.

My father was sitting on an upturned bucket. He had done very little digging. Now he put one hand into the pocket of his good coat and took out a fork.

For a second I was furious. Leo had dug a hole. Janet had made sandwiches. I had spent the morning in a state of tenderness toward my father that was difficult enough to sustain without his producing the whole point of the expedition from his pocket.

Then I saw that his hand was shaking. He wasn't sure how to get the fork into the hole without being seen. He had undertaken, at eighty-three, to perform a piece of magic for the first time in his life, and he hadn't thought to rehearse.

My husband tipped over the bucket.

It was an excellent diversion. There was a shout; my father caught my husband's sleeve; Janet rescued the plate of sandwiches. When order was restored, a silver tine poked out of the soil beside Leo's shoe.

Leo drew the fork out slowly. He wiped it on his trousers. He looked at my father.

“It's one of yours,” he said.

My father nodded.

“You brought it.”

“Yes.”

Leo turned the fork over. “Then you've only got ten at home.”

“That's right.”

“The next time you do a trick,” Leo said, “use one of Dad's. He doesn't count.”

We had tea against the warm wall of the garage. Janet kept the marble. Leo kept the ambulance wheel. Nobody wanted the nail.

Years later, when my father was gone and Leo was packing for his first flat, I found him in the kitchen with the pillowcase open on the table. He had taken out two forks.

“Is that enough?” I asked.

“For tonight,” he said, sounding so exactly like his father that I had to turn around and busy myself with the kettle.

After he left, I put the remaining forks away. They went in with the everyday ones, the bent one we used to fish toast out of the grill, the short one that had arrived with a takeaway salad and somehow survived three changes of address. I shut the drawer.

I don't count them. I do sometimes open the drawer on a Monday and move them about with my hand. They make a sound much like a person coming in with keys, someone familiar who doesn't need you to get up.
